title: To all the betting shops littering our high streets: people power is coming and the odds are against you | Dawn Butler | The Guardian
description: Too many shops are blighting too many communities. With the rule change I fought for now on the horizon, ordinary people can fight back, says Labour MP Dawn Butler
Author: Dawn Butler
Headline: Too many shops are blighting too many communities. With the rule change I fought for now on the horizon, ordinary people can fight back, says Labour MP Dawn Butler
Content: Higher-stakes gambling machines can generate an average of £35,000 in gross yield per machine each year.Photograph: Islandstock/AlamyView image in fullscreenHigher-stakes gambling machines can generate an average of £35,000 in gross yield per machine each year.Photograph: Islandstock/AlamyOpinionGamblingTo all the betting shops littering our high streets: people power is coming and the odds are against youDawn ButlerToo many shops are blighting too many communities. With the rule change I fought for now on the horizon, ordinary people can fight backTue 11 Aug 2026 13.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 13.45 EDTShareHow much gambling do you want in your high street? Are you happy with all the betting shops, the problems they cause, the effect on your environment?It’s worth asking because for years, local councils have been expected to say yes to new gambling venues, even when communities made clear they did not want them. Now, undernew rules announced on Monday, that’s about to change. And about time.Speaking to local residents I hear a clear message time and again: people are fed up with seeing so much gambling where they live, while having little say over whether new venues open.I knew grappling with this issue would be an uphill battle. The gambling industry is lucrative and deeply embedded in our communities. When I looked into why councils were struggling to stop new betting shops, casinos and adult gaming centres opening, I discovered the problem.At the heart of it was the outdated “aim to permit” principle in theGamblingAct 2005. It meant councils were effectively working against a presumption that gambling premises should be permitted, leaving them limited ability to say no. This one principle is the root of the crisis on our high streets: it has stripped local people of any real power to shape their own communities, and let the industry expand largely unchecked.So in 2021 I started my campaign to put power back where it belongs: in the hands of councils and local communities. Today, after years of campaigning, I’m delighted to say that we’ve won.The government has announced it is scrapping aim to permit, giving councils and communities greater power over what happens on their high streets. This is a huge victory forLondon, and for communities nationwide. But it took years of pressure and persistence to get here.I took a minister to Harlesden high street to see the reality for themselves. I launched a petition so Londoners could make their voices heard. I organised a cross-party letter backed by more than 280 MPs, councillors, mayors and gambling reform advocates, including the then mayor of Greater Manchester, Andy Burnham. I took the campaign into parliament too, raising it at prime minister’s questions and leading a debate.During my summer tour last year, I took the campaign into communities across London, listening to what people wanted to see on their high streets, and meeting families affected by gambling harms, such as the campaigner Jackie Olden, who watched her mother’s lifespiral out of controlthanks to a slot-machine addiction.It was a shock to discover how much gambling machines generate: B3 (higher-stakes) gambling machines – essentially slot/fruit machine-style games, found in places such as betting shops, adult gaming centres and casinos – generate an average of £35,000 in gross gambling yield per machine each year – more than the roughly £26,400 a year earned by someone aged 21 or over working 40 hours a week on the national living wage. The scale of the problem is clear in Brent, where gambling premisesoutnumber supermarkets in 17 of Brent’s 22 wards. We have 81 licensed gambling venues across the borough. For my constituents, this is about improving the places they live and raise their families. People want to be proud of their high streets again.The consequences of gambling-related harm can be devastating.A 2023 reportestimated there could be between 117 and 496 gambling-related suicides in England each year. I’ve worked with campaigners and advocates with lived experience of gambling harm, and highlighted organisations such asGambling with LivesandGambling Harm UK, whose expertise helped make the case for reform.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI’m grateful to residents who signed my petition, representatives who backed my campaign, councils including Brent council that pushed for this change, and every reform advocate who helped build momentum. I’m also grateful to Andy Burnham, who followed through on his support by committing to make this bold change.Our high streets should work for local people – not for companies profiting from harm. No longer should residents feel powerless when they see changes on their doorstep. That is why scrapping aim to permit matters: it will make a real, tangible difference to people’s lives.With the support of Londoners and campaigners across the country, we fought, organised and delivered. So, this is your chance: take back your high streets. Get involved, hold your council to account – use these new powers to demand and shape the neighbourhoods you deserve.Dawn Butler is the Labour MP for Brent EastDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: ‘I feel motherly towards them’: the nature reserve manager sharing her office with a wasp nest | Insects | The Guardian
description: Eilish Rothney’s first instinct was to get rid of the wasps entering her converted shipping container in Norfolk. Now she enjoys their constant hum
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Eilish Rothney’s first instinct was to get rid of the wasps entering her converted shipping container in Norfolk. Now she enjoys their constant hum
Content: The intricate wasp nest on Eilish Rothney’s bookcase of files for the Trinity Broads nature reserve.Photograph: Eilish RothneyView image in fullscreenThe intricate wasp nest on Eilish Rothney’s bookcase of files for the Trinity Broads nature reserve.Photograph: Eilish RothneyInvertebrate of the year 2026Insects‘I feel motherly towards them’: the nature reserve manager sharing her office with a wasp nestEilish Rothney’s first instinct was to get rid of the wasps entering her converted shipping container in Norfolk. Now she enjoys their constant humSafeerah AhmedTue 11 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 14.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen wasps began streaming through a rusted gap in her office door one June morning, Eilish Rothney’s first instinct was the same most people would have: get rid of them. The reserve manager for the Trinity Broads, part of the NorfolkWildlifeTrust, had discovered a wasp colony taking up residence in her office, a converted shipping container.“They just built the nest inside my door,” she says. “My first thought was: ‘Oh no, I have to get rid of that now.’ But then I realised: ‘Wait, why? Why do I have to do that?’”Two months on, Rothney is in a co-working arrangement with the nest, which is now more than a metre tall and swallows an entire bookshelf of ring binders. It has papered the inside of her office in what she calls “lovely layers of colours”, with thousands of chewed wood pulp cells stacked like the world’s strangest filing system.Rather than evict her new colleagues, Rothney adapted. She opened the window to give the wasps a clear flight path. “I just stroll past like I’m a browsing cow, calmly going about my day,” she says. “The wasps were fine with me being there. The longer I was there, the more I felt relaxed being alongside them.”Wasps building a nest in a Norfolk Wildlife Trust office on Trinity BroadsThe queen lays eggs continuously, while worker wasps forage and bring food back to feed the larvae. That, in turn, exudes a sugary liquid that the adult workers drink. Rothney describes a low purring sound rising off the nest, which she believes comes from thousands of wings beating to keep the colony cool. “It’s almost like the colony in itself is a living organism,” she says.She says she isn’t worried about being stung – “it wouldn’t be a whole lot worse than mosquito bites” – and her advice for anyone less enthusiastic than her is: “Insects learn that certain individuals won’t harm them. Just keep calm, they will sense that and won’t feel threatened.”Rothney traces her convictions about wildlife back to an ecology field trip at university, and to what she describes as “a kind of poetry and beauty in understanding the intricate relationships between everything”. She says she has become increasingly frustrated by how easily the label “pest” becomes a green light for extermination. “It’s fair enough if people don’t like wasps,” she says, “but we need to move away from things just being killed out of convenience. We cause a lot of damage with that approach.”View image in fullscreenEilish Rothney working on the Broads: ‘All I want is for people to be more tolerant of wasps, and of nature generally.’Photograph: Matthew RobertsShe is quick todefend the waspswhich interfere with picnics every August, too. By late summer, the larvae stop producing their sugary secretion, leaving the adult workers suddenly cut off from their main food source, she says. “The poor things are starving. It’s not a battle between them and me. They’re desperate. Let’s provide them with that sugar and maybe draw them away from someone’s real ale in the evening.“All I want is for people to be more tolerant of wasps, and of nature generally. I’m proud to be working where I am, and it’s our 100th anniversary this year – so maybe the wasps are celebrating too!”As the weather turns this autumn, Rothney says, the queen will stop laying, the males and worker wasps will die off, and next year’s queens will leave to hibernate alone. By winter, the nest will be empty.“It’ll be sad when they leave. I do feel motherly towards them,” she says. “It’ll be odd when they’re gone, because even the noise itself is amazing.”And when the nest is empty? “I’m going to try to take it apart very carefully when they leave so I can see what it looks like inside.”Until then, the shelves belong to the wasps.It’sinvertebrate of the yearagain! From 3-12 August, every day we will profile one of the thousands of amazing invertebrates that our readers have nominated. And then, when you’ve heard about all of them, we’ll open the voting so you can choose your favourites. title: We’re reading less. And it’s making us stupid |  | The Guardian
description: Books have never been trendier, but studies show that as more and more things compete for our frazzled attention spans, we’re reading less and less. This is a problem because reading has a wealth of cognitive benefits that we’re in danger of missing out on.To find out why declining literacy could affect everything from memory to IQ, Madeleine Finlay speaks to the Guardian’s science editor, Ian Sample. She also hears from Prof Falk Huettig, an experimental psychologist at the Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics and author of The Perks of Being a Bookworm

title: ‘Living fossil’: the blue-blood arthropod that has changed little in 445m years | Marine life | The Guardian
description: Tenacious and confounding, the horseshoe crab pre-dates dinosaurs and has copper-based blood vital to vaccine safety
Author: Oliver Milman
Headline: Tenacious and confounding, the horseshoe crab pre-dates dinosaurs and has copper-based blood vital to vaccine safety
Content: The mangrove horseshoe crab – one of the species in the horseshoe familyIllustration: Petra Korlević/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe mangrove horseshoe crab – one of the species in the horseshoe familyIllustration: Petra Korlević/The GuardianInvertebrate of the year 2026Marine life‘Living fossil’: the blue-blood arthropod that has changed little in 445m yearsTenacious and confounding, the horseshoe crab pre-dates dinosaurs and has copper-based blood vital to vaccine safetyOliver MilmanTue 11 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 07.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThey pre-date dinosaurs, eat food using their legs and contain blue blood that we use to keep us healthy. Horseshoe crabs are the supreme, if offbeat, survivors of the invertebrate world.Often called “living fossils” for visually obvious reasons – horseshoe crabs resemble a sort of prehistoric helmet (their Japanese name translates as “helmet crab”) – these animals have barely changed appearance along a lineage that stretches back 445m years.But even for a species that looks like it is stuck in a sort of Jurassic period costume party, horseshoe crabs still have the ability to confound people. For starters, they are not even crabs (they are arthropods but are more closely related to scorpions than crustaceans).They have nine eyes scattered about their bodies and six pairs of legs, but only five of them are for walking – the last pair are used to crush up food such as clams and worms and shovel them into their mouths. They have a sharp, deadly looking tail called a telson which is, in fact, completely harmless and only used to flip them the right way up if they are turned over.When situated dome-up, horseshoe crabs have a formidable defence against predators because of their shells. Draw their blood, though, and you may be surprised to see it is blue, not red.This copper-based blood provides an incredible link in time between the era before stegosauruses and your routine vaccination appointment at the doctor or pharmacy, as it is used by the biomedical industry to help determine if there are any harmful toxins in vaccines.View image in fullscreenAn adult mangrove horseshoe crab on a beach in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh.Photograph: Ihsan Eesa/AlamyHorseshoe crabs are found in North America along shorelines from Maine to Mexico, while a related species, the mangrove horseshoe crab (Carcinoscorpius rotundicauda,above), is found in India, Bangladesh and south-east Asia.The animals use beaches as a sort of nursery, much like sea turtles. Female horseshoe crabs will deposit about 4,000 eggs in clusters in the sand, usually at high tide and during a full moon. Many of these eggs become essential food for shorebirds.While the species has survived several mass extinctions so far, the horseshoe crab now face a novel challenge due to the impact of humanity. Sea level rises and coastal development are squeezing out suitable habitat for the creatures, leading to some concerns over their long-term future.“There’s a worry that rising sea levels are eroding sandy beach habitat, and once that spawning area on the beach is gone then it’s gone,” said Prof Mark Botton, who has studied horseshoe crabs for nearly 50 years.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBotton, whose interest in these creatures as a young man was initially piqued by witnessing a documentary crew from David Attenborough’s BBC Life on Earth series filming horseshoe crabs in the Delaware Bay, has found, though, that the species is unusually hardy.As well as having an internal cocktail of chemicals that helps them survive hostile conditions, horseshoe crabs are adept at eking out a place to survive even if the odds are against them. You do not get to hang around for 445m years without a certain tenacity, after all.“They are very good at finding small patches of sandy habitat even if a coastline has been almost completely concreted over,” said Botton, an ecologist at Fordham University. “Don’t expect them to go extinct any time soon. We shouldn’t sell them short or write them off just yet.”It’s invertebrate of the year again! And then, when you’ve heard about all of them, we’ll open the voting so you can choose your favourites. title: ‘A horrible nightmare’: the shocking story of the eBay harassment scandal | Documentary films | The Guardian
description: Jaw-dropping documentary Whatever It Takes details an aggressive stalking campaign targeted towards a couple whose reporting criticized the tech company
Author: Andrew Lawrence
Headline: Jaw-dropping documentary Whatever It Takes details an aggressive stalking campaign targeted towards a couple whose reporting criticized the tech company
Content: David and Ina Steiner arrive at the federal courthouse for the sentencing hearings of former eBay Inc security executives in Boston, Massachusetts, on 29 September 2022.Photograph: Brian Snyder/ReutersView image in fullscreenDavid and Ina Steiner arrive at the federal courthouse for the sentencing hearings of former eBay Inc security executives in Boston, Massachusetts, on 29 September 2022.Photograph: Brian Snyder/ReutersDocumentary films‘A horrible nightmare’: the shocking story of the eBay harassment scandalJaw-dropping documentary Whatever It Takes details an aggressive stalking campaign targeted towards a couple whose reporting criticized the tech companyAndrew LawrenceTue 11 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 15.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Massachusetts husband-and-wife team Ina and David Steiner launched their reporting careers covering Silicon Valley at the turn of the century, the tech beat was still cozy enough to feel personal. The startups were still emerging from garages, and the journalists covering them were often filing stories from their own kitchen tables. Ebay was still a young online auction company founded on the principle that “people are basically good”.Ebay and ex-executives to pay $55.7m to couple sent cockroaches in harassment campaignRead moreAs digital retail took off, the Steiners launched an e-zine called EcommerceBytes, catering to a growing community of small business owners who were increasingly using platforms likeeBayto sell their wares. “We talked about this being an opportunity for just average people, disabled people, elderly people to make extra income,” says David of a community that has grown alongside EcommerceBytes, which now has more than 600,000 readers. “We were really excited about that.”Their first 19 years on the beat were a dream, the kind of happily-ever-after usually reserved for Hallmark Christmas movie couples. But like any successful partnership, it depended on a division of labor. Ina handled what got published, and David handled how it got done. “Back when we started there was no WordPress,” Ina says. “He had to somehow conjure up his own system where we could still publish within budget.”But they never expected the dream to turn into a nightmare, with them as the targets of a relentless cross-country harassment campaign orchestrated by the very company behind their livelihood. “This was a Stephen King nightmare, a horrible nightmare,” Ina says. “And then to find out the company that I had covered for 20 years was doing this is surreal. It’s taken an enormous toll on us physically and mentally.”View image in fullscreenDavid and Ina Steiner in their living room.Photograph: Big Pond FilmsThe Steiners have become a startling example of the modern dangers reporters can face simply for doing their jobs. Last month, the Steiners obtained a$55.7m settlement from eBayafter six years of criminal and civil proceedings against the company in connection with its former employees’ efforts to intimidate the couple into silence. The macabre campaign unfolded over several weeks in 2019, with the Steiners receiving online threats and disturbing deliveries at their suburban Boston home: live spiders, a bloody pig mask modeled after the one worn by the killer in the Saw franchise, a book on surviving the death of a spouse. Pornographic magazines addressed to David were deliberately sent to the Steiners’ neighbors, and their home was listed online as a destination for pop-up yard sales and swingers’ parties.The Steiners had scant idea who was behind the threats or what they had done to deserve them. “I thought it was some lone psychopath,” Ina said. “I reached out to my sister and said: ‘I have a stalker. Please tell everyone to disengage and disconnect from me on social media.’ We were so terrified and afraid for our family. I was feeling this sort of shame.”They went into self-preservation mode, jury-rigging noisemakers from pots and pans to alert them of potential home intruders, installing cameras throughout their house and sleeping in separate beds to ensure one had enough time to call for help if the other was attacked. All the while, local police were left dumbfounded by the case. They didn’t really start figuring it out until the Steiners provided a license plate number from a car that had been monitoring them, which they traced back to an eBay employee who had rented the vehicle with a corporate credit card.From there, the mystery quickly unraveled: eBay was under pressure – struggling to keep pace with competitors, facing activist investors and embarrassed by Ina’s matter-of-fact reporting on then CEO Devin Wenig’sbloated compensation package. Text message exchanges between executives suggested how far they were willing to go to make the Steiners go away, and just how personal the vendetta had apparently become – a far cry from the cozy Silicon Valley of yesteryear:“Take her down,” Wenig wrote.“I want to see ashes,” wrote chief communications officer Steve Wymer. “As long as it takes. Whatever it takes.”View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Big Pond FilmsAccording to investigators, the company’s security chief, James Baugh, acting on orders from on high, then directed a group of young women who worked for him to target the Steiners – even as he was also harassing them and, in one case, was extramaritally involved. In 2020, the Department of Justice charged seven eBay executives and employees with cyberstalking. In 2022, Baugh was sentenced to 57 months in prison. In 2024, federal prosecutors entered into a deferred-prosecution agreement with eBay itself. The company admitted to a detailed statement of facts, was charged with six felony counts (including interstate-travel and electronic-communications stalking) and agreed to pay the maximum $3m criminal penalty.Meanwhile, the Steiners’ $55.7m civil settlement – in which eBay admitted fault and apologized but disclaimed legal liability – brought a nearly two-year legal battle to a close. Wenig, whostepped down as eBay’s CEOin 2019, agreed to pay $2m to the Steiners and $1m to a first amendment rights charity in Ina’s name (he was not charged in connection with the harassment campaign). But the formal resolutions haven’t exactly brought an end to the Steiners’ personal and professional nightmare. Since their 2019 ordeal, they have each been diagnosed with PTSD, see therapists and take medication to manage anxiety. A simple grocery run still feels like a fraught proposition after all the stalking. David is still haunted by the memory of celebrating his 31st wedding anniversary with Ina over tuna and dry spaghetti, as their provisions ran dry. “Every time we went out or I tried to shop, something would happen and I’d have to run home,” he says.The Prime Video documentaryWhatever It Takes, directed by Jenny Carchman, retraces the Steiners’ ordeal with the pace of a paperback thriller – among other things, revealing an eBay corporate security operation that scans like a cross between an NSA counter-terrorism strike force and a frat house. The couple was vehemently against the idea of participating at first. But the documentary has helped their friends and neighbors understand the gravity of their situation, and why they were so cagey about accepting help. “We felt toxic,” David says. “We certainly didn’t want anybody else involved in something that was directed at us – so we just stayed in our bunker.”Somehow, though, the Steiners managed to summon the resolve to continue publishing – partly to keep the scandal from swallowing the brand they built from scratch. “When people were writing about eBay targeting us, it was as if my 20 years of being a reporter didn’t exist,” Ina says. “I was reduced to: that lady who wrote the story about executive compensation.”Given their own experience of being targeted, I wondered if they could empathize with the female employees who also found themselves caught up in the scandal.“The New York Times did this interview with [one of the female eBay employees] and it was very sympathetic to her,” Ina says, reaching for empathy. “But from my point of view, it was like: she was harassing and terrifyingme.”David feels more guarded. “Ina, she’s a very forgiving person. But I’m just not there yet.”View image in fullscreenIna Steiner in her office.Photograph: Big Pond FilmsThe biggest victory in the Steiners’ civil settlement might be the absence of an NDA. They can speak publicly about the case and their ordealandkeep reporting on unfolding developments. While pursuing the civil case, they received a trove of more than 68,000 documents that have given them a far fuller picture of the internal effort to harass them and the executive failures that essentially let it happen. It’s tempting to describe the whole sordid affair as an early form of corporate terrorism. But given Wenig’s past experience as CEO of Thomson Reuters, home of one of the world’s largest newswire services, it reads more like news-on-news crime.It’s a reminder of how much Silicon Valley has changed since the Steiners started on the tech beat, and how much their plucky operation stands apart from the industry-friendly coverage that dominates the mainstream. For the Steiners, the $55.7m settlement is not the payoff for a fight they wanted to win and leave behind for another chance at a happily-ever-after – on a tropical island where eBay is blocked, maybe. Rather, it underscores the honor of their fight, the value of their integrity and that principled journalism is still well worth doing.Not surprisingly, EcommerceBytes’ loyal readers understood the value of that work already. “We get emails and comments that are like: ‘We know you guys deserve a break, the compensation and the security, but please don’t stop publishing,’” Ina says. “That is really meaningful to find.”Whatever It Takes is now available on Amazon PrimeExplore more on these topicsDocumentary filmseBayfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to safely watch the solar eclipse | Space | The Guardian
description:
On August 12, the moon will pass in front of the sun, completely obscuring it in a solar eclipse. According to Nasa, parts of Greenland, Iceland, Spain, Russia and Portugal will experience a total solar eclipse. In the UK, there will be a partial eclipse, with up to 96% of the sun covered, the deepest eclipse the country has seen since 1999.

But no matter where you’re hoping to watch from, it’s important to protect your eyes. The Guardian’s Sarah Ann Harris explains.

title: Richard Tice accused of ‘nasty tactics’ over legal threat to the Guardian | Richard Tice | The Guardian
description: Reform deputy leader condemned for seeking disclosure of documents that could reveal reporter’s sources
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Reform deputy leader condemned for seeking disclosure of documents that could reveal reporter’s sources
Content: Richard Tice’s lawyers wrote to the Guardian over reporting about financial transactions that were referred to the National Crime Agency.Photograph: Thomas Krych/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenRichard Tice’s lawyers wrote to the Guardian over reporting about financial transactions that were referred to the National Crime Agency.Photograph: Thomas Krych/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockRichard TiceRichard Tice accused of ‘nasty tactics’ over legal threat to the GuardianReform deputy leader condemned for seeking disclosure of documents that could reveal reporter’s sourcesGuardian staffTue 11 Aug 2026 14.15 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleReform’s deputy leaderRichard Ticehas been accused of using “nasty tactics” in an attempt to intimidate journalists and deflect attention from his own financial affairs after issuing a legal threat to the Guardian.In a letter sent from his lawyers, a Guardian correspondent was singled out for her reporting on a series of Tice’s financial transactions that were referred to the National Crime Agency.Tice is now suing the NCA, claiming that the information could only have come from an officer within the agency.In a separate letter to the Guardian, Tice’s lawyers made clear they would be seeking disclosure of documents that could reveal the details of sources.John Whittingdale, a former Conservative culture secretary, condemned the move.“The essence of a free press is that journalists can use verified information from sources without being forced to reveal who they are. This betrays a failure to understand how important that principle is to journalism.”Margaret Hodge, the peer and former Labour MP and anti-corruption campaigner, said: “It is never acceptable for individuals to seemingly abuse our laws to silence investigative journalism and close down public criticism. That’s why we need to urgently reform our laws to stop rich people using their wealth to close down legitimate scrutiny.”Jemimah Steinfeld, the chief executive at the Index on Censorship, added: “This has the appearance of an attempt to force a journalist to break the golden rule: that sources must be protected.“This has been vital public interest reporting by the Guardian. The sources of such journalism are sacred. If the facts are incorrect, then they can be challenged, but the sources should not be chased down.“This appears to be a tactic designed to not only silence journalists but those who talk to them. It is a nasty tactic and we should all be concerned.”Theo Bamber, the chief executive at the News Media Association, said that “robust protection for journalists’ sources is absolutely fundamental to ensuring that reporters can scrutinise authority and hold the powerful to account on behalf of the people impacted by their actions and decisions.“The use of legal threats by an individual or organisation trying to force journalists to disclose their confidential sources is an attack on this important principle, and one that must be resisted at every turn.”Tice and Reform’s leader,Nigel Farage, have been under intense scrutiny in recent months because of a continuing investigation by the Guardian into their financial affairs.The Guardian revealed in a series of detailed reports that Reform UK received a secret £1m donation via a fundraising vehicle run by Tice and asecret £5m giftmade to Farage shortly before he announced he would stand in the 2024 general election.The Guardian also revealed that these and other transactions were reported by bankers to the National Crime Agency over fears they could involve laundered money.Throughout its reports the Guardian has referred to financial industry sources.Tice has suggested in a document filed at the high court that the Guardian’s award-winning City editor, Anna Isaac, could not have had sources at multiple banks.The tangled financial web at the heart of Reform UKRead moreIn legal correspondence sent directly to Isaac, Tice’s lawyers suggested he is seeking to unmask sources based on his own assessment of the reporter’s work.Farage has also issued proceedings against the NCA.A GNM spokesperson said: “Richard Tice’s legal threat against the Guardian appears to be a calculated attempt to deflect attention away from legitimate questions about his financial affairs and the funding ofReform UK.“Instead of providing answers to those questions, he seems intent on intimidating journalists and seeking to expose sources.“The Guardian will oppose these attacks on the freedom of the press and will not be deterred from public interest-driven investigations into politicians and the parties they represent.”Farage previously claimed – without providing any evidence – that the details of the £5m gift must have come from Russian spies hacking his phone.The Guardian described Farage’s claim as “absurd” and “an attempt to deflect attention from legitimate scrutiny of his financial affairs”. The spokesperson added: “Nigel Farage is once again hiding behind a baseless attack on the media rather than facing up to scrutiny from journalists and politicians.”Explore more on these topicsRichard TiceReform UKNigel FarageThe GuardianNewspapers & magazinesNational newspapersNewspapersnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Real struggle’ to tame New Forest blaze as UK set for hottest summer on record | UK weather | The Guardian
description: Key tourist route closed and residents rallying round as battle against wildfire expected to go on for several days
Author: Sandra Laville
Headline: Key tourist route closed and residents rallying round as battle against wildfire expected to go on for several days
Content: A firefighters’ hose and smoke in the distance in the New Forest on Tuesday.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA firefighters’ hose and smoke in the distance in the New Forest on Tuesday.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianUK weather‘Real struggle’ to tame New Forest blaze as UK set for hottest summer on recordKey tourist route closed and residents rallying round as battle against wildfire expected to go on for several daysSandra Lavillein the New ForestTue 11 Aug 2026 11.49 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe battle to contain a large wildfire spreading across the New Forest will go on for several days, experts have said, as wind changes and a desiccated landscape fuel the flames.Smoke billowed above the deserted A31 road, the main tourist route into the New Forest national park where tens of thousands of families are on holiday, late on Tuesday while a helicopter flew above the blaze.Firefightersat the scene said they were trying to contain several hotspots across the more than 100 hectares (247 acres) of dried heathland as winds swirled over the area.Roads, including the A31 dual carriageway, will remain shut until at least Thursday, Hampshire’s fire service said, adding that “significant” repairs were needed to the surface, barriers and fencing.One source at the scene said: “They are really worried that as they dampen down the top, the peat underneath is still alight and spreading the fire. It is too dry, too windy, and it is a real struggle.”July was the busiest month on record for wildfires, the National Fire Chiefs Council said on Tuesday. Its services have responded to 966 wildfires this year, including 458 in July alone.Parts of England are bracing for a fifth heatwave of the summer this week as climate breakdown makes extreme heat, drought and wildfires more likely. The Met Office said on Tuesday that the UK was on course for its hottest summer on record by average temperature. On Monday, authoritiesdeclaredalmost three-quarters of England officially in drought.Hampshire fire and rescue service said it was facing many challenges, including maintaining a water supply and dealing with difficult terrain and changes in wind direction, but it was trying to mount a larger-scale attack on the blaze. Britain owns no dedicated water-bombing aircraft of the kind used by fire crews in Europe.View image in fullscreenA horse stands in the shade next to a truck.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian“Thanks to the efforts of firefighters, we are managing to contain the fire,” it said. “We have been using a mix of fire engines and off-road vehicles to damp down and cool the edges of the area … to prevent spread and escalation. The police drone is being used to enable us to prioritise hotspot areas and manage flare-ups.”As the emergency services worked through the night, a spokesperson for the Fire Brigades Union said it was calling for therecruitment of 5,000 more firefightersto cope with the extreme climate conditions.Firefighters have been at the scene since Sunday evening when a lorry caught fire on the A31 at Ringwood at about 5.21pm, sparking the blaze.Each summer, millions of tourists camp, hike and cycle in the New Forest national park. This year the human-caused climate crisis, which is driving extreme heat, has turned the green English heartland of Hampshire – which has not had rain for 59 days – into a landscape more akin to Arizona in the US.The A31 dual carriageway, which in August is normally nose to tail with tourist traffic, remained closed on Tuesday with no timetable for when it would reopen. Along the abandoned route, two Shell petrol stations stood empty and closed outside the village of Burley.View image in fullscreenA closed petrol station near Ringwood.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianA yellow high-pressure water pipe stretched 5 miles along the empty highway from a stream near the village to the blaze, where more than 120 firefighters from stations across the country continued to try to contain the blaze.Debbie Tann, the chief executive of Hampshire and Isle of Wight Wildlife Trust, said: “It is devastating. It is just dry tinder across the whole forest. It has spread really quickly because of these dry conditions. The New Forest is one of the most important habitats in Europe. It has so many rare species in the heathland – reptiles, adders, lizards, and then the birds like nightjars. This is going to have a devastating impact.”Sue Oatway, who lives in Burley, said people had come together to support the firefighters, many of whom are volunteers, collecting food and drink for them. On a community WhatsApp group, firefighters thanked the “amazing community” for the support.Outside Oatway’s home, New Forest ponies sheltered from the heat under brown, dried-out trees amid withered bracken. Oatway said: “I have never seen it so dry here. Someone posted a world map today on a social media group. I knew about the wildfires in Canada and Europe, but the scale of themin the United StatesI didn’t know. They are everywhere, and now here on our doorstep.”View image in fullscreenBurnt branches on dry ground.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianWith the A31 closed, tourist traffic was forced on to back roads through the forest, causing jams on narrow lanes. Holidaymakers were continuing to try to enjoy their break but as the battle to contain the wildfire entered its fourth day, the reality of the threat was becoming clearer.Jason Bunsell had been camping with a friend at Ashurst on Sunday night when the fire began. “We were coming back on our bikes and saw this big thick black cloud above, we thought it was a storm,” he said. “Then we got back to our campsite and my wife sent a message to me saying: ‘How far are you from the fires, are you all right?’”Ian Buckman, a district lead volunteer for Arundel and Littlehampton Scouts, who was guiding 26 scouts and explorers on a cycle ride through the forest outside Burley, said: “I have never seen the forest so dry. The environmental impact is massive.”Tourism is the largest single industry in the local economy. Within the national park boundaries, leisure and recreation trips account for £107.6m in income each year. But the threat of fire spreading and the impact of air pollution have prompted appeals for tourists to stay away.ForestryEngland, which manages about half of the national park, said the operation to contain the fire could last for several days. Its spokesperson Esta Mion said: “We are very much asking people to stay away … it’s unpredictable. We just don’t know how long this incident could go on for. We’re certainly thinking it could be the next few days, for sure.”Emma Howard Boyd, the chair of the independent National Heat Risk Commission and a professor in practice at the Grantham Research Institute on Climate Change and the Environment, said: “As the prime minister tours every region of the UK, it will be hard to miss the impacts of this extraordinary summer: wildfires, drought, parched farmland and people struggling to work in extreme heat. The government must now act with urgency to prepare the country for a hotter climate, cutting emissions while investing in the resilience of our homes, infrastructure, farms and public services.”Explore more on these topicsUK weatherDroughtWildfiresFirefightersHampshireEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Households near new pylons to get £250 taken off annual energy bills | Energy industry | The Guardian
description: Discounts confirmed near more than 40 locations across Great Britain amid biggest upgrade to electricity grid since 1960s
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: Discounts confirmed near more than 40 locations across Great Britain amid biggest upgrade to electricity grid since 1960s
Content: People living within 500 metres of new or upgraded overhead transmission lines will receive up to £2,500 over 10 years.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAView image in fullscreenPeople living within 500 metres of new or upgraded overhead transmission lines will receive up to £2,500 over 10 years.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAEnergy industryHouseholds near new pylons to get £250 taken off annual energy billsDiscounts confirmed near more than 40 locations across Great Britain amid biggest upgrade to electricity grid since 1960sJillian AmbroseEnergy CorrespondentTue 11 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHouseholds living near new power pylons will have £250 a year taken off their energy bills as the UK government prepares to push ahead with more than 40 grid upgrade projects across the country.The government has promised hundreds of thousands of homes living within 500 metres of new grid infrastructure a saving of up to £2,500 on their energy bills over 10 years in return for “hosting vital infrastructure” which will help the UK transition away from fossil fuels.One of the biggest grid upgrade drives since the 1960s will mean communities in over 40 locations across the country will be eligible for the payments as the government hopes to prevent a backlash againstincreased the building of pylons and substations.Michael Shanks, the energy minister, said the multibillion-pound upgrades, which will be paid for through household energy bills, were “a vital part of how we deliver secure, homegrown energy and unlock economic growth across the country”.Billionaire to invest £35bn in small modular nuclear reactors rollout across UKRead more“It is a moment of national renewal – upgrading what was built largely in the 1960s for the modern age and is our route to bringing down electricity bills for households across the country,” he said.“It’s vital we build again as a country and we are determined those communities which host pylons should benefit which is why we’re bringing down the energy bills of those hosting this vital national infrastructure,” Shanks added.Grid companies are expected tospend up to £77bn over five yearsto build the new networks and power lines needed to carry renewable electricity, often generated offshore or in more remote parts of the country, to urban areas with high electricity demand.The governmentconfirmed the sweetenerfor local communities near these projects after ruling out proposals to run the new cables underground.It said that research, commissioned by the department for energy and net zero (DESNZ), found that “building pylons remains the most cost-effective way of upgrading Britain’s outdated electricity networks” and would provide “the best value for bill-payers”.The eligible households can expect to receive their energy bill discountsautomatically every six months via their energy supplier. The discounts will begin next year.The government has also called on grid companies includingNational Grid, SSE and Scottish Power to plough millions into a fund which will be used to support projects which benefit the local communities.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSome of the biggest beneficiaries will be those living close to National Grid’s Bramford-to-Twinstead grid reinforcement project which will receive more than £4m in payments to fund community projects.In Scotland, communities near Scottish Power’s Chirmorie overhead line project would be eligible for about £2.4m of community benefit funding.At present, constraints in the country’s ageing grid network mean that wind and solar farms are paid to stop generating electricity if there is not enough demand in the local area to absorb the power.The electricity system operator also pays gas plants to fire up to meet demand, and buys electricity imported from the continent via high-voltage power cables. These payments are expected to total £3bn by 2030.Explore more on these topicsEnergy industryEnergy billsEnergyUtilitiesConsumer affairsInfrastructureNational GridnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham urged by 50 police leaders to prevent early release of PC Harper’s killers | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: Letter signed by every chief constable in England and Wales warns early release could weaken trust in justice system
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Letter signed by every chief constable in England and Wales warns early release could weaken trust in justice system
Content: Ministers are urgently seeking to free up spaces in overcrowded prisons across England and Wales.Photograph: Jeff Morgan/AlamyView image in fullscreenMinisters are urgently seeking to free up spaces in overcrowded prisons across England and Wales.Photograph: Jeff Morgan/AlamyPrisons and probationBurnham urged by 50 police leaders to prevent early release of PC Harper’s killersLetter signed by every chief constable in England and Wales warns freeing pair could weaken trust in justice systemPeter Walker,Rajeev SyalandCaroline DaviesTue 11 Aug 2026 18.47 EDTFirst published on Tue 11 Aug 2026 13.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham is facing an unprecedented mass call from police chiefs to block the early release of PC Andrew Harper’s killers, as unions warned his emergency plan to create more space in jails risked causing confusion or leading to prisoners being freed by mistake.A letter signed by 50 police leaders across the UK, including every chief constable in England and Wales, called on the prime minister to do everything in his power to stop the killers benefiting from a programme designed to free up prison space, saying there was “a profound strength of feeling across policing” that this should not happen.Burnham said earlier he recognised “the depth of public concern” about the proposed early release of Harper’s killers and announced a change to the early release scheme, intended to exclude prisoners convicted of the most serious offences by freeing up new prison places.In their letter, released late on Tuesday night, the leaders, who included the Met commissioner, Mark Rowley, Greater Manchester’s chief constable, Stephen Watson, and the National Crime Agency director general, Graeme Biggar, said: “When the state asks people to run towards danger on behalf of the public, they should be able to trust that the justice system will stand behind them when the worst happens.“Pc Andrew Harper’s case also raises a wider question.“When someone is sentenced for an exceptionally serious offence, how much confidence can victims, bereaved families and the public place in that sentence if subsequent changes to release arrangements result in an offender being released significantly earlier than originally anticipated?”The letter, which was signed by police chiefs from forces across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, added: “Officers and staff understand that the law must be applied as it stands. But they will question what message this sends about the value placed on their service and sacrifice when they put themselves in harm’s way to protect others.“Police officers and staff see first-hand the impact serious crime has on victims and their families. They support people through some of the most difficult moments of their lives and ask them to place their trust in the justice system.“That trust is vital and should not be weakened. We are also collectively concerned that an approach to early release which does not sufficiently distinguish the most serious offending risks undermining public safety, victim confidence and wider confidence in the criminal justice system.”Earlier, unions had warned that Burnham’s plan to stop the early release of PC Harper’s killers, Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, and other serious offenders could increase the risk of some more dangerous prisoners being released by mistake.It was also announced on Tuesday that probation staff had voted overwhelmingly to go on strike due to what they said were unrealistic workloads, in another blow to the proposals announced by the prime minister.How viable are plans to free up prison space in England and Wales?Read moreWhile the vote by members of Napo was not directly connected to the early release plans, the probation officers’ union has previously criticised the proposals as rushed.After an uproar about the proposed release of Harper’s killers, Burnham said on Tuesday morning that he had instructed the justice secretary, Alex Norris, to find more prison spaces so the pair and other serious offenders would not be freed.Writing on Facebook, Burnham said places could be provided by removing foreign offenders more quickly, finding a way to release lower-risk prisoners stuck in jail on indeterminate sentences, and “making greater use of the entire prison estate, including using the female estate for male offenders”.Downing Street had said on Monday that there was no feasible way of exempting just a handful of prisoners from the scheme to block the release of Cole and Bowers, who were sentenced to 13 years for Harper’s manslaughter. Under the scheme, they were due to be freed in January.View image in fullscreenJessie Cole (left) and Albert Bowers, two of three men sentenced over PC Andrew Harper’s death.Photograph: Thames Valley police/PATom Wheatley, the president of the Prison Governors’ Association, said further changes to the scheme could lead to prisoners being wrongly released. “Mistakes are more likely due to having to recalculate sentences against a very tight deadline,” he said.Wheatley said removing overseas prisoners was likely to be difficult as many would resist this and a number did not have proper documentation. He said victims would also want to be sure that anyone sent back to their home countries would properly serve their sentence there.Mark Fairhurst, the national chair of the Prison Officers’ Association, said placing men in women’s prisons would require investment and retraining. “Repurposing women’s prisons to accommodate male prisoners is not something that can simply be achieved by changing the sign above the door,” he said.“There would inevitably be additional staffing, training, security and operational requirements. The physical design and facilities of women’s prisons are not necessarily suitable for a male population, and those differences would need to be properly assessed before any decision was taken.”The Ministry of Justice said it was disappointed by the Napo strike vote and it would continue to engage with the union. Officials in Norris’s department are understood to be working at full speed on preparing detailed and workable plans to free up prison space by September.When the early release scheme was announced, there were exemptions for prisoners convicted of rape, serious child sexual abuse and grooming offences but not manslaughter, prompting pressure to block the release of Harper’s killers, including from police and his family.Officials initially said it would be unrealistic to just block the release of Cole and Bowers and that exempting all manslaughter cases risked not creating enough prison spaces to ease the crisis. But in his Facebook post and speaking to reporters on a later visit to Derbyshire, Burnham said he was aware of the strength of public feeling about the plans.View image in fullscreenPC Andrew Harper was killed in Berkshire in 2019.Photograph: Thames Valley police/PA“It’s my job to speak up for the public on this issue,” he said during the visit. “I take that duty very seriously indeed, and I’m confident that there’s more that can be done, and will be done to address public concern.”He said on Facebook: “I am increasingly confident that a more focused approach along these lines will allow us to reduce the number of people released early and, in the case of the most serious offenders like those convicted of the killing of PC Harper, prevent their early release altogether.”Harper, 28, was fatally injured when he got caught in a strap attached to the back of a car and was dragged down a country road as the killers fled the scene of a quad bike theft in Sulhamstead, Berkshire, in 2019.Cole and Bowers, two of three men sentenced over the police officer’s death, are due to be released halfway through their 13-year sentences, having been convicted of manslaughter in 2020. A petition demanding an intervention has nearly 900,000 signatures.The early release changes were part of the Sentencing Act passed earlier this year that cut the minimum amount of time many offenders would have to spend in prison.Explore more on these topicsPrisons and probationUK criminal justiceIndustrial actionTrade unionsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Abusive’ man found guilty of harassing Stella Creasy MP on tube train | Crime | The Guardian
description: Clifford Wilby, 63, blocked the Walthamstow MP from leaving, filmed her and talked about her ‘failings as a member of parliament’
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Clifford Wilby, 63, blocked the Walthamstow MP from leaving, filmed her and talked about her ‘failings as a member of parliament’
Content: Clifford Wilby, who also filmed the MP on his mobile phone, was found guilty of using threatening, abusive, or insulting words or behaviour to cause harassment, alarm, or distress.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAView image in fullscreenClifford Wilby, who also filmed the MP on his mobile phone, was found guilty of using threatening, abusive, or insulting words or behaviour to cause harassment, alarm, or distress.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PACrime‘Abusive’ man found guilty of harassing Stella Creasy MP on tube trainClifford Wilby, 63, blocked the Walthamstow MP from leaving, filmed her and talked about her ‘failings as a member of parliament’Nadeem BadshahTue 11 Aug 2026 13.46 EDTFirst published on Tue 11 Aug 2026 13.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 63-year-old man has been found guilty of harassing the Labour MPStella Creasyafter he was “abusive and aggressive” to her on a tube train.Clifford Wilby, of eastLondon, saw the MP for Walthamstow in July 2025 on a Victoria Line train, Westminster magistrates court heard.He blocked her from leaving the tube carriage and started talking to her about knife crime and her “failings as a member of parliament” and then filmed her on his mobile phone, the court heard.Other passengers intervened and got in between them before Creasy left the carriage.Sarah Madden, prosecuting, said the pair first met during a Zoom meeting in 2024 in Creasy’s capacity as an MP. The meeting was terminated due to Wilby’s behaviour.Creasy, giving evidence from behind a screen, said during the online meeting he “made a series of very serious allegations”, became abusive and “referred to the fact he had been diagnosed as a psychopath”.She said he started to make a complaint about a constituent and she reminded him that she could not discuss somebody else’s case.He became “abusive, aggressive” and they terminated the conversation, said Creasy.View image in fullscreenStella Creasy, the Labour MP for Walthamstow.Photograph: Nicola TreeCreasy said that on 15 July last year she had boarded a Victoria line train and was intending to move further down the train at the next stop, and looked up to get off the train and made eye contact with the defendant.“He said ‘are you Stella Creasy?’, at that point my memory kicked in and I made the connection because I knew his face, he then confirmed he was Clifford Wilby,” said the MP.“He stood up and blocked my ability to leave the carriage, he began talking to me about his concerns about my constituent, he was shouting although the tube train is a loud environment.”She added: “Obviously I was concerned that I was in an enclosed space with him. He was very close.“I stated very clearly this wasn’t an appropriate conversation to be having.”Creasy said at this point she was backed up against the door of the carriage and was holding her hands out as a gesture “to say stop”.She got off the train at Finsbury Park by exiting through another door further up the carriage.Tess McCarthy, defending, put to the MP that she could have got off the train as the incident continued to which Creasy replied “no”.Wilby said he had been hoping to continue the conversation about the constituent on the tube but the MP “became quite agitated” and he was “quite shocked by her reaction”, so he pressed record on his phone “for my safety”.He added: “At no point did I stand in front of her. When I first spoke to her she was actually getting off the train and she turned around to speak to me, I stood up because it was noisy.”The defendant also denied telling Creasy in 2024 he had been diagnosed as a psychopath.The deputy chief magistrate Tan Ikram found Wilby guilty of using threatening, abusive, or insulting words or behaviour to cause harassment, alarm, or distress and adjourned sentencing until 8 September for reports.Explore more on these topicsCrimeStella CreasyLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: The Office actor Lucy Davis says she has incurable stage four breast cancer | Breast cancer | The Guardian
description: Star, 53, says disease has metastasised to her bones and it is too late for chemotherapy
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Star, 53, says disease has metastasised to her bones and it is too late for chemotherapy
Content: Lucy Davis in 2008. She played the receptionist Dawn in The Office.Photograph: Ian West/PAView image in fullscreenLucy Davis in 2008. She played the receptionist Dawn in The Office.Photograph: Ian West/PABreast cancerThe Office actor Lucy Davis says she has incurable stage four breast cancerStar, 53, says disease has metastasised to her bones and it is too late for chemotherapyNadeem BadshahTue 11 Aug 2026 13.55 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLucy Davis, the actor best known for playing Dawn Tinsley in The Office, has said she has incurable stage four breast cancer.The 53-year-old said she was diagnosed a year and a half ago and the disease had metastasised to her bones including her spine, right hip and ribs. She said it was too late for chemotherapy.Davis wrote on Instagram on Tuesday: “As of now, I’m trying to live out whatever might be left of my life in as fun a way as I possibly can.“I always like to find the teachable moments in anything negative that happens. And cancer has not disappointed in that regard; there’s a lot I have learned from it, and I’m grateful for that.“As some of you will know, the pain can really be something else. Standing and walking for too long a time can be hard, and I need to use a wheelchair sometimes (so if you see me toddling around in one, feel free to give me a push!).”Davis, the daughter of the comedian Jasper Carrott, said one of the most important things that had helped her was humour, asking her friends and family to poke fun at her “as much as possible” and to not treat her like a “sick person”.“There’s nothing that will make you feel more unwell than being treated as if you’re unwell,” she added.“I’m not scared of whatever comes next. I’m at peace with it. I’ll see my Gracie [her late dog] sooner than expected, and for me leaving my physical body just means going home. Any and all grieving is for my family; it’s far harder for them than for me.”Davis rose to fame playing the receptionist Dawn in the original version of The Office, which followed the lives of workers at the Slough paper merchant Wernham Hogg, with the show’s co-creator Ricky Gervais playing the manager David Brent.She played Hayley Jordan on BBC Radio 4’s The Archers for nearly 10 years and appeared in the 2004 comedy Shaun of the Dead opposite Simon Pegg and in the Netflix series Chilling Adventures of Sabrina.She said she would continue working for animal rights and would like to keep working as an actor, a job she said was one of the “biggest joys” of her life.She said: “For those of you on a similar journey to mine, I do wish you well. Cancer asks a lot from us, physically and mentally. And we all get to do it however we choose.”Explore more on these topicsBreast cancernewsShareReuse this content

title: Russia frees ex-US marine four years after sentence disputed by his family | Russia | The Guardian
description: Robert Gilman had been deteriorating rapidly in prison and was said to be in a catatonic state
Author: Pjotr Sauer
Headline: Robert Gilman had been deteriorating rapidly in prison and was said to be in a catatonic state
Content: Robert Gilman on his flight home from Russia to the US.Photograph: truthsocial.com/realDonaldTrumpView image in fullscreenRobert Gilman on his flight home from Russia to the US.Photograph: truthsocial.com/realDonaldTrumpRussiaRussia frees ex-US marine four years after sentence disputed by his familyRobert Gilman had been deteriorating rapidly in prison and was said to be in a catatonic statePjotr SauerTue 11 Aug 2026 11.58 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 17.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussia has freed a former US marine who had been in jail since 2022, after Vladimir Putin granted the ailing American a pardon on humanitarian grounds.Robert Gilman, 32, an English teacher who briefly served in the US Marines, was travelling by train when he was arrested in the southern Russian city of Voronezh in January 2022 for allegedly kicking a police officer while drunk, according to Russian state media. He was later sentenced to four and a half years in prison, though his family has consistently denied the allegations against him.His father, Vladimir Gilman, who emigrated to Massachusetts from Russia, wrote in an October 2024 Boston Globe op-ed that his son had fallen ill when the incident occurred and had accidentally kicked the police officer.Concerns over Gilman’s health had grown sharply in recent weeks, and the White House and the state department had urged Moscow to release him so he could receive medical treatment in the US.Eric Lebson, chief strategy officer at Global Reach, an advocacy group representing Gilman’s family, told Reuters last week that he had been transferred in late June from a prison hospital to the psychiatric ward of a civilian emergency hospital in a catatonic-like state that doctors assessed as a “dissociative stupor”.US president Donald Trump claimed he had spoken directly to his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin about the issue, leading to Gilman’s release.“I am proud to announce that American citizen Robert Gilman, a former United States Marine, is coming HOME!” Trump wrote on Truth Social.“After my discussions with President Vladimir Putin, Russia has agreed to release him, very much on a humanitarian basis,” Trump added.US officials told Reuters that Gilman was already on a state department plane carrying him ‌from Russia to Washington Dulles airport, adding that Gilman would be greeted on arrival by US envoy Steve Witkoff and Sebastian Gorka, a deputy assistant to President Trump.The official who spoke to Gilman said he was walking and talking.“All things considered, he seems to be in good ‌shape,” the official said.Trump stressed on social media that Russia had not sought the release of anyone in return. “No exchange took place,” he wrote.It is highly unusual for Russia to free a jailed US citizen without securing a prisoner in return.The decision to release Gilman is therefore likely to be seen as a signal of Moscow’s eagerness to improve relations with the Trump administration, after several weeks in which the US president has appeared to shift towards a more supportive position on Ukraine.Shortly after Trump returned to office, Washington secured therelease of American schoolteacher Marc Fogelfrom a Russian prison in exchange for a Russian national jailed in the US on money-laundering charges.Gilman was one of at least 10 Americans known to be imprisoned in ​Russia.Explore more on these topicsRussianewsShareReuse this content

title: Bumble drops women-first chat rule as dating apps seek engagement boost | Technology | The Guardian
description: Since Bumble’s launch in 2014, only women ‌could initiate conversations in heterosexual matches on the app
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Since Bumble’s launch in 2014, only women ‌could initiate conversations in heterosexual matches on the app
Content: Move from Bumble ⁠comes as dating-app companies grapple with user fatigue toward swipe-based platforms.Photograph: Mike Blake/ReutersView image in fullscreenMove from Bumble ⁠comes as dating-app companies grapple with user fatigue toward swipe-based platforms.Photograph: Mike Blake/ReutersTechnologyBumble drops women-first chat rule as dating apps seek engagement boostSince Bumble’s launch in 2014, only women ‌could initiate conversations in heterosexual matches on the appReutersTue 11 Aug 2026 13.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBumble on Tuesday said it would begin allowing either person ⁠in a match to send the first message, dropping the women-first messaging rule ⁠that has ⁠been ​a defining feature of the dating app since its launch in 2014.The move ⁠comes as dating-app companies across the globe grapple with user fatigue toward traditional swipe-based platforms and slowing ⁠growth, prompting some, including Bumble and Tinder-owner Match Group, to ​roll out new ‌features and artificial intelligence-powered ‌tools aimed at improving engagement.Since Bumble’s inception, only women ‌could initiate conversations in heterosexual matches on the app, unlike most dating apps, including Tinder, where either user can send the first message.Bumble said tests in Canada have shown higher chat initiation rates, ‌fewer expired chats and more mutual conversations after the changes were introduced.The company ​is also extending the reply window for a match to 72 hours from 24 hours as it seeks to increase conversations and reduce the number of matches that expire ⁠without interaction.The changes are a response to ​demands ​from users for “more flexibility, less ​pressure, and more opportunities to create real, ​meaningful connections”, ‌founder and ​CEO Whitney ​Wolfe Herd said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesPreview latestEnter your title: ‘We are still here’: a day in the life of 12 Afghan women | Afghanistan | The Guardian
description: In the five years since the Taliban’s return to power, the walls have been closing in on the women and girls of Afghanistan. A dozen women and girls have, at great risk to their safety, documented their lives for the world to see
Author: Ellen Wishart
Headline: In the five years since the Taliban’s return to power, the walls have been closing in on the women and girls of Afghanistan. A dozen women and girls have, at great risk to their safety, documented their lives for the world to see
Content: Composite: GuardianView image in fullscreenComposite: GuardianFive years of Taliban ruleAfghanistan‘We are still here’: a day in the life of 12 Afghan womenIn the five years since the Taliban’s return to power, the walls have been closing in on the women and girls of Afghanistan.As the regime has tightened its grip, it has banned girls from education after the age of 12, ejected many women from the workplace and created legal frameworks for child marriage and husbands beating their wives. Taliban rule has ushered in a new era of women being whipped for minor infractions and constant inspections by ‘vice and morality’ officials, with men compelled to become enforcers in their own homes. Even the borders of the online world have been creeping inward, with a new spate of smartphone bans and internet restrictions.Marking the grim anniversary, a dozen women and girls have, at great risk to their safety, documented their lives for the world to seeSupported byAbout this contentTue 11 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 14.04 EDTShareThe soldier stripped of her uniformView image in fullscreendouble quotation markI still dream that I am wearing my uniform and going to dutyHerat provinceEvery day, I wake up to the silence of dawn. I feel as though I am still holding my weapon. I lie on my bed for a few moments, taking deep breaths. With every awakening, I make a promise to myself: if my husband manages to return home safely today, I will thank God even more.My name is Parasto*, and I live in Herat. For six years I served here as a soldier. Within a few days of taking the city, the first thing theTalibandid to me and my female colleagues was hold a meeting and demand that we hand over our uniforms. When they took that uniform, I felt as though I had lost something grand that belonged to me; it was a profound pain.Because my husband and I served with the previous government, the Taliban have summoned him several times to question him about how many Taliban he killed, or how many I killed. We have been threatened with death many times, through phone calls and messages. In the early days, many of my colleagues fled. The Taliban arrested two women whose names I do not wish to mention, and nothing is known of their fate to this day. Where are they? Are they alive or not? We tried to smuggle ourselves over the border to Iran, but were turned back by border guards. Today, we still keep our bags packed and waiting, in case we have to flee.Now, my morning begins with chores. I wake, light the fire, make breakfast, prepare my children for school and my husband so that he can search for a day’s work. I stand by the house gate until they leave. After the gate closes, the house sinks back into silence. I pull the curtains closed again so no one knows who lives here.I spend the days alone in the heat of this house. Sometimes, to keep my mind off the past, I sit behind the sewing machine, thread the needle, stitch the fabric slowly. It is a way to pass long hours of loneliness. The weather is also getting hotter every day, as if fire is raining from the sky.At night, before my eyes close, I think of the days when I would prepare myself for the next day’s shift.I had so many dreams of serving this country more, but the times do not allow me to. I still dream that I am wearing my uniform and going to duty. When I wake up, it takes a few moments to realise that none of it exists any more.As told to GoharshadThe undercover journalistView image in fullscreendouble quotation markTaliban could use the city’s expanding network of security cameras to trace my movements and identify meNorthern provincesThe fear of being exposed is constant. Every time someone knocks on our gate, I panic. Whenever I hear the sound, I immediately hide my laptop under my mattress because of what is held on its screen.I am an undercover journalist in one of Afghanistan’s northern provinces, working under an alias. My writing days unfold in a 12-sq-metre room, with a small desk, a mobile phone and a laptop.Coffee is my therapy. Every morning, as soon as I get out of bed, the first thing I reach for is a cup of coffee. I pick up my phone and check the latest news in Afghanistan. I open my pseudonymous email account to see what assignment my editor has left.I have already lived through two house searches by Taliban officers. Since then, every knock at the gate fills me with dread. What if it is the Taliban? What if they enter the house while I am working on a report about a killing, interviewing a transgender person or writing the account of a survivor of violence? A thousand scenarios race through my mind and fear consumes me.The job of a journalist is to meet people and record their stories – but every time I do so, it holds the risk that I could be betrayed. Last week, I went to interview a woman with a disability who had experienced domestic violence. She lived on the outskirts of the city, so a friend accompanied me. To reach her house, I had to change taxis twice. The trip was filled with anxiety because she lived in an area where restrictions are especially severe: women wear burqas, and it is unacceptable for a woman to move around without a male guardian.We walked along dusty alleyways, winding through countless narrow turns. It was a small, impoverished house with barely any light. As I spoke to her, the entire time I was terrified. I had never met her before; she had only been introduced to me through someone I trusted. I did not know what kind of place I was walking into or whether I could trust the situation.When I returned, I told my editor that we should not publish yet. I feared that, after publication, the Taliban could use the city’s expanding network of security cameras to trace my movements and identify her, or me. This is the reality of working under Taliban rule: reporting in a near-total suppression of press freedom is extraordinarily difficult.By Sophia MalekThe neighbourhood bakerView image in fullscreendouble quotation markI wanted my daughters to have a more informed, comfortable life. What if they end up like me? A difficult life with very limited choices.KabulEvery day, when most people are still asleep, my sister Marzia and I wake at 4am. We light the oven. This is how our day begins.My name is Fatema*. I am 32 years old and a mother of six: four sons and two daughters. Me and Marzia, who herself has eight children, run a small home bakery in a corner of Kabul.Women from all over come to us with dough they have prepared the night before, asking us to bake their bread. This work has been our only stable source of income during these five difficult years.My eyebrows and eyelashes have disappeared because of constant exposure to the heat of the fire. My eyes burn. My knees ache at night, and I no longer feel the burns on my hands. Work is good, but I never wanted such a hard life and such difficult work for my daughters.I pray my morning prayer while the oven is heating up. After the prayer, women begin arriving one by one. Some come from distant neighbourhoods, carrying with them fear and worry. They say: “The Taliban were in such and such alley today.” Sometimes they arrive silently, hand over their dough and wait.We bake the bread, and they return home with fresh loaves.As I work, I always remember my mother. She taught my sister and me the art of breadmaking, and was a wise woman. She encouraged me to attend school so I could learn the Qur’an, and she taught me sewing, baking and caring for my children. All these skills have helped me survive. I still light the oven the way my mother taught me. But the wood, which used to cost 60 afghanis per bundle (70p), has risen to 110 afghanis (£1.25). Now, we use almond shells as fuel – they’re cheaper, but their bitter smell stays with me until the end of the day. We charge six afghanis for each batch of bread. On good days, we might earn about 1,000 afghanis (£11), but usually we earn half of that. My family of eight and Marzia’s family of 10 survive on this.My eldest daughter is now 12, and my youngest is eight. Beyond how difficult the work itself is, my biggest worry is that I cannot do anything for their education. I don’t have enough income to send them abroad to study, and I have no hope that conditions inside Afghanistan will improve soon. I wanted my daughters to study and have a more informed and comfortable life. What if they end up like me? A difficult life with very limited choices.By mid-morning, I can take a break, take off my work clothes, wash my hands and face, eat breakfast and rest a while. In the afternoon, I light the oven again, and the work continues until 7pm.When women come and share stories about their lives, I realise that the lives of women and girls in Afghanistan have never been easy. With the arrival of the Taliban, they have become a living hell.As told to Tarana MohammadiThe 12-year-old bloggerView image in fullscreendouble quotation markWhenever I publish a video, relatives say to my father: ‘The honour and dignity of the family will be destroyed. Why is she blogging?’UndisclosedI wake up to the sound of my parents’ laughter. In the living room, my mother spreads out her flower-patterned tablecloth and prepares breakfast. For me, she makes a boiled egg because she knows I love them. I am 12 years old, preparing for my sixth-grade exams – the last I will be allowed to take.After breakfast, my sisters and I go to our room, where my older sister gets lost in old books and notebooks, studying and writing. She dreamed of becoming a writer whose books would be read around the world. But the Taliban buried that dream inside her. My other sister reached 10th grade before she had to leave. Now she sits for hours, searching social media for scholarships and journalism training programmes.I know that soon the fate that came to my sisters will come for me. I will also remain trapped in this room, our forced refuge for years. Even at night we do not dare pull back the curtains for fresh air, fearing the Taliban or suspicious neighbours. What if someone says: “Three young girls live in this house and move around freely inside it”?On the shelf where we keep our clothes, there is no colour left except black. I put on my black dress, scarf, mask andchador. I must wear mychador,even in this scorching heat – two classmates were arrested and expelled from school for failing to wear it correctly.Finally, I reach the school gate, surrounded by girls. The teacher enters the classroom and places a preparatory exam paper in front of us. But I stare at the exam paper and ask myself: what should I write? What future am I studying for, when that path no longer exists?Every day after school, I go straight to that same room and record my blog. I talk about life, recite poetry and speak about girls whose books have remained closed for years, women prevented from living an ordinary life. My mother brings her phone to record me. I receive encouraging messages from women and girls who relate to my words. But whenever I publish a video, relatives come to our home and fill my father’s ears with criticism. They say: “Your daughter has grown up. The honour and dignity of the family will be destroyed. Why is she blogging? Why is she speaking out against the Taliban?”Every time I hear this, I feel like more walls are being built around my life.
