One greater fear stays with me: that someone might reveal my identity and location to the Taliban. Today, perhaps the Taliban see my videos and do not know who the voice behind them is. But what happens if they find me?Sometimes I imagine that if one day I can return to seventh grade, if I can place my books on a desk again and hold my pen without fear, the first thing I will write will be the story of these days. I am a 12-year-old girl. Hear our voices, before our silent rooms become filled with buried dreams. We are still here.As told to Awa NikyarThe polio survivor who became a master tailorView image in fullscreendouble quotation markMy art has ensured that people do not look at me with pity or condescensionUndisclosedTwenty-five years ago, when I was 10, I contracted polio. Because we were a poor family living through war in a remote village, we had no access to doctors or vaccines. My legs bent at the knees, and walking was difficult. My body and height did not grow like those of average people.As a child, struggling with the muscle pain and paralysis, I realised my life would be different from other people’s. I saw my pace in this world was slow, and that I was viewed as a burden. The pain I saw in my mother’s eyes made me realise how difficult my life was going to be. She never said it out loud, but I read it in her gaze.To escape the pain in my mind and body, I would take a needle and plastic scraps to make clothes for dolls. Gradually, I won my mother’s trust and she let me hand-sew a dress for her. Her faint smile was a stamp of approval. I still remember the first proper garment I ever sewed: a white cotton shirt and trousers for my father. He made my heart swell with joy, saying: “Bravo, my daughter!”This talent was a gift from the creator: I had never had a teacher, but I found I could look at anything, replicate its pattern and sew it. One day, one of my sisters showed me a dress by a skilled tailor and asked if I could make one like it. When it was done, seeing I could work like a master tailor, she promised to buy me a sewing machine – and she kept her promise.From that day on, my reputation spread by word of mouth, and clients began coming from more and more distant villages.When clients arrive, their first look is often searching and sceptical. They ask: “Is the tailor here?” I know exactly what they are thinking. When I tell them it is me, they place their orders with looks of disbelief and curiosity. When they see me using a pen and paper to write down measurements, they ask: “How are you literate?” They have no idea how hard I worked to teach myself to read. I became a student of my own students; in exchange for teaching them tailoring, I had them teach me writing.I sometimes have so many orders that I can earn 6-7,000 afghani (£68-80) a month, helping to support the family. Since my mother died and my father lost his sight due to old age, I run the household myself. I keep thanking God for giving me the strength to do so. Despite my legs and skeleton being ravaged by polio, I have never looked down on myself. My art has ensured that people do not look at me with pity or condescension; instead, they look at me as their trusted tailor.As told to Hura OmarThe aspiring novelistView image in fullscreendouble quotation markPerhaps, one day, someone will read these writings and know there were people who, despite all the walls, still kept a window open to the futureBalkh provinceIf you want to know me, do not start with my name, but with my room’s window. Every morning, before the city fully wakes up, I sit in front of it. The road in front of me is just an ordinary street, but to me it is filled with people, and each has a story that no one has yet written. An old man who slowly drags his cane across the asphalt; a girl who clutches her bag tightly to her chest and walks briskly; a child chasing his ball … Sometimes, before I write the first sentence, I just watch them for a few minutes.I am Mahtab*. I am 23 years old and from Balkh province, and I am writing a novel.I began writing on my own, but now I take online classes as well. One by one, students appear onscreen. Some could be my older sister or even my mother. Every time I see their faces, I think how remarkable it is: here, where the paths to learning grow narrower every day, there are still people who have not given up. Sometimes, the internet disconnects, sometimes the power goes out, but none of this stops the class.Let me tell you about last week: I was missing going to the bookshop, so I adjusted my shawl and set off. The little bell above the door chimed as it opened, and the smell of paper and new books filled the shop. The bookseller smiled and said: “I haven’t seen you in a long time.” I went straight to the fiction shelf. My fingers slid over the spines of the books, and I was holding one in my hand when, through the glass, a few men in official attire passed by. Instinctively, I held my breath.Through the glass, I saw girls passing the shop: one holding her little sister’s hand; one with a book hidden beneath her shawl; another walking so fast, as if she wanted to get away from the street’s gaze. When I stepped out, I held the book tight against my chest. In a time when so much can be taken from a person, the dream of reading, writing and creating cannot be stolen unless one gives it up. For me, writing is not just putting words together; it is a way to preserve what is being lost: dreams, memories, the voices of people who are still hopeful. Perhaps, one day, someone will read these writings and know there were people who, despite all the walls, still kept a window open to the future.When night falls, I sit behind the same window again. I may not be able to change the pain of this city, but I can remember it, write it down and not let it be lost in silence.As told to Sofia MalikThe cleaner and brickmakerView image in fullscreendouble quotation markAlthough this income does not cover our needs, I have no choice but to continue. My children’s hopes are tied to my tired handsJawzjan provinceMy husband used to be the breadwinner in our family. But in 2021, he was in injured in a traffic accident, leaving him unable to stand on his feet or work. From that moment, the responsibility of providing for the family fell on my shoulders.My name is Leilma*. I am 33 years old. I am originally from Faryab province, but I now live in Jawzjan. I am the mother of four children – three daughters and one son.Every day, I wake up before sunrise, pray and begin my household chores. I prepare breakfast for my children and husband, send my children to school, prepare food for our cow and goats and feed them, then tie them under the shade of trees so they can be protected from the scorching sun.Then, I head to the hotel where I work as a waitress and cleaner. From 6.30am until 8 or 9pm, I work continuously.On days when there are wedding ceremonies at the hotel, I arrive early, arrange tables and chairs, and serve guests food. Then I clean every part of the hotel with brushes, mops and brooms, and arrange the tables and chairs again. I wash the tablecloths, chair covers and dining sheets, and dry them on the hotel roof. Once they are dry, I collect them, spread them back on the tables and chairs and return home.For all this work, I earn only 200 afghanis (£2) a day. Although this income is very little and does not cover all our needs, I have no choice but to continue. My children’s hopes are tied to my tired hands.I live with my husband and four children in a very small house with only one room. To be able to build at least one more room, I make raw bricks whenever I have free time.My brother used to do this work so I know how bricks are made: preparing the soil, mixing it with water to make mud. I spend hours pressing and kneading the mud with my feet until it is ready. After that, using a brick-making mould, I shape the raw bricks from the mud and leave them under the sun to dry.Sometimes, there is a wedding ceremony at the hotel while the mud for making bricks is also ready at home, so I cover the mud with plastic and go to the hotel. When I return home at night, I start making bricks again.My neighbours tell me that if I continue putting so much pressure on myself, I will collapse. But I do not know any other way. My children are all still young, and I cannot bring myself to send them to work.I tell myself: I did not have the chance to study and became a cleaner; let them study and become educated.As told to Simin DaneshjoThe teacher at a girls’ schoolView image in fullscreendouble quotation markGirls who are starting school for the first time are happy, energetic and full of dreams. Being around them gives me a sense of joyDay Kundi provinceMy day begins at four in the morning. After waking, I pray and read the Qur’an until the sky begins to brighten. Then I pick up empty water containers and walk to the nearby spring to collect fresh water.I have breakfast with my son – tea, sugar and tandoori bread. We live in a remote village in Day Kundi province, but unlike many other villagers, our table is not filled with eggs or cheeses. My name is Sediqa*. I am 41 years old, and I have been teaching at my village’s girls’ school for 18 years. I studied at this same school. After the fall of the previous Taliban regime, when Hamid Karzai came to power in 2002 and girls’ schools reopened, I was among the first to return – although I was over 20 years old at the time, I started my education from first grade. Eventually, I became a teacher.I married a man who promised to support my work and education, because I hoped to build an independent life. But after my son was born, he failed to support me, did not allow me to study at university and opposed my going to work. Then, when the government collapsed and the Taliban took power, my husband left Afghanistan. My son and I were displaced, moving from one person’s home to another. The house I built through years of hardship and with the money I earned from teaching was taken away from me by his family. We eventually settled in a mud house near the school.In the morning, I prepare dough and go to an area among the trees near my house to gather firewood. I light the clay oven and bake our bread, then leave for school with my son. We each take separate mountain paths and walk to our schools alone. My son walks an hour on foot while my journey takes 45 minutes.Eighteen years ago, many girls and I gathered at this school under a single tent. There were no professional teachers, our school had no building and the tent was unbearable in the heat and cold – yet we gathered beneath that roof with great enthusiasm and a deep desire to learn.Today, our school has a building, and classrooms with desks and chairs. But our girls can no longer study beyond sixth grade. The school uniform has been replaced with large black prayer garments,chador namaz, which education officials come to inspect. The youngest girls are just six years old. Despite their age and the long distances they travel, they must carry these heavy garments through the difficult journey, enduring the heat and cold.I teach first grade, and my day ends with the happy laughter of these young girls. Girls who are starting school for the first time are happy, energetic and full of dreams. Being around them gives me a sense of joy.As told to Nahid NajiThe student locked inside and losing hopeView image in fullscreendouble quotation markIn the darkness, I go into the courtyard and look at the moon and stars. I tell myself that everything will change one dayNangarhar provinceSometimes, when I catch a glimpse of myself in the mirror during the day and see the colour of my face and my hair, I fall silent. I see how much I have truly changed over these past few years. My skin has become pale and lifeless, as if I am fading away; the dark circles under my eyes look frightening. Sometimes, I think the girl I see in the mirror is not me.My name is Leima*. I am 24 years old, and I was studying computer science at a private university in Nangarhar when the Taliban announced the closure of universities. I was in my room, working on a course project. It was 9pm when I finished studying and saw the news on my phone.I fell into a state of shock. When my mother and sisters saw me they became silent. They had wanted to hide the news from me, but I already knew. For days, my family and relatives tried to reassure me that the universities would reopen.When the universities stayed shut, I was left hopeless. My father – who has always supported our education – told me not to worry, that he would find every possible way for me to continue my studies. Eventually, he decided that we should leave Afghanistan and go to Pakistan or Turkey so I could resume my education. But because my younger brother has a physical disability and is paralysed, we were unable to leave.Now, life has reached a point where no ordinary day is truly ordinary. My mind is so filled with thoughts and worries that even when I’m cooking, tears fall from my eyes without me realising.This morning I woke up at 2am, recited prayers and sat on my prayer mat, crying. Every night, I ask God to make everything right. In the darkness, I go into the courtyard and look at the silent sky, the moon and the stars. It gives me a sense of comfort. I tell myself that everything will change one day.There was a time when I would dress up every day. I would lovingly dye and style my hair, apply my favourite bright lipstick, listen to my favourite music at full volume and dance happily in my room. This morning, after brushing my teeth, I wanted to comb my hair. But my worries are making it fall out: so much hair gathered on the brush that I felt as if every strand had died.As I sat there, my eyes fell on my old perfumes sitting beside the mirror. I picked one up and sprayed it on myself; for a moment, my mood changed. I felt like the person I used to be years ago.As told to Hosai Ismail KhanThe prosthetist helping women to walkView image in fullscreendouble quotation markMy 13-year-old daughter has been at home for two years, and it breaks my heart. No one truly understands a mother’s fearFaryab provinceMy workday revolves around plaster, moulds, plastic prosthetics, scissors, screws, rubber, glue and other tools.My name is Nazanin*. I am 42 years old and the mother of four children – two daughters and two sons. For the past 21 years, I have worked as a technician in a hospital, making orthopaedic assistive devices, casts and plastic prosthetic limbs for women and children with physical disabilities.I begin each day with prayer, then wake my two sons, who leave for their classes at 6am. My younger daughter is in second grade, so I take her to school in my rickshaw. My older daughter, however, is 13 and no longer allowed to attend school.Now, she stays home alone. She does all the housework, prepares meals for her father and siblings. She has been at home for two years, and it breaks my heart. No one truly understands a mother’s fear. Every time I close the gate behind me, it feels as though my soul remains on the other side with my daughter.I arrive at work at 8am and check how many orders we have. I produce several casts or artificial limbs most days.I think about my daughter as I work and wonder what she is doing. How long can she keep herself busy with housework? How much television can she watch? I worry that she might harm herself. I worry that she might lose hope.Then I tell myself that there are women who need me – who dream of walking independently and doing everyday tasks on their own. One young woman I worked with was the mother of seven children. Her husband was a farmer and they lived in a remote mountainous district. Before receiving the prosthesis, she had to crawl to do her daily tasks.Now, she can walk powerfully on those uneven fields. Later, when she visited us to have her prosthetic leg repaired, she told us with great happiness: “I went to the market – I saw the market up close. I work on my land now, and I no longer think about the fact that I once did not have a leg.”In the evening, when my husband returns from work, he comforts me about our daughter. He says: “Are you anxious? Well, this is something that has happened to all girls.” He takes our daughters out for a walk and buys them ice-cream or something small. He says: “At least let their faces light up a little.”As told to Tomiris TamgaThe dental assistant who dreamed of being a surgeonView image in fullscreendouble quotation markI wondered how many innocent people this man had helped kill, how many families he had left without loved onesJawzjan provinceGetting to my place of work is never easy. On my way, I pass several mosques and a Taliban-run religious school. When the young men come out, the way they look at me sometimes makes me fearful. Every time I walk that route, I wonder whether I could end up like Farkhunda – a young woman killed by a mob for no reason. The men’s stares reveal how deeply they resent women leaving their homes.My name is Marwa*. I am 23 years old, and once I dreamed of being a brain surgeon. When women were banned from universities, I found I could study an online course in dental prosthetics. Today, I work as a dental assistant in a small private clinic run by a friend of my father’s.When I arrive at the clinic, I push fear aside and focus on my work. Taliban officials and soldiers all come to the clinic. One commander came to have a tooth extracted and asked the dentist about the anaesthetic injection. The soldier with him laughed and said: “Doctor, don’t numb the commander. Our commander has spilled so much blood – let him lose a little blood from his tooth as well.”Hearing that, I wondered how many innocent people this man had helped kill, how many families he had left without loved ones, how many women and children had suffered because of him. Every moment, I worried that he might suddenly become angry.Officials from the Ministry for the Propagation of Virtue and the Prevention of Vice visit the clinic to carry out inspections. They always ask: “Who is this young woman’s guardian and why is she working alone?” Every time, I worry they might shut down the clinic or create problems for us. Whenever they arrive, I hide so they do not see me.This is not the future I imagined for myself. When I was 17 and began preparing for Afghanistan’s national university entrance exam, I told myself I would earn the highest score in my province. I had dreamed of becoming a doctor, but by the time exam results were announced, the political system had changed and I wasn’t able to pursue that. Once, a man who had been my teacher came in for treatment. When he saw me, he said: “You are capable of much more than being a nurse or an assistant. If circumstances had been different, you could have become a better doctor than many practising today.” His kind words meant a great deal.There are months when I feel hopeless. But then, a small sense of hope returns. Maybe the circumstances are not right today, but no one knows what tomorrow will bring. Some girls have lost hope and are searching for a refuge in life – they think if they get married, they can find that refuge in their husbands. But I want to be my own refuge.As told to Atousa AzarThe teacher who fears her students will be married offView image in fullscreendouble quotation markThe most painful part of my work at the school is seeing my students graduate from sixth grade. Their sad faces on their final days are unbearableSamangan provincePeople often say that the beginning of the week starts with motivation and energy, but since the day Afghanistan fell to the Taliban and my studies were left unfinished, I have had no motivation to live. Morning and evening, day and night, every day of the week feels the same: dark and heavy.My name is Fatana*. I am 25 years old and live in one of Afghanistan’s northern provinces. When the Taliban seized control of Afghanistan, I was a third-year student of law and political science, living in a government-run dormitory. Since then, I have been prevented from continuing my education. My six-year-old sister and I get into a rickshaw and go to school – a private school where I have worked as a teacher for nearly two years and earn a monthly salary of 4,000 afghanis (£45). Alongside teaching, I try to encourage my students. I tell them that to achieve success, they often have to work several times harder than boys.One of my students lost her father to cancer last year, and her family is struggling financially. She is a quiet and sorrowful girl who often keeps to herself. In addition to her regular lessons, I teach her English for one hour every day through WhatsApp. Sometimes, I cannot escape worrying about her future. I fear that poverty and family pressure could force her into child marriage – a fate that still shapes the lives of many children.The most painful part of my work at the school is seeing my students graduate from sixth grade. Their sad and hopeless faces on their final days are unbearable for me. Every time I think about those girls, and wonder what conditions they are living in today, my heart aches. I ask myself: how many of them are still holding on to their dreams of education? How many have been forced into marriages they did not choose?As told to Raha Malik* Names have been changedThis report is a collaboration with Zan Times, a collective of journalists inside Afghanistan who write under pen names for their own safety

title: Will Andy Burnham’s everyday fixes be enough to get the public on his side? | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: The prime minister’s money-saving policies are popular but they are yet to convince voters he can take on the big things
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: The prime minister’s money-saving policies are popular but they are yet to convince voters he can take on the big things
Content: Andy Burnham on a visit to Ilkeston, Derbyshire on Tuesday.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham on a visit to Ilkeston, Derbyshire on Tuesday.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersAndy BurnhamAnalysisWill Andy Burnham’s everyday fixes be enough to get the public on his side?Rowena MasonWhitehall editorThe prime minister’s money-saving policies are popular but they are yet to convince voters he can take on the big thingsTue 11 Aug 2026 13.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareIt was last year that Martin Lewis, the money-saving guru, advised the government to find “100 small things that piss people off” and set about sorting them out.That approach has been adopted almost immediately byAndy Burnhamsince entering office, as he began his programme of “everyday fixes” to tackle problems that can be dealt with through minor policy tweaks.Labour strategists say the philosophy behind this is to show that Burnham notices the frustrations of people’s lives, and that he will be decisive about improving these issues.This started withscrapping VAT on electricity billsandcapping bus fares. His latest policy assault is on garish signs on the high street and everything fromexcessive vape and betting shopsto subscriptions that auto-renew without warning.It is applying to politics the “broken window” theory of crime that suggests clamping down on small-scale antisocial behaviour such as littering can help discourage more serious crime.As much as anything,Burnham’s moves against rip-off Britainshould be a warning to companies that the government is paying attention to their behaviour towards voters, as he mulls over how far to go with a programme of increasing public control over essential services.The intention is a long way from Keir Starmer’s promise to be a government that treads more lightly on people’s lives, as the new prime minister has taken a bet that voters want leaders who are active about everyday frustrations as well as embarking on major structural reform.From ticket booking fees to shrinkflation, six other ways Burnham could cut cost of livingRead moreBurnham’s instinct to show the public that he is prepared to act on their behalf is a sound one, according to Peter Kellner, the pollster and former chair of YouGov, who has written recently about the difficulty ofwinning round “ungrateful voters”.“Probably the best any government can do in the short run – short of some educational programme about where our taxes go – is gain the perception that they as politicians are on the voters’ sides. This is the key to the Burnham bounce. Plainly the amounts of money involved on bus fares and VAT and so on are small in the great order of things.“But they are part of a story about where Burnham stands in relation to the responsibility of the government to look after people. How long this lasts I don’t know because we have yet to see what’s in the budget. And if at the end of the day they announce tax rises, then that changes. But if I were his communications adviser, this is what I would have advised him to do.”He said Tony Blair and Margaret Thatcher successfully told the stories of their premierships in their first five to six years, and that Burnham needs to do something similar in terms of building a narrative. “What we have yet to see is Burnham joining the dots of what he’s done so far. And it’s got to be something clearer than Starmer saying life is difficult and we are doing the best we can and we want to make Britain fairer and more prosperous,” Kellner says.However, there is also a risk for Burnham that hailing small changes as achievements will veer into the dreaded territory of consumer gimmicks that American strategist David Axelrod warned against.The former Obama adviser, who was drafted in to help Ed Miliband’s 2015 campaign, memorably branded Labour’s approach on the cost of living in that election as: “Vote Labour and win a microwave”. In other words, it was a consumer retail offer of short-term bargains without an overarching big and inspiring message to pull it all together.Another cautionary tale can be found in the fate of the Joe Biden and Kamala Harris administration. Together they targeted price gouging and unfair consumer practices. But while the overall economy began to improve under Biden, voters never give the US government credit for small changes like holding down medicine bills and expanded child tax credits because they were unhappy about the lasting effects of food and housing costs inflation that had an effect globally.It will be a test for Burnham how far he can reap the rewards of dealing with consumer frustrations at a time when he has little room for bigger giveaways to help with the cost of living while the economy is barely growing.Burnham must also guard against a third possible peril: the potential for mockery if the issues seem too inconsequential for a prime minister to be bothering with – in the vein of John Major’s “cones hotline” for people to report nuisance roadworks.The new prime minister, however, seems aware of these pitfalls. He is openly flagging the policies as small wins – while promising bigger structural change to take place in the longer term on social care and public ownership of utilities.Labour was also ready to paint Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, as out of touch when she tried to ridicule the cost of living policies by saying: “Is that it? The problems go way beyond bus fares and VAT on bills.”Polling so far seems to suggest that voters are tentatively impressed and moving back towards Labour at a time when both Reform UK and the Greens are sliding. However, the latest data from Ipsos Mori says seven in 10 remain dissatisfied with the way the government is running the country. While they make think Burnham is outperforming the other parties and a substantial number feel he is on their side compared with other leaders, voters are still going to take some convincing that the new prime minister really will be able to change their lives for the better.Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamBus faresLabourConsumer affairsTransport policyanalysisShareReuse this content

title: What effect will Donald Trump’s childhood vaccine recommendations have in the US and beyond? | Vaccines and immunisation | The Guardian
description: Is there any science behind the recommendations? Will they result in lower vaccination rates? And will they cause a resurgence of preventable diseases?
Author: Kat Lay
Headline: Is there any science behind the recommendations? Will they result in lower vaccination rates? And will they cause a resurgence of preventable diseases?
Content: Robert F Kennedy Jr looks on as Donald Trump speaks before signing an executive order calling for more research and flexibility on vaccines.Photograph: Jim Watson/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRobert F Kennedy Jr looks on as Donald Trump speaks before signing an executive order calling for more research and flexibility on vaccines.Photograph: Jim Watson/AFP/Getty ImagesVaccines and immunisationExplainerWhat effect will Donald Trump’s childhood vaccine recommendations have in the US and beyond?Is there any science behind the recommendations? Will they result in lower vaccination rates? And will they cause a resurgence of preventable diseases?Kat LayGlobal health correspondentTue 11 Aug 2026 13.14 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 13.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA newexecutive orderfrom the US president, Donald Trump, calls for sweeping changes to childhood vaccine recommendations.His plans would result in fewer vaccines being recommended overall; the combined measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine being replaced with three separate shots, and all childhood immunisations being administered during separate medical visits “to the maximum extent feasible”.Is there any science behind the proposals? And what are the likely implications inside and outside the US border?What impact will this order have in the US?The main outcome will be “confusion for parents”, Dr Aaron Milstone of the American Academy of Pediatrics told Reuters, with conflicting messages likely to mean delayed vaccinations.During any delay, some children may be infected with deadly vaccine-preventable diseases.Measles casesare already at a 30-year high in the US.An executive order has no immediate, legal effect on the public – but it is likely to put pressure on US states to make changes to requirements that children be vaccinated before attending schools. And it sets the stage for legal challenges against states that have implemented their own vaccine recommendations.What about in other countries?The recommendations are unlikely to be copied in other countries, said Ben Kasstan-Dabush, assistant professor in global health and development at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine: “No country would want to deal with the inevitably costly outbreak responses that would occur as a result of this policy decision.”But ideas as well as diseases spread easily across borders. The short-term risk is that parents in other countries get the false impression that the vaccines they are being offered for their children are not safe, and delay or avoid vaccination, putting their own children at risk.The longer-term risk is that the misinformation leads to lower vaccination rates at a population level, and the world sees a resurgence of diseases that could have been prevented.“There is a risk of the confused messaging affecting people outside the US,” said Prof Sir Andrew Pollard, director of the Oxford Vaccine Group. “Confidence in vaccines, and getting jabbed, is critical for the health of a population.”Shortly after Trump’s announcement, the World Health Organization defended the science-based process used to set child immunisation schedules in countries around the world.WHO spokesperson Tarik Jašarević told a press briefing in Geneva it was important that countries’ vaccine schedule recommendations be made by independent experts and “free of industry and political influence”.“When these standards are not upheld, trust in vaccines, health experts and scientific institutions, like WHO, can erode,” he added.Why is Trump doing this?Trump himself has many times repeated discredited claims that vaccination causes autism, and appeared to make the same link when signing the order.The US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, is a leading vaccination sceptic, who has for years amplified misinformation about vaccines.One study foundhe was the top “superspreader” of Covid-19 vaccine misinformation on Twitter (now X) in 2021.Kennedy has tried to reshape US vaccination schedules but hasfound his attempts blockedby a federal judge. A White House official told reporters that was a separate issue to the executive order.In 2025, UK vaccine expertscalled on public health agencies in other countriesto get “Kennedy ready”. They argued that “the political agenda against vaccination in the United States raises implications for routine childhood vaccination programmes in the United Kingdom and countries around the world, due to the transnational spread of diseases and ideas”.Does the MMR jab cause autism?No. There is “strong evidence of no link”, said Helen Bedford, professor of child public health at UCL. “The vaccine has, and continues to save, millions of lives.”False claims of a link between the MMR vaccine and autism were made byBritish doctor Andrew Wakefieldin 1998 in the Lancet medical journal. That paper was retracted, and Wakefield was struck off by the UK’s medical regulator. But he has been lauded by anti-vaccination groups, and attended Trump’s first inauguration.Is there any science supporting breaking up the MMR vaccine into separate shots?“The three vaccines have never been administered as separate doses to young children as part of vaccination policy so that policy’s safety and effectiveness are unproven,” said Bedford. “However, just by delaying protection it would be a serious step backwards for protecting our children’s health.”In fact, says Kasstan-Dabush, giving them separately amounts to “an experiment with children’s health”.Adam Finn, emeritus professor of paediatrics at the University of Bristol, raised a more practical issue for the US and many other countries.“Dividing the vaccine into separate components makes no logical sense and is infeasible at this time in any case asno such vaccines are available,” he added.Would these proposals affect vaccination rates?Studies of communities with low vaccination rates typically find that, while hesitancy can be an issue,accessibility, such as the logistics of getting children to health appointmentsalso play a role. If parents can only get one shot in an appointment, they may not return for the rest.“Spacing vaccines across many separate visits increases the likelihood of delayed or missed doses and leaves children susceptible for longer, with no demonstrated safety benefit in healthy children,” said Azeem Majeed, professor of primary care and public health, Imperial College London.Explore more on these topicsVaccines and immunisationRobert F Kennedy JrMMRDonald TrumpWorld Health OrganizationexplainersShareReuse this content

title: How viable are plans to free up prison space in England and Wales? | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: The PM is proposing three ways of increasing jail capacity – but none offer a quick or straightforward solution
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: The PM is proposing three ways of increasing jail capacity – but none offer a quick or straightforward solution
Content: Andy Burnham has proposed deporting foreign offenders, reducing the number of women in jail and reviewing indefinite sentences.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham has proposed deporting foreign offenders, reducing the number of women in jail and reviewing indefinite sentences.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesPrisons and probationExplainerHow viable are plans to free up prison space in England and Wales?The PM is proposing three ways of increasing jail capacity – but none offer a quick or straightforward solutionRajeev SyalHome affairs editorTue 11 Aug 2026 13.58 EDTFirst published on Tue 11 Aug 2026 13.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnhamsaid on Monday he was “increasingly confident”that PC Andrew Harper’s killers would not be freed in the new year.Determined to ensure that Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole, who were jailed for 13 years in 2020 for manslaughter, serve their full sentences, he has asked the justice secretary, Alex Norris, to examine three options for increasing prison capacity.The options outlined by Burnham are speeding up the deportation of foreign offenders, releasing female prisoners from jail and reviewing indefinite sentences given to “lower-risk” prisoners.How feasible are they?Accelerating the deportation of foreign prisonersThere were 10,134 foreign nationals held in prisons acrossEnglandand Wales at the end of June 2026, according to the most recent Ministry of Justice figures.Removing them from the UK would therefore be a major political coup for Burnham.Burnham ‘increasingly confident’ PC Harper’s killers will not get early releaseRead moreBut there are several major obstacles.Going back to Tony Blair, governments have pledged to clear jails of foreign prisoners, but all have failed.Andrew Neilson, the director of campaigns at the Howard League for Penal Reform, said the government would struggle to achieve any immediate relief for the overcrowding crisis by seeking to deport foreign prisoners.He said: “Reciprocal agreements will have to be drawn up with many of the countries involved and they take time to draw up, and so it does not provide immediate relief to the capacity crisis.”Tom Wheatley, the president of the Prison Governors’ Association, said: “Releasing foreign offenders is difficult because many of them don’t want to go, and quite often they are undocumented. If they have come over on small boats, you do not necessarily know where you might be able to deport them to.“Many victims will want to see that justice has been served. If someone has been physically attacked or raped by someone from a foreign country which is corrupt, it may well be difficult to guarantee that their attacker’s sentence will be served.”Emptying women’s prisons andfilling them with menThis is an option that has been examined and re-examined by successive governments.Ministry of Justice officials have been seriously examining schemes to divert female offenders out of jail for more than a year.Burnham could adopt approaches pioneered by the Greater Manchester authority to steer women away from prison for lower-level offences. These reduced the number being jailed in the region by 55% in eight years.Turning the biggest women’s prison – HMP Bronzefield in Ashford, Surrey – into a men’s jail would free up more than 500 spaces.Neilson said: “There should be scope to reduce the number of women in custody, but it is difficult to assess whether Burnham’s plans would work without more detail.”Wheatley said there would be difficulties in quickly converting women’s prisons so they could hold men.He said: “Many women’s prisons would not meet the security measures needed for male prisoners.“For example, some of the prisoner accommodation at HMP Styal is essentially a set of houses within a secure perimeter. The security standards would not meet the requirements needed for men.“HMP Bronzefield is a newer, secure prison that could be used for men, but it needs to hold women so that women can be brought to London courts.”Releasing‘lower-risk’offenders servingIPPsentencesImprisonment for public protection sentenceswere introduced in 2005 for dangerous offenders whose crimes did not warrant a life sentence. They allowed offenders to be detained for a potentially unlimited period until they could prove that they were no longer a threat to the public. If released back into the community on licence, they could be returned to custody.Although IPP sentences were abolished in 2012, the change was not retrospective, and more than 2,200 people remain in prison despite having served many years beyond their minimum tariff.Neilson said: “Around 70% of IPP prisoners are in category C or D prisons so the system does not see them as a great risk.“But identifying them and then putting in place the structures to be able to help people who have been in jail for many years would not be a quick fix.“People do recognise that people who have been in prison for many, many years will require proper support. It will not free up space immediately.”Explore more on these topicsPrisons and probationUK criminal justiceAndy BurnhamLabourEnglandWalesexplainersShareReuse this content

title: Savage Mountain review – inside the record-smashing mountain climb that ruined lives | Television | The Guardian
description: Former cross-country skiing champion, Kristin Harila had clocked an incredible mountaineering record – but then, halfway up K2, she and her team encountered an injured porter from another expedition …
Author: Rachel Aroesti
Headline: Former cross-country skiing champion, Kristin Harila had clocked an incredible mountaineering record – but then, halfway up K2, she and her team encountered an injured porter from another expedition …
Content: Intense ... Kristin Harila and Tenjen ‘Lama’ Sherpa in Savage Mountain.Photograph: ©GabrielTarso/FieldProductionsView image in fullscreenIntense ... Kristin Harila and Tenjen ‘Lama’ Sherpa in Savage Mountain.Photograph: ©GabrielTarso/FieldProductionsTV reviewTelevisionReviewSavage Mountain review – inside the record-smashing mountain climb that ruined livesFormer cross-country skiing champion, Kristin Harila had clocked an incredible mountaineering record – but then, halfway up K2, she and her team encountered an injured porter from another expedition …Rachel AroestiTue 11 Aug 2026 18.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhy climb a mountain? Really, there’s only one answer: to prove that you can – to yourself, to other people, to the world at large. Is that a good enough reason? Not always, as demonstrated by this thought-provoking but ultimately not particularly revealing documentary about Norwegian mountaineer Kristin Harila.From the off, we know this won’t be a straightforwardly inspiring tale of an ordinary person performing incredible feats against all the odds. That, despite Harila being relatively ordinary – a competitive cross-country skier in her youth, she was working for a furniture company when she took up mountain climbing – and her indisputably incredible achievements. In 2023, she obliterated thespeed record for reaching the world’s 14 highest peaks; the previous fastest time was just over six months; Harila did it in 92 days. The glory, however, was short-lived. In retrospect, the experience was “hell and a nightmare”, she says. Not so much because of the climbs themselves – although the mountainside footage suggests hellish and nightmarish to be broadly accurate descriptors – but because of something that happened during the final ascent, which cast a particularly bleak shadow over all of Harila’s efforts.Savage Mountain begins at the start of Harila’s expedition. Having already spent half a million dollars on a previous attempt, which was scuppered by permit issues, she sells her flat to raise funds while trying and mostly failing to get corporate sponsorship. Logistical nightmares abound; Harila and the expedition company she hired to provide logistical support, Seven Summit Treks, are at the mercy of seasonal constraints, unpredictable conditions and yet more bureaucratic red tape. Eventually, a schedule is drawn up and Sherpas employed – and when Harila’s money does run out, Seven Summit Treks covers the costs.Trailed by various cameramen, Savage Mountain shows just what it takes to climb these peaks. It is extremely difficult – the slightest misjudgment can result in death for the entire team, while exhaustion must be overcome by sheer force of will (at one point we see Harila scale a mountain while suffering from food poisoning, stopping repeatedly to spew orange vomit into the snow). But it is also, in a way, very simple. For Harila, this paradox seems to be the appeal: climbing reduces life to the intense, all-consuming but also uncomplicated act of putting one foot in front of the other.Off the mountain, however, things do get complicated, as multiple narratives swirl around Harila’s accomplishments. She proffers a couple herself: her feats are proof that women are just as strong as men, while her insistence that the same Sherpa accompany her on all her ascents – and therefore share her record – will rectify history’s disregard for these Nepali mountain guides, who have frequently perished assisting westerners. Admirable in theory, but undoubtedly riskier for the Sherpa, a shy father of two, Tenjen “Lama” Sherpa.Then there’s the unexpected tragedy that ends up tainting everything. While climbing the final peak, K2,Harila and her team find a man– Mohammad Hassan, a porter employed by another expedition company (although the documentary doesn’t make this very clear) – hanging upside down from a rope. Although some climbers try to save him, they don’t succeed. By the time they descend, Hassan has died.Initially, Harila does not mention this event to the media, so when it is reported weeks later, people are horrified. It is horrifying, but this documentary implies there is nothing Harila could or should have done differently, bar having told the story herself from the outset and therefore commandeered the narrative. Regardless, she is inundated with horrendous abuse online and sponsors desert her, leaving her in $700,000 (£520,000) of debt.But worse is to come. Lama, now a treasured friend, has acquired a reputation as a Sherpa who can help break records. In October 2023, he is killed by an avalanche while assisting a mountaineer who was racing to become the first American woman to summit the same 14 peaks as Harila.Harila is floored by this news, and sets up a foundation in his memory. We are left with the sense that competitive mountain climbing can be a toxic pursuit, especially when climbers try to attract sponsors by performing “extraordinary” feats, as Harila puts it. In fact, she seems so disillusioned that I was surprised to discover what happened after filming finished: she went back to her record-breaking ways, and this year became the first woman to complete the Everest “triple crown”.These records seem pretty hollow in light of the human cost, but those who pursue them clearly feel they’re worth the risk. Savage Mountain does lightly psychoanalyse Harila, tracing back her steeliness and self-sufficiency to her childhood, but it also has an almost hagiographic cosiness with its subject that means it never asks the difficult questions required to elicit proper insight. Harila is certainly no villain, but you may be left unconvinced that her expensive and extremely dangerous hobby makes her much of a hero either.Savage Mountain aired on Sky Documentaries and is available on NowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewDocumentaryMountaineeringFactual TVreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Suri Core 1.0 electric toothbrush review: this new budget model is still sustainable – and the one I’d buy | Health & wellbeing | The Guardian
description: With wireless charging, a battery that lasts up to four weeks and recyclable heads, Suri’s latest eco-friendly model doesn’t lose much in the cost-saving process
Author: Alan Martin
Headline: With wireless charging, a battery that lasts up to four weeks and recyclable heads, Suri’s latest eco-friendly model doesn’t lose much in the cost-saving process
Content: Clean sweep … the Suri Core 1.0 offers many of the Pro 2.0’s features for less.Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenClean sweep … the Suri Core 1.0 offers many of the Pro 2.0’s features for less.Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianThe FilterHealth & wellbeingReviewSuri Core 1.0 electric toothbrush review: this new budget model is still sustainable – and the one I’d buyWith wireless charging, a battery that lasts up to four weeks and recyclable heads, Suri’s latest eco-friendly model doesn’t lose much in the cost-saving processThe best electric toothbrushes for every budgetSuri Pro 2.0 toothbrush reviewAlan MartinTue 11 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Last year’sSuri 2.0 toothbrushwas a huge improvement on its predecessor. It fixed a handful of things that made the original hard for me to recommend, while continuing to focus on sustainability with recyclable heads made of cornstarch and castor oil.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.But that kind of innovation doesn’t come cheap, and the Suri 2.0 brush costs£105 with the charging case, or £85 without(an option that wasn’t available at launch).Now Suri has sought to tackle that problem with a cheaper brush: the Suri Core 1.0. It’s £65, and keeps the key improvements of Suri 2.0 (now rebranded as Suri Pro 2.0), making it a strong option for those who put sustainability at the top of their shopping priorities.View at SuriView at BootsHow I testedView image in fullscreenPutting it to the test … the Core 1.0 was used daily for a fortnight and compared with the Pro 2.0.Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianHaving tested more than 30 brushes for the Filter’s guide to thebest electric toothbrushes, this isn’t my first toothbrushing rodeo, if you’ll excuse the confusing mental image. In short, youbrush, brush and brush again– well beyond the twice-a-day recommendation of dentists and into obsessive territory.While brushing, I look for grip, how it feels in the mouth and – most importantly – how clean my teeth feel after use. That may sound pretty basic, but having tested so many electric toothbrushes, some really do feel more effective than others, and clearly cope better with stubborn plaque.Fortunately, Suri gave me the Core 1.0 brush two weeks ahead of launch day, so I’ve been using it every day since. I also have a Suri Pro 2.0 brush for direct comparison.Suri Core 1.0 electric toothbrush: what you need to knowView image in fullscreenCore values … Suri’s cheaper toothbrush retains a pressure sensor and wireless charging.Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianView at SuriView at BootsThe Suri Core 1.0 is Suri’s first attempt at a lower-cost brush. Given the 1.0 in the title, it’s safe to assume it won’t be the last, either.Fortunately, the cost-cutting required to produce a cheaper toothbrush hasn’t seen a return to the weak spots of the now-retired first-generation Suri brush. The Suri Core 1.0 has a pressure sensor and a wireless charging cradle – not the more easily breakable spring-pin base of the original.It also uses the same cornstarch and castor oil heads that you can send back free for recycling. There’s also a two-minute timer with a friendly buzz every 30 seconds to remind you to move on to the next mouth quadrant.So what is it missing, exactly? The motor is slightly weaker, producing 28,000 sonic vibrations per minute, rather than the 30,000 on the Suri Pro 2.0, and the battery lasts up to four weeks, rather than more than four weeks as the more expensive model promises. Its plastic handle is made from more than 90% bio-circular material (including used cooking oil and other waste feedstocks), rather than the aluminium of previous models (it’s still IPX7 waterproof).But the biggest change is that the Suri Core 1.0 brush doesn’t come with a case. Granted, you can nowbuy the Suri Pro 2.0 without a case, but you can always buy one at a later date. Not so with the Suri Core 1.0: it’s slightly shorter than the more expensive model, so doesn’t fit snugly, and it won’t charge within it either.However, for travel, there’s a plant-based head cover included, and there’s a travel lock to stop it going off in your bag.All of this will set you back £65. For comparison, the Suri Pro 2.0 is £105 with a charging case, or £85 without.Suri Core 1.0 specificationsType:sonicModes:two (clean and polish)Power:up to 28,000 BPMPressure sensor?YesBattery life:up to four weeksApp?NoWarranty:one year (extended to two years with registration)What we loveView image in fullscreenFresh feeling … the Core 1.0 offers a similar level of mouth cleanliness to the pricier Pro 2.0.Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianThe main thing to celebrate about the Suri Core 1.0 is how little the company has had to cut to make a cheaper brush. It would have been easy for the company to simply stuff the now-retired original Suri brush’s innards into the new bio-circular plastic shell, flaws and all.But Suri hasn’t done that: a pressure sensor and wireless charging – by far the biggest improvements in Suri Pro 2.0 over its predecessor – are present. Given I got through no fewer than three spring-pin chargers on my original brush, that’s quite a big deal.double quotation markThere’s little difference in performance between the Core 1.0 and Pro 2.0What’s more, if I were to do a blind test on the Suri Pro 2.0 and Suri Core 1.0 – something I’d not advise if you don’t want to spend the rest of the day cleaning your mirror – I’m not convinced I’d be able to tell the difference in performance either. The motor speed is only 6.7% lower, after all, and while the Suri Pro 2.0 is weightier and clearly more premium with its cold-to-the-touch aluminium finish, there’s not much in it.Trying both side by side reveals a similar feel, and a similar level of mouth cleanliness. And while the Core 1.0 has a battery life that’s “up to a month” rather than “over a month”, it doesn’t feel that this will make much of a difference in practical terms. Indeed, Suri tells me the Core 1.0 has a 700mAh cell to the Suri Pro 2.0’s 800mAh, so not a huge difference.And then, of course, there’s Suri’s main selling point: its sustainability credentials. Like its pricier sibling, the brush uses heads made from cornstarch with castor oil bristles. These can be sent back to Suri for recycling, with compostable postage-paid envelopes supplied to make the process as frictionless as possible. Apack of threecosts £14.99, but you can subscribe and receive two every six months for £8.98 so you’re never stuck using a head past its best.The Core 1.0’s head is white, giving the brush a two-tone designwith whichever base colour you pick. The heads are the same for every model, so there’s nothing stopping you getting a colour designed for the Suri Pro 2.0 instead – though it won’t exactly match the colour of the base. This is a deliberate design decision, according to Suri, to prevent people confusing the Core 1.0 with the 2.0.What we don’t loveTackling the elephant in the room first, is the lack of travel case a problem? For me, not particularly. With Suri Pro 2.0, the company introduced a travel lock and a plant-based travel head cover, and both are present here. Once capped and locked with a long press of the power button, you can toss the Suri Core 1.0 in your bag and not worry about it getting dirty or being misidentified as a bomb threat.ThePro 2.0 caseon its own costs £30, so this seems like a sensible cost-saving decision – and more sustainable too, given that the case contains a battery (used to power a UVC light cleaner).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markThe Core 1.0 offers a respectable clean, but some cheaper rivals pack more punchBut you can’t decide to simply buy this case later, as the Core 1.0 is slightly shorter than the 2.0, meaning it rattles around rather than fitting snugly. And it won’t charge in the case either, even when cleanly touching the base. You can still use the UVC light on it, as the size difference isn’t huge. All the same, this feels like artificially weakening the Core 1.0 to give users more reason to buy the Suri Pro 2.0, and that leaves a slightly bad taste in the mouth.Speaking of bad tastes in the mouth, while both of Suri’s brushes offer a very respectable clean that’s far superior to any manual toothbrush, their maximum power of 28,000/30,000 BPM feels considerably less powerful than most of their electric toothbrush rivals.You don’t have to spend a fortune for something more powerful, either: the Odonta PowerPlus brush reaches 42,000 BPM, andit costs just £29.99. Though I have to say that it pays to go higher: theLaifen Wave Pro(66,000 BPM) andSpotlight Pro(50,000 RPM, both about £99) have been my go-to when teeth have felt extra furry after a night on the cider.SustainabilityView image in fullscreenHeads up … Suri’s plant-based brush heads can be returned for recycling.Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianSustainability, as ever, is Suri’s strongest suit. The world of electric toothbrushes isn’t an especially sustainable one, but B Corp-certified Suri is at least making efforts in the right direction.Beyond the recyclable plant-based heads, the packaging is moulded sugarcane pulp and the new shell is made from more than 90% bio-circular material – plastic made from cooking waste, largely – to reduce reliance on petroleum-based materials. It’s debatable whether this is a more ecological choice than the aluminium used on the original Suri, but the lack of bundled travel case means one fewer plastic, battery-containing accessory.There are limitations to Suri’s ecological ambitions – you can’t make an electric toothbrush without a built-in battery, after all – but the founders acknowledge it’s not a “perfect business” in the company’s latest impact report. “As we continue to grow we want to fully own what that growth creates – the emissions, the complexity, the gaps we haven’t yet closed,” it reads.Still, the progress is promising: two tonnes of brush heads collected (with the companyusing some to make soap dishes), 201kg of packaging removed by changes to its design, and a clearer idea of where the majority of its carbon emissions come from, which it says will help it make further reductions. You can read the2025 impact reportfor yourself.Suri Core 1.0: should I buy it?It would have been easy for Suri to repackage its retired 1.0 brush in a new plastic coating and call it a new product. But the company hasn’t taken that route, instead maintaining a pressure sensor, travel lock, plant-based travel head cover and wireless charging of the Suri Pro 2.0 model.For me, the compromises over the Suri Pro 2.0 brush are so minor that if I had to pick a Suri toothbrush today, the Core 1.0 is the one I’d choose. Sure, there’s no travel case, but that’s a minor inconvenience, and better for the planet.But I have to admit that other toothbrushes I’ve tested have offered a better clean than either of these Suri brushes, so it really depends on your priorities. If you want the best clean possible or need a more affordable brush, I’ve included some alternatives below. But if sustainability is your number-one concern, then this is a toothbrush you should certainly consider.View at SuriView at BootsSuri Core 1.0 vs …Suri Pro 2.0 electric toothbrushView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianFrom £85 at SuriFrom £85 at BootsWhen I wrote mySuri Pro 2.0 review, it was £105 with the case included. You can now buy it as a stand-alone brush for £85, so is it worth spending the additional £20 or £40 over the Suri Core 1.0?My feeling is “no” for the former, and “maybe” for the latter. The brush has 2,000 BPM more power in the motor, a slightly longer battery life and an aluminium frame, all of which are – as far as I’m concerned – nice to have rather than essential. But given the Suri Core 1.0 doesn’t support the travel case, the £105 bundle is a different proposition for frequent travellers, or germophobes who want to take advantage of the built-in UVC disinfection light.Laifen Wave Pro electric toothbrushView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Martin/The Guardian£99.99 at AmazonMost electric toothbrush heads either vibrate or oscillate to clean. Laifen has discovered this doesn’t have to be an either/or decision, building a toothbrush that does both.The result is by far the most thorough clean my teeth have had outside a dentist’s chair. With three modes on the brush, all customisable to 1,000 different combinations in the app, you can get up to 66,000 BPM and 60 degrees of oscillation for two types of cleaning on your teeth. If you’re put off by having to use an app, rest assured that, once you’ve set it to your liking, you can forget it exists.Odonta PowerPlus electric toothbrushView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Martin/The Guardian£29.99 at AmazonIf money is tight, you can’t do better than the Odonta PowerPlus. At just £29.99, it’s the cheapest brush I’ve tested that comes with a built-in pressure sensor (an upgrade that usually starts around the £65 mark). On top of that, it features 42,000 BPM of power across five different brushing modes, IPX7 water resistance and three weeks of battery life.For the same price, Odonta also hasthe PowerLite, which is aimed at people who want something lighter for travel. Despite having a smaller frame, it doubles the battery life, but you do lose the pressure sensor and a little power, at 40,000 BPM.For more:The best electric toothbrushes for every budgetHow to make your toothbrush last longerThe best water flossers – testedAlan Martin is a writer who has been putting products – including phones, gaming devices and wearables – through their paces for more than a decade. Although he wouldn’t call teeth brushing a hobby, it’s something he’s been doing for decades with a degree of aptitude that has largely satisfied dentistsExplore more on these topicsHealth & wellbeingThe FilterGadgetsHygieneBeautyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘There is no age-limit on love!’: Lesley Manville and Peter Mullan on their heart-melting TV romance | Television | The Guardian
description: Ten years later, the actors are stopped in the street to talk about their chemistry in the fantastic BBC sitcom Mum. The pair open up about joy, naughtiness and Tinder swiping
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Ten years later, the actors are stopped in the street to talk about their chemistry in the fantastic BBC sitcom Mum. The pair open up about joy, naughtiness and Tinder swiping
Content: ‘What a great basis for a romance’ … Lesley Manville and Peter Mullan in Mum.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘What a great basis for a romance’ … Lesley Manville and Peter Mullan in Mum.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyMaking loveTelevision‘There is no age-limit on love!’: Lesley Manville and Peter Mullan on their heart-melting TV romanceTen years later, the actors are stopped in the street to talk about their chemistry in the fantastic BBC sitcom Mum. The pair open up about joy, naughtiness and Tinder swipingMore from our series Making Love:‘We met and two minutes later we were kissing’ – how Gavin and Stacey became Britain’s most bang tidy TV coupleHollie RichardsonTue 11 Aug 2026 11.07 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 11.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTen years ago, Stefan Golaszewski introduced us to 59-year-old Cathy in his sitcom Mum. It was the day of the funeral of her husband, Dave, in the chaos of her suburban semi-detached before setting off. Her dopey son, Jason, was there with his goofy new girlfriend, Kelly, as was Cathy’s pushover brother, Derek, and his snobby partner, Pauline. Dave’s parents were picking at nibbles, too, making borderline problematic comments. And there was a quiet, kind man, Michael, trying to reach Cathy in this mayhem to give her a bouquet of flowers.Michael was an old friend of Cathy and Dave. Over the next three seasons, he slowly revealed his true feelings to Cathy. It started with a little hand grab. Then came the admission that, after Michael’s mum died, the last thing he talked to her about was, “You.” Garden centre trips followed (“We’ve been to three and you still haven’t bought any chairs!”) as did Cathy’s doubts (“What if I just miss Dave?”). Then, one day, she gave in to her feelings: “It sort of crept up on me.” After a final declaration of love in the rain, the pair walked off into the sunset with a bag of crisps and bottle of bubbly.Fresh from his first hit relationship sitcom, Him & Her, only Golaszewski could make the line “Thanks for helping me scrape shit off my drive” sound romantic. Peter Mullan as Michael was the master of longing, whileLesley Manvillecaptured Cathy as a woman at long last putting her own happiness first. The show picked up multiple Bafta nominations, and won the hearts of viewers who rooted for this quieter love story between two ordinary people in their 60s. After all, how often does TV celebrate that?“Lesley, are you hiding?” Mullan says on an early morning video call, as we meet to mark this decade anniversary.“I was on stage last night and was on until very late, I’ve only just got up!” Manville says. “I was told it was audio only, so I’m still in my jim-jams.”It’s true that there has been some miscommunication, but the one blank square, somehow, stirs the chemistry.“You’re the sex siren of the West End!” he tells her. Laughter erupts.“You wouldn’t think that if you saw me now,” she insists, later adding: “Just look at the poster for Les Liaisons Dangereuses. That’s how I want you to remember me.”Do you remember meeting for the first time?LM:We’d met at Dinard film festival years before and then I guess we next met at the read-through for Mum? We’d just said “hello, nice to meet you” blah blah, then the next thing you know we’re on a round table with all these amazing people.[I ask how they feel about being Golaszewski’s first choices.]LM:Well, it would have been terrible if you’d started this interview by asking: “So, Lesley, I hear you were the 15th choice for this.”What do Cathy and Michael love about each other?LM:You’ve got these three people and they’re so close and one of them dies, and the other two are still mourning the loss of this person. Cathy and Michael’s friendship is as strong as it always was. What a great basis for a romance! It’s an amazing friendship; it’s crucial. So, I can kind of understand that. Can you, Peter?PM:Yeah! I’ve got friends to whom that has happened in real life.LM: Oh really?PM:Yeah, there were three – and very, very close – then one died and the other two got together.LM:Wow.PM:That’s since Mum … but not because of Mum!LM:Jason kind of frowns on it, partly because he doesn’t want his mum to be with someone other than his dad. But also because there’s a kind of stigma: “You can’t be with dad’s best friend.” But he had to get over that.What were your favourite romantic moments?PM:For me, it was the declaration of love in the rain.LM:Oh God, Peter, yes!PM:Yeah, that was quite special. Not least because it’s the only time Stefan didn’t pull me up on the fucking lines.LM:He is a stickler for the lines being absolutely spot on … I’ve just remembered what you said, Peter: “You melt me like butter!”PM:It was the only time Michael had ever brought all of this forth. He’d held all of that in. So from an actor’s point of view it was great to finally allow that.LM:There’s also the little lovely moment with the fireworks and you just see their fingers connecting. I think that’s the first time there’s ever any acknowledgment that there’s something going on between them that’s quietly gone beyond friendship. Hands touching is a gorgeous thing. It reminded me of The Age of Innocence: the scene where Daniel Day-Lewis takes Michelle Pfeiffer’s glove off really slowly and it’s the most erotic thing.Is there anything you wish Cathy and Michael did differently?LM:I think it ended pretty perfectly because it was a little anarchic sweet moment, kind of childlike, of them just prancing off into the woods with a bottle of champagne and leaving the whole bonkers family behind. I wouldn’t have changed a thing!PM: I agree completely.LM:It was joy and naughtiness. People tend to equate middle-aged people with not being naughty any more. But these two are and it’s just delightful.When did you realise this was a love story for the ages?PM:I was really surprised. I wasn’t expecting the kind of reactions we got. I knew it was a really lovely show and beautifully written and acted. But I was very taken by people [asking] “Will they/won’t they?”, which was really sweet. I’ve never been in anything else like that!LM:From my experience of strangers talking to me about it, they were really pleased to see a love story about people who weren’t in their 20s or 30s.PM:Oh totally!LM:People at that age can fall in love, Jesus Christ!PM:What was interesting, too, was that young [people] weren’t disgusted by it. As many youngsters came up to me and talked about it as did people of our vintage. Which was really interesting because, quite rightly, when you’re young, Jesus, who wants to see two old fogies get together? I mean, remember, when you’re young, 40 is ancient!What has been the most intense fan reaction to Cathy and Michael?LM:It’s the thing that people stop me to talk about the most. Just this week, someone stopped me and said: “Oh I love Mum, it was my favourite!” And they’re always asking, “Are you gonna do any more?”PM:I’m the same, I get it at least every couple of weeks.LM:And 10 years on! How many shows can you say that about from 10 years ago?PM:Absolutely.LM:We’re bigging ourselves up here, aren’t we? We’re marvellous!How romantic are you in real life?LM:Oh, that’s a bit personal. You can start this one, Peter.PM:I’m a romantic at heart, yes.LM:Yeah, me too.PM:We all are. I don’t believe there’s a human being on earth who’s not a romantic. Whether they show it or not is a different issue, but we all share that gene.LM:I mean, who wouldn’t want romance? Who wouldn’t want somebody sharing, receiving, giving … Who wouldn’t want that in this messed-up world we’re living in? Keep it simple, just a little bit of good, honest, basic to and fro, love, romance.PM:More!LM:Yes, more of it please. I’m not on Tinder, in case anyone is wondering.PM:At least not at this time in the morning …LM: Not in my PJs, I’m not! I wouldn’t think Tinder is very romantic anyway. Scroll right, scroll right, scroll right. No that’s not my idea of romance.Did you keep something from set that reminds you of Cathy and Michael?LM:When we finished, Lisa McGrillis, who played Kelly, had somebody make us these little dolls of our characters. I’ve got a little Cathy doll with a striped T-shirt, which Cathy wore quite a lot. I certainly didn’t steal any of Cathy’s costumes. [Manvillepreviously saidCathy’s “terrible jeans” made her bum “look as if it goes on for ever”.]Did you steal any of Michael’s costumes, Peter?PM:No, and I didn’t steal any of Cathy’s either. But I’ve got a cup and we’re all in a selfie on it. I do have the utterly bizarre little model: mine looks like Beetlejuice.But in all seriousness, most actors wouldn’t take props because they would jump on you. You can get arrested for it. I can say this now, I guess: I nicked a nose and a pair of ears from Lord of the Rings. I’ll not say who gave them to me but they were terrified.LM:The nose police are going to be after you now.PM:Quickly followed by the acting police.What was your real relationship like off camera?LM:We do lots of work and people come and go in our lives but you can’t put them all in your phonebook. But Mum was utterly unique. The core of it was the eight of us. We have a WhatsApp group and it’s still going. We were all close.PM:Baby, I’m with you 1,000%. It’s the only show I’ve ever done where we’ve all kept in touch after. It’s very rare. And in my case, it’s the only one where [we] still keep in touch with that little band of brothers and sisters. It’s beautiful.LM:And sometimes if we haven’t heard from somebody for a while, somebody will check in and just say: “Has anybody heard from whoever?”What can Cathy and Michael teach us about love?PM:It comes in all shapes and sizes and we should have more of it.LM:Yeah. And for Cathy, at the most awful time of her life, you could never have imagined that this little acorn of love was brewing right there in front of her.There’s this amazing bit in series one, when – oh God yes, Peter it was amazing what you did – Cathy’s ordering some takeaway for them both and Michael’s just watching her and that’s all he needs to do. It’s just sublime. Cathy is dealing with this grief and Michael is just allowing her to deal with it. You see the love is already there for him and it’s been there for years. The scene of him just watching her open the cupboard looking for a menu … it’s gorgeous.It’s a beautiful, slow-burning love story. I guess the big thing is, there is no age limit on falling in love.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionMaking loveLesley ManvillePeter MullanfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Hard work or humour? Take the British values quiz | Social trends | The Guardian
description: Poll finds consensus on what makes people proud to be British but deep divisions on issues such as immigration
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: Poll finds consensus on what makes people proud to be British but deep divisions on issues such as immigration
Content:
Three-quarters of the 6,000 adults surveyed believed British people shared a common set of values.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThree-quarters of the 6,000 adults surveyed believed British people shared a common set of values.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianSocial trendsHard work or humour? Take the British values quizPoll finds consensus on what makes people proud to be British but deep divisions on issues such as immigrationAlexandra ToppingPolitical correspondentTue 11 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou may think it’s a commitment to buying a round, the ability to chat at length about the weather, or making a proper cup of tea. But when it comes down to what makes people proud to be British, there is a consensus across all ages, demographics and political groups – and tea, pints and the weather don’t get a look-in.Hard work, fair play and community are the values that voters – no matter which political party, age group, social class or region they come from – instinctively believe capture what it means to be British, according to a large-scale study of British values by Public First.“When you talk to people across Britain it’s clear they have a shared set of values – if fairness is Britain’s moral compass, hard work is its character and community the thing that binds us,” said Olivia Walsham, the director of social policy at the policy and polling research firm.But the research found that while most voters could agree on this core set of values, they were deeply pessimistic about finding common ground: more than 65% of respondents felt that in a post Brexit-era, Britain is more divided than ever.1.What makes the most Brits feel proud to live in the UK today?Iconic products like tea and fish and chipsThe NHSBritish humourOur sporting achievementsReveal2.Which quality do Brits most associate with British people?PoliteHumorousHard-workingReservedReveal3.How many Brits say that when they make themselves a cup of tea, they always ask if anyone else
wants one?Around 4 in 10Around 6 in 10Around 8 in 10Reveal4.Which country do Brits think has values most similar to our own?The United StatesAustraliaFranceIrelandReveal5.What proportion of Brits say they have a 'stiff upper lip'?Around a thirdAround a halfAround two thirdsReveal6.How many Brits get frustrated when someone tries to skip the queue?55%70%85%Reveal7.'When at a pub, everyone should buy a round.' How many Brits agree?Around 45%Around 65%Around 85%Reveal8.Which historic event do Brits most say exemplifies what it means to be British?The end of the Second World WarThe creation of the NHSThe Battle of HastingsThe BlitzReveal9.Who do Brits think plays the biggest role in upholding British values today?PoliticiansThe Royal FamilyFamilies and parentsSchools and teachersReveal10.62% of people who volunteered in the last month feel optimistic about the future of their local area.
What’s the figure for people who have never volunteered?25%40%55%RevealAs Andy Burnham embarks on asummer “listening” tourof the UK and vows to“bring back hope”, thereportsuggests he has his work cut out, with fewer than one in three people feeling hopeful about the UK’s future, and seven in 10 feeling that things have become worse in the last five years.But three-quarters of the public believed British people shared a common set of values – ranging from 70% of Reform UK voters to 83% of Labour-leaning voters.In the study, which polled 6,000 adults and spoke to 300 people in focus groups, participants were asked to choose which values they thought were the most important – forcing them to make trade-offs.View image in fullscreenPlatinum jubilee celebrations in south London. Only 27% of those polled thought the royal family played the biggest role in upholding British values today, however.Photograph: Jill Mead/The Guardian“Hard-working” topped the list of qualities the public associated with British people, with 70% describing hard work as a British value. “Community” was also key, with 80% of people agreeing Britain was at its best when neighbours looked out for one another. Contributing to society boosted positive views: 62% of those who had volunteered in the last month said they were optimistic about their local area’s future, compared with 25% of those who had never volunteered.Unsurprisingly for a population that can’t pass a queue without joining it, the notion of “fairness” or waiting one’s turn was the clearest shared value. Asked for examples of what described British life at its best, citizens referenced queueing, the NHS, fair play, taking turns, treating people equally, and the expectation that everyone should play by the rules.The report also exposes deep-seated division, especially on immigration.
