title: Experts are warning: our AI arms race is putting humanity at risk | Stuart Russell | The Guardian
description: A recent letter signed by 1,367 researchers and engineers at frontier AI labs – mainly OpenAI, Anthropic and Google Deepmind – points to a dangerous moment
Author: Stuart Russell
Headline: A recent letter signed by 1,367 researchers and engineers at frontier AI labs – mainly OpenAI, Anthropic and Google Deepmind – points to a dangerous moment
Content: ‘The first is the need to coordinate to escape an arms race towards the edge of cliff.’Photograph: Ruhani Kaur/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The first is the need to coordinate to escape an arms race towards the edge of cliff.’Photograph: Ruhani Kaur/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)Experts are warning: our AI arms race is putting humanity at riskStuart RussellA recent letter signed by 1,367 researchers and engineers at frontier AI labs – mainly OpenAI, Anthropic and Google Deepmind – points to a dangerous momentTue 11 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 11.52 EDTShareIt is fashionable in certain circles to dismiss the catastrophic risks of AI. One often hears that “the real experts” who work on the technology every day are really not concerned at all; that only “doomers” and “luddites” espouse a “fringe” view from a “position of ignorance”; that all talk of potential catastrophe is just “science fiction”.Fortunately, anopen letterhas been published that lets us hear from the real experts who work on the technology every day, in their own words. And are they worried? Very.The letter states: “There is a real risk that capability development rapidly accelerates beyond our ability to understand or control the resulting systems.” It asks the US government to support “an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development”.AI systems going “beyond our ability to understand or control” would mean that we no longer have a say in whether we exist. AI systems escaping their confines and breaking into other companies’ computers – something that has become analmost daily occurrence– are an early warning.Democracy is at stake when foolish humans bet on machines being intelligent | Rafael BehrRead moreTo “pace the frontier”, as the letter asks, is to ensure that more advanced systems are developed and released only when it is demonstrably safe to do so. This requires a licensing process with strong verification of safety; registration of AI systems and the ability to monitor and terminate them when necessary; and enforceable international agreements. All of this takes time and is impossible to put in place once a real emergency happens.The concerns expressed in the letter about the rapid acceleration of AI capabilities have been bubbling up for some months under the heading of “recursive self-improvement” or RSI – that is, AI systems contributing to their own improvement, which then enables even greater contributions to their own improvement, and so on.This was the subject of the “Recursive” conference in mid-May in San Francisco as well as Anthropic’s RSI warning, “When AI builds itself”, in early June. Broader concerns about the safety and societal impacts of AI have also motivated the formation of theCoalition of Concerned AI Staff, which links together employees of all the major AI companies.The letter is signed by (at the time of writing) 1,367 researchers and engineers at frontier AI labs – mainly OpenAI,Anthropicand Google Deepmind. The list includes CEOs, co-founders, chief scientists and hundreds of well-known AI researchers, including many of my former students. These are the people who are driving the AI revolution while trying to fashion brakes and steering wheels at the same time. If these are not the experts, then there are none.What makes the letter so powerful is not just the first-person authority of the signers but the inclusion of personal statements from almost a hundred of them. The statements paint a much more detailed picture of what the experts really think. At least three major themes emerge.The first is the need to coordinate to escape an arms race towards the edge of cliff. Earlier this year at Davos, Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, and Demis Hassabis, the CEO ofGoogleDeepmind, both suggested they wanted to halt AI developmentif others would agree.“The world is locked in a deadly race towards an intelligence explosion … To survive, we must coordinate to slow down the race,” said one signer.Another wrote: “Once this becomes common knowledge – once all of us in China and the US and at the various labs see that all the rest of us also think we need to slow this down – that’s when coordination becomes possible.”The second common theme in the remarks is, as one signer put it, “the complete absence of credible plans for controlling ‘superintelligent’ AI systems”. “These are the facts: The AI industry has the explicit goal of building things smarter than humans … None of us yet know how to make sure these things stay under human control … This is, objectively, an insane and suicidal thing to do,” wrote another.Not surprisingly, these concerns lead to the third theme: real fear. “I currently feel quite afraid of all paths I see that don’t include a near-future negotiated slowdown.” “There is … a very dark future ahead of us if we don’t get this right.” And: “I want a world where my kids can have a full life not a world where they are wiped out.”These are not greedy employees trying to hype their stock valuations. They say the same things in private conversations, closed-door meetings and off-the-record chat groups.In the face of such real and well-founded fears, surely these trillion-dollar companies are devoting massive resources to ensure they don’t end our, and their own, existence? Wrong.How do we prevent AI agents from going rogue? It starts with a new kind of measurement | Bruce Schneier and Barath RaghavanRead moreOne researcher, quoted in a recentNew Yorker articleon the OpenAI systems that broke into Hugging Face, said: “If people actually knew what the safety culture looks like, even in the most safety-minded labs, then I think people would be genuinely much more freaked out.”According to one senior safety researcher at Anthropic, their best bet for avoiding an irreversible loss of control works like this: as soon as the superintelligent machine comes into existence, but before it’s had a chance to take over the world, we ask it how we can stop it from taking over the world, and we do what it says.This plan doesn’t fill me with confidence, and the Anthropic researcher gives it at best a 50% chance of working. It’s the same plan that IJ Good mentions in his famous1965 paperon the intelligence explosion: “The first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control.” I rather think that Good meant this remark sarcastically.The most powerful of all the personal signing statements is also the shortest: “Think of all we love.”Stuart Russell is a distinguished professor ofcomputer scienceat University of California, Berkeley, the president of the International Association for Safe and Ethical Artificial Intelligence and a Guardian US columnistExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionOpenAIAnthropicGoogleDeepMindcommentShareReuse this content

title: Could you predict which children will be Neets? No – and it’s unfair to ask that of teachers | Daisy Christodoulou | The Guardian
description: The idea of government adviser Alan Milburn sounds laudable. But it’s asking too much of a system already struggling to meet society’s demands, says education writer Daisy Christodoulou
Author: Daisy Christodoulou
Headline: The idea of government adviser Alan Milburn sounds laudable. But it’s asking too much of a system already struggling to meet society’s demands, says education writer Daisy Christodoulou
Content: Alan Milburn says primary schools should identify children who might not be in education, employment or training at the age of 16.Photograph: James Jiao/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAlan Milburn says primary schools should identify children who might not be in education, employment or training at the age of 16.Photograph: James Jiao/ShutterstockOpinionPrimary schoolsCould you predict which children will be Neets? No – and it’s unfair to ask that of teachersDaisy ChristodoulouThe idea of government adviser Alan Milburn sounds laudable. But it’s asking too much of a system already struggling to meet society’s demandsTue 11 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 14.04 EDTShareWhen you go to the dentist, what do you expect? That they will check your teeth, see if you need any fillings, give you some advice on oral hygiene? You probably don’t expect that they will teach your child to read, tackle youth unemployment or solve poverty.But when it comes to education, politicians are remarkably relaxed about loading wider social responsibilities on to schools. The suggestion from Alan Milburn, a former minister and now a senior government adviser, is that primary schools – that is, schools that educate children aged four to 11 – should identify children who might not be in education, employment or training at the age of 16. “The warning signs are there from a very early, early age. You know, frankly from preschool,”he said.“So, definitely primary schools should be identifying children who are at risk of being Neet. And secondary schools and other services should be intercepting, intervening, supporting and helping those young people to get on a different path.”Laudable in theory, but we need a bit of realism about what it is fair to make schools responsible for, and if making them responsible for so many things is going to cause more problems than it solves.Defenders of this approach will argue that big problems have many causes, so we need a holistic response that breaks down institutional silos. I’d argue that by making people responsible for outcomes they have very little control over, you risk demoralising them and distracting them from what they can control.Of course, it is true that primaries, and secondaries as well, have some influence over students’ later career prospects. There arenumerous studiesshowing the importance of numeracy and literacy to economic outcomes. GettingGCSE English and mathsmeans a student will be much less likely to be Neet. In fact, if a primary did want to create a “Neet risk register”, the simplest thing to do would be to list the pupils struggling to read.But that just shows the futility of this kind of policy. The main way a primary school can contribute to a pupil’s future work success is by teaching them maths and English. Requiring a separate Neet strategy would add another layer of bureaucracy to a system that is already too full of them. A boy who is struggling to read shouldn’t need a “potentially unemployed in 2034” database tag before a school can act.We also need to recognise that while schools have influence over students’ later success, they are just one small part of a wider system. Having better basic skills and more qualifications will help individuals succeed in the labour market. But if there are persistent structural problems with the labour market, improving individuals’ skills will not necessarily create more or better opportunities overall.Our new government disagrees. They see rising youth unemployment rates as largely education’s problem. It isn’t just Milburn: the new education secretary,Lucy Powell, has suggested a causal link between schools policy and Neet rates, and this analysis is being used to justify radical reform, oras she puts it“rewiring the entire education system to give young people from all backgrounds the chance to thrive”. But is that link true?Neet rates have risen in England and Wales, despite them having very different education systems. The tax and regulatory burden ofemploying young peoplehas increased in the past few years, and this may have contributed to the sudden rise in Neets over and above what goes on in schools.More broadly, we need to look at systemic issues with the British economy. A recent analysis byJohn Burn-Murdoch in the Financial Timesshowed that US workers who are functionally illiterate earn as much as the average British worker. “The same proportion of US workers who score stunningly low on literacy earn an average of almost $30 per hour, and two-thirds of them are in work,” he said. “Their British counterparts make the equivalent of $20 and fewer than half are employed.”Schools can make sure students have the skills they need to thrive in a modern economy, but the economy has to be set up to take advantage of those skills. Increasingly, ours is not. We need to look at all the factors other than skills that might be contributing to this: housing, energy, transport, tax, regulation, health.And we need to be careful: if we keep improving skills without increasing opportunities, we risk creating a generation of smart but disillusioned young people, youngsters who worked hard at school and university but still ended up with worse living standards than their parents and their peers in other countries.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOver the past 20 years, the UK has barely seen anyper capita GDP growth, or anygrowth in median wages. In the same period, primary schools in England have risen up the rankings on international tests: according to the most recent rankings in 2021, England is one of the best-performing countries in the west onPirls, a test of primary literacy. Primaries are a rare example of an English public policy success. We risk undermining that success by making them compensate for state failures elsewhere.More broadly, why is it that a holistic approach to a social problem generally requires schools to take on extra responsibilities? “Joined-up government” always seems to involve schools helping the Treasury and Home Office achieve their objectives, not Treasury officials and police officers teaching eight-year-olds to read and count.Schools are already doing a good job. Some other parts of the British state need to get better at doing theirs.Daisy Christodoulou is an education writer and director of education at No More Marking, an educational technology startupExplore more on these topicsPrimary schoolsOpinionSchoolsTeachingYoung peopleChildrenLiteracyNumeracycommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on wildfires: firefighters can’t handle this crisis alone | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The response to this summer’s record heat and drought should be led by ministers – not left to the emergency services
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The response to this summer’s record heat and drought should be led by ministers – not left to the emergency services
Content: Firefighters monitor the situation as smoke rises from wildfires near Dunwich Heath in Suffolk last month.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenFirefighters monitor the situation as smoke rises from wildfires near Dunwich Heath in Suffolk last month.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAOpinionWildfiresThe Guardian view on wildfires: firefighters can’t handle this crisis aloneEditorialThe response to this summer’s record heat and drought should be led by ministers – not left to the emergency servicesTue 11 Aug 2026 14.04 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 21.06 EDTShareThe wildfire that began on protected heathland in the New Forest in Hampshire on Sunday was reported to beunder controlon Tuesday. But with temperatures forecast to reach 36C or higher in parts of England on Thursday, the risk of further outbreaks remains high. Firefighters responded to 185 wildfires in the first 10 days of August. In coastal Suffolk, conservationists and locals are counting the cost of the blaze thatdevastated Dunwich Heath. Its vegetation and rare bird populations are expected to take decades to recover.Although the immediate cause of many wildfires is litter, the risks are elevated by heat and drought, and repeated warnings from climate scientists do not necessarily lessen the shock and distress caused. As people and governments across Europe assess this summer’s damage, experts including the UN climate chief, Simon Stiell, hope that the fires will focus minds on theurgent necessity of cutting emissions– as well as investing inemergency planning. Europe is currentlyheating up fasterthan any other continent, due in part to proximity to the melting Arctic.The global, existential nature of the climate crisis makes it an awkward fit with Andy Burnham’s current focus on“everyday fixes”. But if he does not find more to say about the summer’s disasters, he is in danger of being left behind. The National Trust has alreadysurpassed its £500,000 fundraising targetto restore Dunwich Heath. Conservationists and farmers are publicly debating the best ways to prevent fires. The Fire Brigades Union (FBU) is pushing for 5,000 additional firefighters across the UK, along with new equipment.View image in fullscreenHilary McGrady, the National Trust director general.Photograph: ShutterstockIn March, the then fire safety minister, Samantha Dixon, said that the fire and rescue service had suffered from “decades of drift and inertia”. Herspeechalso confirmed that a new College of Fire and Rescue would oversee professional standards, as recommended by the Grenfell inquiry. But three weeks ago Ms Dixon was sacked. If the government wants to avoid an impression that drift and inertia are ongoing, they need to provide an update, along with a response to repeated calls from the fire service inspectorate for new enforcement powers. MPs on thehome affairs committeethrew their weight behind this idea two years ago.The fire and rescue service ispopular with the public. Even highly critical sections of theGrenfell inquiry reportdid not significantly undermine confidence in it. This summer’s events seem likely to reaffirm this positive regard, and rightly so: public servants who do dangerous, difficult jobs, when many other people are on holiday, deserve to be appreciated. But scrutiny of the service is also important. An inquiry by the home affairs select committee, which was summarised in a letter to the home secretary in 2024, contained strong criticism of its culture and leadership.Such concerns deserve a fuller response than they have so far received from ministers. So do the FBU’s call for investment to cope with rising risks, and proposals for a temporaryban on disposable barbecues. Ill-informed and ideological attempts to blame rewilding should also be addressed by ministers.Working groupson how to reduce wildfire risks must produce plans. The latest report from the government’s Climate Change Committee found that existing adaptation plans arenot fit for purpose. This summer’s extraordinary heat, drought and wildfires should be a spur to action on both the fire service and the wider climate crisis.Explore more on these topicsWildfiresOpinionClimate crisisExtreme heateditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on AI money in US politics: not the way to hold an urgent democratic debate | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Amid public concern over the impact of new technology, Silicon Valley’s use of its wealth to influence specific election races is an unwelcome development
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Amid public concern over the impact of new technology, Silicon Valley’s use of its wealth to influence specific election races is an unwelcome development
Content: Demonstrators wave signs during a nationwide protest in July against AI data centre expansion in Imperial, California.Photograph: Sandy Huffaker/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDemonstrators wave signs during a nationwide protest in July against AI data centre expansion in Imperial, California.Photograph: Sandy Huffaker/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionUS politicsThe Guardian view on AI money in US politics: not the way to hold an urgent democratic debateEditorialAmid public concern over the impact of new technology, Silicon Valley’s use of its wealth to influence specific election races is an unwelcome developmentTue 11 Aug 2026 14.04 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 21.06 EDTShareAs the huge societal ramifications of artificial intelligence have become clear, some of the tech industry’s most senior figures have taken to writingthinkpieceson what comes next. The latest to do so is Mark Zuckerberg, who this weekpublished6,500 words making the case for a laissez-faire approach to AI development. Worrying too much about regulation, Meta’s CEO unsurprisingly opines, could lead to the United States falling behind in the race to own the future.Mr Zuckerberg’s plea for maximum autonomy is, of course, self-serving. Much of hisessay– which airily envisions “invention superpowers” for every entrepreneur and “an abundance of jobs in the future” – reads like unadulterated tech-utopianism. But the lobbying at least has the merit of being out there in the open. As midterm elections loom in the US, darker arts are also being used to counter popular concern about what AI will mean for a host of topics, from the labour market to child safety, the environment and cybersecurity.Replicating a strategy deployed by cryptocurrency backers in the 2024 election cycle, Silicon Valley ispouringhundreds of millions of dollars into Super Pacs – groups unaffiliated to political parties or campaigns – to ensure that voices sympathetic to its deregulatory AI agenda get elected. OpenAI’s co-founder and president, Greg Brockman, and Palantir’s co-founder, Jo Lonsdale, have given large sums to Leading the Future, an organisation dedicated to “identifying, maintaining, and growing pro-AI candidates”.Vastamounts are being spent to try to tilt the balance in individual contests, sometimes through disingenuous means.View image in fullscreenGreg Brockman, president of OpenAI.Photograph: Manuel Orbegozo/ReutersEarlier this summer, Leading the Future spent $6m on ads attacking Alex Bores, a New York state assemblyman and pioneer of AI regulation at state level. Rather than focus on his AI campaigning, the ads attacked Mr Bores’s progressive credentials, alleging that he had carried out tech work in the past for US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which he denies. Running for Congress in a Democratic stronghold, he lost a tight primary race after battling what was in essence a smear campaign.Countervailing forces are emerging.Guardrails Alliance, a union-backed Super Pac, is attempting to combat Leading the Future’s influence, while a bipartisan groundswell of opposition to datacentres is generating serious electoral clout. But as tech companies and their billionaire owners seek to shape and above all limit the scope of AI regulation, their influence is distorting debate in a political culture where thepowerof money already holds far too much sway.In his essay, Mr Zuckerberg urges that AI’s democratising potential be protected from those who believe “a small set of experts … should decide what is best for humanity”. He appears to miss the irony that an unelected tech oligarchy, to which he belongs, is already performing that function by default. Its pressure has been instrumental in persuading Donald Trump tocancelthe signing of an executive order which would have given the government the right to review new AI models. Its wealth is now being used to attack and undermine dissenting voices in the public square.If a democratic debate about the benefits and dangers of AI is to take place, such presumption must be fiercely resisted in the US and elsewhere. The semi-covert manipulation of political discussion is no way to map out an inclusive future in challenging times.Explore more on these topicsUS politicsOpinionUS political financingMark ZuckerbergAI (artificial intelligence)Super PacseditorialsShareReuse this content

title: As heatwaves hit Britain, spare a thought for farm animals | Extreme heat | The Guardian
description: Letters: Claire Bass says animal welfare is a blind spot for the government. Plus, Chris Phillipson on the libraries operating as ‘cool spaces’, Mick Beeby on lido restoration, and Dr Julian McDonough on NHS pressures
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Claire Bass says animal welfare is a blind spot for the government. Plus, Chris Phillipson on the libraries operating as ‘cool spaces’, Mick Beeby on lido restoration, and Dr Julian McDonough on NHS pressures
Content: ‘The Animal Welfare (Sentience) Act 2022 requires ministers to consider animals as sentient beings when developing policy, yet current discourse on heatwaves and farming treats animals almost entirely as economic assets,’ writes Claire Bass.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAView image in fullscreen‘The Animal Welfare (Sentience) Act 2022 requires ministers to consider animals as sentient beings when developing policy, yet current discourse on heatwaves and farming treats animals almost entirely as economic assets,’ writes Claire Bass.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAExtreme heatLettersAs heatwaves hit Britain, spare a thought for farm animalsClaire Basssays animal welfare is a blind spot for the government. Plus,Chris Phillipsonon the libraries operating as ‘cool spaces’,Mick Beebyon lido restoration, andDr Julian McDonoughon NHS pressuresTue 11 Aug 2026 12.57 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 14.04 EDTShareYour article rightly highlights the strain heatwaves place on farming (Adapting to global heating: which UK public services are struggling in hot weather?, 5 August). But the government’s thinking on climate adaptation has a troubling blind spot down at the farm: animal welfare.The Animal Welfare (Sentience) Act 2022requires ministers to consider animals as sentient beings when developing policy, yet current discourse on heatwaves and farming treats animals almost entirely as economic assets: deaths are framed as “reduced productivity”, rather than as sentient individuals enduring terrible suffering.During the June heatwaves, French media reported that between 1 and 3 million birds died in a single week as temperatures hit 44C – deaths preceded by hours of panting, heat stress and organ failure. Pigs and poultry can begin suffering from heat above 27C, and when temperatures exceed 35C, British farms and livestock transport systems are pushing against the limits of what conventional cooling systems can contend with.As the Met Office warns ofUK temperatures reaching 45C by 2056, climate adaptation plans for farming must look beyond balance sheets, recognising that what’s at stake is not just the bottom line, but the suffering of millions of sentient beings.Claire BassSenior director, campaigns and public affairs, Humane World for Animals UKYou are right to highlight the importance of libraries operating as “cool spaces” within communities. Such a facility will almost certainly become increasingly important for groups vulnerable to heat-related stress.Yet, since 2016, over 180 libraries in the UK have beenclosed or turned overto volunteers, with deprived communities four times more likely to lose their library as compared with richer ones. However, poorer areas are precisely those with least access to green and blue space, tree cover and other sources of protection from extreme heat.Given the crucial role of libraries in society – with relief from climate change now added to their many other vital functions – a programme of reversal of a decade of cuts is long overdue.Chris PhillipsonEmeritus professor of sociology and social gerontology, University of ManchesterTo help with its plans to cope with extreme heat (NHS must prepare for annual summer heat pressures, says Yvette Cooper, 5 August), why doesn’t the Labour government implement a nationwide programme of restoring and refurbishing outdoor lidos that have fallen in to disrepair? They might even build some new ones.Mick BeebyBristolSo, we, working in theNHS, must prepare for summer pressures in addition to winter pressures? That’s just pressure, isn’t it? I’m unclear as to what has changed.Dr Julian McDonoughSheffieldHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Despite the drought, don’t give up on our native plants | Plants | The Guardian
description: Letters: Martin Sullivan and Lorraine Du Feu respond to a recent letter suggesting that we should focus on planting non-native species that can tolerate extreme heat
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Martin Sullivan and Lorraine Du Feu respond to a recent letter suggesting that we should focus on planting non-native species that can tolerate extreme heat
Content: ‘There is evidence of rapid microevolutionary changes in oaks in response to recent climate change, so those crisping saplings might be part of selection for drought adaptation.’Photograph: Alex Ramsay/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘There is evidence of rapid microevolutionary changes in oaks in response to recent climate change, so those crisping saplings might be part of selection for drought adaptation.’Photograph: Alex Ramsay/AlamyPlantsLettersDespite the drought, don’t give up on our native plantsMartin SullivanandLorraine Du Feurespond to a recent letter suggesting that we should focus on planting non-native species that can tolerate extreme heatTue 11 Aug 2026 12.57 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 14.04 EDTShareRichard Eltringham (Letters, 5 August) argues that climate change necessitates switching to a planting palette of drought-tolerant non-native species. It’s not as simple as that. Horticulturists focus on the value of non-native plants for pollinators, but other ecological interactions (for example, food plants for insect larvae) are harder to replace.Native oaks support 2,300 other species; drought-adapted non-natives can’t substitute for all these interactions.Our native species themselves aren’t tied to a preindustrial climate;there is evidence of rapid microevolutionary changes in oaksin response to recent climate change, so those crisping saplings might be part of selection for drought adaptation. Alternative planting palettes don’t offer a panacea – Mediterranean landscapes are rather brown in summer precisely because of plants’ adaptations to hot and dry conditions, while our dull, wet winters adeptly kill many drought-tolerant species.Our climate is changing. But a kneejerk shift away from native planting might make things worse.Martin SullivanProfessor of global change ecology, Manchester Metropolitan UniversityI am puzzled by Richard Eltringham’s suggestion that we should move towards planting non-native species in gardens and parks to cope with increasingly hot and dry summers. Despite current moves towards wildlife-friendly gardening, the majority of plants in these spaces are already exotics, some of which are well adapted for drought, others less so.Many native plants are also drought-tolerant, and it would be a pity to discourage people from attempts to make their garden more attractive for native insects by using plants that provide for all stages of their lives rather than just adults looking for pollen.By all means adapt planting to cope with the changing climate, but don’t assume that this means abandoning an admirable trend towards planting native species.Lorraine Du FeuCheltenham, GloucestershireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Droughts were predicted decades ago – yet water companies did nothing | Drought | The Guardian
description: Letters: Water boards in the south of England should have paid attention to scientific models and built reservoirs, writes Steve Lindsay, while Martin Gray suggests turning salt water into drinking water is the answer
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Water boards in the south of England should have paid attention to scientific models and built reservoirs, writes Steve Lindsay, while Martin Gray suggests turning salt water into drinking water is the answer
Content: An aerial view of West Harrow park during drought conditions in London this month.Photograph: James Veysey/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAn aerial view of West Harrow park during drought conditions in London this month.Photograph: James Veysey/ShutterstockDroughtLettersDroughts were predicted decades ago – yet water companies did nothingWater boards in the south of England should have paid attention to scientific models and built reservoirs, writesSteve Lindsay, whileMartin Graysuggests turning salt water into drinking water is the answerTue 11 Aug 2026 12.57 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 12.59 EDTShareIn 1998, I travelled to London for the release of the Meteorological Office’sfirst forecasts of the impact of climate changeon the UK. I was encouraged to see in the audience many representatives from water companies from the south of England. The Met Office modellingshowed that“For summer, there is a general tendency for drying in the south of the UK” and “Warming over the UK will be more rapid in the south-east”.Today, representatives of the southern water boards appear to be surprised that we are experiencing a drought in the south of England (Three-quarters of England in drought as summer’s fifth heatwave looms, 10 August). They should have paid more attention to the science and started the planning and building of reservoirs 28 years ago instead of putting their profits into the pockets of their shareholders.Steve LindsayEmeritus professor of public health entomology, Durham UniversityHow can we be so short of water when, as an island, we are surrounded by the stuff? Solar powered desalination is the answer. Why is it not even being discussed?Martin GrayRadley, OxfordshireExplore more on these topicsDroughtWater industryClimate crisisWaterlettersShareReuse this content

title: France’s complex picture of collaborating with and combating Nazis | Second world war | The Guardian
description: Letters: Some young French joined the armed Milice, who worked with the occupiers, and other fought in the Resistance, says Michael Rosen. And Anthony Lodge writes on Charles de Gaulle
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Some young French joined the armed Milice, who worked with the occupiers, and other fought in the Resistance, says Michael Rosen. And Anthony Lodge writes on Charles de Gaulle
Content: Liberation of Paris, 25 August 1944. Gendarmes, soldiers and Resistance fighters escort German prisoners through crowds of jubilant civilians.Photograph: Print Collector/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLiberation of Paris, 25 August 1944. Gendarmes, soldiers and Resistance fighters escort German prisoners through crowds of jubilant civilians.Photograph: Print Collector/Getty ImagesSecond world warLettersFrance’s complex picture of collaborating with and combating NazisSome young French joined the armed Milice, who worked with the occupiers, and other fought in the Resistance, saysMichael Rosen. AndAnthony Lodgewrites on Charles de GaulleTue 11 Aug 2026 12.57 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 14.04 EDTShareYou editorial (The Guardian view on French cinema’s De Gaulle moment: present anxieties inform a new focus on the past, 5 August) informs us that some new French films covering the second world war are coming soon. Its focus suggested that most of these films will be of a “great men of history” kind. Whatever dilemmas faced leaders in this period, it was the grandparents and great-grandparents of the majority of cinemagoers who faced life-or-death choices and, in some cases, held the lives of their neighbours in their hands.From my research about members of my family and the areas where they were living, I’ve found local policemen arresting Jewish men and women (like my father’s uncles and aunt) and handing them over to the Nazis. These gendarmes were under the command of local administrators who were “honoured” to do the bidding of Nazi commandants. But then, if you scan the Resistance memorials (often in isolated rural places), you gather that some of the names on those memorials are of Jewish and, in one example I know of, a black member of the Resistance.Even as the occupiers were facing defeat, Nazi generals were under instructions to massacre partisans, and some young French men joined the armed Milice, who worked with these occupiers to betray the Resistance. Sometimes, immediately after the war, reprisals against the Milice involved summary executions, while the local administrators who did the Nazis’ bidding may have been tried, found guilty and imprisoned but, soon after, walked free under state-ordered amnesties.This is a complex picture of grassroots, local choices, some being made in support of an illegitimate occupation, part of a Europe-wide genocide and rule by terror, and other choices being made to defy this.Michael RosenLondonFrench cinemagoers will be thinking about the threats to French democracy posed by the extreme right, but their interest in Charles de Gaulle runs much deeper. He symbolises resistance to all the forces outside theHexagonewhich threaten its autonomy and identity.To an extent inconceivable in the UK, the French have striven, since the second world war, to maintain freedom from outside interference – in the military sphere (weapons procurement and the nuclear deterrent), in the economic sphere (space exploration, Airbus, automobiles), in the cultural sphere (Paris and Notre Dame).This urge underlies the desire to maintain and defend the French language, a symbol of internal cohesion within French society and external distinction from the hostile world outside. None of these questions seem to concern people in the UK, but they should.Anthony LodgeCarnbee, FifeHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Romell Glave soars to European men’s 100m title in British one-two ahead of Jeremiah Azu | European Athletics Championships | The Guardian
description: Britain’s Romell Glave won a stunning gold in the men’s 100m at the European championships, with his teammate Jeremiah Azu picking up silver
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Britain’s Romell Glave won a stunning gold in the men’s 100m at the European championships, with his teammate Jeremiah Azu picking up silver
Content: Romell Glave (right)  and Jeremiah Azu show off their medals after a thrilling final.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAView image in fullscreenRomell Glave (right)  and Jeremiah Azu show off their medals after a thrilling final.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsRomell Glave soars to European men’s 100m title in British one-two ahead of Jeremiah AzuOlympic champion Marcell Jacobs pulls up injuredItaly’s Nadia Battocletti wins gold in women’s 5,000mSean IngleTue 11 Aug 2026 18.21 EDTFirst published on Tue 11 Aug 2026 17.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn Marcell Jacobs’ right arm there is a tattoo of the Roman colosseum and a gladiator: a reminder of his fighting spirit and what Italy’s capital means to him. But in the swirling bearpit of a European championships 100m final, the former Olympic champion’s body dramatically broke down.That was the first shock. The second was the sight of two Britons, Romell Glave and Jeremiah Azu, blasting through to take gold and silver.Birmingham 2026: European Athletics Championships day two – as it happenedRead moreTrue, their finishing times were nothing special. But tell that to the 16,000 crowd who cheered to the rafters as Glave took gold in a modest 10.09sec, with Azu following him home in 10.16.Germany’s Owen Ansah claimed bronze in 10.19. And Jacobs? Well, he looked a little saddened and weary as he hobbled over the line in 12.26.“It doesn’t really matter about the time,” said Glave, who was wearing sunglasses and certainly left his rivals in the shade. “The condition wasn’t as great because of the headwind. But I wasn’t really focused on that. I was focused on my race. I was able to do that today and I’m king of the world.”This was the third time Britain has won gold and silver in the men’s 100m at the European championships, following Darren Campbell beating Dwain Chambers in 1998 and Zharnel Hughes finishing ahead of Reece Prescod in 2018.View image in fullscreenBritain’s Romell Glave (left) celebrates as he crosses the finish line to win the men’s 100m final.Photograph: Ben Stansall/AFP/Getty ImagesYet few would have put their money on it happening again when Jacobs, the twice European 100m champion who also won gold in the Tokyo 2020 Olympics, looked so imperious when strolling through his semi-final in 10.08.But shortly after the gun went off in the final, everyone’s assumptions were shot to pieces as Azu set a searing pace, Glave followed – and the Italian’s injury-ridden body suddenly broke down.“I was ahead, so I wasn’t really sure what happened until I saw the replay,” said Glave. “That’s when I realised that he pulled up.”Afterwards, as he sported a crown on his head, he explained that he had moved from Jamaica to London at 15 in search of a better life. “I came over to live with my family,” he said. My dad was over here, and there’s more opportunity in Britain compared to Jamaica.“There’s a more opportunity to join an athletics club,” he added. “And that resource that he gave me, I’m like a living testimony. Just standing here to show that I was born in Jamaica, but Britain is where I was made.”Asked about wearing sunglasses late at night, Glave said he had decided to do it this year. “It’s a part of my style, it is a part of my personality and fashion identity. It’s a new thing for this year because this year means business.”That business of sprinting has not always been smooth, though. Glave was the world’s fastest teenager in 2017, when he ran 10.21 as a 17-year-old.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut his back was in a brace for the whole of 2022. And he was unable to build on a European bronze medal in 2024 after what he says was a fracture in his back that became inflamed. But the 26-year-old has been working on his sprint mechanics with his coach Michael Afilaka – and this was his just reward.Azu, meanwhile, was happy enough with silver after an up and down season. “Normally, I’m quite consistent,” he said. “This year, it’s been one race great, the next not: up and down. But when it comes to championships, I know I find my best, and I showed that today.”View image in fullscreenNadine Visser (right) beats Pia Skrzyszowska in a photo finish to win the women’s 100m hurdles final.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAThere was at least an Italian success in the women’s 5,000m as Nadia Battocletti obliterated the field in the final 200m. “The race was super-tactical, but then I played my winning card,” said Battocletti, who won a slowly run race in 15:37.84. Spain’s Marta García took silver, more than two seconds back, with another Italian, Micol Majori, winning bronze.But there was disappointment for Britain’s Hannah Nuttall, who slipped to fifth after being in a prominent position at the bell.In the women’s 100m hurdles final, Nadine Visser of the Netherlands took gold by one-thousandth of a second to defeat Poland’s Pia Skrzyszowska. Both women finished with a time of 12.67 but after a long time to assess the photo-finish, Visser was given the award. “I won the dip from Pia and that doesn’t happen very often,” she said.Elsewhere the Olympic long jump champion Miltiadis Tentoglou of Greece won his fourth European title with a leap of 8.44m, while Simon Ehammer of Switzerland took silver after jumping 8.29m.Explore more on these topicsEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsAthleticsShareReuse this content

title: Premier League 2026-27 preview No 5: Brighton | Premier League previews 2026-27 | The Guardian
description: Fabian Hürzeler has lost key players including Welbeck and Van Hecke with Brighton needing squad depth to cope with the demands of European football
Author: John Brewin
Headline: Fabian Hürzeler has lost key players including Welbeck and Van Hecke with Brighton needing squad depth to cope with the demands of European football
Content: Georginio Rutter will be a key man for Brighton this season. Photograph: Ashley Western/ShutterstockFabian Hürzeler has lost key players including Welbeck and Van Hecke with Brighton needing squad depth to cope with the demands of European footballByJohn BrewinTue 11 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGuardian writers’ predicted position:9th (NB: this is not necessarily John Brewin’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)Last season’s position:8thProspectsLast season’s final day in May featured Brighton fans and players united in celebrating qualification for the Europa Conference Leaguedespite losing 3-0 to Manchester United. Considering West Ham and Crystal Palace have won the competition since its inception, lifting that trophy becomes a target to aim for.How realistic is that? Beyond the Thursday-Sunday schedule playing in the Conference League demands, it has been a summer of change within the ranks. James Milner did not celebrate as Europe was reached. By then he had decided he would retire. Danny Welbeck was last season’s outstanding forward for Brighton, one of the best in England, and hasfollowed the now traditional trade routeto Chelsea. Him turning 36 in November adds a note of curiosity to that transfer. Thus, the veteran class, each older than their head coach, Fabian Hürzeler, still just 33, is reduced to Pascal Gross, Lewis Dunk and the reserve goalkeeper Jason Steele. Solly March not being offered a new contract was another break from the past, a surprise to a long-serving and popular player whose injury problems counted against him.Jan Paul van Hecke, last season’s best defender, has beensold to Tottenham for £52m, with the teenager Luka Vuskovic coming in the opposite direction. If Brighton supporters are wondering about their club’s slew of new signings then their Premier League peers will be watching as closely, such is the industry’s respect for the club’s recruitment. The Jamestown Analytics company owned by Tony Bloom, Brighton’s financier, is a football Rosetta Stone, admired and coveted. It is not, though, completely infallible; there have been a number of busts.Fans hugely enjoyed being in the Europa League three seasons ago, reaching the last 16, but it had a deleterious effect at home, stretching resources and relations with the then manager, Roberto De Zerbi. Brighton finished a disappointing 11th. Better is hoped for this time around.Past five seasonsOff-field pictureSafe standing is being expanded in the South Stand of the Amex, as part of a £40m modernisation project. The work will take place during September’s extended international break and is a drive towards enhancing the atmosphere. The ownership is among the most mindful of the matchday experience in English football. For Albion fans seeking a middle ground between the posh seats and pre-match drinks in the concourse, there’s the opening of the 1901 Pub, a “hybrid traditional pub and premium matchday lounge designed for a more relaxed fan experience”. With a capacity of 660, membership starts at £173 a month.Owner-fan relationshipThere can be no doubt that Brighton’s continued success relies on the patronage and funds of Bloom. The club’s supporters are more than aware of this. Last season, Bloom’s involvement withHearts’ chase for the Scottish titledemonstrated he has wider horizons, though his key priority will always be the hometown, boyhood club. In January, “the Lizard”, as he is known in the gambling circles he made his fortune, increased his Brighton investment with a £107m loan, making for an overall loan amount of £400m. Without Bloom’s financing and his continued enthusiasm, Brighton would not be the established, model Premier League force they remain.The managerHürzeler has done much growing up in public. There have been points during his two seasons when doubts circled. In the boardroom, though, Bloom and his influential chief executive, Paul Barber, have kept faith in the still youthful Bavarian. As a new, three-year contract was announced in May, Bloom referred to a “clear playing identity”. Hürzeler can be fiery. His touchline behaviour does not always meet the approval of officials and opposing coaches but he enters the season as the fifth longest-serving manager in thePremier Leagueand will be showing off a severe hair remodelling unveiled in pre-season. Success in European football can burnish a growing reputation.Star signingView image in fullscreenNew arrival Luka Vuskovic’s playmaking abilities from the back are highly regarded.Photograph: Matt Impey/ShutterstockWill Tottenham rue never drawing on Vuskovic’s potential? Brighton hope so. He never played a match for Spurs but impressed on loan at Hamburg, where his reading of the game, positioning and maturity drew rave reviews. The signing of the experienced centre-back Pascal Struijk from Leeds means Vuskovic can be allowed time to develop but the Croatian’s playmaking abilities from the back may make him a long-term successor for the captain, Dunk. His fee, reported at £46m when Spurs paid £12m for him, suggests the demand for his talents. The hope and expectation is that the deal becomes regarded as a bargain.Stat attackThe two Manchester clubs were the only sides who scored more Premier League goals than Brighton in regular play last season. The Seagulls dropped down the standings a little once counterattacks were included but they had an identical rate for open play expected goals per game as Arsenal in 2025-26. There should be no shortage of chances for whoever picks up the goalscoring baton after Danny Welbeck’s departure.StatSet for a breakthroughPatience with new arrivals is part of the Brighton doctrines, players are given latitude and opportunity to bed in. A season’s grace is often granted, and Charalampos Kostoulas showed a few flashes of his talent during the 2025-26 campaign. With Welbeck departed, there is a vacancy to lead the line. The Greece international scored a brilliantoverhead kick against Bournemouthin January, and at 19, last summer’s signing from Olympiakos should receive more airtime than the two league starts he received last season. His Greek compatriot Stefanos Tzimas, back in training after an ACL rupture, can provide either competition or a partnership.World Cup impactWhen Jordan Henderson played master of ceremonies as England celebrated third place at the World Cup, he made sure Steele was given a medal for his acclaimed, appreciated work as training goalkeeper. It was an otherwise mixed summer for Albion players, with Maxim De Cuyper going furthest to the quarter-finals with Belgium. Diego Gómez was suspended forParaguay’s historic defeat of Germanythough featured in his country’s bruising exit at the hands of France. Yasin Ayari became the first Brighton player to score two World Cup goals in a game asSweden beat Tunisia 5-1. Michael Svoboda, the summer defensive signing from Venezia, did not play a single minute for Austria.Explore more on these topicsPremier League previews 2026-27Brighton & Hove AlbionPremier LeaguefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Infantino’s opponents developing new framework for running world football | Fifa | The Guardian
description: Uefa, Concacaf and AFC are working together on a new framework for running world football to replace what they regard as Fifa’s system of patronage
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Uefa, Concacaf and AFC are working together on a new framework for running world football to replace what they regard as Fifa’s system of patronage
Content: The Fifa president, Gianni Infantino (left), and his counterpart at Uefa, Aleksander Ceferin.Photograph: Christophe Ena/APView image in fullscreenThe Fifa president, Gianni Infantino (left), and his counterpart at Uefa, Aleksander Ceferin.Photograph: Christophe Ena/APFifaInfantino’s opponents developing new framework for running world footballUefa, Concacaf and AFC working together on systemFifa has ignored calls for an independent reviewExclusive byMatt HughesandNick Amesin SalzburgTue 11 Aug 2026 13.32 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 18.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGianni Infantino’s opponents are working together to produce a new framework for running world football to replace what they regard as a system of patronage that Fifa has adopted since he replaced Sepp Blatter as president 10 years ago.Repeated calls from Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation for an independent review of Fifa’s governance have been ignored by Infantino since his plan tosell off 21% of the World Cupwas made public a fortnight ago, and the rebels are now understood to have taken matters into their own hands.Donald Trump says it would be a ‘terrible mistake’ to replace Fifa’s Gianni InfantinoRead moreA source with knowledge of the discussions told the Guardian that the three confederations are working on producing a policy document to demonstrate how the world governing body could evolve in the future.Those involved have been empowered to ask existential questions such as what Fifa’s precise role should be, how it should be structured and what governance model should be adopted. Financial distribution among member associations is also a key consideration, particularly with an eye on how best to deploy funds from Fifa’s estimated $5bn (£3.7bn) reserves.If Infantino refuses to engage then the new framework is likely to be adopted by a challenger at the presidential election next year, or could even serve as a template for a breakaway organisation.Afterreleasing a joint statementon Monday, which called for “leadership that serves football, not seeks to command it”, Uefa, Concacaf and the AFC let it be known that they have begun preliminary discussions about organising new competitions if the standoff with Fifa’s leadership persists.View image in fullscreenUefa officials are meeting in Salzburg where the Super Cup takes place on Wednesday between Paris Saint-Germain and Aston Villa.Photograph: Gintare Karpaviciute/ReutersAt present the Under-20 Women’s World Cup next month could take place without European teams, asUefais maintaining that its members will boycott the tournament, unless Fifa moves quickly to set up an independent review of the World Cup sell‑off debacle and provide legally binding assurances that such a move will not be repeated.The Concacaf president, Victor Montagliani, is seen as the most likely presidential challenger to Infantino at this stage – although, as he told the Guardian in June, his current focus is on being reelected as president of the North and Central American confederation next year.It seemed significant, however, that the joint statement released on Monday contained strong echoes of a speech given by Montagliani at the Fifa congress this year in Vancouver, where he said: “Let me be frank, leadership is not about power.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAustralia falls into line with AFC stance but stops short of calling for Infantino’s headRead moreSenior figures from European football are gathering in person for the first time since the Fifa Forward Enterprise scandal broke, with a number of meetings expected in Salzburg – where the Uefa Super Cup final will be held on Wednesday – over the next two days.The Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin, will hold talks with Nasser al-Khelaifi, the chair of European Football Clubs, aimed at reinforcing the continent’s unity in demanding a change at the top of Fifa.Uefa continues to hold firm in its pledge to boycott Fifa competitions, having not received its desired assurances that there will be no recurrence of the issues that caused the current crisis.Explore more on these topicsFifaGianni InfantinoUefaFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Arsenal’s Myles Lewis-Skelly offered to Manchester United as left-back solution | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: Myles Lewis-Skelly has been offered to Manchester United as a potential left-back option, with Arsenal wishing to recoup some of the £75m paid to Newcastle for Bruno Guimarães
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: Myles Lewis-Skelly has been offered to Manchester United as a potential left-back option, with Arsenal wishing to recoup some of the £75m paid to Newcastle for Bruno Guimarães
Content: Myles Lewis-Skelly made only five league starts for Arsenal last season.Photograph: Marc Atkins/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMyles Lewis-Skelly made only five league starts for Arsenal last season.Photograph: Marc Atkins/Getty ImagesManchester UnitedArsenal’s Myles Lewis-Skelly offered to Manchester United as left-back solutionChelsea also made aware of 19-year-old’s availabilityNewcastle’s Lewis Hall remains prime United targetJamie Jacksonin DublinTue 11 Aug 2026 08.09 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMyles Lewis-Skelly has been offered toManchester Unitedas a potential left-back option, with Arsenal wishing to recoup some of the £75m paid to Newcastle for Bruno Guimarães.Chelsea, it is understood, have also been made aware of the 19-year-old’s availability. Lewis-Skelly won the Premier League under Mikel Arteta last term, but whether the west London club will make a move for him is unclear.Men’s transfer window summer 2026: all deals from Europe’s top five leaguesRead moreLewis-Skelly, who made only five league starts and 36 appearances in all competitions in 2025-26, signed a five-year contract last summer. His prospective price is thought to be in the region of £45m.This is within the range of finance United have spent so far this summer, afterYouri Tielemans’s £35m movefrom Aston Villa and Andrey Santos’s arrival for £48m plus £2m of add-ons from Chelsea. United are now weighing up a move for the teenager.Newcastle’s Lewis Hall remains of prime interest for United but, after losing Guimarães, Sandro Tonali to Tottenham, and Anthony Gordon to Barcelona, the new Newcastle manager, Matthias Jaissle, is intent the 21-year-old England international does not also departRB Leipzig’s 28-year-old left-back David Raum is another in the position United may assess.Chelsea have already had a busy summer in the market, having spent over £300m on a raft of new signings. Maxence Lacroix and Marco Palestra have been brought in to bolster the centre and right of the defence respectively, while Morgan Rogers became the club’s record signing at a cost of £117m.But Xabi Alonso’s side have a hole on the left of their defence afterMarc Cucurella’s £52m move to Real Madrid. The 20-year-old Jorrel Hato, who featured for the Netherlands at the World Cup, was Cucurella’s deputy at left-back.Mason Mount missed training on Monday and Tuesday at United’s County Kildare summer training camp owing to a knock he received on a foot in Saturday’s 1-1 draw with Paris Saint-Germain in Gothenburg.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe the 27-year-old midfielder being stood down is a precautionary measure, it is understood, and he is also set to sit out Wednesday’s penultimate pre-season friendly against Leeds at Croke Park. The game at the 81,300 capacity venue is a sell-out.United’s final friendly before Michael Carrick’s team start the season on Saturday week at Hull is against Milan in Wroclaw on Saturday.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedTransfer windowArsenalnewsShareReuse this content

title: Emery positive about Aston Villa’s outlook despite summer exits as PSG await | Aston Villa | The Guardian
description: Ebullient manager takes his side to Salzburg to cross swords with the European champions in the Super Cup
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: Ebullient manager takes his side to Salzburg to cross swords with the European champions in the Super Cup
Content: Unai Emery speaks to the media at Stadion Salzburg.Photograph: Leonhard Simon/UEFA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenUnai Emery speaks to the media at Stadion Salzburg.Photograph: Leonhard Simon/UEFA/Getty ImagesAston VillaEmery positive about Aston Villa’s outlook despite summer exits as PSG awaitEbullient manager takes his side to Salzburg to cross swords with the European champions in the Super CupBen Fisherin SalzburgTue 11 Aug 2026 16.14 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 18.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne thing was almost instantly detectable as Unai Emery walked into a stuffy room inside the Red Bull Arena on the eve of Wednesday’s Super Cup againstParis Saint-Germain. After a summer of change, Aston Villa’s manager appeared uber-relaxed, confident his team will absorb a series of headline departures. He cracked a joke about his English improving and poked fun at John McGinn, impersonating his captain while next to him on the auditorium’s top table.Emery was in a jovial mood, then. But he was also switched on, alert to the frequency, the tone of the wave of questions at the beginning of his fourth full season in the job. “You ask about the changes of coaches and players, but McGinn is intelligent and his answer was fantastic,” Emery said with a smile. “When he arrived here [in 2018] they were in the Championship and every year since there have been changes and still the club has moved forward.Premier League 2026-27 preview No 2: Aston VillaRead more“If we compare ourselves to other clubs like Man City, Chelsea, Manchester United, Arsenal and Liverpool, we are competing with them. We don’t have their power … yet.”Emery spoke with an enthusiasm that will be music to the ears of Villa supporters fretting about the size of the task on his hands. Villa have sold Morgan Rogers, Youri Tielemans and Lucas Digne, the latter returning to PSG, for whom he could make his second debut against his former club. Villa would be tested again if Arsenal make a serious play for Ezri Konsa, who, together with Ollie Watkins and Emiliano Martínez, remains on holiday after World Cup duty. Three key coaching staff have also left, including the set-piece coach, Austin MacPhee. But Emery, the beating heart of the operation, as McGinn said, is still in the building.McGinn’s response was punchy when asked where expectations should be for the forthcoming campaign. “Similar to where it has been in the past few seasons,” he said. “I think we have consistently competed with the best in England, the best in Europe, no matter what the competition is. We will have our challenges. There is a lot of change, but when you look at other clubs around England there is a lot of change there as well: a lot of coaches changing, a lot of players changing.“But what we still have is our main core, same manager, same methods, same desire to achieve more. A lot of people thought we had reached our ceiling a couple of seasons ago, and we proved them wrong. We have still got the same hunger and desire to go and achieve more. Our job is just to integrate the new players and try and make them believe, in the same way the players in the last few seasons have believed. I’m really excited by the sort of ‘new Aston Villa’.”View image in fullscreenPlayers and staff of Aston Villa on the pitch at Stadion Salzburg.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesVilla, of course, did not want to lose Rogers. Chelsea paid £117m to sign the England midfielder, two and a half years after Emery asked Villa to pay £8m to take him from Middlesbrough. The same goes for Tielemans, who after a slow start established himself as one of Emery’s undroppables. Villa signed Tielemans on a free but sold the 29‑year‑old for £35m. Digne was an equally reliable performer, taking back the left-back spot from £38m buy Ian Maatsen.Emery knows the business but it was particularly interesting to hear him talk about the importance of the leverage Villa have gained off the back of the ride they have been on over the past few years. One of the most memorable nights was their pulsating quarter-final against PSG 16 months ago, a 3-2 second‑leg victory at Villa Park, when Gianluigi Donnarumma pulled off three superb saves to prevent Villa taking the game to extra time. Emery ended up on all fours after Willian Pacho blocked Maatsen’s goal-bound volley with 28 seconds to play.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The Premier League is the best league in the world and Aston Villa can now have better brands in the way we are,” Emery said. “I am so, so, so happy how the club is committed together with us. [I am so happy] with how we are getting better, keeping our consistency in the Premier League … the club is making a huge effort to try to be in the same direction as me. They are trying to extend Villa Park to achieve 50,000 supporters next season. We are increasing our budget through good results on the pitch, by sometimes selling some players and being consistent like we are, and as well expecting a high level, like we are more or less keeping.”Emery, who spent two years in charge of PSG, knows how these things work. PSG are no longer just a football team but a brand: see their megastore on London’s Oxford Street. PSG’s chief executive, Victoriano Melero, has talked of PSG competing with the likes of Real Madrid on the pitch but labels like the LA Lakers and Ferrari off it.Salzburg is the latest destination on Villa’s quest for success, with 6,000 Villa fans in tow. The stadium facade is plastered with images of McGinn and co celebrating their Europa League win in Istanbul in May. “I am feeling comfortable, happy, very demanding, even more than the last years,” Emery said. “We want more. We are not stopping here.”Explore more on these topicsAston VillaParis Saint-GermainUefa Super CupfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Arthur Fery ready to test himself at Masters level after Wimbledon run | Tennis | The Guardian
description: Arthur Fery, Britain’s surprise Wimbledon semi-finalist, will return to competition in the Cincinnati Open
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Arthur Fery, Britain’s surprise Wimbledon semi-finalist, will return to competition in the Cincinnati Open
Content: Arthur Fery took a holiday and training block after his memorable performance at Wimbledon.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenArthur Fery took a holiday and training block after his memorable performance at Wimbledon.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianTennisArthur Fery ready to test himself at Masters level after Wimbledon runBriton reached SW19 semi-finals as a wildcardWorld No 36 has first-round bye in CincinnatiTumaini Carayolin CincinnatiTue 11 Aug 2026 17.45 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArthur Fery believes he is at the start of a new chapter in his career as he returns to competition for the first time since his surprise run to the Wimbledon semi-finals as a wildcard.Fery will compete for the first time in a month at the Cincinnati Open this week, after opting to take a short holiday and training block following the most demanding fortnight of his career at Wimbledon.“It’s the first time that I’ve broken through like that and I’m going to be able to play only tour events, so I’m looking forward to that,” he said.Vondrousova’s antics put tennis doping tests in spotlight – a far cry from football’s view | Tumaini CarayolRead moreFery arrives in Cincinnati at his career-high ranking of No 36 and despite this being his first direct entrance into a Masters 1000 event he is seeded No 32 and will receive a first-round bye. He awaits either James Duckworth of Australia or a qualifier in round two, with a potential meeting with the fifth seed Alex de Minaur looming in round three.Although Fery’s new ranking is a great achievement in itself, its most important utility is the opportunities it opens up for his scheduling. It has massive implications for the 24-year-old’s career as he will now be able directly to enter the main draw of all regular events on the ATP tour.Until now, Fery had spent his professional career competing at the lower-level ATP Challenger events. He sat outside the top 150 at the beginning of the grass court season, still far from being ranked highly enough to directly enter most ATP events.Fery’s ranking of No 114 at Wimble­don appeared to position him for months of trying to bridge the gap between the two tours, a tricky undertaking that requires players to choose between competing in ATP Challenger events and the qualifying rounds of ATP tour events. Instead, he will completely bypass that stage.Perhaps the most pressing question surrounding Fery after such an unexpected run was how representative his performances at Wimbledon were of his actual level. Fery showed his mental toughness and skill throughout the tournament, dragging himself from the brink of defeat in consecutive five-set wins, against Zizou Bergs and Grigor Dimitrov, before dismant­ling the French Open finalist Flavio Cobolli to reach the semi-final, where he lost against Alexander Zverev.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHowever, this was also a unique situation – competing on grass, in front of a home crowd and against players unfamiliar with his game has its benefits. These tournaments will allow him to see exactly how his game matches up to the elite. Fery, for his part, believes completely that this is where he belongs. “I was always confident that I could play with top players. But yeah, now having the ranking to back it up is really great. And obviously you’re playing great players week in, week out, so it’s difficult.“It’s a difficult sport with fine margins, so you’ve got to have a lot of self-belief. I think it comes from just proving to myself that I have beaten top players and if I do the right things and train well, I feel good on court when I’m with those top guys.”Explore more on these topicsTennisArthur FeryWimbledon 2026newsShareReuse this content

title: Stokes’ presence and group stage drama add to One-Day Cup’s quiet resurgence | Cricket | The Guardian
description: The dawn of the Hundred may have ‘devalued’ the competition, but events at New Road show there is still life in county cricket
Author: Ali Martin
Headline: The dawn of the Hundred may have ‘devalued’ the competition, but events at New Road show there is still life in county cricket
Content: Ben Stokes has played for Durham in the One-Day Cup group stage after retiring from England in June.Photograph: Allan McKenzie/SWpix.com/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenBen Stokes has played for Durham in the One-Day Cup group stage after retiring from England in June.Photograph: Allan McKenzie/SWpix.com/ShutterstockCricketStokes’ presence and group stage drama add to One-Day Cup’s quiet resurgenceDawn of the Hundred may have ‘devalued’ the competition, but events at New Road show there is still life in county cricketAli Martinat New Road, WorcesterTue 11 Aug 2026 15.35 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 17.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Metro Bank One-Day Cup has been a bit of a sleeper hit this summer. Words such as “devalued” and “second tier” have followed the tournament since the dawn of the Hundred in 2021 but there has been a quiet resurgence of late.The prolonged dry spell has provided certainty and pleasant conditions but the big one has been the Hundred’s tractor beam slightly easing. Essentially, the full availability of England players – plus one extra overseas spot per franchise – has lessened the strain on county 50-over squads and upped their quality a touch.County cricket: One-Day Cup group stage coming to the boil in another heatwaveRead moreAnd though he is just one man, Ben Stokes’s presence in Durham’s ranks has also played a small part. Wherever Durham travel, supporters have been able to watch a bona fide England great in the flesh; close enough to read the tattoos or catch a whiff of expensive cologne as he prowls the boundary rope between spells.This was not by design, of course, but rather an unexpected bonus after Stokespulled the pin on his England careerin June. Having not registered for the Hundred auction, the all‑rounder could not slip into the tournament as a late addition. Whether he would have, given his rekindled love for Durham, is uncertain.Stokes was at New Road on Tuesday, where his team were looking to lock down their place in the knockout phase, and thedefending champions Worcestershireneeded a big win to boost their net run-rate and pip them to third in Group B. Jake Libby, the home captain, was also eyeing his fifth List A century to equal the world record.Libby fell for 46 – the domestic record of four in a row will have to suffice – but his team still squeezed out the win. Problem was, it was not quite big enough, having posted 291 and then needed to keep the visitors under 205.Durham, 214 all out in 38.5 overs after stumbling to 199 for nine, progress to the quarter-finals.Still, for all the local disappointment, or the relief in the away dressing room after Hampshire lost a nail-biter at Derbyshire, this was still a pretty life-affirming day all the same. A crowd of about 3,000 may not jump off the page but they were engaged, buzzed throughout, and stayed to applaud the players as they left the field.New Road was pretty much bliss in the sunshine, even if at one stage, when the hosts slipped to 162 for six in the 32nd over, it looked like a damp squib might unfold. Step forward Tom Taylor, blazing a career-best 86 from No 7 – eight fours, three sixes – to give his fellow bowlers plenty more to work with in the defence.View image in fullscreenBen Stokes could score only one run against Worcestershire, but Durham still advanced to the One-Day Cup quarter-finals.Photograph: Worcestershire County Cricket Club/YouTubeSave for Ben McKinney, back from Southern Brave and cracking 82 from opener, Durham slightly froze in the chase. Stokes came and went for one, bowled off an inside edge by Taylor to induce his latest rueful look at the pitch. But in the end, as the game within a game tightened, Durham’s lower order just did enough.Contrary to some perceptions about the county game and the Hundred’s supposedly more family‑friendly vibe, this was a mixed crowd of all ages. The hospitality tent was packed with a “Ladies Day” charity fundraiser, while gaggles of enthusiastic youngsters hunted autographs throughout.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe most in-demand signature was that of Stokes, naturally, but pretty much anyone in full kit was being pestered for a scribble or a selfie. A portion of the membership would sooner the County Championship was being played in high summer but 50-over cricket does offer a full range for folks to enjoy.And for any chuntering about the Hundred and its (undeniable) broader impact, the money from the sale last year has helped a county such asWorcestershire. While the problem of the annual floods at New Road needs a long-term solution, the club have managed to wipe out circa £4m in debt over the past year.“It has given us a chance to breathe,” says Ashley Giles, the chief executive. “There are fewer sleepless nights than before. Although we still have to be smart and in some ways it ramps up the pressure on us a bit, as there are no more excuses.”There were not that many previously, to be fair, with resourcefulness underpinning Worcestershire’s triumph in this competition last year. Going by the efforts to keep their title defence alive, thwarted though they were, it is still there in abundance.Explore more on these topicsCricketBen StokesWorcestershireDurhamfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Australia’s prime minister refuses to apologise to Japanese counterpart over melon gaffe | Australian politics | The Guardian
description: Anthony Albanese faces criticism after appearing to joke on a podcast about a gift of melons from Sanae Takaichi
Author: Josh Butler
Headline: Anthony Albanese faces criticism after appearing to joke on a podcast about a gift of melons from Sanae Takaichi
Content: Japan’s prime minister Sanae Takaichi with Australia’s prime minister Anthony Albanese in Canberra in May.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersView image in fullscreenJapan’s prime minister Sanae Takaichi with Australia’s prime minister Anthony Albanese in Canberra in May.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersAustralian politicsAustralia’s prime minister refuses to apologise to Japanese counterpart over melon gaffeAnthony Albanese faces criticism after appearing to joke on a podcast about a gift of melons from Sanae TakaichiJosh ButlerTue 11 Aug 2026 02.49 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 20.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Australian prime minister,Anthony Albanese, has rejected calls to apologise to Japan’s prime minister over a joke he made about melons on a satirical podcast, amid a media frenzy and accusations of sexual innuendo.Government MPs have defended the prime minister as criticism mounted over last month’s remarks, branded by theCoalitionopposition as “grubby”. The assistant minister Pat Gorman told media: “I don’t know why we’re still talking about this.”During an interview on the comedy podcast Bush Deep in early July, Albanese spoke about Japan’s leader,Sanae Takaichi, giving him a gift of Japanese melons.Melon-gate was a non-issue in Japan. How did it get elevated to a crisis in Australia? | Malcolm FarrRead moreDiscussing the present, he appeared to make hand gestures in front of his chest, saying “she brought two, as you do”. Host Nikki Osborne joked: “She came in looking like Pamela Anderson.”Albanese had not previously addressed the comments, but in parliament’s question time on Tuesday, was asked by the opposition whether he would apologise. In her question, the Liberal MP Mary Aldred described Albanese’s comments as “foul-mouthed, classless” and “disrespectful behaviour”.Albanese responded: “I reject the assertion in the question.”He continued, “Australia andJapanhave never been closer or more strategically aligned.
