And my government has taken our special strategic partnership to new heights,” noting recent economic, strategic and security collaborations between the countries.During his answer, one Liberal MP interjected: “Why didn’t you say that in the podcast?”Aldred later asked again whether Albanese would apologise, to which he again noted various meetings with Takaichi and the close relationship between Japan and Australia.The melon comments have since been canvassed regularly by media outlets including The Australian, the West Australian and the Australian Financial Review. But it resurfaced as a political issue after The Australian ran a comment piece on Monday from the former Japanese ambassador Shingo Yamagami, who claimed Albanese had insulted Takaichi.In an op-ed titled “sexist melon joke was not only ungracious, it betrayed the close bond of our two nations”, Yamagami – who left his post in 2023 and previously had a less-than-warm relationship with some in Labor – called out “crude jokes”.The Australian reported on Tuesday that Japan’s government had sent a diplomatic cable to Australia in July, days after the podcast originally aired, claiming there had been “sensationalised reporting in the Australian media” and saying they detected no “ill intention” in Albanese’s statement.The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, on Monday demanded Albanese apologise, while his deputy, Jane Hume, claimed the melon comments were “grubby” and “beneath the office of the prime minister”.Shiro Armstrong, the director of the Australia-Japan Research Centre at the Australian National University, told Radio National last week there had been “no mention of [Albanese’s comments] in Japan until weeks later”, calling it a “non-issue” in the country.Yamagami told News24 on Tuesday that Albanese should consider visiting Japan this year to meet Takaichi, claiming the issue was a topic of debate in his country.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnthony Albanese’s ‘shag, marry, date-gate’ underscores the double-edged sword of social media appearancesRead more“We need to move on, but I think we need to show mutual respect to each other,” Yamagami said.Labor MPs have closed ranks around Albanese, defending the prime minister and deflecting questions about his remarks.Asked whether an apology was needed, Gorman said: “There is no need for that.”The resources minister, Madeleine King, referred to the Japanese cable saying there had been “sensationalised reporting”, and claimed Albanese’s comments had been “mischaracterised”.The agriculture minister, Julie Collins, said Albanese had rejected “the type of inference that you’re applying” while the environment minister, Murray Watt, said “some media interpretations of that episode of that podcast have been misinterpreted”.The same podcast interviewearlier attracted controversyafter Albanese nominated singer Kylie Minogue while playing a game of “shag, marry, date”with Osborne. After the podcast, Albanese said he apologised “unequivocally” for those comments.The host later said attention on the game had been a“moment taken out of context”.Explore more on these topicsAustralian politicsAustralian foreign policyAnthony AlbaneseSanae TakaichiJapanLabor partyCoalitionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hotel prices in Europe jump before total solar eclipse | Travel & leisure | The Guardian
description: Rooms in Icelandic capital Reykjavík cost double usual rate and Spain also enjoying strong bookings
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Rooms in Icelandic capital Reykjavík cost double usual rate and Spain also enjoying strong bookings
Content: Tourists in Reykjavik have been shelling out £587 on average for a room, according to Lighthouse Intelligence.Photograph: Oliver Sved/AlamyView image in fullscreenTourists in Reykjavik have been shelling out £587 on average for a room, according to Lighthouse Intelligence.Photograph: Oliver Sved/AlamyTravel & leisureHotel prices in Europe jump before total solar eclipseRooms in Icelandic capital Reykjavík cost double usual rate and Spain also enjoying strong bookingsEurope’s total solar eclipse: the best place to see itKalyeena MakortoffTue 11 Aug 2026 06.50 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 17.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHotel prices have surged in key European cities as hundreds of thousands of tourists flock to see the first total eclipse visible from the continent this century.Iceland’s capital, Reykjavík, has seen one of the biggest jumps in hotel room prices, being one of the few accessible locations to see the full eclipse before evening on Wednesday.Tourists there have been shelling out $793 (£587) on average to secure a room on Wednesday, a 98% jump compared with the same day last year, according to data from the travel and hospitality data group Lighthouse Intelligence.Spain is also steeling itself for an influx of tourists, as one of the best places on the European continent toview the total solar eclipse. The finance ministry said on Monday that it expected 460,000 overseas tourists to visit specifically to see the eclipse.The rate for a room in A Coruña in the north ofSpainwas up 135% compared with last year to $451 on average, while prices in Mallorca, where the eclipse is expected to be visible on the horizon at sunset, were up by 24% at about $448. In Santiago de Compostela and Bilbao, hotel room prices have risen 34% and 67% respectively.Solar eclipse mapAccommodation in small towns and villages in the eclipse’s path, as well as makeshift observatories set up by local enthusiasts, have been booked for months. There have been reports of US travellers taking part in house exchanges with people living in Spain’s Castilla y León, which is one of the best regions to view the eclipse.However, authorities in Spain are worried about an increased risk of fires, with police expecting 1.5m more car journeys than usual on Wednesday. They have warned that extraordinarily dry temperatures mean the smallest spark could lead to devastating forest fires, while traffic could end up blocking access for emergency vehicles if fires break out in rural areas.Authorities will undertake out a massive police operation and safety campaign, with plans to deploy 35,000 officers to help minimise risks. Virginia Barcones, the secretary general for civil protection and emergencies at Spain’s interior ministry, said: “We’ve had an extremely tough summer in Spain, with yet another series of major forest fires. That’s why we must restrict any kind of activity that could generate a spark.”Parking on hard shoulders or close to dry vegetation has been banned in Spain, as have barbecues and fireworks. The València region has closed its natural parks and banned walking on rural footpaths.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs of Monday evening, three large wildfires were burning in the provinces of Huelva, Segovia and Huesca. Fires have already scorched about 200,000 hectares this year – six times more than by the same date in 2025, according to the environment ministry.For those unable to make the journey, the US space agency Nasa has installed four high-powered telescopes in the small village of Villalibado in north-west Spain in order to livestream the eclipse to more than 10 million people.A partial solar eclipsewill be visible across the UKon Wednesday, where it will reach its maximum coverage at 7.12pm in London.Explore more on these topicsTravel & leisureSolar eclipsesIcelandSpainEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: University of Cambridge whistleblower who reported alleged bullying wins employment tribunal | University of Cambridge | The Guardian
description: Prof Wyn Evans, who raised concerns over treatment of female staff at Institute of Astronomy, was subject to ‘baseless’ investigation, judge rules
Author: Daisy Ayliffe
Headline: Prof Wyn Evans, who raised concerns over treatment of female staff at Institute of Astronomy, was subject to ‘baseless’ investigation, judge rules
Content: Prof Wyn Evans told a tribunal hearing in June that Cambridge’s Institute of Astronomy had ‘a bad history of misogyny’.Photograph: Sophia Evans/The ObserverView image in fullscreenProf Wyn Evans told a tribunal hearing in June that Cambridge’s Institute of Astronomy had ‘a bad history of misogyny’.Photograph: Sophia Evans/The ObserverUniversity of CambridgeUniversity of Cambridge whistleblower who reported alleged bullying wins employment tribunalProf Wyn Evans, who raised concerns over treatment of female staff at Institute of Astronomy, was subject to ‘baseless’ investigation, judge rulesDaisy AyliffeTue 11 Aug 2026 11.18 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 17.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAUniversity of Cambridgewhistleblower who alleged bullying of female staff inside the university’s Institute of Astronomy has won a tribunal against his employer.Prof Wyn Evanstold a tribunal hearing in Junethat the institute suffered from “a bad history of misogyny”. He claimed that one woman in the department had been “hounded out of a job”, another was “left a frightened woman”, and a third had faced “aggressive professors” at the institute.The tribunal found that after raising concerns, Evans was “subjected to a prolonged nearly two-year investigation by the university”, even though the allegations against him “contained scant particularisation, and no evidence to support them”.The tribunal said its job was not to “conduct a public inquiry into alleged bullying or misogyny within the Institute of Astronomy at the University of Cambridge” but concluded it was “satisfied that the claimant genuinely believed that there was a problem within the institute about the way female administrators were being treated”.It found that Cambridge “did not even want to consider” Evans’s complaints under its whistleblowing policy, and described “an institutional mindset” that viewed the professor of astrophysics as “a source of difficulty and continuing reputational risk due to his protected disclosures which might damage the institute and the university”.The judgment comes at a torrid time for senior leaders at Cambridge, where academicsare calling for an independent inquiryinto the processes and circumstances that led to Jason Arday being appointed as the university’s youngest professor. Arday, who was appointed in 2023,stepped down earlier this monthamid allegations of plagiarism and embellishing his CV.View image in fullscreenThe investigation into Prof Wyn Evans after he made his complaints was ‘baseless’, ‘filed in retaliation’ and ‘likely malicious and vexatious’, the tribunal ruled.Photograph: Sophia Evans/The ObserverAfter the tribunal in Bury St Edmunds, Employment Judge Graham found serious failures in the university’s handling of complaints by Evans, with 11 of 14 alleged detriments upheld against the university or individual respondents including the vice-chancellor.The investigation into Evans was found to be “contrary to natural justice”. The tribunal ruled it was “baseless (as nothing had been provided to support it) and it had been filed in retaliation … and was therefore likely malicious and vexatious”.“By contrast, a number of the claimant’s detailed concerns or complaints were dismissed out of hand without a proper process,” it said.The tribunal also concluded that senior figures at Cambridge relied on correspondence and processes prepared for them by HR or administrators.The vice-chancellor attended the tribunal in person in June and claimed that she had drafted a response to Evans “with the assistance of” the then university registrary, Emma Rampton. The tribunal rejected Prof Deborah Prentice’s evidence. “We find that it was written solely by Ms Rampton and then presented to the vice-chancellor as a fait accompli. Professor Prentice had very little to do with it, save for putting her name to it.”“Ghostwriting was a consistent and a concerning theme throughout this matter,” the tribunal concluded. “In one example the person being complained about drafted the response to the claimant rejecting his complaints against them.”View image in fullscreenEvidence submitted by Prof Deborah Prentice, University of Cambridge’s vice-chancellor, was rejected by the tribunal as she ‘had very little to do with it, save for putting her name to it’.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianEvans, who last year stood to be the University of Cambridge’s chancelloron an anti-bullying manifesto, has said the tribunal judgment raised questions about the vice-chancellor’s fitness for office.“Never rains but it pours for Cambridge,” he said. “Cambridge University has lost the whistleblowing tribunal, with vice-chancellor Deborah Prentice among the respondents found to have retaliated against a whistleblower. That comes on top of serious concerns about her leadership during the Jason Arday crisis. Taken together, these events raise a fundamental question: is Deborah Prentice actually in control of the university she is supposed to lead?”During the hearing, Akua Reindorf KC, for the University of Cambridge, had suggested Evans’s emotional testimony in court about the suicide of a former colleague amounted to “crocodile tears”. The tribunal found “we were not persuaded that the claimant’s expressed emotion in the hearing was false or dramatised for our benefit”.In a statement the University of Cambridge said: “We acknowledge the employment tribunal’s judgment of 10 August 2026 and are carefully reviewing it. We will now take time to reflect on the findings in detail.”Damages in the case are due to be decided at a further hearing in January.Explore more on these topicsUniversity of CambridgeUniversitiesBullyingEmployment tribunalsDiscrimination at workEnglandCambridgenewsShareReuse this content

title: The return of the caspian tiger: how a species feared extinct has come back to Kazakhstan | Wildlife | The Guardian
description: The wild capture and release of a female big cat into a nature reserve is the first step towards reintroducing a population that hasn’t been seen for 70 years
Author: Patrick Greenfield
Headline: The wild capture and release of a female big cat into a nature reserve is the first step towards reintroducing a population that hasn’t been seen for 70 years
Content: A tiger is released into Kazakhstan's wilderness as part of a repopulation programmeThe age of extinctionWildlifeThe return of the caspian tiger: how a species feared extinct has come back to KazakhstanThe wild capture and release of a female big cat into a nature reserve is the first step towards reintroducing a population that hasn’t been seen for 70 yearsThe age of extinction is supported byAbout this contentPatrick GreenfieldTue 11 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 06.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn 31 July, “Umit” – which means hope in Kazakh – was released into a nature reserve on the edge of Lake Balkhash after more than a decade of careful planning to return the caspian tiger to the region. With this release,Kazakhstanbecame the first country to restore its tiger range after they had been thought extinct, with the last reliable sighting in the country recorded more than 70 years ago.Umit – a wild-caught female tiger transported from the Russian far east – will be joined by more big cats in the coming years, with plans to establish a self-sustaining population of about 50. A wild-caught male flown from Russia is still being monitored by authorities and will be released when he is judged fit to survive alone. Two wild tiger cubs are also being reared on the reserve in special enclosures, with as little human contact as possible, and are likely to be released into the marshlands next year, to feast on boar, deer and kulans, a type of wild donkey.“Today, we became witnesses of a truly historic event,” declared Yerlan Nysanbayev, Kazakhstan’s environment minister, after the release. “There is a lot of work ahead on monitoring tigers and forming a stable population, but today the first and very important step has been taken.”Amur tiger in Kazakhstan after being released into the wildernessThe caspian tiger was considered extinct in the 1970s after decades of fur hunting, habitat destruction and eradication campaigns. Its range once spanned from eastern Turkey to north-west China, including Armenia, Azerbaijan, Iran and swathes of central Asia, mostly in forest highlands and along the edges of lakes and rivers, particularly inTugai foreststhat were widely destroyed for agriculture.It was officially declared extinct in 2003, but a scientific breakthrough just six years later laid the foundation for the recent release. DNA analysis of the tiger’s genetic historyrevealed thatthe caspian tiger and the amur tiger found in eastern Siberia were almost identical, with populations probably intermingling until the early 1900s before they were isolated by hunting. What became known as the caspian tiger spread west from Siberia and were separated from the amur tiger by a single letter of genetic code.A map of Kazakhstan and surrounding countries“For all intents and purposes, this is the return of the caspian tiger, only this time they flew instead of walking,” said Dale Miquelle, an authority on Siberian tigers who headsWildlifeConservation Society’s Russia programme. “The idea of bringing back a subspecies of tigers that has disappeared is very exciting. This is as close as we’re going to get to that process.”Today, it would be practically impossible for the caspian tiger to re-establish its former range. A2017 feasibility study identifiedtwo places in the region with enough suitable habitat to re-establish populations, both in Kazakhstan. The most promising was thought to be Ile-Balkhash, where Umit was released, which the Kazakh government made a nature reserve in 2018.While this summer’s release is the first example of a cross-border tiger translocation, there have been several successful releases in the Russian far east as part of efforts to restore the amur tiger’s former range. One scheme involved rescuing orphaned cubs whose mothers had been shot by hunters in Siberia, and then releasing them into former ranges when they were strong enough. The project, which Miquelle worked on, was a huge success – especially because there was no human contact with the young big cats.“The success rate was pretty close to 100% after the release. These animals adapt amazingly quickly. One young female killed a Himalayan black bear within 24 hours of being released and others have learned to hunt on their own in the wild really quickly,” he says.But it is not all good news. Wild tigers have suffered a catastrophic century, withnumbers fallingfrom about 100,000 at the beginning of the 20th century to about 5,500 today. In many parts of Asia, they are still declining – and facing new threats from climate breakdown and disease. In recent years in Russia, African swine fever wiped out enormous numbers of wild boar, a tiger’s favourite prey,causing many totarget human settlements. Ensuring there is enough food for the returning caspian tigers is key to their survival, says Miquelle.“I am very hopeful this can work. In Russia, a number of translocations resulted in the recolonisation of tiger habitat. So there’s a blueprint that suggests that this can work as long as there is suitable habitat and sufficient prey,” he says.Find moreage of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reportersRebecca Ratcliffe,Phoebe WestonandPatrick Greenfieldin the Guardian app for more nature coverage.Explore more on these topicsWildlifeThe age of extinctionExtinct wildlifeAnimalsKazakhstanSouth and central AsiaRewildingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Drought, water rationing and dry rivers: our water crisis is here | Peter Gleick | The Guardian
description: It doesn’t have to be this way. We know what needs to be done
Author: Peter Gleick
Headline: It doesn’t have to be this way. We know what needs to be done
Content: ‘No new technology needs to be invented to provide safe water and sanitation to the billions of people who still lack it.’Photograph: Marco Bertorello/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘No new technology needs to be invented to provide safe water and sanitation to the billions of people who still lack it.’Photograph: Marco Bertorello/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionClimate crisisDrought, water rationing and dry rivers: our water crisis is herePeter GleickIt doesn’t have to be this way. We know what needs to be doneTue 11 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 11.56 EDTShareDisturbing news about our water resources is now constant and unrelenting. In just the past few weeks, media have reported that Puerto Rico issuffering a deep water crisisas severe drought has cut water supplies to thousands. TheRhine and Po riversin Europe areat record low levels. The seven states sharing theColorado Riverin the US arefighting over unprecedented shortages, while its major reservoirs have shrunk to their lowest levels since they were built.Hungary’s only nuclear power plant is on the verge of shutting down because there isn’t enough water in the Danube River to cool it. Toxic chemicals have been found inall English water bodies.Desalination plants in the Middle Easthave been bombedin the ongoing war with Iran and municipal water systems in the United Statesare being hacked.The worstEl Niñoin recorded history isunfolding in the Pacific, affecting weather and water around the world. Violence over wateris worsening, with more water-related conflicts than at any time in recorded history. And communities are mobilizing toblock water-hungry datacenters, concerned that their water resources will be drained away.As AI guzzles water and energy, we are already facing a choice: datacentres or homes? | John HarrisRead moreAt any given moment, there are always places around the world suffering from droughts or floods or experiencing water scarcity – a normal consequence of the natural variability of our climate and weather.But what we’re experiencing now is not normal; it is the direct consequence of accelerating human-caused climate changes, on top of decades of neglect and underinvestment in our water institutions and infrastructure.For years, climate scientists have warned that continued emissions of greenhouse gases from burning fossil fuels and other human activities would alter the planet’s climate, raise temperatures, disrupt weather patterns and worsen extreme events, raise sea levels, and accelerate the spread of disease vectors. Those warnings were ignored, dismissed, downplayed. And now we are reaping what we’ve sown.Yet our politicians continue to prevaricate, refusing to take actions to protect water resources; or worse, rolling back earlier efforts. The Trump administration’s EPA has halted efforts to regulate new water pollutants and weakened regulations put in place by previous administrations – both Democratic and Republican.The administration has also continued to push forbillions of dollars of cutsto other federal agencies that coordinate research on water resources and climate, including the National Science Foundation, the US Geological Survey, and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.If governments continue to fail to address water and climate crises, the coming decades will inevitably see worsening water-related violence and conflict and deteriorating public and ecological health.It doesn’t have to be this way. People care deeply about water. Inpollafterpoll, concern for water resources – both quantity and quality – consistently ranks at the top, above all other environmental challenges.Europe’s rivers are running dry, and the knock-on effects are disastrous | Yiannis BabouliasRead moreAnd we know what needs to be done. No new technology needs to be invented to provide safe water and sanitation to the billions of people who still lack it. The cost of providing water to all and cleaning up the consequences of unregulated and uncontrolled water pollutionis far less thanthe costs of failing to do so.Violence over shared water resources can be lessened by international agreements and diplomacy over shared watersheds – which is the focus of a majorFinnish water diplomacy initiative.Smart investments in water efficiency technologies and regulations and in advanced wastewater treatment systems canimprove the resilienceof existing water infrastructure to extreme events.Far more food can be grown with far less water with efficient irrigation systems, reducing pressures on overtapped aquifers and rivers.And the rapid expansion of renewable energy systems and the rapid phase-out of fossil fuels will both slow the rate of climate change and reduce the amount of water required to produce the energy we all require – a win-win.We also need more public education about both water threats and solutions by our schools and media, more bipartisan actions by our politicians, and more investment by governments, corporations and communities in the technologies and policies that we know work but are failing to pursue with the urgency the growing crises demand. Constant news about worsening water problems must not become the new normal.Peter Gleick is author of The Three Ages ofWater(2023) and When the Well is Dry: How Water Fuels Violence and Shapes Peace (2026)Explore more on these topicsClimate crisisOpinionWaterAccess to waterDatacenters – USMiddle East and north AfricaTrump administrationcommentShareReuse this content

title: Meta glasses banned from courts in England and Wales | Meta | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Court service says anyone trying to enter buildings with glasses will have them confiscated and returned when they leave
Author: Matthew Weaver
Headline: Exclusive: Court service says anyone trying to enter buildings with glasses will have them confiscated and returned when they leave
Content: Mark Zuckerberg wearing a pair of Meta glasses, which have been labelled ‘pervert glasses’ amid concerns about people taking videos without consent.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMark Zuckerberg wearing a pair of Meta glasses, which have been labelled ‘pervert glasses’ amid concerns about people taking videos without consent.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesMetaMeta glasses banned from courts in England and WalesExclusive:Court service says anyone trying to enter buildings with glasses will have them confiscated and returned when they leaveMatthew WeaverTue 11 Aug 2026 06.29 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 14.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCourts inEnglandand Wales have joined a number of restaurants, theatres and pubs in banning Meta glasses, amid a mounting backlash against what has been described as “spyware”.Last month courts inNew York announced a banon the controversial glasses, which can record video footage while being worn.Now His Majesty’s Courts & Tribunals Service (HMCTS), which is responsible for all criminal, civil and family courts in England andWales, has made clear that Meta glasses will be confiscated from anyone entering its judicial buildings.A spokesperson told the Guardian: “There are clear restrictions on taking images or videos within courts and tribunals which is why the use ofMetaglasses is prohibited.”Taking images or videos in court buildings is prohibited in the UK without official permission and can be prosecuted as contempt of court. While lawyers and members of the public are allowed to enter courts with smartphones, which can record both video and audio, theHMCTS made clear that no such exception would be made for smart glasses.A source said: “Users who bring Meta glasses into courts or tribunals will have them confiscated on entry and they will be returned when the owner leaves the building.”They said smartphones were allowed on the condition they would not be used for recording court procedures.Earlier this year, aclaimant was accused by a judge of wearing smart glassesin the high court and getting “coaching” through them while giving evidence.Laimonas Jakštys was told to remove the glasses during a case over the directorship of a property company. Raquel Agnello KC, sitting as a judge of the high court, said Jakštys had been “assisted or coached in his replies to questions put to him during cross examination”. Jakstys denied using the smart glasses to receive answers, and denied they were connected to his phone.HMCTS does not hold figures on the number of incidents of smart glasses being used or taken into courts.In February, members of the security team for Meta’s chief executive, Mark Zuckerberg, were seen wearing Meta glasses during a high-profile trial in California about social media addiction.The judge, Carolyn B Kuhl,threatened the security guards with contempt of courtif they had recorded any of the proceedings.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNew York’s court system said it was banning smart glasses to ensure “individuals cannot surreptitiously record court proceedings”. It added: “No individual possessing smart glasses will be permitted to enter a UCS [unified court system] facility unless they voucher the smart glasses for safekeeping by uniformed personnel while the individual remains in the facility.”Last year Meta sold 7m pairs of the glasses, which cost between £269 and £469.Fears about Meta glasses being used to film people, especially women, without their consent has led to them being labelled “pervert glasses”. A number of restaurants, theatres and pubs in the UK, including Wetherspoons, havebanned Meta glasses over privacy fears.A spokesperson for Meta said the company did not want to comment on the court ban. They said when the glasses were recording a pulsing light was visible to people in the vicinity, and that frequently updated tamper detection technology is deployed to stop users covering this light during recordings.This article was amended on 11 August 2026 to correct the name and abbreviated form of HM Courts and Tribunals Service (HMCTS)Explore more on these topicsMetaUK criminal justiceCameras in courtContempt of courtEnglandWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Doctors at remote Devon hospital get ‘crash course’ after maternity unit shut | Devon | The Guardian
description: Staff at North Devon district hospital given training in difficult births in case mothers-to-be cannot get to Exeter
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Staff at North Devon district hospital given training in difficult births in case mothers-to-be cannot get to Exeter
Content: Some staff are worried that North Devon district hospital in Barnstaple is being downgraded.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSome staff are worried that North Devon district hospital in Barnstaple is being downgraded.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianDevonDoctors at remote Devon hospital get ‘crash course’ after maternity unit shutStaff at North Devon district hospital given training in difficult births in case mothers-to-be cannot get to ExeterSteven MorrisTue 11 Aug 2026 08.07 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 17.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDoctors at one of England’s remotest hospitals have been given a “crash course” in birth emergencies after its maternity unit was shut and as fears grow that the safety of women and babies may be put at risk.From Tuesday, the maternity service at North Devon district hospital (NDDH) in Barnstaple has beensuspended indefinitelyowing to staff shortages, leaving many pregnant women facing a journey of at least an hour and a half when they go into labour.Women have told the Guardian they may be forced to give birthwithout medical help at home or even in a laybyas they try to get to hospital in Exeter, more than 50 miles away, on roads often choked with traffic during the summer months. Some have said they will move from the area to give birth.A doctor at the hospital has now revealed that emergency staff at the NDDH have been given training in dealing with difficult births if mothers cannot get to Exeter.The doctor, who asked not to be named, said: “I’m hoping that we won’t see such emergencies and women will birth their babies without a problem and both will be fine, but there is a potential that we will see women who can’t make it to a maternity unit who have to be diverted to the hospital.“There’s been a crash course in learning how to deal with emergencies such as shoulder dystocia or postpartum haemorrhage. It’s been an intense time and we’re all pretty shocked. We’re capable but they’ve thrown us into a potentially very serious situation. There’s a physical risk to the public.“The emergency department and its staff are familiar with dealing with emergencies without the direct help of specialities but it’s the unfamiliarity of an obstetric emergency or neonatal collapse and having no one nearby on site to assist that is confronting.”RoyalDevonuniversity healthcare NHS foundation trust has described the suspension as temporary but cannot put a date on when maternity services at the NDDH may return.The doctor said: “This has the potential to put a lot of strain on the emergency department. It has to deal with a high volume of patients, especially over the summer when the tourists come. It also has to deal with a large elderly population.”Some staff are worried that the hospital is being downgraded. The doctor said: “It feels like they are slowly stripping away services and moving them. It’s like they’re dismantling our hospital. That’s not fair on the public or on staff. This has hit staff morale as people are questioning what this means for the future of our hospital.”View image in fullscreenJemima Knight, left, and her sister Harriet Knight.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianJemima Knight, who is 18 weeks pregnant, lives two hours from the nearest hospital – and her last birth took only two hours.She said: “This is my third baby. My first required a hospital transfer in an ambulance and luckily that transfer was only 20 minutes. I do not know what the outcome of that birth would have been if the transfer time had been two hours. My second baby was born in two hours.“Even if I knew this labour would be longer than two hours, anyone who has ever had a baby knows that being strapped into a car seat in August heat in the holiday traffic whilst in active labour would be a horrific, dangerous and traumatising experience akin to torture. No woman should ever have to go through that, and that is what the hospital trust are asking us to do.”She said she was considering relocating her family to Bristol, where they could stay with relatives for her birth. “The travel time proposed for us is like suggesting that it would be appropriate to close a hospital in Bristol and tell the pregnant women they have to go and give birth in London.Knight is also worried for her sister, Harriet Knight, who is 34 weeks pregnant. Jemima said: “A safe and respectful birth is a fundamental human right, and that right has been removed for hundreds, potentially thousands, of women in Devon.”Aspecial Devon county council meetinglater this month will discuss the closure. The council leader, Julian Brazil, said: “This closure is extremely concerning. It is not a decision which would be countenanced in other parts of the country and we should not accept second-rate NHS provision here.”The trust has said it is trying to recruit extra consultants and doctors but has not been able to hire enough to run a safe service.A spokesperson for Royal Devon university healthcareNHSfoundation trust said: “The safety of women, babies and families is our top priority. We carefully considered all options but the greatest risk was continuing to provide births without sufficient medical staffing.”The trust said it recognised that some women were vulnerable and had put in place a range of support, including help with transport and finances.On the “crash course”, they said: “We have worked closely with colleagues in our urgent & emergency department, maternity services and SWAST [the ambulance trust] to agree clinical pathways for managing emergency presentations.”Asked about staff morale, the spokesperson said: “We recognise the impact this has had not only on women and birthing people, but also on our colleagues. We are actively supporting our colleagues through these temporary changes alongside our focus to reopen birthing services in north Devon as quickly as possible.”The trust denied that more services may go from the hospital. It said: “This is not the case. We are committed to providing the core acute hospital services that people in north Devon rely on. Most services continue as normal, and millions of pounds are being invested in north Devon.”Explore more on these topicsDevonHospitalsWomen's healthNHSHealthEnglandChildbirthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Driver who broke sound barrier sets new speed record in hydrogen-powered car | Utah | The Guardian
description: British driver Andy Green reached 406.320 mph in car powered by two hydrogen internal combustion engines
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: British driver Andy Green reached 406.320 mph in car powered by two hydrogen internal combustion engines
Content: Andy Green after breaking the land speed record for diesel-powered vehicles in Bonneville Salt Flats, Utah, on 22 August 2006.Photograph: Richard Meredith-Hardy/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAndy Green after breaking the land speed record for diesel-powered vehicles in Bonneville Salt Flats, Utah, on 22 August 2006.Photograph: Richard Meredith-Hardy/ShutterstockUtahDriver who broke sound barrier sets new speed record in hydrogen-powered carBritish driver Andy Green reached 406.320 mph in car powered by two hydrogen internal combustion enginesAssociated PressTue 11 Aug 2026 13.48 EDTFirst published on Tue 11 Aug 2026 08.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe only person to break the sound barrier in a car earned another world record on Tuesday in a show of force for hydrogen power.British driver Andy Green reached 406.320mph (653.908km/h) in a car powered by two hydrogen internal combustion engines with a combined 1,600 horsepower, setting the record for that vehicle category, according to the Fédération Internationale de l’Automobile, the international governing body of motor sports.The 64-year-old retired Royal Air Force pilot rocketed across the crystalline crust at Utah’s famous Bonneville Salt Flats in a 32-ft (9.75-meter) car engineered by British construction equipment manufacturer JCB. The engines, adapted from those used in the company’s heavy machinery, mix pressurized hydrogen gas with air and ignite it to create bursts of power.To be clear, Tuesday’s feat didn’t come close to approaching the overall land-speed record, which Green set with jet power in 1997. That year, he climbed into the Thrust SSC, a black needle sandwiched between two cartoonishly large jet engines, and drove it to an outright record of 763.035 mph (1,227.985 kph), breaking the sound barrier and achieving a feat no one has come close to matching. His runs in Nevada’s Black Rock desert produced sonic booms that shook the nearby town of Gerlach.Footage from 1997 shows Andy Green’s fastest land speed world recordIn 2006, Green also set the land-speed record for a diesel-powered car – 350.092 mph (563.4 kph) – at the Bonneville Salt Flats. He returned there Tuesday with the goal of beating that mark using hydrogen power, which he has called the “fuel of the future”.In targeting his diesel speed, Green easily topped the previous hydrogen combustion world record of 185.5 mph (298.5 kph). He had a 10-mile (16-km) straightaway to build speed. A few dozen JCB staff members and reporters watched from a distance through cameras and binoculars.A remnant of a prehistoric lake bed, the Bonneville Salt Flats are about 100 miles (160 km) west of Salt Lake City and sit atop a shallow aquifer that cools the tires. The low-friction surface and dry desert air are conducive to speed and have beckoned drivers since the first race there in 1914.Green was no stranger to speed when he took his first racing job. He had been flying supersonic military jets when he spotted a 1994 British newspaper ad seeking a high-speed driver to break the sound barrierGreen did not approach supersonic speeds on Tuesday, but JCB engineers hope his feat with hydrogen power will shake up the clean-energy industry.The company’s chairman has argued that hydrogen can better handle the demands of heavy industries than electric power.Hydrogen is only as clean as its source, and the vast majority is currently produced from fossil fuels. JCB signed a deal to buy green hydrogen, which is created using renewable energy but makes up a tiny fraction of global hydrogen production.Explore more on these topicsUtahWorld recordsAutomotive industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Syrian court sentences Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia for war crimes | Syria | The Guardian
description: Verdict relates to atrocities committed during the country’s 14-year civil war in which about 500,000 people died
Author: William Christou
Headline: Verdict relates to atrocities committed during the country’s 14-year civil war in which about 500,000 people died
Content: Bashar al-Assad (pictured on the poster) and his brother Maher, who was also sentenced to death, fled to Moscow in December 2024.Photograph: Omar Sanadiki/ReutersView image in fullscreenBashar al-Assad (pictured on the poster) and his brother Maher, who was also sentenced to death, fled to Moscow in December 2024.Photograph: Omar Sanadiki/ReutersSyriaSyrian court sentences Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia for war crimesVerdict relates to atrocities committed during the country’s 14-year civil war in which about 500,000 people diedWilliam Christouin BeirutTue 11 Aug 2026 06.40 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 17.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Syrian court has sentenced the country’s former presidentBashar al-Assadand his brother Maher to death in absentia for crimes against humanity and war crimes during the 14-year civil war, in which about half a million people died.The two men fled to Moscow after being ousted by a lightning rebel offensive in December 2024 whichtoppled the dictatorial regime in just 11 days.The former president and his brother, who commanded the feared fourth division and was considered the regime’s top security official, oversaw a brutal crackdown in which government forces killed, arrested and tortured indiscriminately to crush protests that started in 2011.The court said Bashar al-Assad had been sentenced to death for crimes of “premeditated and intentional murder of more than one person and of children” as well as “torture, arbitrary arrest and crimes against humanity”.View image in fullscreenBashar al-Assad in 2023 at the signing of a  comprehensive programme of strategic and long-term cooperation between Iran and Syria in Damascus.Photograph: Matin Ghasemi/Borna News/ATPImages/Getty ImagesIt said it would pursue international legal avenues to try to prosecute the two men, but Russian officials have previously declined requests to extradite its former Syrian allies.The court also sentenced Atef Najib, Assad’s cousin and the former head of political security in Daraa, to death. Najib was responsible for the torture of a group of 15 young boys who had graffitied anti-Assad slogans on a wall in 2011 – an event that kicked off mass protests in the southern Syrian province, which then spread to the rest of the country.Najib’s trial was highly publicised, with pictures of him listening to proceedings while dressed in a prison uniform and held in a cage in court. The Syrian government has presented his trial as a landmark case in its pursuit of transitional justice, something experts say is key to healing divisions in the country.View image in fullscreenAtef Najib on trial in Damascus.Photograph: Mohammed Al Rifai/EPASyria has experienced explosions of violence in the post-Assad era. About 1,500 mostly Alawite civilians were killed in a wave of retaliatory killings in March 2025 after militants loyal to al-Assad attacked security forces. Al-Assad belonged to the Islamic Alawite sect – a minority group in Syria – and enjoyed strong support in the group’s coastal heartland during his rule.In July 2025, more than 1,700 people were killed in massacres in the Druze-majority province of Suweida when local fighting evolved into sectarian killings. Low-level violence has continued in northern Syria until the present day, particularly targeting Alawite civilians.View image in fullscreenSyrians celebrate the ruling outside the palace of justice in Damascus.Photograph: Bakr Alkasem/AFP/Getty ImagesSyrian authorities have taken steps towards transitional justice, establishing committees and arresting Assad-era officials, in an effort to end intercommunal violence.Al-Assad became president in 2000 at the age of 34, inheriting power from his father, Hafez. He had trained as an ophthalmologist in London and was not initially supposed to be president, but became the heir after his brother, Basil, died in a car accident.Though styled as a young reformer who was supposed to allow some liberalisation in Syrian politics and its economy, his legacy was largely defined by his brutal response to the country’s revolution. Under his rule, Syria’s fearsome security apparatus was given a free hand to arrest, torture and kill civilians on an industrial scale.Explore more on these topicsSyriaBashar al-AssadWar crimesMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Every minute counts’ as rescuers race to find survivors after deadly Colombia earthquake | Colombia | The Guardian
description: People being pulled from collapsed buildings day after 7.4 magnitude quake hit, in response experts say contrasts favourably with Venezuela’s
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: People being pulled from collapsed buildings day after 7.4 magnitude quake hit, in response experts say contrasts favourably with Venezuela’s
Content: Rescuers race to find survivors as Colombia rocked by 7.4-magnitude earthquake – videoColombia‘Every minute counts’ as rescuers race to find survivors after deadly Colombia earthquakePeople being pulled from collapsed buildings day after 7.4 magnitude quake hit, in response experts say contrasts favourably with Venezuela’sTom Phillipsin Rio de Janeiro andThomas Grahamin BogotáTue 11 Aug 2026 11.31 EDTFirst published on Tue 11 Aug 2026 10.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleColombian rescue workers are racing to find survivors afterthe country’s deadliest earthquakethis century killed at least 240 people and left at least 3,000 missing.In Cali, one of the worst affected cities, firefighters said they had pulled a 35-year-old man from the wreckage of a collapsed building shortly before 4am on Tuesday – nearly 24 hours after the 7.4 magnitude quake rattled westernColombia.“We have found life under the debris … Every minute counts,”the fire department wrote on Xalongside a video of a survivor being rescued from beneath a concrete beam.On Tuesday afternoon there wasa sudden burst of applauseafter a 31-year-old woman named as Diana Troncoso was also rescued by firefighters after a 16-hour effort. “Getting out of there is a miracle,” her father, Álvaro Troncoso Torres,told journalistsfrom local newspaper El País as he stood by the ruined building.Civilians reportedly pulled at least five survivors from a partly collapsed hotel, although elsewhere the bodies of some of the city’s 95 confirmed victims could be seen lying on the street under sheets.View image in fullscreenExhausted rescue workers and volunteers rest during the search for survivors in Cali.Photograph: Joaquín Sarmiento/AFP/Getty ImagesColombia’s president, Abelardo de la Espriella, wassworn into powerin Cali only last Friday. On Monday night he was back in his country’s third-largest city, telling reporters that 5,000 homes had been destroyed and 188 people were missing in the surrounding department of Valle del Cauca.“We will get through this together,” Cali’s mayor, Alejandro Eder, told its 2.3 million citizens during a televised meeting with the new president.Eder said emergency responders had rescued 37 people from some of the 40 buildings that had completely collapsed in Cali. De la Espriella, who won power in June by vowing to launch a major crackdown on illegal armed groups, said more than 1,000 troops were being mobilised to avoid public disturbances amid reports of looting.The situation in Pereira, a city 130 miles to Cali’s north, appears similarly dramatic, with at least 53 people reportedly trapped in some of the 58 buildings that collapsed. Eleven people are missing, according to the local newspaper El Diario.GraphicOn Monday, Pereira’s mayor, Mauricio Salazar,broke down in tearsas he described the damage inflicted on his city, where at least 66 deaths have been confirmed.“Pereira is living through a historic and tough situation,” Salazar told reporters, his voice breaking as he explained how local hospitals were struggling to keep up with the influx of patients.The earthquake, which struck at 7.34am on Monday, is Colombia’s deadliest since a 6.2 magnitude temblordevastated parts of the same western coffee growing regionin January 1999, killing more than 1,000 people.View image in fullscreenColombia’s president, Abelardo de la Espriella, left, was sworn in only last week.Photograph: Gabriel Aponte/Getty ImagesThe natural disaster poses an immediate and severe challenge to De la Espriella, a far-right populist with no experience of politics or governing who took office less than 72 hours before the earthquake.The acting leaders of neighbouringVenezuelawere castigated by civilians for what many considered their lethargic and incompetent initial response to the twin earthquakes that struck its north coast on 24 June, killing at least 6,300 people.Buildings damaged after strong earthquake hits ColombiaIn the crucial 72 “golden hours” after Venezuela’s earthquakes, survivors said government officials and troops were nowhere to be seen, something widely attributed to years of economic crisis, corruption and the mismanagement of the armed forces, as well as foreign sanctions.Colombia’s earthquake on Monday appears to have caused substantially less damage than Venezuela’s far shallower and more destructive earthquakes. But the official reaction – at least so far – appears to have been far more organised, proactive and transparent than in Venezuela, where civilians were often left to their own devices to dig victims from the rubble.In the hours after Colombia’s earthquake, De la Espriella quickly declared a state of emergency and said he would personally lead the disaster response, making a trip to the department of Chocó, before travelling to Cali. He has sent teams led by various ministers in his recently named cabinet to each of the worst affected places. Government officials have offered regular updates on the situation. De la Espriella is due to fly to Pereira on Tuesday.View image in fullscreenPeople search through the debris of a damaged building in Pereira, Colombia.Photograph: Carlos Ortega/EPAExperts attribute the two countries’ contrasting responses to their starkly different political realities.Venezuela has suffered more than a decade of authoritarian rule under the recently abducted dictator Nicolás Maduro, during which time the country’s institutions, media and civil society withered and international aid groups and NGOs struggled to operate.Critics have voicedfears over a possible authoritarian tackunder Colombia’s recently installed pro-Donald Trump leader. But the country remains a vibrant multiparty democracy with strong institutions and an energetic civil society.Christopher Sabatini, a senior fellow for Latin America at Chatham House, believed those very different systems explained the dramatically different responses to the natural disasters.Sabatini recalled how after June’s twin earthquakes, Maduro’s secretive authoritarian heirs – who have retained power with Trump’s blessing under acting president Delcy Rodríguez – had gone into “a defensive crouch” as citizens were abandoned to their own fate. “They just went quiet,” in the hours after the disaster, he said.In contrast, Sabatini sensed in Colombia “a quick, sharp, public-facing and immediate response” from officials such as Cali’s technocratic mayor, and even the controversial new right-wing president, in what was “an efficient, effective state”.“It shows the democratic DNA of both sides,” Sabatini said of the contrasting earthquake reactions in Colombia and Venezuela.Orlando Pérez, a Latin American politics expert from the University of North Texas at Dallas, also noted major differences in the responses, although he recognised that Venezuela’s disaster was more severe.“Everybody is praising de la Espriella’s quick response – and I’m willing to give him his due. He has reacted in a much more public way and shown leadership in an overt manner. The Colombian military has been deployed in a much more effective and quick [manner] than in Venezuela,” said Pérez, noting how conservative social media influencers were explicitly pushing the comparison between Rodríguez’s sluggish response and the seemingly rapid reaction of her Colombian counterpart.“But things could go south pretty quickly if the initial burst of energy and activity is not followed up with effective reconstruction and recovery and assistance for the … people who have lost their homes and their jobs,” Pérez added.“We have seen in other places where initial responses are positive and then recovery doesn’t come quickly enough, and people get frustrated.”Explore more on these topicsColombiaEarthquakesVenezuelanewsShareReuse this content

title: Spotify to distinguish AI artists from real people – and stop recommending them | Spotify | The Guardian
description: Music streaming platform creates ‘AI persona’ label that will appear on profiles and track listings in crackdown on fake performers
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Music streaming platform creates ‘AI persona’ label that will appear on profiles and track listings in crackdown on fake performers
Content: AI-generated artists will be labelled as an ‘AI persona’ on their profile, in search and in track listings.Illustration: Spotify UKView image in fullscreenAI-generated artists will be labelled as an ‘AI persona’ on their profile, in search and in track listings.Illustration: Spotify UKSpotifySpotify to distinguish AI artists from real people – and stop recommending themMusic streaming platform creates ‘AI persona’ label that will appear on profiles and track listings in crackdown on fake performersDan MilmoGlobal technology editorTue 11 Aug 2026 09.40 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 17.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSpotify is to label AI artists and exclude them from algorithm recommendations as part of a crackdown on fake performers.The world’s largest music streaming platform is creating a label for AI-generated artist identities called “AI personas” that will appear on the artist profile and on track listings on playlists.It means that from September AI-generated artists such as theVelvet Sundownwill carry the persona label and will be blocked from personalised recommendations by default. The aim is to differentiate these deepfake artists from real performers who might lose out on streams to artificial rivals.Spotify said: “True artist-fan connection can only be built on a foundation of trust and authenticity. In music, that means listeners need to be able to trust that the artist behind the music is who they say they are. That’s more essential than ever in the age of generative AI.”Last year Spotify revealed it had removed 75m spam tracks from its platform over a 12-month period as AI tools created a flood of fake music. Spotify’s legitimate catalogue stands at 100m tracks.Spotify will allow music creators to reveal if their identities are AI-created – and will then label them as an AI persona – but it will not rely on self-disclosure alone. The company said it would use human review and AI investigative tools to determine if artists were fake. Although the new rule technically applies to AI “identities”, Spotify says AI-generated profiles are invariably a front for AI-made tracks as well.The company said: “Listeners have been clear in telling us that they don’t like seeing an artist profile that seems human, only to find out that the persona is AI-generated.”Last year there was debate about the origins of the Velvet Sundown – a 70s-style US rock band – before the band’s social media channels confirmed the subterfuge. A statement described the group as an AI creation that was “somewhere in between” human and machine.The Velvet Sundown has 117,000 monthly listeners on Spotify but its page has no clear AI labelling, although the artist profile describes the four-piece as a “synthetic music project”.In January there was further discussion about Sienna Rose, a soul singer who entered Spotify’s viral top 50 but did not appear to be real, having never played a gig or released any videos despite releasing a prolific burst of material over a 10-week period. The Spotify profile for Rose, who has more than half a million monthly listeners, does not clarify whether she is AI or not.Explore more on these topicsSpotifyAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: Delivery drivers to be paid minimum $31.30 an hour across Australia in ‘world-leading’ decision  | Gig economy | The Guardian
description: Fair Work Commission issues a new minimum standards order for gig workers to come into effect 17 August
Author: Catie McLeod
Headline: Fair Work Commission issues a new minimum standards order for gig workers to come into effect 17 August
Content: Under the changes, delivery platforms will have to organise and pay for personal accident insurance that ‘provides a reasonable minimum level of cover’ for their workersPhotograph: Martin Berry/AlamyView image in fullscreenUnder the changes, delivery platforms will have to organise and pay for personal accident insurance that ‘provides a reasonable minimum level of cover’ for their workersPhotograph: Martin Berry/AlamyGig economyDelivery drivers to be paid minimum $31.30 an hour across Australia in ‘world-leading’ decisionFair Work Commission issues a new minimum standards order for gig workers to come into effect 17 AugustGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastCatie McLeodConsumer affairs reporterTue 11 Aug 2026 04.25 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 05.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDelivery drivers in Australia will be paid a minimum rate of $31.30 (US $22.05/£16.35) an hour and insured for injuries on the job under a landmark agreement approved by the industrial umpire that could set a precedent in other countries.The Fair Work Commission (FWC) on Tuesday issued a new minimum standards order for gig workers who perform on-demand delivery of food, drinks, or groceries, and the operators of the digital platforms who engage their services.Hospitality recruitment app Supp calls gig-workers contractors. Some users say it leads to casual work without entitlementsRead moreThe Transport Workers’ Union, representing the gig workers, had jointly applied with major platforms DoorDash and UberEats for the new protections in 2024, after years of talks.After taking public submissions on new standards for the industry, including from gig workers and other interested parties including Amazon and Auspost, FWC has greenlit the conditions, to come into effect from 17 August.The deal is likely to have involved concessions from either side of the negotiating table, including the union agreeing to call the workers “employee-like”.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailIn a joint statement on Tuesday, the TWU, UberEats and DoorDash said the new standards would provide an “industry-wide safety net for hundreds of thousands of [workers] while preserving the flexibility that sits at the heart of on-demand work.”The TWU national secretary Michael Kaine said the new standards were “world-leading”.Under the new standards, workers will be responsible for maintaining third-party insurances on the vehicles they use for deliveries, so if they get in an accident and damage another vehicle the delivery platform will not be liable for the cost.On the other hand, delivery platforms will have to organise and pay for personal accident insurance that “provides a reasonable minimum level of cover” for their workers, although experts have previously pointed out this is open to interpretation.While they were proposed by the TWU, UberEats and DoorDash, the conditions are expected to apply to any on-demand platforms that sell food, drinks or groceries, as well as the people they hire on an ad hoc basis to deliver products.The new conditions include “safety net” pay rates for workers, who will initially receive hourly rates ranging from $31.30 to $32 depending on the class of vehicle – for example, whether they are riding a push bike or driving a car.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe minimum rates – which are designed to ensure delivery workers are paid even if they are, for example, waiting for a restaurant – will increase by 50 cents from 1 January 2027.The new standards cover a range of issues and, among other provisions, are intended to provide clearer dispute resolution and workers the right to unpaid time off.The TWU, DoorDash and UberEats made the joint application to the FWC after the Albanese government introducedworkplace reforms in 2023, which included empowering the industrial umpire to set minimum standards for gig workers.The workplace relations minister, Amanda Rishworth, on Tuesday said the resulting standards were a “milestone”.“This [FWC] order is a big step in delivering Australia’s world-leading gig worker protections and means food delivery workers don’t have to trade off flexibility for fairer protections,” she said.Explore more on these topicsGig economyUberCouriers/delivery industrynewsShareReuse this content
