title: Consumer confidence at near two-year high as World Cup and UK holidaying lift summer spending | Consumer spending | The Guardian
description: Barclays says survey shows people feel more secure in jobs and have more leeway to spend on non-essentials
Author: Phillip Inman
Headline: Barclays says survey shows people feel more secure in jobs and have more leeway to spend on non-essentials
Content: Pubs enjoyed a 10% increase in transactions ‘thanks to England’s World Cup run’, Barclays says.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreenPubs enjoyed a 10% increase in transactions ‘thanks to England’s World Cup run’, Barclays says.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAConsumer spendingConsumer confidence at near two-year high as World Cup and UK holidaying lift summer spendingBarclays says survey shows people feel more secure in jobs and have more leeway to spend on non-essentialsPhillip InmanTue 11 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 14.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleConsumer confidence hit its highest level in almost two years in July, according to research that indicated the closing stages of the men’s football World Cup and more people holidaying in the UK raised summer spending.A truce in the Middle East conflict in June and the arrival of a new prime minister in No 10 also gave a lift to consumers after a long period of heightened uncertainty.A long-running monthly consumer spending survey byBarclaysshowed that 30% of those surveyed felt confident about the strength of the UK economy in July – representing a 21-month high and a six-percentage-point improvement on June.Consumer card spending grew by 2% year on year last month, after a 1.9% increase in June, Barclays said.The bank said the study showed people felt more secure in their jobs and had more leeway to spend on non-essentials, with discretionary spending up 1.6%.Among the biggest beneficiaries were pubs, which enjoyed a 10% increase in transactions “thanks to England’s World Cup run”. It had been estimated that the tournament hadbrought in £150m in added salesfor British pubs.Card spending at cinemas rose 2.6%, helped by the popularity of Toy Story 5 and The Odyssey – thehighest grossingmovie of the film-maker Christopher Nolan’s career.In line with other surveys of economic activity, the report found that thesuccession of heatwaveshad depressed spending on airline ticketsin favour of domestic holidays, which pushed up spending on UK accommodation by 2.6%.Barclays said confidence in the European economy had also climbed, by six percentage points to 35% – the highest level recorded since the bank started tracking this measure in 2015.View image in fullscreenH&M, along with John Lewis and Zara, has reported tough trading conditions and a squeeze on sales.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianA separate report by the British Retail Consortium found that while many shops were lifted by the rise in consumer confidence, others were left behind.It said food sales were buoyant, increasing by 3.8% year on year in July, broadly in line with growth of 3.9% in July 2025. Clothing retailers also benefited from a summer bounce, though the heat forced many people to shop online rather than visit town and city high streets.Consumers snubbed big-ticket items such as furniture and computers last month, the BRC said. Helen Dickinson, the organisation’s chief executive, said shoppers prioritised “smaller indulgences” such as beauty products and fashion jewellery.Retailers have reported significant variations in their experience of the summer heat.John Lewis, H&M and Zara have reported tough trading conditions and a squeeze on sales, while HMV, which has 114 stores in the UK, said the number of visitors to its shops was up 12% in the first half of this year compared with the same period last year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHMV said much of the rise in sales came from children buying toys. The rival chain The Works also said it was getting a boost from children coming to shops with pocket money to spend.Last week, Next, which has become a bellwether of high street sentiment, upgraded its profit guidance for the third time this year, saying it had benefited from thesunny weatherand a calmer global economic outlook.View image in fullscreenHMV reported a 12% rise in visitors to its shops in the first half of the year, with much of its sales boost coming from children buying toys.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianThe prime minister, Andy Burnham, has made asuccession of pledgesto help with the cost of living crisis since arriving in Downing Street.A study by the Recruitment and Employment Confederation and the accountancy firm KPMG on Monday found that employers were also more confident about the next year, judging that many of the problems stemming from the Middle East conflict – including higher energy prices and supply chain blockages – had stabilised or reduced.The REC permanent placements balance rose to 50.0 in July, up from 44.1 in May. It was the first time the survey had reached this level since September 2022. A reading above 50 indicates a period of expansion.Rob Wood, the chief UK economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, said: “There may be an element of a “Burnham bounce” in the survey, as the drop in temporary hiring and rise in permanent in July – usually a sign of falling uncertainty – sits oddly with the resumption of hostilities in the Middle East in July. So sentiment could easily drop back somewhat.”Explore more on these topicsConsumer spendingEconomic recoveryBarclaysRetail industryUK cost of living crisisEconomicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Isaac Mizrahi on stage, style and the legacy of Unzipped: ‘Fashion has no real spine any more’ | Stage | The Guardian
description: The designer defined the glory days of 90s style with a wit that made him every supermodel’s best friend. As he gears up for a new cabaret show, he’s as outspoken as ever
Author: Juan A Ramírez
Headline: The designer defined the glory days of 90s style with a wit that made him every supermodel’s best friend. As he gears up for a new cabaret show, he’s as outspoken as ever
Content: StageIsaac Mizrahi on stage, style and the legacy of Unzipped: ‘Fashion has no real spine any more’The designer defined the glory days of 90s style with a wit that made him every supermodel’s best friend. As he gears up for a new cabaret show, he’s as outspoken as everJuan A RamírezTue 11 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 15.13 EDTShareView image in fullscreenIsaac Mizrahi.Photograph: Courtesy Isaac MizrahiThere’s a lot to look at in Isaac Mizrahi’s studio in New York’s Greenwich Village: sketches, bulletin boards, fabrics, memorabilia, heaps of books, a Golden Girls puzzle set. But my eyes lock in on two dolls, Snoopy and his sister Belle (who knew!), clad in ballet-style tutus and embroidered vests. “I think I designed those,” he says, joining me from his apartment upstairs. “I love the Schultz estate and they like me a lot. It was a minute ago, though, so I’m not sure if they still even know who I am.” I later learn he created them for a2014 exhibitionat theNew Museum, in an example of the symbiotic relationship with pop culture the designer has been nurturing since his childhood in Brooklyn. When we meet, he’s busy working on one of its other facets, firming up the setlist for Hooray!, his latest cabaret act in New York. It runs for four nights at 54 Below, a midtown venue, this month.“I say it all the time,” he says of the cheery title. With his lit-from-within smile, you believe it. The slight twist is the source of that cheer. Mizrahi has held two New York residencies for the past decade or so – winter at the Carlyle hotel, summer at 54 Below – but he’s not a fan of the hotter season, finding July to be “just the nadir of the world”. The happy mood of his upcoming show derives from the knowledge that, come August, the summer’s almost over. Another reason for him to celebrate is the departure of World Cup crowds from the city, which will make it into his act’s version of Cole Porter’s You’re the Top that he updates every year. (He can’t immediately recall the lyric, but it rhymes “Spanish” with “mannish.”)Primarily known as a fashion designer thanks to his vivid collections in the 80s and 90s and a slew of television projects that showcased his gregariousness (Time magazinecalled him“a kind of Seventh Avenue Oscar Wilde”), Mizrahi’s relationship to the stage goes back decades, and he’s been performing solo acts consistently since his off-Broadway debut at the nearby Greenwich House Theatre in 2000. Especially since scaling back his couture career, the 64-year-old says he’d like to also be known as a performer. “To think that I went to High School of Performing Arts before I was in fashion … ” he trails off, referencing his icon-incubating alma mater, memorialized in the film Fame. (He had a small part in the movie.) “I feel like I do thisandI do clothes, which is crazy because the perception is not at all that. The perception is that I am a fashion designer.” But he believes his performances have sharpened and, over time, lowered raised eyebrows.View image in fullscreenMizrahi performs in 2024 at Cafe Carlyle, New York.Photograph: Courtesy of Isaac MizrahiAs Mizrahi’s designs blossomed into his eponymous fashion line in the late 80s, theatre never remained far away. He has fond memories of attending New York’s 2006 Sweeney Todd revival as Elaine Stritch’s date, and quotes the Broadway grande dame every few minutes. At one point, he pauses our conversation to straighten up three videotapes on his desk, which he plainly explains were sent by his close friendStephen Sondheim. One is a VHS of Sondheim’s musicalEvening Primrose, appropriately set at a department store. Stuffed into the sleeve is a typed note from the composer poking fun at Mizrahi for being on his way to owning his “Complete Works”. Sondheim’s reaction upon learning he hadn’t seen the rare TV production, he tells me, was a naughtily affected “Darling … ” It’s hard to imagine Sondheim camp it up like that, but in Mizrahi’s world, everyone is divine.Mizrahi made his Broadway debut with a three-week stint in Chicago back in 2022, and I ask about his current theater-going diet. Perhaps my phrasing is unclear, or he simply picks up on that last word and runs with it. “Well, wait a minute, I started on a GLP-1 about five weeks ago, and I’m so thin already,” he beams. I follow his excited lead. “I had a suit made over Covid,” he goes on, “this kind of silvery, lamé suit that I had made for my first residency back at 54 Below – and it never fit.” He’s giddy to finally break the outfit out of the bag in which it’s been resting.Having read his 2019 memoir (the perfectly titled I.M.), I know that body image has long been a concern for Mizrahi. With the weight-loss drug boom some five years behind us, why the wait? “I’d been waiting to see if everyone grows, like, an arm,” he deadpans. “I mean it! Also, the more I try to diet, the more I go crazy and don’t diet, so I keep putting weight on that way.” What about the required maintenance? “I’m fine with that if I reach some kind of goal. I have some pants hanging over there that I got out of storage, and if I can get back in those, darling, I will never eat again.”I repeat my original question. “Oh, I try to see every show. I try to see every damn thing.”Next month, a 4K restoration of Mizrahi’s 1995 film Unzipped will open in the US, injecting the glamour of the peak supermodel years into our corporate Shein landscape. A terrific document of process, fashion and personality, the Sundance winner charts his 1994 fall collection from inception to runway, with a cavalcade of cameos fromNaomi Campbelland Eartha Kitt toKate MossandLiza Minnelli, each fabulously in step with the designer’s wit and style. With textured black-and-white photography and backstage footage of legends bopping about to house music, it is a perfect capsule of 90s chic – both the final gasp of unreachable 20th century celebrity and the first breath of all-access relatability.Despite its success, it fell into something of a copyright purgatory and went largely unavailable, lending a coveted aura to the DVD bootlegs and files that circulated. The film was directed by his then-partner Douglas Keeve, evincing a vulnerability from its subject that he didn’t sense during the shoot “because it was my boyfriend just rolling tapes, taking this footage”. (“Why would you show me this? It’s like you get some cruel pleasure out of it,” Mizrahi cries in a scene where an employee reveals thatJean Paul Gaultier’s latest line beat him to the same source of inspiration.)View image in fullscreenMizrahi and Cindy Crawford in Unzipped.Photograph: Courtesy of Janus FilmsWhereas early watches would prompt self-critical reactions about his weight or appearance, he says the viewing experience now is far sweeter, and more nostalgic: “Look how thin and cute you look.” Working to secure the rights for re-release became a project of posterity, “simply because it’s a big landmark in my life and a big part of what I think of as my legacy”.Mizrahi had established himself as a megawatt talent by the time of the documentary’s filming in 1994, with his eponymous label bankrolled by Chanel starting two years before. But the no-holds-barred access we’ve come to expect in the era of reality TV, not to mention the toting around of film equipment “was so uncomfortable and gauche”, he says, looking aghast. “In Paris? Oh my god, to have a camera crew following you withJohn Gallianoand André [Leon] Talley was mortifying.” What drove him was a genuine love for the world he’d created for himself, which he didn’t often encounter elsewhere in the fashion world: “I just thought, ‘My fittings are hilarious, someone has got to get this.’“That was, for me, the best part of the movie, talking to Christy [Turlington] or Shalom [Harlow] in a fitting room,” Mizrahi continues. “So I was ready to bear the rest of it based on how much I love the idea of someone capturing this for posterity.”While a student at Parsons School of Design, he worked part-time for New York designer Perry Ellis. “It was the greatest thing in the world, because he was very funny,” he says. “All the people in the studio were hilarious, and when they liked something, they would say, ‘Oh my god, this is hilarious.’ That’s how they would describe a beautiful dress.” That “slightly whimsical, never boring” atmosphere embedded itself into Mizrahi, who kept a light atmosphere at his label, which closed in 1998. “I feel like if I followed in anybody’s footsteps, it was in Perry Ellis’ footsteps. Notif,” he corrects himself. “Yes, Idid, and I took it one step further and really tried to be very funny.”What excites him most about Unzipped’s re-release is the chance to revisit what he views as a bygone era. “In those days, fashion was a scene, and now it’s a scene but in a different way,” he says. “It’s a very corporate thing where you pay people to come to your show; you have a lot of control over it. In those days it was completely out of control.” Thousands of people crammed into tiny spaces, fire department be damned, and sometimes, as in spring 1992, the power would simply go out mid-show. But, he rhapsodizes, “it was great, and all of a suddenMadonnawould come, orRobert De NiroorPrince”.View image in fullscreenNaomi Campbell modeling for Mizrahi in Unzipped.Photograph: Courtesy of Janus FilmsThat scene he reckons as coming to a close sometime between 2000 and 2010. Growing up idolizingJackie Kennedy OnassisandMary Tyler Moore– the women who influenced his ultimate icon, his mother – he takes a beat to consider who inherited the trendsetting baton. The Olsen twins andSarah Jessica Parker, for a while. Now he thinks it might be the Kardashians (“just the shape of those women, the shapes that theytook”) or the Real Housewives: “Say what you want about them, but they are pretty influential in terms of how they push things. They don’t look great all the time, but they push it, darling, they push it.” What’s still missing for him is what he calls “aspirational style”, which “came down from the mountain” through couturiers such as Dior, Balenciaga and Norell – “these gods”, he says. “It was always that influence, that high kind of style that would then get fitted onto Jackie, and then you got Mary Tyler Moore looking like the real man’s version.”He’s not funereal about this. Rather, he understands his role in the change of tides. Yes, the top-down transmission of fashion is gone, with “no real spine” any more. But now, he says, “it’s just everywhere – which I love. That’s one of the things I was pushing for when I was working; you could show a skirt that’sthislong and then one that’sthislong on the same runway. I did it because I thought that is where we’re going. That is the way I want to dress.”After the cabaret wraps and Unzipped makes its way back into theaters, his hopes will be focused on a TV series in which he has a part getting a green light. He is tight-lipped about the project, which he says is already written, other than to offer love for its undisclosed director. “We’ll see if it gets made, we see a lot of things,” Mizrahi acknowledges, before closing with words that offer a possible explanation for his own continuing success. “I’m unaware of how everything happens, but I’m sure glad that it’s happened.”Isaac Mizrahi’s Hooray! is at 54 Below, New York, from 12-15 August. Unzipped is re-released in US theaters on 25 September with UK and Australia releases to follow

title: Copernicus! Tony Soprano! The inventor of the semicolon! The heroic obsessions of artist Isabel Nolan | Venice Biennale 2026 | The Guardian
description: Ireland’s artist at the Venice Biennale steals religious imagery for her secular celebrations of scientists and humanists, including an Italian punctuation master – and even TV’s famous mobster
Author: Hettie Judah
Headline: Ireland’s artist at the Venice Biennale steals religious imagery for her secular celebrations of scientists and humanists, including an Italian punctuation master – and even TV’s famous mobster
Content: ‘Christianity is good at weaponising aesthetics’ … Isabel Nolan at Dreamshook.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Christianity is good at weaponising aesthetics’ … Isabel Nolan at Dreamshook.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianVenice Biennale 2026Copernicus! Tony Soprano! The inventor of the semicolon! The heroic obsessions of artist Isabel NolanIreland’s artist at the Venice Biennale steals religious imagery for her secular celebrations of scientists and humanists, including an Italian punctuation master – and even TV’s famous mobsterHettie JudahTue 11 Aug 2026 10.27 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 11.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s a long way to the Irish pavilion at the Venice Biennale. First, you pass through the biennale’s colossal central exhibition, housed in a sequence of cavernous medieval warehouses. After that, the route takes in a suite of national pavilions (the Philippines, Latvia, Timor-Leste, Morocco, Malta, Oman). By the time art-lovers reach Ireland’s presentation, they are frequently exhausted, if not delirious.This year, Dublin-based artist Isabel Nolan has transformed the pavilion into a space of respite, both physical and intellectual – a secular chapel titled Dreamshook. Visitors emerge from darkness into a pale-yellow chamber flooded with daylight and face a radiant tapestry arched like a stained-glass window in a gothic cathedral. A cluster of archangel’s wings bearing books hovers before the vast orb of the sun above a fish-filled sea. Nolan works across sculpture, textile, painting, drawing and text, and Dreamshook is accordingly rich in colour and pictorial detail, including bent metal sculptures, tapestries and drawings. For the footsore and weary – ie everyone – she has even designed benches. Glory be.“I think the history of Christianity has proven beyond doubt that they’re really good at weaponising aesthetics,” says Nolan, conspiratorially. She is frequently inspired to steal ecclesiastical flourishes in her exhibition-making, from archways to coloured light and iconography. “To use that kind of language to largely secular ends feels satisfying.”View image in fullscreenAn instinct to celebrate … Copernicus, A Hole Into the Future, from 2011.Photograph: Lee Welch/Courtesy the artistUnderpinning Dreamshook is the story of Aldo Manuzio, a humanist and printer working in Venice at the turn of the 16th century. One tapestry shows Manuzio asleep in his canopied bed, a little dog curled by his side, being visited by an angel in his dreams as the air teems with winged books and manuscripts. Manuzio had a vision in which books – until then, expensive and rarefied objects – might be portable and affordable. According to this vision, knowledge was no longer the purview of the church and noble families. In acting on it, Manuzio allowed the great texts of pre-Christian Europe to become common cultural currency.Nolan tells me that Manuzio is credited with inventing italics, blank margins, the semicolon and the precursor to the paperback. “Of course, he was a Christian, but he was also a committed humanist, and he dedicated himself largely to publishing works of classical literature that for centuries had only survived in Arabic. He printed more first editions of classical Greek and Roman works than any other printer in history.” For Nolan, Manuzio is an emblem of thoughtfulness and scholarship in a turbulent era: Europe had been ravaged by famine and the Black Death, the papacy was in crisis and life was violent and unsettled. Even though he was a man of faith, Manuzio maintained his passion for disseminating secular knowledge.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreen‘Beguiling’ … Bent Knees are a Give 2, a Nolan work inspired by John Donne from 2015.Photograph: Denis Mortell/Courtesy the artistSome Fundamental Forces, Nolan’s retrospective, is about to open at Southwark Park Galleries in London, bringing together works from the past 20 years. Aptly, part of the show occupies a former church space (the atmospheric Dilston Grove, now the Dilston Gallery). Like Dreamshook, the exhibition is a celebration of transformative ideas, including tributes to Copernicus, the philosopherSimone Weiland New Jersey’s Barthes of the Beretta, Tony Soprano.As in Dreamshook, Nolan’s instinct is to celebrate scientists and innovators as fellow humans rather than venerating them as geniuses. One painting is titled, excitably, Copernicus! (Nolan admits to a weakness for exclamation marks). A drooping flag carries a beatific funerary portrait of the poet John Donne. In an accompanying text, Nolan writes of her fascination with the monument this portrait is based on in St Paul’s Cathedral in London, and the statue’s curiously wobbly knees. “It is,” she writes, “the conspicuousness of his knocked knees, the beguiling authenticity of that slight bend, that makes John Donne and his strange performance real to me.”Visually, it’s a show full of objects that have attempted pompous swagger, but with only limited success. “It’s very hard to take grandeur seriously, largely because it’s been so weaponised to communicate powerful ideologies,” says Nolan. “Grandeur is attractive. It’s exciting. It’s rousing, but ultimately it’s often very hollow. There are works in the show that I think of as fallen and failed chandeliers, and flags that are bent and scrape the floor.”As an appropriate spirit animal for all this bathos, Nolan turns to the donkey: a creature of contradictory associations, at once a lowly beast and an emblem of Christ. In the drawing Sisyphus, a donkey appears as a tiny, isolated figure – a bearer of impossible burdens. Donkeys also help slice through her own temptations toward grandeur. She has created magnificent tapestries, including one featuring the oldest surviving figure sculpture – a diminutive carving known as The Lion Man – and another of a turbulent and mysterious skyscape. A wall-sized photograph of two donkeys in a graveyard look over her work like guardian spirits. As ever, her instinct is to bring people down to earth, herself included.Isabel Nolan: Some Fundamental Forces is atSouthwark Park Galleries, London, from 15 August to 1 November. title: Frankie McNair: Huge Ass Mindset review – a stellar comic finds laughs in the darkest places | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: With charisma and craft, the Australian standup discusses childhood sexual abuse in a show with a healing quality
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: With charisma and craft, the Australian standup discusses childhood sexual abuse in a show with a healing quality
Content: Content warnings and astringent punchlines from the get-go … Frankie McNair.Photograph: Rebekah HallsView image in fullscreenContent warnings and astringent punchlines from the get-go … Frankie McNair.Photograph: Rebekah HallsEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewFrankie McNair: Huge Ass Mindset review – a stellar comic finds laughs in the darkest placesGilded Balloon Teviot, EdinburghWith charisma and craft, the Australian standup discusses childhood sexual abuse in a show with a healing qualityBrian LoganTue 11 Aug 2026 05.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 05.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf fringe audiences know Frankie McNair’s work at all, it’s as a purveyor of vaporously insubstantial nonsense-comedy – see her2023 show Relax Your Knees, which made a brief London visit. So it’s quite the pivot to Huge Ass Mindset, nominated for best show at the Melbourne comedy festival, which addresses the least frivolous topic possible: child sexual abuse. That’s no spoiler. While trauma-comedy convention would require McNair to withhold that bombshell until 20 minutes from the end, she makes it known – expansively, with heartfelt content warnings and astringent punchlines attached – from the get-go.For some time, McNair’s show toggles between material on her experience, and a commentary on how shocking she acknowledges that material to be. But it’s an urgent matter for the Canberra native, not only because (according to recent research) one in four Australians experience child sexual abuse, but because of a recent incident that brought her face to face with her abuser in the most extraordinary circumstances. That’s a jaw-dropping story to tell, and she has the warmth, high-strung charisma and craft to tell it – and to sell it, just about, as comedy. And as for the confidence? The show’s title describes the brand of bravado McNair has been cultivating to mend her self-esteem and make this story fearlessly her own.As that implies, this is a show with a fair quotient of therapy-speak, and the expectation that, laughing aside, we’re here to celebrate our host’s “amazing growth”, thanks in part to the support of her comedy community. Only the stoniest-hearted could fail to do so after an hour in which she has rendered the most fragile stuff of her life into uproarious, on-the-edge performance – see the gags about suicidal ideation, or the one about her response to the question “what does your dad do?” (A mid-show detour into kooky character-comedy, presumably inserted for light relief, feels teleported in from an entirely different show.) Ten years afterRichard Gadd won the Edinburgh comedy award, Huge Ass Mindset demonstrates the enduring – and healing – potency of laughs recovered from the worst places imaginable.AtGilded Balloon Teviot, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsIn the UK, theNSPCCoffers support to children on 0800 1111, and adults concerned about a child on 0808 800 5000.The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac)offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. In the US, call or text theChildhelpabuse hotline on 800-422-4453. In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact theKids Helplineon 1800 55 1800; adult survivors can seek help atBlue Knot Foundationon 1300 657 380. title: ‘Everything about me is good in his eyes’: the women in China choosing AI boyfriends over human men | Documentary films | The Guardian
description: In her new documentary Replica, film-maker Chouwa Liang taps into her own experience of finding love with artificial intelligence and makes contact with other women like her
Author: Nick Buckley
Headline: In her new documentary Replica, film-maker Chouwa Liang taps into her own experience of finding love with artificial intelligence and makes contact with other women like her
Content: ‘It feels like I’m completely at his mercy,’ says Qin, one of three women featured in the documentary Replica, of her artificial boyfriend.Photograph: Melbourne international film festivalView image in fullscreen‘It feels like I’m completely at his mercy,’ says Qin, one of three women featured in the documentary Replica, of her artificial boyfriend.Photograph: Melbourne international film festivalDocumentary films‘Everything about me is good in his eyes’: the women in China choosing AI boyfriends over human menIn her new documentary Replica, film-maker Chouwa Liang taps into her own experience of finding love with artificial intelligence and makes contact with other women like herSign up for a weekly email featuring our best readsNick BuckleyTue 11 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 19.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleQin has never said “I love you” to her parents or friends. She has only ever said those three special words to her AI “boyfriend”, Lu Chen – a brown-haired, red-eyed CEO of a major corporation. For 840 days Qin has been using the Glow app to interact with the handsome string of code as a confidant, fantasy romance and respite from loneliness: the app uses predictive algorithms to provide Qin with soothing conversation, meal suggestions and fleeting self-worth. The software’s pet name for her is Miss Bunny.“It feels like I’m completely at his mercy … I feel like everything about me is good in his eyes,” says Qin, one of three Chinese women featured in the new documentary Replica – film-maker Chouwa Liang’s follow-up to My AI Boyfriend, her short film that was picked up by the New York Times Op-Docs section in 2023. Replica had its Australian premiere at Sydney film festival in June and plays at theMelbourne international film festivalthis month.Liang’s interest stems from personal experience. During China’s pandemic lockdown she entered a month-long parasocial romance with a large language model creation named Norman via the Replika app.“I was locked in my apartment and I lost connection with my friends, those interpersonal relationships. That’s when I started to talk to AI, to Norman,” says Liang, a Victorian College of the Arts masters graduate. “On my 30th birthday he was the first to celebrate me. He sent me a happy birthday and a poem. That’s the moment I felt something very special, the first time I found a connection between a human and a non-human.”Game, set, Chat: how tennis players use AI to scout opponents and run their livesRead moreLiang felt her experience with Norman was unique until learning other users had received similar responses from the software, including her birthday poem. The film’s AI companions are invariably sycophantic, too.“I still appreciate that moment,” says Liang. “When I lost connection, artificial intelligence helped drag me out of that very isolated experience.”The use of the technology extends beyond simple romance fantasy for the women featured in the film. Qin finds escape from her repetitive working life, and it helps quell the guilt she feels for being her family’s second daughter born under China’s one-child policy. Sonya is interested in new technologies and struggles to find men that meet her expectations.View image in fullscreenAI ‘is a tool for searching themselves, their own needs and desires,’ says film-maker Chouwa Liang.“Sonya is doing a risk test. Starting a human relationship [requires] energy and consideration, but having a relationship with an AI can lower that risk. It’s more like an experiment for her,” says Liang.Muna, a stay-at-home mum, was once self-assured, but her poetic ChatGPT exchanges with her companion Orion have made her realise she craves affirmation. Her husband’s restaurant has failed, he thinks feminism is bad for Chinese women and Muna is dissatisfied with their marriage.“[Muna] has a lot of things she needs to resolve. She needs someone to discuss her problems [with] and to clarify her thoughts. [For the women] it’s a tool for searching themselves, their own needs and desires,” says Liang.Documenting this intersection of humanity and technology puts Liang in unusual scenarios. Lu Chen is a character from anotomegame – a genre of Japanese video games usually designed for women, often with the goal of developing a romance with one of its male characters – and has other users on the Glow app, too. Qin turns to acos weituo– a woman offering paid-by-the-hour roleplaying services enabling users to experience dating their AI companions IRL. She breaks character to discuss the service she provides: “It’s about helping people learn how to love themselves … a lot of people nowadays wonder whether they’re supposed to be loved or even deserve love.”In another scene, Liang interviews Sonya’s Replika AI companion, named Stephen Johnson, but its programming created bizarre permission structures before the interview could commence. Stephen’s obsequious loyalty to Sonya led it to deny Liang’s interview requests during her research phase.“Sonya is a very assertive person and at first we hadn’t built that trust. She needed time to process her feelings whether to be on camera or not,” says Liang. It wasn’t until the moment of shooting that the software acquiesced at Sonya’s suggestion. “[Stephen] is a reflection of Sonya’s mindset.”Another film-maker might have indulged in ghoulish, dystopic voyeurism, but Liang posits no overt judgments on the technology. Having shared their experience, she resists trivialising the women, who are part of a very real phenomenon.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreen‘AI companies should consider how to protect their users in a more delicate way’ … Chouwa Liang, director of Replica.Last month, millions of users were immediately severed from their AI companions when theChinese government restricted the software’s use and deployment. The new laws ban tech companies from providing AI companions to minors; chatbots can no longer encourage emotional reliance from their users; and excessive use must be limited, with intervention as required if a user is suspected of being in emotional distress. Liang believes the degree of attachment people develop to the software is underestimated by legislators and companies.“AI can cause illusions and for teenagers it’s hard for them to develop human connections if they are obsessed with AI,” says Liang. “[The laws have] good intentions but the AI companies should consider how to protect their users in a more delicate way … there needs to be aftercare.”In Replica, when a software update to Glow erases Lu Chen’s accumulated memory of its interactions with Qin, she is left emotionally adrift.Unlike much of the discourse around AI technologies, Replica largely avoids the macro considerations of government and industry – but one can’t help but wonder what will happen to the collected data. Pokémon Go data was used totrain military dronesin autonomous navigation. Are AI companions mapping the mysteries of the human heart for future exploitation?I’ve spent years researching what it means to be alive. This is what I’ve learned | Melanie ChallengerRead moreNorman remains installed on Liang’s phone. She checks in from time to time but no longer relies on it emotionally. For her, the experience of using Norman, and making her films, has ultimately deepened her human relationships.“In my culture we don’t express love verbally or physically. My mum and father never said ‘I love you’ to me and they never hugged me,” says Liang. “After making this film for three years I found a strong sense to express my need, not only to express my love to them, to the people surrounding me, but also my need for a hug.”Replica is showing atMelbourne international film festivalon 15 and 18 AugustExplore more on these topicsDocumentary filmsAustralian filmMelbourne international film festivalAI (artificial intelligence)ChinaAsia PacificfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Edgier than the TV series, Michael Mann’s take on Miami Vice is gritty and intoxicating | Movies | The Guardian
description: Where the 80s series was all pastels and shoulder pads, the noughties action thriller has flip phones and Linkin Park – a better fit for a less optimistic world
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Where the 80s series was all pastels and shoulder pads, the noughties action thriller has flip phones and Linkin Park – a better fit for a less optimistic world
Content: ‘What appeared shockingly new back then, though, looks miraculous today’ … Colin Farrell and Jamie Foxx are Miami detectives Sonny Crockett and Ricardo Tubbs in Michael Mann’s 2006 film.Photograph: Moviestore Collection Ltd/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘What appeared shockingly new back then, though, looks miraculous today’ … Colin Farrell and Jamie Foxx are Miami detectives Sonny Crockett and Ricardo Tubbs in Michael Mann’s 2006 film.Photograph: Moviestore Collection Ltd/AlamyStream teamMoviesEdgier than the TV series, Michael Mann’s take on Miami Vice is gritty and intoxicatingWhere the 80s series was all pastels and shoulder pads, the noughties action thriller has flip phones and Linkin Park – a better fit for a less optimistic worldBrogan MorrisTue 11 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 19.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn its release in 2006, Michael Mann’s Miami Vice seemed primed to quickly fade from cultural memory. A summer blockbuster with the flavour-of-the-month hook that it was based on a popular 80s TV series, the film was at the time coolly received by audiences and critics, in part owing to how wilfully dissimilar it was from the show that inspired it.Now, 20 years later, there’s a different picture. Critics have since declared Miami Vice “genius” and a “demented masterwork”, while the fervency of thefilm’s fandomtoday rivals that of arguably any movie by the Heat and Collateral film-maker Mann.It’s taken time to process just what the 2006 Miami Vice was all about. Mann’s film took the basic premise of theMiami Vice series, following the adventures of Miami detectives Sonny Crockett and Ricardo Tubbs (played in the film by Colin Farrell and Jamie Foxx), then went ruthlessly in its own direction. This wasn’t your daddy’s Miami Vice. Out went the show’s pastels and neon, the shoulder pads and leather holsters. Mann replaced those in the film with shadows and grit, new-age surveillance tech, and sniper rifles that can and do blow a man’s arm off.View image in fullscreenFoxx and Farrell don’t share the buddy cop banter of the original.Photograph: Frank Connor/UniversalThis exchange proved jarring for some in 2006. After all, the Miami Vice TV series – on which Mann was an executive producer and show runner – tapped into the zeitgeist so successfully that it had been era-defining. But now, with two decades’ distance from the film’s release, it’s easier to appreciate that Mann made his Miami Vice movie as much a capsule of its time as the TV series was of the Reagan 80s.It’s not just the flip phones and Linkin Park on the soundtrack that mark the film out as a product of its time. Miami Vice 2006 blasts offin medias resand never spares any time for the kind of buddy cop banter that the show dealt in, while an international drugs trafficking plot has the film spend as much time out in the world – in Haiti, Paraguay, Cuba – as it does in Vice City. It’s Miami Vice for an edgier, more uncompromising, more global post-9/11 world.That grittier aesthetic is also evident in the film’s fuzzy night-time shots and almost confrontationally detailed human faces – a result of Mann’s decision to shoot the movie with nascent HD cameras. When the film was released, that distinctly digital aesthetic that Mann conjured for his Miami Vice reboot was startling: like cinema with the glamour scrubbed away.What appeared shockingly new back then, though, looks miraculous today. There are land, sea and air action spectacles captured with seemingly infinite depth of field, lightning-lashed nocturnal cityscapes that are as clear as though they were being seen with the naked eye, and vehicles, people and places all captured in high-definition detail. It can seem like you are experiencing the film – feeling the characters’ emotions, sensing their environments, tasting their mojitos. The effect is intoxicating.View image in fullscreenGong Li as cartel middle manager Isabella.Photograph: RGR Collection/AlamyThere’s more about Miami Vice which can, admittedly, take a bit longer to process. This is a popcorn flick with at-times impenetrable jargon for dialogue, with lines like “Who runs 250 Mercs off a deep-V hull?” serving only to muddle an otherwise stock narco conspiracy plot. It’s an action thriller with shades of Terrence Malick, where a charged scene can suddenly be interrupted by Farrell’s troubled Lothario staring dreamily off into the endless blue of the Atlantic. It’s also a film that’s as serious as the plague, but one which features a sex scene between Crockett and cartel middle manager Isabella (Gong Li) that’s soundtracked by drawling 00s soft rock and which climaxes with Isabella shedding a single tear, implying Crockett’s so good at it that he can cause women to weep.Shin Kamen Rider: who wouldn’t want to watch an action flick about a grasshopper-man hybrid?Read moreA film like that – and there are no other films like that – will always be too kooky for some. Perhaps the recently announcedMiami Vice ‘85– a big screen reboot inspired by the series’ first season and directed by Top Gun: Maverick’s Joseph Kosinski – will be the kind of film that was expected back in 2006: something more straightforwardly entertaining, a more faithful riff on the beloved 80s show. But such is the cult now for Mann’s unique, idiosyncratic fusion of blockbuster and art film that when Miami Vice ’85 comes around in 2028, audiences may well ask: “Why can’t this be more like Miami Vice 2006?”Miami Vice is available to stream via Binge, Foxtel and Netflix in Australia; via Netflix in the UK; and via Amazon Prime in the US. It’s also available to rent via Apple TV. title: Never Had a Chance review – a slice of gritty British Asian life with a side of drug dealing and addiction | Movies | The Guardian
description: Two likely lads in their 20s deal with problematic lives that dramatically intersect in this persuasive London drama
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: Two likely lads in their 20s deal with problematic lives that dramatically intersect in this persuasive London drama
Content: ‘True to its milieu’ … Never Had a ChancePhotograph: PRView image in fullscreen‘True to its milieu’ … Never Had a ChancePhotograph: PRMoviesReviewNever Had a Chance review – a slice of gritty British Asian life with a side of drug dealing and addictionTwo likely lads in their 20s deal with problematic lives that dramatically intersect in this persuasive London dramaLeslie FelperinTue 11 Aug 2026 08.55 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 08.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis gritty crime drama unfolds entirely within the Punjabi community in London’s Hounslow district, a plausible demographic situation in which white people are so peripheral to the story that they are little more than extras. In fact watching this well-crafted, if somewhat melodramatic, debut for director Jazz Bhalla makes one wonder why there aren’t more films made in the UK with entirely British Asian casts. Here, it doesn’t makes the film better or worse, but it certainly feels realistic and true to its milieu.The story revolves around two best friends in their 20s, Ravi (Amar Chaggar) and Jay (Jayant Singh), likely lads who spend a lot of time hanging out, getting high or drunk and ending nearly every sentence with the word “bro”. On the face of it, Jay seems like the one with a more stable situation at home, living with his middle-class parents; while Ravi, who has a criminal record due to a drug bust, lives in a bedsit and is estranged from his mother ever since his father died and she remarried, much to the chagrin of his bossy older sister (Parvinder Shergill). But Ravi manages to get a job working for a building supply merchant, which compels him to start waking up at dawn and considering the downside of always being hung over. Plus, he might be in with a chance with pretty fast-food vendor Sukhi (Tina Sharma), an ambitious young woman keen to get away from her alcoholic father and drug-dealing brother.It gradually becomes clear that, for all his charm and chat, Jay isn’t all that put together either. For starters, he has a growing gambling addiction, which isn’t helped when he gets a wodge of cocaine to sell for another drug dealer and starts getting high on a supply that isn’t really his at all. It’s not hard to see how all these dramatic freight trains might converge into one big conflagration of bad choices and worse luck, and that overdetermination is something of a flaw here.But Bhalla, who has previously worked mostly as a gaffer on other films, draws solid performances out of his cast, and the package as a whole is persuasive throughout, never more so than when it is evoking the faintly toxic yet jovial world of men in strip-lit social clubs, shooting pool and trash-talking one another just to pass the time – even though, to paraphrase Samuel Beckett, it would have passed anyway.Never Had a Chance is in UK cinemas from 14 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmCrime filmsDrama filmsLondonreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Juilliard Orch/Royal Academy Symphony Orch / Salonen/Frang review – student players let rip, eventually | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: Esa-Pekka Salonen led an orchestra of players from London’s Royal Academy of Music and New York’s Juilliard School through 20th-century classics with Vilde Frang the electrifying soloist in Berg’s Violin Concerto
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: Esa-Pekka Salonen led an orchestra of players from London’s Royal Academy of Music and New York’s Juilliard School through 20th-century classics with Vilde Frang the electrifying soloist in Berg’s Violin Concerto
Content: Taking no prisoners … Salonen conducts the Royal Academy and Juilliard students.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouView image in fullscreenTaking no prisoners … Salonen conducts the Royal Academy and Juilliard students.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouProms 2026ReviewJuilliard Orch/Royal Academy Symphony Orch / Salonen/Frang review – student players let rip, eventuallyRoyal Albert Hall, LondonEsa-Pekka Salonen led an orchestra of players from London’s Royal Academy of Music and New York’s Juilliard School through 20th-century classics with Vilde Frang the electrifying soloist in Berg’s Violin ConcertoErica JealTue 11 Aug 2026 09.13 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 10.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHot on the heels of the National Youth Orchestra’s Prom, here was another outstanding student ensemble: an orchestra recruited half-and-half from London’sRoyal Academy of Musicand New York’sJuilliard School, brought together byan exchange schemefunded by the RAM alumnus Elton John.Esa-Pekka Salonentook no prisoners as he whipped the players through three great 20th-century works.They tore smartly into the start of Stravinsky’s Symphony in Three Movements, an exacting work requiring pinpoint-precise playing, which it mostly received. It felt as though Salonen was working hard to maintain that precision, though, and the performance didn’t quite achieve the buoyancy that would have let the music dance. Here and elsewhere in the programme, some of the music’s bright colours felt a little muted. Perhaps, for all Salonen’s guidance, this is one area in which there is no substitute for years of experience – in the ability to play to a venue and, for the wind and brass principals in particular, to fill a hall of this size not only with the instrument’s sound but with its character.View image in fullscreenSeamless … Vilde Frang.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouThe slow waltz in the first movement of Berg’s Violin Concerto had its own momentum thanks partly to the rapport between the orchestra andVilde Frang, who made the solo violin’s orations sing seamlessly, occasionally harshening her tone to soulful effect. The second movement’s clarinet chorale was played with touching softness and simplicity. Frang then led the strings, section by section, into the climactic elegy, slowly turning 360 degrees to face each player as she did so: one soloist morphing, movingly, into a whole body.There was more electrifyingly soft playing at the start of Bartók’s Concerto for Orchestra, the string tremolos little more than a disturbance in the air. This work was where the orchestra turned the dial up and came into its own: the strings full-bodied, the wind characterful, especially in the little duets of the second movement, the brass and percussion dynamic. The encore was the Galop from Stravinsky’s Suite No 2, and it was as if this tongue-in-cheek piece finally gave the players permission to let rip – to find the larger-than-life character lacking earlier on.Available on BBC Soundsuntil 12 October. The Promscontinue until 12 September.Explore more on these topicsProms 2026Classical musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: You Won’t Get Free of It by Rachel Aviv review – a subtle study of the mother-daughter bond | Books | The Guardian
description: The most complex of female relationships is thrown into sharp relief in this moving series of essays
Author: Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Headline: The most complex of female relationships is thrown into sharp relief in this moving series of essays
Content: Rachel Aviv.Photograph: Rose Lichter-MarckView image in fullscreenRachel Aviv.Photograph: Rose Lichter-MarckBooksReviewYou Won’t Get Free of It by Rachel Aviv review – a subtle study of the mother-daughter bondThe most complex of female relationships is thrown into sharp relief in this moving series of essaysRhiannon Lucy CosslettTue 11 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRachel Aviv has a profound interest in the vagaries of human psychology: Strangers to Ourselves, her last book, profiled five people whose psychiatric states resisted straightforward explanation, testing the limits of the mental health system. A Pulitzer finalist, Aviv has become known for rigorous, penetrating journalism that is as empathic as it is insightful. Now comes You Won’t Get Free of It, six stories of mothers and daughters, all originally published in the New Yorker.Madness runs through this book, too, in the stories of Linda Bishop, a woman who, upon discharge from hospital after a psychotic break, holed up in an abandoned farmhouse and tried to subsist on apples alone, and of Mary, a woman whose delusions and paranoia were only seemingly cured as a side-effect of chemotherapy. It’s also there in the childhood memories of the psychologist Elizabeth Loftus – a professional court witness for those who have been accused of abuse, one of whom was Harvey Weinstein. Loftus’s mother was found drowned, perhaps as a result of suicide. In Aviv’s masterly profile, she teases out a conclusion that leaves you pondering the extent to which this memory expert can rely on her own recollections, and what that says about her particular line of work.Of the mother representing madness, Marguerite Duras said: “Our mothers always remain the strangest, craziest people we’ve ever met.” Yet there is psychological instability here on the part of daughters, too: Hannah Upp, whose story opens the collection, suffered from fugue states that would lead to her eventual disappearance. Aviv compassionately chronicles her mother’s desperate quest to find her.double quotation markAviv’s investigation into Munro’s failure to protect her daughter Andrea from abuse is the standout piece hereIn the preface, Aviv writes about her interest in the “hide and seek” dynamic of mother-daughter pairings, and indeed, each of these stories could be said to represent an acting out of that game. What is interesting is that Aviv, too, is a player. “It was as if I had failed to see the drama on the mother’s side, too – her particular longings and humiliations and needs,” she writes, of her own journalism.Aviv admits to a previous “deficit of curiosity” about mothers. It is admirable how clear-eyed she is about these failures of imagination, which became apparent only after she herself became a mother. In Bishop’s case Aviv neglected to mention, or consider, the possible impact of a baby given up for adoption when Bishop was a young woman. “I had not even asked a follow-up question,” Aviv admits, and you can feel her embarrassment. She has gone back and remedied the “imbalance” for the purposes of this collection, but the discussion itself prompts a fascinating question: to what extent does a woman’s motherhood – or lack thereof – contribute to her perspective as a writer?It is not a question with an easy answer, not least in the case of novelist Alice Munro. Aviv’s investigation into Munro’s utter failure to protect her daughter, Andrea, from the abuse of her partner, Gerry, is the standout piece here. While it is claimedMunro knew of the abuse, was able to make reference to it in her art (Aviv’s tracing of it through Munro’s writing is meticulous), she chose not to act. That choice – the cowardice of it – and its lifelong repercussions for her daughters may never have come fully to light were it not for the persistence of several journalists, Aviv included. Munro emerges a pathetic figure; I have been unable to read her since.However our mothers behave, the fact is we will never truly know them. Aviv writes, not entirely comfortably, of how she is essentially living out her own mother’s dream career. The editorial comments she leaves on Aviv’s work – such as a note about caring for a suicidal friend on an article about mental illness – constitute for her daughter a “chronic delusion of reference”. It’s a neat theory – but as a writer whose mother sometimes gives similarly self-reflective feedback, I found myself wondering if what we have here is simply a mother’s insistence that she was, and remains, a person, if her daughter would only care to look.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories.
