title: Virtue and a Sledgehammer – take a literal hammer to your past | Games | The Guardian
description: What do you do when you return to your home town, with your dead mother in your car boot, to find the inhabitants have been turned into robots?
Author: Malindy Hetfeld
Headline: What do you do when you return to your home town, with your dead mother in your car boot, to find the inhabitants have been turned into robots?
Content: Taking ‘20 pounds of physical media’ to her town … Virtue and a Sledgehammer.Photograph: Devolver DigitalView image in fullscreenTaking ‘20 pounds of physical media’ to her town … Virtue and a Sledgehammer.Photograph: Devolver DigitalSummer games previewsGamesVirtue and a Sledgehammer – take a literal hammer to your pastWhat do you do when you return to your home town, with your dead mother in your car boot, to find the inhabitants have been turned into robots?Malindy HetfeldTue 11 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the boot of her car, Pratelle carries the corpse of her mother and a giant sledgehammer. Her mission is simple: take the hammer to her home town. As you enter shops and homes through the door and leave them through the opposite wall, it becomes clear that the robots who either attack you or flee are all digital versions of your old neighbours.Pratelle, with her close-cropped hair and dungarees, read to me as a queer woman, but interestingly, testers of the game often mistook her as a man. The team at developer Deconstructeam and longtime collaborator Selkie Harbour didn’t anticipate this confusion but found it fits the character perfectly, especially in this setting based on a small Spanish town like those in which the developers grew up.“These towns are culturally living a couple of decades behind, especially regarding subjects such as queerness,” says game director, writer and Deconstructeam CEO Jordi de Paco. “Maybe these communities aren’t ready to acknowledge that they have other identities within them – and Pratelle is exactly that. She is someone who doesn’t fit the community, but her very existence makes the community ask questions about identity, even if it’s through confusion and anger.”View image in fullscreenDigital versions of your old neighbours … Virtue and a Sledgehammer.Photograph: Devolver DigitalMany of the robot villagers react to Pratelle with vitriol, but some flee or beg for their lives, which feels harrowing despite their identical bodies. The villagers remember what it was like to have a body, a plot point the full game will explore in detail.The most important part, however, is Pratelle’s story, which you uncover by hitting glass statues around town that contain fragments of memory. It seems as if Pratelle’s own sister turned everyone into robots, which is one of the reasons she rebels with what she calls “20 pounds of physical media”. But Virtue isn’t meant to be read as a critique of our increasingly digitised lives. Instead De Paco created a family story of a “sometimes embarrassing teenager” to contrast with the otherwise futuristic themes of the game.“Back in 2024 we designed a prototype with a pretty stereotypical story about transhumanism,” he says. “We had some friends play it and got the feedback that the themes were stale, so we decided to use the setting as more of a metaphor and came up with the feeling of not belonging. Suddenly the aesthetics and themes felt really powerful in contrast with the destruction of buildings and facing robots.”A game about straightforward destruction seems to fit oddly with Deconstructeam’s prior body of work, such as the thought-provoking narrative experiences The Red Strings Club and Many Nights a Whisper. “We’re constantly joking about this being our first actual game because you’re not making a proper game unless you destroy something,” laughs De Paco, who even tried to take a sledgehammer to a real ruin for research.“In Virtue, you’re being made to destroy the place you grew up in. Despite the combat, the game is a narrative experience. It’s not meant to be challenging; it’s more of an aesthetic choice. We think of Virtue like a walking simulator: you go through a space and solve the narrative, and the game isn’t designed around combat. We want everyone who plays this game to reach the end.”Virtue and a Sledgehammer is in development forPC. Release is planned for later in 2026Explore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsPCfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ten Ways to Die Happy review – gameshow invites you to don a robe and treasure time | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Audience members are invited to examine what they will do with their lives in this earnest shared thought experiment
Author: Kate Wyver
Headline: Audience members are invited to examine what they will do with their lives in this earnest shared thought experiment
Content: Even if you are one of the chosen ones, the show’s pace remains fairly sedentary … Ten Ways to Die Happy.Photograph: Sisifo ProductionView image in fullscreenEven if you are one of the chosen ones, the show’s pace remains fairly sedentary … Ten Ways to Die Happy.Photograph: Sisifo ProductionEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewTen Ways to Die Happy review – gameshow invites you to don a robe and treasure timeUnderbelly, Bristo Square, EdinburghAudience members are invited to examine what they will do with their lives in this earnest shared thought experimentKate WyverTue 11 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 15.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you could hold the years of your life in your hands like coins, would you choose to spend them differently? This is the thoughtful, earnest tone of Ten Ways to Die Happy, an existential but somewhat formulaic Italian production (performed here in English) created by Emanuele Aldrovandi and Jacopo Giacomoni. In this gentle gameshow, we are asked not just to consider how we would use the finite time we have, but to put this thought experiment into practice.Eight people are plucked at random from the audience. My number is called, so I don a white robe, choose a new name for my new life, and take a seat on stage. Perla Ambrosini is our ethereal host, standing in fabric armour in a shallow pool of water. Each of us has a tray of flowers that we throw into the pool, every plastic bud representing the “energy” available to invest in work, art and family. Once our supply is up, we’re dead.Ambrosini efficiently guides us across the years, Dungeon Master-like, through fumbling sex, consuming grief and boring jobs. Over the course of our lives, we control little counters to mark our levels of happiness. “The aim of the game,” Ambrosini tells us, “is to die happy.”Spin Cycle review – romcom hits full speed as couple air their dirty laundryRead moreThere’s no doubt the show induces more of an elevated heart-rate if you’re on the top table – though there are opportunities for broader audience participation. But even if you are one of the chosen ones, the show’s pace remains fairly sedentary.Some of the interaction is cringe, and while there’s never a sense that you’ll say something wrong, neither is there ever a truly difficult dilemma, nor a decision that feels more poignant than if you were casually playing the board game Catan. While the performance is conducted with an intense sense of ceremony, the drama of the actual game would be improved by greater stakes. But in its blunt reflections and visual confrontations, Ten Ways to Die Happy is a welcome reminder that we should all make the most of the time we have.AtUnderbelly, Bristo Square, Edinburgh, until 31 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalFestivalsTheatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Game of Thrones, Shakespearean? What fools these mortals be!  | Theatre | The Guardian
description: The Mad King may bring more dynastic disputes and dotty despots to the RSC – but a ‘mayhap’ or a riddling aphorism does not a Shakespeare play make
Author: Michael Billington
Headline: The Mad King may bring more dynastic disputes and dotty despots to the RSC – but a ‘mayhap’ or a riddling aphorism does not a Shakespeare play make
Content: Endless jousters … Game of Thrones: The Mad King.Photograph: Johan PerssonView image in fullscreenEndless jousters … Game of Thrones: The Mad King.Photograph: Johan PerssonTheatreGame of Thrones, Shakespearean? What fools these mortals be!Michael BillingtonThe Mad King may bring more dynastic disputes and dotty despots to the RSC – but a ‘mayhap’ or a riddling aphorism does not a Shakespeare play makeTue 11 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTShareAs a latecomer toGame of Thrones, I am struck by how many people tell me it is “very Shakespearean”. It is as if they need to justify its heady escapism and heavy reliance on bonking and brutality. But its debt to the Bard – apart from the rivalry between the houses of Lannister and Stark – rests mainly on the casting. Watching the first 11 episodes, I noticed four Lears past and to come (Julian Glover, David Bradley, Oliver Ford-Davies and Roger Allam), a Macbeth (Sean Bean), a Hamlet and Henry V (Iain Glen) and a Cassius (Michelle Fairley) among many others.Because it is presented by the Royal Shakespeare Company and staged by Dominic Cooke, who memorably directedThe Hollow Crownon television, we shall doubtless hear the same arguments aboutGame of Thrones: The Mad Kingat Stratford. But, although there are frequent nods to Shakespeare, they totally lack the resonance of the original. Our first sight of Michael Shaeffer’s King Aerys with a white beard, a leafy crown and no shoes almost screams “Lear on the heath”. But where Lear gradually declines into insanity (“O fool I shall go mad”) and comes out the other side, Shaeffer’s Aerys is a dotty despot from start to finish. The use of tournaments to settle dynastic disputes also reminds us of the opening of Richard II – but where that event is aborted and ultimately causes the king’s downfall, here the image of embattled jousters is endlessly repeated.View image in fullscreen‘How many crows may nest in a grocer’s jerkin?’ … Harmony Rose-Bremner as Lyanna Stark and Michael Abubakar as Eddard Stark in Game of Thrones: The Mad King.Photograph: Johan PerssonBut there are two other reasons why the use of tropes from the Stratford playwright doesn’t make a play Shakespearean. The most obvious is the language. Where Shakespeare allows even minor characters unforgettable verse (the first murderer’s “the west yet glimmers with some streaks of day” in Macbeth) or plangent prose (the second carrier’s “peas and beans are as dank here as a dog” in Henry IV Part I), Duncan Macmillan’s dialogue rarely glistens. There is a heavy dependence on riddling aphorisms (“Every step we take from our destiny leads us towards it”) and repeated archaisms (such as “mayhap” for “perhaps”) that put me in mind of Max Beerbohm’s magnificent parody of a historical drama, Savonarola Brown, where Lucrezia asks: “How many crows may nest in a grocer’s jerkin?”The other aspect of Shakespeare’s genius, signally missing here, is the ability to enliven dynastic conflict with social detail and to traverse the nation. Even in an early Marlovian play such as Henry VI Part Two, there is a wonderful scene where the seemingly sightless Simpcox is exposed as a faker. By the time we get to a masterpiece like the two parts of Henry IV, Shakespeare takes us from the council chamber and the battlefield into the Eastcheap taprooms and the Cotswold countryside. But in the nearly four hours of Stratford’s Games of Thrones, we get little sense of the impact of the struggle for power on the commonwealth. This is a story of feuding families and warring tribes with scant acknowledgment of its impact on the people who are simply battle-fodder.‘Can’t stop smiling!’ The wait is over for epic Game of Thrones prequel The Mad KingRead moreBut there is a larger point. While marginalising Shakespeare, the RSC seems fixated on fiction. After this play, inspired by the novels of George RR Martin, the company offers adaptations ofGeorge EliotandAlexandre Dumas. Yet there is a great historical novelist with genuine echoes of Shakespeare hiding in plain sight: Walter Scott. I know he is unfashionable but I have read most of theWaverley novelsand been astonished by their narrative vigour and richness of character. Jonathan Bate in The Genius of Shakespeare, while quoting the endorsement of the novelist’s greatness by a Marxist critic, makes the case for Scott’s indebtedness to the man from Stratford far better than I could and I would urge the RSC’s directors to read it.Of course, they could do something even more radical than ransack the library shelves for work that is supposedly “Shakespearean”. They could stage more of the plays that Shakespeare actually wrote – but that might be a step too far.Game of Thrones: The Mad King is at theRoyal Shakespeare theatre, Stratford-upon-Avon, until 5 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreRoyal Shakespeare CompanyGame of ThronesGeorge RR MartinWilliam ShakespeareDuncan MacmillanDominic CookecommentShareReuse this content

title: Spin Cycle review – romcom hits full speed as couple air their dirty laundry | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: There is crackling chemistry between Zofia Zerphy and Rhiannon Bell while their washing gets done but this play remains a puzzle
Author: Kate Wyver
Headline: There is crackling chemistry between Zofia Zerphy and Rhiannon Bell while their washing gets done but this play remains a puzzle
Content: ‘How will you use your 50 minutes?’ … Zofia Zerphy, left, and Rhiannon Bell.Photograph: Sofia Salazar StuderView image in fullscreen‘How will you use your 50 minutes?’ … Zofia Zerphy, left, and Rhiannon Bell.Photograph: Sofia Salazar StuderEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewSpin Cycle review – romcom hits full speed as couple air their dirty laundryUnderbelly Bristo Square, EdinburghThere is crackling chemistry between Zofia Zerphy and Rhiannon Bell while their washing gets done but this play remains a puzzleKate WyverTue 11 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 14.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNames go missing like lost socks in this laundry-based, amnesia-laced romcom. With crackling chemistry but a holey structure, Zofia Zerphy’s Offie award-winning story of a queer meet-cute asks what you hold on to once a relationship is over, and whether it’s ever better to forget the mistakes you both made.In the liminal space of a launderette, with their encounter framed by a washing machine’s 50-minute timer, Kitt (Zerphy) and Noel (Rhiannon Bell) talk over each other at full speed. “How will you use your 50 minutes?” Kitt asks. Their connection is easy and instant as they use them to bicker and flirt, discussing art, exes and the correct laundry tabs to use. Kitt is the rich, confident American, more privileged than Noel, the messy, Northern Irish, non-binary stranger. Except they don’t feel like strangers. With Bethan Rose’s direction making the most of the small stage, the pair lean close over the whirring machines, unpacking the ways they’ve been shaped by past relationships, and admitting they’ve both dated someone very like the other. In fact, they could swear they’ve met before.Roleplay review – Fleabag producer scores again with one woman’s life as a ‘slutfluencer’Read moreAs memories are tumbled up, this breezy romcom devolves into an airing of dirty laundry. Occasionally slipping into shouting matches, the story sings when they admit their feelings slowly, almost side-on, like Noel inspecting Kitt as if she’s one of their sculptures, tracing a tingling line from wrist to shoulder on her skin.The memory-loss set-up creates a thrilling puzzle, but it’s never pieced together. No explanation is given for the selective memories that build the story, so we have no idea why one remembers something when the other doesn’t, or what prompts that memory to fade. Without this structural scaffolding, the mystery loses its momentum. The attraction between Kitt and Noel is evident. We just need to understand the rules of their memory-muddled world to feel our 50 minutes is well spent.AtUnderbelly, Bristo Square, Edinburgh, until 31 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalFestivalsTheatreComedy (Stage)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Harriet Dyer: Easily Distra … review – how to sell a single shoe on eBay and other stories | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: A comic on the verge of the big time offers one ‘very silly hour’ around the highways and byways of her madcap life
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: A comic on the verge of the big time offers one ‘very silly hour’ around the highways and byways of her madcap life
Content: Semaphores punchlines with windmilling physicality … Harriet Dyer.Photograph: Matt StrongeView image in fullscreenSemaphores punchlines with windmilling physicality … Harriet Dyer.Photograph: Matt StrongeEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewHarriet Dyer: Easily Distra … review – how to sell a single shoe on eBay and other storiesMonkey Barrel, EdinburghA comic on the verge of the big time offers a ‘very silly hour’ around the highways and byways of her lifeBrian LoganTue 11 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 10.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAformer winner of the Sean Lock awardfor comic originality, Harriet Dyer richly delivers on that promise of oddity in her latest show, Easily Distra … As its title suggests, you can shelve any expectation of coherence or narrative consistency here: it’s 55 minutes of switch-backing reminiscence, as Dyer meanders across the landscape of her peripatetic life. From Cornwall to Birmingham to Bristol, our scatty host moves and moves on, and yet eccentric incident follows her everywhere. The real-world Harriet may justifiably be nonplussed by this (in quite the backhanded compliment, an old school friend tells her she’s not changed at all since she was four years old) – but no doubt it’s a gift to her comedy.Not that her comedy needs gifts: an increasingly familiar TV face, she’s teetering on the verge of the big time. But here in a cave in Edinburgh, it’s hard to imagine a more marginal figure, a tattooed West Country screwball rummaging her props bag for DIY comedy accoutrements, semaphoring punchlines with a windmilling physicality and oral SFX. Previous fringe shows, including 2022’s acclaimedTrigger Warning, have addressed more significant subject matter, but this one is “a very silly hour indeed”, in her own estimation, as our host fantasises about growing feathers, accidentally sells a single shoe on eBay and memorialises the occasion when a seagull filched her beekeeping brother’s bratwurst.Cathy review – snappy comedy with a perfect role for Elaine C SmithRead moreThere’s material that contains within it the germ of several fringe shows, like the routine about her closeted gay dad, or another about her teenage enthusiasm for alcohol. While mental health is not the emphasis here of a performer whoopenly engages with that subject elsewhere, there are plenty of jokes whose battiness only barely conceals something more troubling – like the one about breaking her own arm to escape a dead-end job. Yikes. But quirky is persistently the top-note in Easily Distra …, and Dyer keeps things upbeat with consistently strong gags (see the one about the roundabout, or the “al dente” variety of traffic accident) and arresting anecdotes. It adds up to nothing more, nor less, than a divertingly dotty autobiographical standup hour.AtMonkey Barrel, Edinburgh,until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Edinburgh festivalFestivalsComedy (Culture)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Feel the burn: why holidays from hell make for blistering fiction | Books | The Guardian
description: Family fallouts, failing marriages, sunburn, food poisoning ... from Deborah Levy’s hypnotic and disturbing Hot Milk to All In, Claire Powell’s all-inclusive nightmare, Leon Craig looks at the best novels about vile vacations
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Family fallouts, failing marriages, sunburn, food poisoning ... from Deborah Levy’s hypnotic and disturbing Hot Milk to All In, Claire Powell’s all-inclusive nightmare, Leon Craig looks at the best novels about vile vacations
Content: High-end holiday hell … TV series The White Lotus.Photograph: HBO/Home Box Office, Inc.View image in fullscreenHigh-end holiday hell … TV series The White Lotus.Photograph: HBO/Home Box Office, Inc.BooksFeel the burn: why holidays from hell make for blistering fictionFamily fallouts, failing marriages, sunburn, food poisoning ... from Deborah Levy’s hypnotic and disturbing Hot Milk to All In, Claire Powell’s all-inclusive nightmare, Leon Craig looks at the best novels about vile vacationsLeon CraigTue 11 Aug 2026 09.24 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 09.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvery summer, we long for a much-needed break from daily life, dreaming of self-reinvention in some distant paradise. But really, holidays can be absolute hell. Instead of relaxation we encounter heaving crowds, lumpy beds, the caprices of our loved ones and the grim truth that we can escape neither their worst failings nor our own, however far we travel.Small wonder, then, that the disaster holiday has become a booming subgenre in fiction. For most of us, the levels of luxury promised by hit TV seriesThe White Lotusare pure fantasy, yet we’re all vulnerable to the expensive promises we’ve been sold. Two of the smartest offerings in fiction this summer come from Claire Powell’s All In and Chloë Ashby’s Family Friends. In the former, a struggling couple whose marriage is on the rocks go on an all-inclusive Spanish weekend break, paid for by a rich brother. Poignant and extremely funny, the frictions that ensue are all too believable.So, too, is the implosion of Ashby’s group of friends who have a decades-long custom of holidaying together in the south of France. This year, however, their marriages are threatened by one husband’s deceit, the lingering attraction between old friends and the arrival of a vivacious teenage stepdaughter. Poised and gripping, it uses a sweltering Mediterranean setting to amp up tensions to dramatic effect.In Sabine Durrant’s superb thriller Dead Heat, meanwhile, a failed journalist, his more successful media friend and a former school contemporary, now a Gatsbyesque billionaire, find their Greek adventure transformed not only into a shameful reminder of racism in their shared past, but something outright murderous. Being thrown together to brave blazing summer heat only intensifies existing tensions as Durrant expertly brings the drama to a head.Many characters seeking escape find that a change of scene only makes problems worse. Deborah Levy’sHot Milk, adapted as a film last year by Rebecca Lenkiewicz, chronicles a family unravelling in a Spanish fishing village. Rose pays thousands to a clinic to cure her mysterious paralysis while Sofia distracts herself with local beauty, Ingrid, as unresolved conflicts between mother and daughter start to boil over.A fateful holiday also inspires the scathing, semi-autobiographical play in Jo Hamya’s novelThe Hypocrite. Sophia is taken out of school to act as her novelist father’s amanuensis, though he spends much of his time in Sicily seducing local women instead of bonding with his daughter. Years later, he is appalled to see that Sophia has adapted his parenting failures for the stage, though the novel cleverly hints at aspects of her own behaviour on that holiday which Sophia may have conveniently chosen to forget.The fancier the surroundings, the worse a fictional holiday is likely to be. In William Rayfet Hunter’sSunstruck, an invitation to his university friend Lily’s parents’ chateau is the catalyst for unwelcome epiphanies about the class and race differences between the narrator and Lily’s family, even as he becomes involved with her wayward brother. Lucy Foley’sThe Midnight Feastalso plays with this trope to great effect, when the opening weekend of a high-end wellness retreat in the West Country is disrupted by revelations from a guest’s disastrous stay many years before.Our attempts to get away from it all can often lead us right back to what we left home to avoid. In Deepa Anappara’s ambitious, multilayeredThe Last of Earth, Victorian adventurer Katherine hopes her journey into the forbidden kingdom of Tibet will help her overcome difficult feelings about her heritage. Unfortunately, disguising herself as a male pilgrim to cross dangerous unknown terrain only serves to underline Katherine’s alienation as she attempts to become the first European woman to reach Lhasa.View image in fullscreenPainful self-awareness … Olivia Colman (Leda) in the film adaptation of Elena Ferrante’s The Lost Daughter.Photograph: Yannis Drakoulidis/NETFLIX © 2021.In an unfamiliar setting, relaxed and away from our usual points of reference, we are more vulnerable to danger. Patricia Highsmith’s classic The Talented Mr Ripley posits the holiday abroad as a perfect space for murder and identity theft. In Sean Gilbert’sI’ll Be the Monster, a murderous husband and wife encounter an old university acquaintance while on a trip to Istanbul to revive their marriage. This unsettling novel disorients us by asking who is really the predator, and who is the prey.The self-discovery that travel can bring is not always benign. Thirty years ago, Alex Garland’s cult bestseller The Beach lured in the reader with the promise of a mysterious idyll on a remote Thai island. However, the narrator’s true awakening is to how easily manipulated he and most of the other would-be lotus eaters really are. Painful self-awareness don’t come to a stop with parenthood, either. In Elena Ferrante’s The Lost Daughter, Leda allows a new acquaintance, downwardly mobile young mother Nina, to use her beach cottage for an illicit rendezvous. Even as Leda hypocritically judges Nina for struggling in the way that she once did, she is forced to come to terms with her own temporary abandonment of her daughters.At once longed-for and disruptive, any break from place or routine can be double-edged. In my own debut novel, The Decadence, a group of former university friends break lockdown to holiday in a remote Devon country house during the pandemic. Too quarrelsome and intoxicated to notice that the house is in fact haunted, they do not realise they must band together against the danger until it is almost too late.Despite all these fearsome warnings, venturing far from home can still bring vital insights. In EM Forster’s A Room With a View, Lucy Honeychurch scandalises her chaperone with the realisation that she must break off her engagement after being impulsively kissed by George Emerson in a field above Florence. David Nicholls’ bestsellingYou Are Herebrings together lonely divorcees Marnie and Michael for a rainy hike across the Lake District, with love growing unexpectedly as they emerge from their self-protective shells.We don’t always get exactly what we want from our holidays, but the adventure is in breaking away from the familiar. Even our most unpleasant travel experiences can be revelatory, and the best can transform us into new versions of ourselves, especially once they are safely behind us.The Decadence by Leon Craig is out in paperback on 6 AugustExplore more on these topicsBooksFictionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Fancy a Nobbly Bobbly? Or a Jelly Terror? The eye-popping guide to the greatest ice lolly wrappers ever | Design | The Guardian
description: From Fonzie to Elvis to the Daleks, from a Mini Milk to a Seaside Saucy to a Freak Out, incredibly rare vintage ice lolly wrappers have now been memorialised in a 96-page, nostalgia-inducing delight
Author: Daniel Dylan Wray
Headline: From Fonzie to Elvis to the Daleks, from a Mini Milk to a Seaside Saucy to a Freak Out, incredibly rare vintage ice lolly wrappers have now been memorialised in a 96-page, nostalgia-inducing delight
Content: Three greats … Happy Days, Rock Around the Choc and Zoom.Photograph: Trunk RecordsView image in fullscreenThree greats … Happy Days, Rock Around the Choc and Zoom.Photograph: Trunk RecordsDesignFancy a Nobbly Bobbly? Or a Jelly Terror? The eye-popping guide to the greatest ice lolly wrappers everFrom Fonzie to Elvis to the Daleks, from a Mini Milk to a Seaside Saucy to a Freak Out, incredibly rare vintage ice lolly wrappers have now been memorialised in a 96-page, nostalgia-inducing delightDaniel Dylan WrayTue 11 Aug 2026 04.52 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 08.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSeven years ago, Jonny Trunk entered the house of a hoarder in Stockport that was bursting at the seams with a goldmine of British ephemera from the last half century. “You couldn’t get into the house,” recalls Trunk, who is an avid pop culture collector, as well as a writer, DJ, broadcaster and record-label owner. “It was full of all this stuff he had collected indiscriminately.”Growing up in an orphanage in Surrey, John Townsend began collecting milk bottle tops and by the 1950s had amassed a huge collection of cigarette and tobacco cards. He then simply continued at full speed. “He never stopped collecting ephemera,” says Trunk. “If it was a printed piece of paper with something on it, he’d have it.” Townsend died in 2016, leaving every inch of his five-bedroom house, as well as the caravan and summerhouse, bursting with fizzy drinks cans, sweet wrappers, crisp packets, cereal boxes, flyers, cigarette cards and countless other items.View image in fullscreenLyons Maid Red Devil, Star Wars, Freak Out.Photograph: Trunk RecordsTrunk was given access to the collection – some of which featured in his 2020 book, Wrappers Delight – and he has now focused on one particular area from this vast haul for a new book: Fancy an Ice Cream? A Collection of Vintage Ice Lolly Wrappers. He bolstered this with his own personal collection. When Trunk posted some on Instagram in May, the rush of responses suggested there was a book in this. When he then announced one, film director Edgar Wright declared: “This is my dream book!”Over 96 pages, it’s an eye-popping collection of nostalgia-inducing icy delights from roughly 1970-80. There are familiar names such as Feast, Fab, Mini Milk, Nobbly Bobbly, Cider Lollies and Lemonade Sparkle, alongside long-forgotten designs that were specific to the era, featuring everything from Kevin Keegan football lollies to Star Wars, Dr Who’s Daleks and Fonzie from Happy Days. “Read about my fight against evil on the back of this pack,” reads one cartoon strip for Captain Rainbow’s lemonade and strawberry or banana lolly, complete with a chocolate dip base. One rock’n’roll themed ice lolly bears a wonky image of Elvis and features an Elton John trivia game on the wrapper.View image in fullscreenFizz Bang, Lord Toffingham, Cider Barrel and more.Photograph: Trunk RecordsThey clearly resonate with people. Trunk, who is 60, also sells prints, of everything from Lord Toffingham toffee ice creams to Lolly Gobble Choc Bomb, and gets requests from as far away as Las Vegas. “Some people now look at them from a design point of view,” he says, “because you’re seeing weird colours that don’t normally come together. And you see graphic styles that are now a bit lost. But it’s probably 75% nostalgia.”Trunk reckons it taps into a very particular period of childhood for a certain generation. “The peak period for these is around 1972-75,” he says. “That’s when a lot of those classics originated. And it was a grim time, wasn’t it? But summer in England was always a brilliant time and these wrappers are symbolic of that joy. They reflect that throwaway happiness of getting an ice-cream. Because when I was growing up, it was a real treat. We were lucky if we got one. I used to have to beg for 5p to get a Fizz Bang.”Trunk says it’s something of a miracle that a book like this could even exist, since 1970s ice lolly wrappers are far from durable. “They’re wax paper,” he explains. “And the other thing you’re dealing with, which makes them even more fragile, is they’re wet. So you’ve got wet paper. It’s also something you tear off, so they usually get destroyed.” All of which makes this collection a real one-off. “This stuff is so unbelievably, stupidly rare,” he says. “You’ve got no idea how rare an ice lolly wrapper from 1974 is. It’s ridiculous. Also, a lot of these only came out for a single season.”View image in fullscreenJelly Terror, Goal and Score ice lolly wrappers.Photograph: Trunk RecordsWithin a niche community, wrappers can exchange hands for £30 to £150 each. However, there is one that has eluded him and he’s now in a perpetual hunt for it: Walls’ Midnight Mint – a brown choc ice wrapper with an owl on it. “I’ve never seen one of those in however many years of collecting this stuff,” he says. “That would be the Holy Grail.”View image in fullscreenA Superman ice lolly wrapper.Photograph: Trunk RecordsGiven the scarcity of these wrappers and the lack of information about them, tracing down their designers is a problem. “It’s impossible,” says Trunk. “Unless someone comes out of the woodwork after this book and goes, ‘Oh, my mum did the drawing for the Fab lolly.’ None of it is ever credited. These places don’t keep archives. They were in-house designers and it was throwaway. Who was interested? This stuff was never seen as worth documenting properly. It’s such a shame.”● Fancy an Ice Cream? title: Yeehaw! Bring on the tap-dancing cowgirls! How the Edinburgh Military Tattoo suddenly got cool | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: With its marching bands, billowing flags and precision drills, the Tattoo has never exactly been cutting edge. But now an experimental theatre-maker has been let loose on it …
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: With its marching bands, billowing flags and precision drills, the Tattoo has never exactly been cutting edge. But now an experimental theatre-maker has been let loose on it …
Content: Hoedown at the castle … tap-dancers in action on opening night.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenHoedown at the castle … tap-dancers in action on opening night.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026Yeehaw! Bring on the tap-dancing cowgirls! How the Edinburgh Military Tattoo suddenly got coolWith its marching bands, billowing flags and precision drills, the Tattoo has never exactly been cutting edge. But now an experimental theatre-maker has been let loose on it …Mark FisherTue 11 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDusk has settled onEdinburghCastle and now a laser beam is scribbling a route across its ramparts and high into the sky. The voice of actor Richard Rankin is talking solemnly about lonely soldiers answering a call, while a ferocious light rises in the gatehouse. Out of it emerge scores of drummers and pipers, their sound both melodic and awe-inspiring. They crisscross the esplanade to the stirring lament of The Skye Boat Song.This is the Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo, an event often overlooked amid the festival cacophony – and yet its popularity eclipses any other event in the city. Last year, it played to 230,000 and raised £1.5m for charity. Like an outsize variety show, it is a formidable spectacle: fireworks, projections, flags dragged over the audience and a soundtrack that ranges from Carmen to Star Wars.double quotation markIt’s a living, breathing thing that speaks to the momentI speak to Susan from Aberdeen who is here with her daughter for the third year in a row. They love the highland dancing. “The atmosphere is amazing,” she says, delighted to be back. From New Zealand, Francesca tells me she is staying with family in Glasgow and is here for the night. “It’s a bucket-list item,” she says. “I was going to go when it toured to Auckland in February but I was told I had to see the original one first.”View image in fullscreenElectric dreams … the New Zealand army band at the castle.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianStaff Sgt Ross Yorkstone, drum major with the New Zealand army band, is equally pleased to be here. Performing for the sixth year, he can think of no equivalent. “The closest would be the Basel Tattoo but it’s nowhere near as big as this,” he says. “We always come here with our top A-game.”On a hot summer afternoon, I sit down with Alan Lane, the creative director, in West Princes Street Gardens to talk about the event’s phenomenal appeal. Our meeting place is deliberate: next to us is a statue of a kilted soldier with a rifle across his knees. He is the figure voiced by Rankin in A Call to Gather, the name of this year’s Tattoo show, and is looking poignantly towards the Scottish National War Memorial high above us in the castle grounds. Known as The Call 1914, the memorial is a tribute to the American expats who came to fight in the first world war. It is Lane’s inspiration. “It’s a celebration of those who will lend a hand,” he says. “If you’re my friend, I’m going to come when you call.”But which Alan Lane am I talking to? There seem to be two. One is the kind of man you would expect to be commanding a military display: a reservist who trained at Sandhurst as an officer in the Royal Engineers and who, as a wide-eyed 18-year-old, set his heart on directing the Tattoo. He is 1.9 metres tall (6ft 3in) and holds himself with a soldier’s bearing.View image in fullscreen‘I was obnoxiously leftwing’ … Alan Lane, who evacuated Sheffield Crucible as part of a show.Photograph: Duncan McGlynnThe other Alan Lane is more surprising. A lifelong member of the Labour party, he is the founding artistic director of Slung Low, the Leeds-based theatre company with a speciality in large-scale community events. He was behind Flood, a four-part epic with a cast of 58 for Hull, UK City of Culture, andCamelot: The Shining City, a dystopian fantasy in which the audience was evacuated from the Sheffield Crucible as part of the show.This Lane set up a community college on a doubledecker bus, took charge of a working men’s club and, for a year during the pandemic, coordinated afree food delivery service in Holbeck and Beestonin Leeds. He is a vegetarian who today has shown up in pink shorts. “Having run a food bank and working men’s club, there aren’t many theatre directors who are more obnoxiously leftwing than I was,” he laughs, keeping an eye on Bolt, his spaniel, who has come along for the walk.You can understand why Lane is not keen on singular thinking. If others see a contradiction in his background, he does not. “The beach commanders on D-day were part of the Labour cabinet five years later,” he says. “I don’t get how it isn’t leftwing to believe we need a military and that there is some honour in that.”double quotation markThis year, we’ve got the Americans and the Qataris in a show – that’s not by accidentStill, the organisation took some adjusting to. After his appointment in April 2024, he was kitted out with tweed, tartan and ties. He is not joking when he says that the Tattoo has a crisis meeting when attendance for the 8,800-capacity show drops below 96% – a figure that any arts company could only dream of. “But actually what I’ve found is, fundamentally, we’re not that different,” he says. And anyway, for Lane differences are there to be bridged. “Where that gets us to in this year’s Tattoo is a sharing of culture in order to understand each other,” he says. “This year, we’ve got the Americans and the Qataris in a show – that’s not by accident.”View image in fullscreenWords of wisdom … backdrop to the performance space.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianThe juxtaposition is plain to see. The Qatar Police Academy Band and Drill Team, with its sky-blue tunics, strident song and Islamic projections, comes on straight after a section called Bright Brave World in which US culture is represented by the Jackson 5, country music and tap-dancing cowgirls. Slogans of the nation’s founding principles are splashed across the castle walls: “All men are created equal”, “A new nation conceived in liberty”, “The pursuit of happiness”.Launched in 1950, the Tattoo established elements that remain to this day. There will always be marching bands and traditional songs, and they could not do without the lone piper, the solitary player on the ramparts who casts a spine-tingling hush across the audience.But every year, two-thirds of the event is created anew by the organisation’s own dancers and musicians – 133 of them, one of the largest amateur companies in the country. “In the same way you wouldn’t go: ‘Oh no, I’ve seen Scottish Ballet,’ you’d say: ‘What are they doing this year?’” says Lane. “They’re turning those skills and talents to a different story.”View image in fullscreenThe Qatar Police Academy Band and Drill Team at Edinburgh Castle.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianIf he is trying to capture the moment, this is nothing new. In 1962, the audience crowded on to the esplanade to dance to Chubby Checker’s Let’s Twist Again, a hit only a few months earlier. In 2022, theUS army Field Band brought hip-hop to the castle, with rappers Lamar Riddick and Nicholas Feemster taking to the mics for a cover of Clean Bandit’s Rather Be.“It’s a living, breathing thing that speaks to the moment,” says Lane. “The show has to have a specific creative intent at every moment. It’s not enough to say: ‘The New Zealand army band are coming – they’ll do their thing.’ There has to be something worth saying.”What, then, is worth saying in 2026? “People paying attention to each other’s cultures,” says Lane without hesitation. “This job involves me sitting with lots of military leaders telling me their plans for the next three or four years. All of them involve war. Notpreparingfor war – actual war. Looking five years out, every one of them says: ‘At that point, we are at war.’ This is a good time to be doing this show, where can we find common ground because they keep telling me war is coming.”View image in fullscreenLight fantastic … performers at the castle last week.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianBut what of those who see the Tattoo as acelebration of military might? Sensitivities feel especially acute this year, when the Tattoo, like the Edinburgh international festival, is marking the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence at the same time as the US is firing missiles at Iran. Is this really the best moment to bring on the US army Field Band performing the “best of Americana”?Magic tricks, Palestinian circus, and a ‘kinky Hamlet’: the must-see shows at 2026’s Edinburgh fringeRead more“The Tattoo doesn’t celebrate the military,” says Lane, unruffled by the suggestion. “I sit in meetings with people who wish it would do that, but it’s not our job. The Tattoo is unapologetically Scottish in its celebration of heritage. We genuinely love it. We’re zealots. But it doesn’t speak to militarism in those ways at all.”He continues: “The thing I’m sure of is: in times of difficulty, talk more, not less. The challenges for an American band to come here are real, and it would be very easy for them to decide they didn’t want to waste any political capital by coming. And it would be very easy for us not to invite them. I think we would be lesser for it because we would forget the great philosophical and poetic ideas of America. It’s brilliant to be reminded of them and to think: ‘Ah, this too shall pass.’”A Call to Gather, the Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo, is at Edinburgh Castle until 29 August. He has presented shows including Million Pound Menu, Gordon, Gino and Fred’s Road Trip, Remarkable Places to Eat, and the travelogue series Tour de Fred, and authored the booksSeriously British, Wine Uncorked andFirst Dates: The Art of Love.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Originally from Limoges, France, Sirieix cut his teeth in a number of top restaurants before becoming general manager of Michelin-starred Galvin at Windows. His charity,The Right Course, which teaches hospitality skills to prisoners, is opening restaurants in three prisons this year. He lives in London with his wife, affectionately nicknamed “Fruitcake”.What’s the last treat you bought for yourself?A Hampton greenhouse – it’s the Rolls-Royce of greenhouses. It’s being finished right now. I’m really excited about it. My first attempt at propagation failed miserably, but I’m growing courgettes, tomatoes, thyme, watermelon … you name it.View image in fullscreenCauseway greenhouse£40,300 at HamptonWhere do you buy your food from?Local shops I’ve been going to for years in south London: William Rose butchers in East Dulwich, Beaumont fruit and veg shop, and FC Soper fishmonger, both in Nunhead. It’s nice to buy stuff from people you know, where you know the quality.Visit William Rose ButchersVisit F C Soper FishmongerWhat’s the best present you’ve given?My wife’s engagement ring – it’s big, it’s prominent on the finger, it’s beautiful. She picked it herself, which I think is the key to making a woman happy with an engagement ring.… and the best present you’ve received?A book given to me two Christmases ago by my wife and son, full of pictures of them.What’s your favourite online store?Amazon – it’s very practical; you can be sitting here, order what you want, and it comes the next day.What’s your favourite bricks-and-mortar shop?Hedonism Wines in Mayfair, London. I last bought a bottle of Krug there for someone as a gift – they’ll mail it anywhere in the world for you.View image in fullscreenVine and dandy: Mayfair’s Hedonism Wines.Shop wine at HedonismWhat’s the gadget you use most often?At the moment, my Niwaki secateurs to deadhead roses.View image in fullscreenNiwaki GR Pro secateursFrom £80 at Niwaki£90 at BurfordFor more, read the Filter’s guide to thebest secateursWhat’s the purchase you regret the most?I bought a big, beautiful brown leather sofa. I won’t name the brand, but it’s the most uncomfortable thing, and it has just collapsed on itself. C’est la vie.What’s the thing(s) you get delivered?Everything other than food. I like to touch my tomatoes before I buy them or talk to the butcher about the meat.Where do you buy your underwear?My wife, “Fruitcake”, buys them for me from Calvin Klein or Hugo Boss.View image in fullscreenShop men’s underwear at Calvin KleinShop men’s underwear at Hugo BossWhat would you buy with £20?In London, two pints of Guinness.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. I wasn’t taught to moisturise as a boy but my wife got me into it and my skin feels so different – this stuff is by far the best.View image in fullscreenLa Roche-Posay Lipikar moisturiser£25 at Lookfantastic£25.50 at BootsFor more, read the Filter’s guide to thebest moisturisersHow do you make your coffee at home?My L’Or coffee machine. title: The myth of Anthony Bourdain: how the bad boy chef became a hero to boozehounds and bullies | Anthony Bourdain | The Guardian
description: The author of Kitchen Confidential has inspired a new movie, Tony, about his days as a dishwasher. But do today’s chefs still admire his self-sabotaging rock’n’roll spirit – or have they outgrown it?
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: The author of Kitchen Confidential has inspired a new movie, Tony, about his days as a dishwasher. But do today’s chefs still admire his self-sabotaging rock’n’roll spirit – or have they outgrown it?
Content: If you can’t stand the heat … Anthony Bourdain in Sydney, 2005.Photograph: Fairfax Media/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIf you can’t stand the heat … Anthony Bourdain in Sydney, 2005.Photograph: Fairfax Media/Getty ImagesAnthony BourdainThe myth of Anthony Bourdain: how the bad boy chef became a hero to boozehounds and bulliesThe author of Kitchen Confidential has inspired a new movie, Tony, about his days as a dishwasher. But do today’s chefs still admire his self-sabotaging rock’n’roll spirit – or have they outgrown it?Zoe WilliamsTue 11 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe trope of the Angry Young Man was not born in a kitchen, but Anthony Bourdain’s particular myth-making created what might be the prototype forfin de(20th)sièclemasculinity. As the director ofTony, the new biopic of Bourdainfocusing on his first job, has said, the film is about “a magical world where nothing can go wrong and a young man who’s angry about it”.Bourdain arrived in that job, as a dishwasher in a restaurant in Provincetown, Massachusetts, aged 19. He was hellbent on a life of formless, self-sabotaging rebellion, and found his tribe. But when he published his book Kitchen Confidential in 2000, a quarter of a century later, he set the ethos of that kitchen tribe in stone, and attracted an ever-replenishing pool of chefs who, if they weren’t already just like him, were prepared to die trying.However, that anger, like everything about Bourdain, wasn’t real – it was performative, playful. He compared himself once to thechef Eric Ripert, saying they both had a “live and let live energy”, but Ripert “believes in karma … I believe in vendetta”. That fabled anger never sounded quite real.View image in fullscreenBourdain in New York, 2002.Photograph: Chris Floyd/CAMERA PRESSKitchen Confidential starts with Bourdain travelling through France as a child with his brother and his moneyed American parents of European inclinations and heritage. He is a little prick to his family, for no reason, and he’s also a git to the French kids, before returning to the US to be a jerk to flatmates and girlfriends in his private liberal arts university (Vassar) before dropping out. He’s still in his teens in 1975, when he takes that lowly job in Provincetown. There, he’s a minnow among absolute sharks of delinquency – a chef might turn out an impromptu service for a 100-strong post-wedding party, then bang the bride against the bins afterwards. The staff scored drugs you’ve never heard of, and drugs you’d never have needed if you hadn’t taken all those other drugs.In that kitchen, Bourdain finds his spiritual home, “a subculture whose centuries-old militaristic hierarchy and ethos of ‘rum, buggery and the lash’ make for a mix of unwavering order and nerve-shattering chaos,” he wrote in Kitchen Confidential. That book, remembers the journalist, cookery writer and cook Diana Henry, 63, described “a world we didn’t have an in on, and suddenly we did”. (Henry did, in my view, thebest late-era interview with Bourdain, two years before his death.)Bourdain described his cheffly mission: “Your body is not a temple, it’s an amusement park. Enjoy the ride.” In his writing, as in his cooking, he prioritised pace and crunch over elegance and fuss. Relationships in this brigade system were tightly bonded and savagely caustic. “As an art form, cook talk is, like haiku or kabuki, defined by established rules,” he wrote. “All comments must, out of historical necessity, concern involuntary rectal penetration, penis size, physical flaws or annoying mannerisms or defects.” Between the drugs, the shagging, the late nights, the contradictory, hurtling imperatives of discipline and self-indulgence, the contempt for self-care and the penis jokes, this was a definitionally masculine ideal, and not even for so childish a reason as that you’d need a dick in order to dip it in someone’s Vichyssoise. There’s just no female model for being beautiful, high and still smashing it at work: the women in this space (just off the top of my head, Nancy Spungen, Amy Winehouse) end up dead.View image in fullscreenTom Kerridge: ‘Chefs love the energy of being chefs – it becomes your way of life.’Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianIn many ways, Bourdain was just saying what he saw: this was the reality of kitchens across decades and continents. Tom Kerridge, 53, describes being drawn in by exactly the same atmosphere: “Every chef will tell you the same thing – they don’t come into kitchens because they love food.Chefslove the energy of being chefs. It becomes your way of life, as opposed to what you do – it’s what you are.” Kitchens might have their hierarchies imported from the French army, their insubordination penalties only a fraction less violent, yet at the same time, Kerridge continues, “they’re building sites, they’re construction zones, they’re full of people using sharp things and burning themselves, who are all really tired”.Andrew Clarke, 48-year-old co-owner and exec chef at Acme Fire Cult in east London, and the founder of Glandstonbury (yes, it’s an offal festival), said of his first colleagues – nowhere fancy, a pizza place in Bluewater, in the late 90s: “They were these pirates. None of them were proper chefs. They needed a job without a CV, without any qualifications – some of them had been in prison, and the kitchen was very accepting of that.” The word “pirate” is used constantly, by everyone, and the ex-con thing is real: in 2009 the Clink charity was established, opening restaurants in High Down, Brixton and a couple of other prisons, teaching prisoners skills for when they got out. And there’s a reason they were trained up for professional kitchens, not ice-cream parlours.Clarke remembers arriving “in a kitchen that was very French, very disciplined, very trained. Bourdain’s book was just out, and I just started reading little passages, and I thought, ‘That’s me. That’s the person I am, that’s where I’ve been, that’s what I’ve done.’” Sally Abé – 38, former head chef at the Pem in the Conrad, St James’s, London, and, lately, her own bistro, Teal – had an all-female senior team at the Pem, but did not enter the business in 2007 wanting to throw over its hyper-masculine conventions. “To be honest, I’m a very stubborn, determined person,” she says. “When I was 21, I thought, ‘I can be one of the boys,’ and I got swept up in it. It was really fun.”View image in fullscreen‘I saw chefs being drunk in service, and quite often that was me’ … chefs Andrew Clarke (left) and Daniel Watkins.Photograph: Sophia Evans/The ObserverYet at the same time, Bourdain’s writing was so vivid, his character so magnetic, his joie de vivre so complicatedly credible and so contagious, that he built the world in the act of describing it.As much as it pains me to pour cold water over it, Bourdain’s myth – the bit that was neither rooted in reality, nor prefigurable by force of will – was that the quintessential chef’s life could just proceed without consequence. “Bourdain romanticised that sort of life,” Henry says, “taking coke, drinking too much.” He ended up in rehab in the early 90s, but remained a heavy smoker and drinker. In kitchens the world over, says Clarke: “All roads led to the bar: a good service, you go to the bar, a bad service, you go to the bar. I saw chefs being drunk in service, and quite often that was me. I’d have a skinful at lunch and then do a dinner.” Kerridge has talked in the past about hisjaw-dropping alcohol consumption, before he went teetotal in 2013.In 2015, Clarke suffered a terrible depressive episode. When he posted about it onInstagram, a huge number of people in the industry shared their own experiences with him. He has since set up a mental health charity for people working in the hospitality industry calledPilot Light. “While we wanted to raise awareness of mental health in the business, it inevitably led to people talking about bullying, sexism and racism in the industry. I’m a chef – I wanted to keep it very clean and simple. For me it was about mental health. But it was Pandora’s box.”It’s worth making a distinction between the ludic, juvenile macho vibe Bourdain immortalised and a more modern toxic masculinity, designed to undermine, control and exclude women (having come of age in the 90s, I could spend forever insisting on that distinction). However, Bourdain himself, a subtle and self-critical person, could see how the first provided cover for the second. As he told an audience at his alma mater, the Culinary Institute of America, in 2017: “If there’s a harasser in the kitchen who’s a jerk, chances are he’s got a copy of my book on his station. And I’m going to have to live with that.”View image in fullscreenSally Abé … ‘I thought, ‘I can be one of the boys.’Photograph: Sophia Spring/The ObserverThere were also a lot of real bullies operating under the cover of play-bullying, and it’s interesting, looking back, how widely this was accepted in the industry. It was an open secret when Noma – the experimental Danish restaurant – was huge in the 2000s that its founder, René Redzepi,terrorised his staff. When theNew York Timespublished evidence in March that Redzepi had “punched employees in the face, jabbed them with kitchen implements and slammed them against walls” leading to “lasting trauma from layers of psychological abuse, including intimidation, body shaming and public ridicule”, the collective sound of people feigning horror at a thing that we’d all known for 20 years was really something.That’s not just kitchens, of course. “Not only does it look like an awful way to treat people, it’s become unacceptable,” Henry says. “You can’t bully anybody anywhere.” She recalls her experience working as a TV producer on food programmes. “Even the way I behaved in television, making researchers stay late because they hadn’t done enough, I wouldn’t get away with that now. We don’t like it any more.”Abé has no problem differentiating between mischief, intensity, ego and harassment. “Kitchens are always going to be high-pressure places – once you’re in the service, you’re in the service. If the food’s not ready, you’re an idiot. But I’ve taken all those environments I worked in and turned them on their head. My kitchen’s nothing like that now.”Clarke is done with the macho bullying (“It’s deeply uncool,” he says), and when he started Acme in 2022, he did a thing that would doubtless have had Bourdain, back in the day, exploding in 2,000 colourful words. “We have very physical, long days; none of us look after ourselves like athletes and perhaps we should. We were doing yoga classes in the space, checking in, talking to each other. Doing everything a little more holistically.” It’s not as anti-Bourdain as it sounds, Clarke says: “He got into jiu-jitsu in his 50s. He was fully at the point of: ‘I’m going to look after myself.’”Bourdain never understood his own propensity for self-sabotage, as well as other-people-sabotage. It’s laced through his writing: there he always is, making trouble for no good reason. And he said as much to Henry when she interviewed him. “What is it that gave him the pain that he carried around with him?” she asks. “His childhood sounded perfectly OK. He was just always a bit of a wreck until he got to be a chef. It’s strict – you can’t not deliver. You’ve got to be in, you’ve got to see your crew, you’ve got to do your service. There are completely set rules and you can’t disobey them.” Kitchens were a haven for people who needed rules as much as they hated them, and could only reconcile those warring urges in a cacophony of appetites.View image in fullscreenRené Redzepi, founder of the experimental Danish restaurant Noma, who stepped down amid accusations of physical and psychological abuse of his staff.Photograph: Reuters/AlamyPerhaps inevitably, through some combination of a little foresight and a changing world, the pirate spirit that defined kitchens for so long is being replaced by a new intellectualism. “Chefs nowadays are like bloody poets,” Henry says. “Stevie Parle, Merlin Labron-Johnson – all these people have got degrees. Once they would have been doing a master’s and a PhD; instead they’re focusing on growth and animals and flavour combinations and technical stuff.”It’s not a sanitised world. It surely still has the plenty of what Bourdain wrote were the fundamentals of “good food and good eating ... blood and organs and cruelty and decay”. An intellectual kitchen just doesn’t invite chaos, or torment, or madcappery, but you wonder what will become of all the people who were mainly in it for those things.Tony, the biopic ofAnthony Bourdain, is in cinemas from FridayDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in our letters section, please click here.Explore more on these topicsAnthony BourdainChefsMental healthFoodRestaurantsBullyingfeaturesShareReuse this content
