Author: Paddy Maddison
Headline: Whether you’re commuting, training or riding for fun, we asked specialists to break down what to know before you buy – from specs and safety to price
Content: Paddy Maddison enjoys the ‘meditative’ process of climbing coastal roads on his trusty steed.Photograph: Paddy Maddison/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPaddy Maddison enjoys the ‘meditative’ process of climbing coastal roads on his trusty steed.Photograph: Paddy Maddison/The GuardianThe FilterCyclingHow to buy a bike: expert tips for finding the right budget, frame and fitWhether you’re commuting, training or riding for fun, we asked specialists to break down what to know before you buy – from specs and safety to priceThe best bike locks for every budgetPaddy MaddisonTue 11 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.For me, cycling is therapy. It’s calming, meditative and uncomplicated. But there’s a catch. To experience the simple joy of riding a bike, you first have to navigate the maddeningly complex process of buying one.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Make no mistake: this is not a straightforward case of marching into Halfords, saying, “One bike, please!” and leaving with a shiny new steed. But, while complicated, it needn’t be stressful.Before you buy, ask yourself three questions: how will I use it? How much am I willing to spend? And what features do I want? Based on your answers, this guide will arm you with what you need to make a confident, informed purchase – no engineering degree required.To help, I’ve enlisted two experts: David Arthur, founder of cycling-tech YouTube channelJust Ride Bikes, and Stephen Roche, owner of bike-fitting and custom-build studiothe Bike Tailor.How to buy a bikeWhat type of bike do you need?View image in fullscreenChain reaction: start your bike search by getting to know the different types available.Photograph: Paddy Maddison/The GuardianThe best bike for you depends largely on where and how you intend to use it. To make matters more confusing, the bike industry is constantly coming up with new types of bicycles. Thankfully, they can all be grouped loosely into one of five main categories.HybridBest for:running around townHybrids fuse elements from road and mountain bikes, prioritising comfort for everyday use. They’re popular in urban environments when journeys are short, and speed isn’t a primary concern. They’re usually among the most affordable options, too. “These bikes are perfect for commuting and casual leisure cycling due to the flat handlebar and upright riding position,” says Arthur. “That said, they can feel slow compared with road bikes.”View image in fullscreenScott Metrix 30 EQ bike£949 at Scott SportsView image in fullscreenTrek Verve lowstep equipped 2027£800 at Team Cycles£800 at Evans CyclesRoad bikeBest for:riding farther, faster on paved surfacesWith drop handlebars that allow the rider to get low down and tuck in, road bikes are made to go fast. They’re designed for aerodynamic efficiency and low weight, featuring slick tyres that roll smoothly over tarmac. “The downside is that the low-slung riding position can be uncomfortable at first,” says Arthur. “The relatively narrow tyres combined with a stiff frame can be jarring on rough roads.”View image in fullscreenVan Rysel Shimano 105 Di2 Endurance£2,999.99 at DecathlonGravel bikeBest for:hopping between tarmac, towpaths, bridleways and light trailsThe fastest-growing category in cycling, this relatively new breed of bike is essentially an off-road version of a road bike. It still has the drop bars and fundamental shape, but with wider tyres to grip on rough ground, lower gears for traction on unpaved ascents, and a longer wheelbase for increased stability. “Gravel bikes are designed to handle a variety of terrain,” says Arthur. “They’re the perfect all-rounders – as at home on country lanes as they are blasting through a forest or tackling the daily commute. The trade-off is they’re slower than road bikes on the road and less capable than mountain bikes on the rough stuff.”View image in fullscreenCanyon Grizl CF 6£1,899 at CanyonView image in fullscreenLiv Devote 2£1,199 at TredzMountain bikeBest for:full-blown off-road ridingIf you intend to do most of your riding away from roads and paths, a mountain bike could be a good option. They have thick, knobbly tyres for grip on loose surfaces, flat handlebars for increased control, and often feature suspension to smooth out bumps when riding on rough ground. “These comfort-focused features – including easy gearing and a relaxed riding position – make mountain bikes great for beginners,” says Arthur. “Unfortunately, big tyres and suspension systems add weight and mechanical complexity.”View image in fullscreenTrek Marlin 4 Gen 3£525 at Tredz£525 at Cycles UKView image in fullscreenBoardman MHT 8.6 women’s mountain bike£650 at Halfords£650 at TredzCargo bikeBest for:reducing car useA cargo bike offers a genuine alternative to travelling by car. These bikes often have a large platform or bucket at the front or rear that can be filled with anything from shopping to children, allowing you to transport large loads with relative ease. “Many cargo bikes have pedal-assist motors too,” says Arthur. “But they’re expensive and bulky to store, so you’ll need the money and the space first.”View image in fullscreenTrek Fetch+ 4 750Wh electric cargo bike£4,500 at Trek BikesFolding bikeBest for:city living and short commutesFor those without much storage space, housing something the size of a pony isn’t realistic. This is where folding bikes come in. With smaller wheels and compact frames, these metal bikes can be packed away quickly when not in use, conserving floor space.Born in London during the 1970s,Bromptonhas a well-deserved reputation as one of the most reliable names in the category. Its genericisation has made it a household name, but it is by no means the only option. Dahon, for example, also makes excellent folding bikes, often at a slightly lower price. That being said, if your budget can stretch to a Brompton, it’s perhaps worth forking out for the superior build quality.View image in fullscreenDahon Mariner D8£799 at DahonWhat else do you need?View image in fullscreenGet kitted out: consider essential and desirable accessories you’ll need once you have your bike.Photograph: Justin Paget/Getty ImagesHelmetHelmetsaren’t mandatory for cyclists in the UK, but most people still choose to wear one. It can be the difference between life and death if you have a nasty crash. Pick one that’s comfortable and adjustable for a snug fit. It should feel secure without any significant movement when you shake your head.LightsIf you’re cycling on the road at night,bike lightsaremandatory. Depending on where you’re riding, you’ll want them to see and/or be seen. By law, you should have a red light mounted on the rear and a white light mounted on the front.The best bike lightshave rechargeable batteries, multiple blinking and static modes, and can be removed or adjusted easily. The Knog Blinder came top in my test of bike lights; this mini set from the same range features a front and rear light.View image in fullscreenKnog Blinder mini square light£38.99 at Fawkes Cycles£52.99 at Ribble CyclesFor more, read thesafety essentials cyclists won’t leave home withoutskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLockA lock is a good idea if you’re using your bike to commute or run errands. The best ones are heavy and cumbersome but provide peace of mind if you’re leaving your bike unattended for extended periods. For 10 minutes here and there, something smaller and more discreet will usually do the trick. Wearable chain locks, such as the classic Hiplok, are a good middle ground, as they’re portable but still offer robust protection.View image in fullscreenHiplokLite wearable bike lock£42.75 at Fawkes Cycles£59.99 at HalfordsFor more, read our guide to thebest bike locks for every budgetBasic toolsMechanical issues can and do occur. The basic ones can be fixed at home or even in the middle of a ride, provided you have the right tools. A simple multitool is a cyclist’s Swiss army knife. It has several different Allen key heads for making adjustments to the bike, and some of the higher-end ones even include things like chain-link removers. You should also arm yourself with two pumps: a floor-standing track pump for home to inflate tyres quickly and easily, and a mini pump that can be shoved into a pocket, pannier or backpack for adding air on the go.View image in fullscreenLezyne V Pro 7 multitool£16.49 at Fawkes Cycles£16.99 at Merlin CyclesView image in fullscreenTopeak JoeBlow Max II floor pump£28.54 at Halfords£28.54 at AmazonView image in fullscreenTopeak Peakini II mini pump£14.99 at HalfordsLubeA bike’s chain, cassette and chainrings (known collectively as the drivetrain) will wear over time, but you can extend their life by keeping them lubricated. Choose a purpose-designed lubricant for dry or wet conditions based on where you ride, and apply it to the side of the chain that contacts the teeth of the cassette and chainrings. Do this approximately every 100 miles, or more frequently in wet weather.View image in fullscreenFinish Line dry chain lubricant, 60ml£4.99 at Tredz£9.99 at AmazonView image in fullscreenMuc-Off wet weather lube, 120ml£7.99 at Decathlon£5.99 at AmazonClothingHigh-visibility clothing is always a good idea if you’re riding on roads, but you may even want to consider things like padded shorts and close-fitting jerseys if you’re planning to ride longer distances for hours at a time. Padded “bib shorts” or “bib tights” have a soft foamy pad stitched into the seat to keep you comfortable on the saddle for longer.View image in fullscreenProviz men’s waterproof reflective cycling jacket£79.99 at Proviz£88 at Mountain WarehouseView image in fullscreenProviz women’s reflective active jacket£44.99 at Proviz£49.50 at Mountain WarehouseHow much should you spend?You can spend as much or as little as you like, but the experience improves noticeably as you move up through the prices … up to a point. The good news is that there are solid options to suit almost every budget. Pricing is a broad spectrum, ranging from a few quid for a Facebook Marketplace clunker to £12,000+ for a Tour de France-worthy “superbike”. Your best bet is to aim somewhere in the middle. Here’s what you can expect for your money.SecondhandThere are incredible deals to be had for those bold enough to navigate the used bike market. However, some rudimentary knowledge is essential to avoid a bad experience, so get to know yourSramfrom yourShimano(if that’s a foreign language to you, you know where to start Googling).Found something that looks like a good fit? Don’t just blindly go in offering the asking price. Instead, hunt online for the same bike and see what the going rate was when it was new. You can use that information, coupled with the age and current condition, to determine whether the price is fair or not. Make sure you’re comparing models from the same year. If the year isn’t stated on the listing, search Google Images for the exact same colourway, as manufacturers tend to change these annually. If you can find one the same, chances are it was made at the same time.A word on carbon: any used bicycle comes with the possibility of hard-to-spot structural damage, but the risk is greater with carbon. This material is strong and lightweight, which has made it the go-to for high-end bikes, but it can fail catastrophically if cracked even slightly. The trouble is, such cracks are often barely visible, so you’ll need to conduct a thorough inspection, looking for deep scratches, flaking paint or any other suspicious signs. If in doubt, you could always pay a professional mechanic to check it for you.In terms of where to buy, local bike-specific Facebook sales-and-wants groups often yield the best results: do a bit of digging to find the best ones in your area. Alternatively, eBay can be a safe bet, or, better still, spend a day visiting local bike shops to browse in person.Under £400At the bottom end of the price scale, you’re looking at basic entry-level bikes built with affordability in mind. Options in this bracket will be mostly low-grade aluminium or steel with budget components, such as mechanical brakes as opposed to more powerful hydraulic brakes. As a result, they’ll probably be heavy and clunky to operate. Plus, cheap parts tend to wear out faster. That’s fine for short, occasional miles or getting a feel for cycling, but if you want to spend hours in the saddle, you may find yourself shopping for an upgrade sooner rather than later.£500-£1,000Expect lighter aluminium frames and entry-level shifting-and-braking components (known collectively as groupsets) from reputable, industry-standard brands such as the aforementioned Shimano and Sram. Closer to £1,000, this may include hydraulic disc brakes, which provide superior stopping power, wet-weather performance and control when compared with their mechanical counterparts. This is a good place to aim for most people looking for a solid bike for commuting and leisure who aren’t concerned about having the “fastest this” or the “lightest that”.£1,000-£2,000Carbon fibre begins to creep in here – if not the full frame, then possibly fork and/or seatpost. Bikes in this bracket will generally be lighter and provide a noticeably smoother ride thanks to better-quality components, such as wheels, tyres and groupsets. Speaking of which, respectable mid-range shifting can be found easily for this sort of money, such as Shimano’s bestselling 105 system – affectionately referred to by some as “the groupset of the people” – which is renowned for offering excellent bang for the buck.£2,000+This is where things get serious. These are mid- to high-end bikes, probably featuring full carbon-fibre frames, premium groupsets, carbon wheels and possibly even electronic gears. On mountain bikes in this bracket, you should expect full suspension, and for cargo bikes, you’ll probably see mostly motor-assisted options.What should you look for?Frame materialAluminium, steel, carbon and titanium: these are the four most common frame materials, and each comes with its own benefits and drawbacks.“Carbon fibre is the most desirable material in cycling due to its low weight, stiffness and strength, but it comes with a premium price,” says Arthur. “But aluminium should not be ignored. It’s more common at lower prices, and it offers the best value for beginners.”Steel and titanium are good options, too. Both are easy to repair, but where steel is affordable and heavy, titanium is expensive and light.GearsIt’s easy to fall down a rabbit hole when trying to understand gears, but don’t get too caught up in it. Unless you’re a professional road racer, ignore the fancy stuff and focus on fuss-free functionality.“Don’t be swayed by flashy top-of-the-range electronic groupsets,” says Arthur. “A lot of cheaper groupsets still offer exceptional performance, and their simplicity leads to lower maintenance and cheaper replacement parts when things do eventually wear out.”TyresBroadly speaking, wide, knobbly tyres inflated to low pressures provide cushioning and grip on uneven ground, while narrow, slick tyres inflated to higher pressures are faster and more efficient on paved surfaces. Consider where you’ll be riding and which you value most: comfort or speed. Choose your rubber accordingly.BrakesBrakes are a divisive topic in the cycling world. Rim brakes, which work by gripping a braking surface on the outer edges of the rim, used to be the default. In recent years, they’ve been usurped by disc brakes, which use a rotor attached to the wheel’s hub. Many purists swear by rim brakes, praising their low weight and simplicity. But when it comes to pure stopping power, disc brakes win.Disc brakes come in two forms: mechanical and hydraulic. Mechanical disc brakes are cheaper and operate with a cable mechanism. Hydraulic disc brakes are more expensive and use hoses filled with brake fluid – much like the brakes in a car.“If your budget allows for an upgrade to hydraulic disc brakes, it’s worth spending the extra money,” says Arthur. “They offer far superior braking performance in all weathers and can genuinely boost confidence when riding fast.”SizeMost brands provide a chart to give you a loose idea of what size to go for based on certain measurements, but it’s always best to sit on different options before making a decision. The Bike Tailor’s Stephen Roche agrees, adding that you should know your measurements – height and inseam at a minimum – before you start shopping.“You can also look at the bike measurement known as reach,” he adds. “This is the horizontal distance from the bottom bracket to the top of the head tube. If you find that your arms are outstretched and you’re bending from the neck, you probably need a smaller frame size.”Another option, Roche suggests, is to pay for a professional bike fit. “It takes any guesswork out of the equation.”For more, read:The best bike lights to see and be seenThe best bike panniers and handlebar bagsHow to make your bike last longerPaddy Maddison is a consumer journalist, outerwear enthusiast and exercise addict. If he’s not hiking in the hills, he’s grinding up them on his bike, hurtling down them on his snowboard, or lacing up his running shoes and hitting the pavements. As a result, he gets plenty of time to put all the latest and greatest gear through the wringer for the FilterExplore more on these topicsCyclingThe FilterFitnessHobbiesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: José Pizarro’s recipe for peach and moscatel granita | Food | The Guardian
description: Something light, cooling and refreshing to finish a big summer meal
Author: José Pizarro
Headline: Something light, cooling and refreshing to finish a big summer meal
Content: José Pizarro’s peach and moscatel granita.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The Guardian. Food styling: Aya Nishimura. Prop styling: Polly Webb-Wilson. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence.View image in fullscreenJosé Pizarro’s peach and moscatel granita.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The Guardian. Food styling: Aya Nishimura. Prop styling: Polly Webb-Wilson. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence.FoodJosé Pizarro’s recipe for peach and moscatel granitaSomething light, cooling and refreshing to finish a big summer mealJosé PizarroTue 11 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor me, the best desserts are often the simplest. In Spain, we often finish a meal with something light, something that refreshes rather than fills you up. This is exactly that. It has a lovely texture that sits somewhere between a drink and something you eat, and is perfect at the end of a long meal. It feels relaxed but still special, the kind of thing you enjoy on a warm day, when all you want is something fresh and uplifting.Peach and moscatel granitaWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appPrep5 minCook40 min, plus chillingFreeze3 hr+Serves6500ml moscatel wine125g caster sugar5-6lemon thyme sprigsPared zest of1 unwaxed lemon, plus the juice of ½ lemon6 ripe peaches or nectarinesPut the wine and sugar in a pan with the lemon thyme and lemon zest, then heat gently until the sugar dissolves. Add 500ml water and bring to a simmer.Lower the peaches into the liquid and poach for four to five minutes, until tender. Lift out the peaches with a slotted spoon, transfer to a plate or tray and leave to cool. Once cool enough to handle, remove the skins from the peaches and add these to the pan of poaching liquid. Put the peeled peaches in the fridge to chill.Bring the poaching liquid to a boil, then simmer for 15-20 minutes, until it reduces slightly and turns a lovely pink colour. Strain into a jug, pressing the juice from the skins, then stir in the lemon juice: you should have about 700ml syrup. Leave this to cool, then chill in the fridge until cold.Pour the chilled syrup into a shallow tray and put in the freezer for 30 minutes. Stir with a fork then repeat, stirring every half an hour or so. You will need to do this five or six times, until you have a lovely granita.Serve scoops of the granita with a whole poached peach, or cut the fruit in half and remove the stones.Explore more on these topicsFoodFruitSummer food and drinkIce-cream and sorbetSpanish food and drinkDessertrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Car hire firm told me I was a ‘no-show’ so I lost £185 | Money | The Guardian
description: I was delayed, but I had prepaid through Holiday Autos and had provided my flight number as requested
Author: Anna Tims
Headline: I was delayed, but I had prepaid through Holiday Autos and had provided my flight number as requested
Content: The flight was severely delayed and the car had been rehired.Photograph: IJzendoorn/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenThe flight was severely delayed and the car had been rehired.Photograph: IJzendoorn/Getty Images/iStockphotoConsumer championsMoneyCar hire firm told me I was a ‘no-show’ so I lost £185I was delayed, but I had prepaid through Holiday Autos and had provided my flight number as requestedAnna TimsTue 11 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 06.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI booked a car hire at Heathrow through Holiday Autos on a visit to the UK and provided my flight number as requested.My flight was severely delayed, and when I reached the car hire desk, I was toldI’d been marked down as a “no-show” and that my car had been rehired.Under duress, I was forced to hire a larger car for twice the price, and was told I would not be refunded the original £185 hire fee.Since then, the car hire company has told me to complain to Holiday Autos, and vice versa.BF, AustraliaThe terms and conditions of your contract state that a definition of a “no-show” is a customer who arrives late because of a flight delay without having provided a flight number. You had provided your number, so the supplier would have been able to verify your flight status, but neither party would accept this when you complained.Holiday Autos tells me your car was no longer available owing to “operational constraints”. But you had prepaid, so there would have been no financial loss to the hire firm if it had held the vehicle until your arrival.It insists that cars cannot be held indefinitely even if flight details are provided, but it did not mention this in the terms.Holiday Autos says an upgraded vehicle was offered instead, without disclosing that you were forced to pay handsomely for the privilege.The company has, however, performed a magnanimous U-turn.“While the additional charges were agreed directly between the customer and the car rental supplier, we recognise the impact this experience had on the trip,” it says. “As a gesture of goodwill, we have refunded the costs of the original rental plus the additional upgrade and insurance costs incurred.”We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. Email us atconsumer.champions@theguardian.comor write to Consumer Champions, Money, the Guardian, 90 York Way, London N1 9GU. Please include a daytime phone number. title: Do you have to be hot at work? Eight people on how looks influence their jobs | Beauty | The Guardian
description: Due to the rise of GLP-1s and cosmetic surgeries, professionals who weren’t usually subject to high beauty standards are facing new pressures
Author: Alaina Demopoulos
Headline: Due to the rise of GLP-1s and cosmetic surgeries, professionals who weren’t usually subject to high beauty standards are facing new pressures
Content: ‘If someone likes looking at you, they’ll hire you,’ says YaGass Sey, a social media consultant from Florida.Photograph: The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘If someone likes looking at you, they’ll hire you,’ says YaGass Sey, a social media consultant from Florida.Photograph: The Guardian/Getty ImagesBeautyDo you have to be hot at work? Eight people on how looks influence their jobsDue to the rise of GLP-1s and cosmetic surgeries, professionals who weren’t usually subject to high beauty standards are facing new pressuresAlaina DemopoulosTue 11 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 13.05 EDTShareIn 1975, John T Molly’s book Dress for Success became a national bestseller. It promised the American workforce “scientific” proof that certain clothes could “increase your income” and “boost your status”. It offered searing advice like: “Sweaters give out nothing but negative impulses … they say ‘lower middle class’ and ‘loser.’”For those with office jobs, the workplace has long been a place where fashion counts. Molly’s book gave rise to ideas like power dressing and the adage about “dressing for the job you want, not the one you have”. But a new casual office culture, spurred by San Francisco tech companies where hoodies are the norm, plus the work-from-home revolution, was supposed to ameliorate some of those pressures.Instead, things have gotten worse, as appearing on camera and keeping an active social media presence has become the norm. Now, the focus is no longer just on appropriate attire for the professional class, but a wide range of beauty and body standards for people in professions who never previously had to worry as much about what they look like. In the social media age, there is no such thing as having a face for radio.Surgery, shame and self-erasure: four female writers on the tyranny of impossible beauty standardsRead moreA slew ofrecentstudiestell us that hot people make more money. There’s a term for this workplace phenomenon: “lookism”, or a bias against people perceived as unattractive. One 15-year survey found that hot MBA candidates had a higher probability of holding more desirable jobs than their “plain-looking counterparts” – the authors called this an “attractiveness premium” corresponding to over $2,500 in higher salaries. Another 2018 report called attractiveness “an enduring, positive labor market characteristic”.Visible, successful people now sport ubiquitous features that increasingly come courtesy of needles and scalpels: airbrushed skin, impossibly high cheekbones, thinned noses. We expect this of celebrities, but filler, semaglutides and cosmetic surgeries are now commonplace for people in professions from childcare to administration. Ageism is a big factor: in asurvey last year, for example, 15% of people over the age of 45 said they would consider cosmetic surgery to get on at work, a figure which rose to 20% for Botox and fillers.Below we spoke to welders, home builders and lawyers – all of whom say they never thought the way they look would influence their work this much.Hannah HembreeBell: ‘I have hair appointments all the time’View image in fullscreen43, divorce lawyer atHembree Bell Law Firmand owner ofMy Confident Divorce, a law firm that represents only women, Austin, TexasLooks matter more now than they did 10 years ago, 1,000%. Along with being a lawyer, I’m trying to grow as a thought leader for women in the divorce space – that means more forward-facing, PR-type things.Whether you like it or not, social media is a big component of growing a brand or company. I work with a stylist, I have hair appointments all of the time, and I go to a medi-spa for all the aesthetics one gets when they’re 43. I’m spending four figures a month on things like Botox, filler and beauty appointments.There’s a pressure to always be on as a woman. I go on morning news shows to talk about divorce stories and trends. Now, when I go on vacation I have to think about the clothes I pack, the hair tools I bring, in case I need to shoot content while I’m away. That’s another thing I wasn’t dealing with 10 years ago. Literally right now, I am vacationing on the beaches in Delaware with my family. I got a call from my PR team to go on TV in New York. I had to have some clothes shipped from my house, and I went on a shopping trip, to get something appropriate to wear. That took time away from my family.View image in fullscreenYaGass Sey: ‘I’m not trying to look good for other people’27, social media consultant, Jacksonville, FloridaIf someone likes looking at you, they’ll hire you. I’ve known this from the start of my very first job, at the [chain store] Rue21. I was 16 and essentially the cute personality hire. They had me standing at the front of the store selling perfume to bring people in, and I did nothing else. I was the only person who ever had that job, in front of the store, to this day.Two years ago, I made a TikTok about pretty privilege – the idea that people treat you better if you’re attractive. It really took off and became one of my best viral videos. (I now have over 247,000 followers on TikTok.) I made a scale of pretty privilege, with levels from one to four, with the treatment getting better based on someone’s looks. People in the comments were asking me what level they were. There were so many comments. I was bored at home. So I was just like, “all right, Cash App me $5” and they would get a reading on my personal thoughts of their pretty privilege, or where they were on the scale. I was not expecting people to go through with it, but it took me weeks to get through everyone and I made a few thousand dollars off of it. It was proof of concept that I could make money off of nothing, or just from my personal opinion.I think people saw me as an authority on this because of my delivery. When you’re in the consulting business, looks absolutely matter. And being attractive gives you a level of confidence that people are attracted to.When I was in a front-facing positions such as restaurants, I was spending maybe $500-$600 on my presentation: different hairstyles, nails, lashes. Now, I work from home, so, even though I am still visible on TikTok a lot, I find I spend a lot less. Not doing as much has made me appreciate my natural beauty more. My nails don’t break because I’m not in the salon getting them drilled off all the time. My lashes are longer because I’m not having something glued to them all the time. My hair’s not breaking off. Everything’s healthy, and I’m not trying to look good for other people, so I feel pretty all the time.View image in fullscreenLindsey Hover: ‘My botox and nails don’t stop me from working hard’39, welder and content creator, Huntington Beach, CaliforniaMy appearance has definitely helped me get jobs. I know for a fact that I got one welding job through Instagram, because they wanted their shop to get more exposure through my page.I got into welding through an ex-partner. He was into cars. I bought a truck that was full of rust and bullet holes, and he said he’d help me restore it. Then we broke up, so I had to figure out how to do it on my own. After that I apprenticed for a while, working as a bikini bartender to get by. Then I went to fabrication school. It was important to me that I didn’t come off as some stripper to the guys, I needed to do the work to prove myself.As I built my reputation as a welder, I started getting a lot of attention online. People were like “Who’s the blond welder?” so I used that to my advantage and made the Instagram The Blue Collar Barbie.I work a blue-collar job, but I also embrace my femininity. I always have. I’ve spent thousands of dollars on my hair. I have Botox. I have fake tits. I get my nails done. But that doesn’t stop me from getting dirty and working hard.I do think there was resentment from other people who do this work. A lot of men were like, “Why is she getting all this free shit from brands?” But I stuck with it and became a better welder than a lot of men out there, and that’s how I earned respect in my field. When I got better at my job, I started showing off more skin, because why not maximize everything I can? Why wouldn’t I? That doesn’t negate the fact that I’m actually a really badass welder.View image in fullscreenDe’Laney Ortiz: ‘I signed up with an agency for good-looking dog walkers’30, actor and gig worker in New York CityI’ve done pretty much every side gig imaginable. Hospitality, babysitting, watching someone’s dog, coaching kids’ basketball. I’ve noticed people treating me better, or sometimes worse, because of how I look. I would say people can be standoffish and on guard, especially in the hospitality industry, because they think that people must tell you that you look good all the time. They treat you a bit meaner to humble you. Which is weird, because all I’m trying to do is ask if they want some wine or a cocktail. I’m not trying to hit on anybody.I’ve just signed up with a dog-walking service, Hot Dogz, which is an agency for people who want good-looking people to walk their pets. Since I do a lot of gig work, I’ve gotten used to these weird job experiences. When it comes to dog walking, people like the idea of somebody kind of cute that they get to deal with on an every other day basis. They do vet us – it’s not a gimmick, and it’s not guys looking for a sugar mama. We can talk and joke around, but I try to be professional. When there’s that mutual respect, whether it’s a client or myself, then I’m like, “OK, we can connect here and it’s not all about what I look like.”View image in fullscreenCarter Sherman: ‘Getting camera-ready has added an hour to my day’32, co-host of the Guardian podcast Stateside with Kai and Carter,New York CityI majored in magazine journalism, at a time when I wasn’t thinking at all about being on camera or what I looked like. Now as a podcast host,I’m on camera up to four to five times a week. I love what I do. At the same time, getting ready has added an hour to my day. And I don’t think I’m even seriously investing that much in my appearance. I’m doing the bare minimum to look professional. I’m going through my makeup much faster, and straightening my hair more often than I have since high school. I couldn’t put a dollar amount on how much I’m spending on my appearance, but I’m definitely paying more to replenish products than I did before.I haven’t gotten many comments from viewers on my looks, but the ones that I do unfortunately stick with me more than I’d like. I got one comment, below the line, that said I needed to eat a hamburger. I was like, if I was heavier, you’d be making comments about that. There’s no way to win. When I don’t get those comments, that probably means I hit the acceptable threshold of what I should look like.I’m at the age where I’m noticing lines forming on my face. I have friends who have gotten Botox or filler, but I have deep feminist misgivings about it. I have decided that I would prefer to not do it at all, but if I get to a place where I really feel uncomfortable and unable to do my job because of my insecurities, then I would give myself permission to do something about it. I go back and forth wondering, what is the right way to think about this? It does take a lot of mental energy trying to figure out what my stance is on this exactly.View image in fullscreenCalvin Rust: ‘I tell my crew to brush their hair’24, home builder and content creator, Meridian, IdahoMy dad is an engineer, so I come from a more white-collar background. I think in the home-building industry more generally there’s a bit of stigma about dwelling on your appearance; it’s like, your work speaks for itself. But your first impression can help with your goals. I now have a crew of guys. I always tell them that you can’t control many things, but what you can control says a lot about you. So it’s the little stuff: brushing your hair, working out, taking care of your body. I tell my guys: if you’re currently working on my crew but you want to be a job site super, looking good is going to set you apart.Our TikTok started because we just had a slow day. I threw a couple of videos up, and one took off. We thought it was fun, so we kept doing it. Over time, it morphed into a brand. Now we have 500,000 followers. We’re aiming to be a pretty big custom builder in the Idaho area. Before TikTok, we just framed houses. Now, we’re building them. That brings this more self-imposed pressure, because a framer can dress one way, but a general contractor works with clients, who appreciate someone who dresses well.Retention is really important in social media, so we take note of what works well, and so much of that is visual: cowboy boots versus work boots, or tennis shoes versus basketball shoes. It’s a little micro social experiment with every video we put out.When it comes to TikTok, there is a specific look that does well. The workwear company Brunt once sent me this jacket. It’s a nice olive green with a hood. I got it for free, but it probably costs over $100. I’ve noticed that when I wear that jacket, my videos do really well – 30-40% better than the ones where I do not wear that jacket.View image in fullscreenJaime Maser Berman: ‘It starts to feel like The Substance’48, publicist, New JerseyPublicists and beauty journalists often get to try treatments for free and I think people are just like, “I would never be able to pay for this on my salary, or that sounds like a fun story to write so maybe I will go and get this.” And all of these women kind of start to morph in a way that feels ever so slightly like Demi Moore in The Substance. And it’s a little bit trippy. But I realize I’m talking out of both sides of my mouth – like I do the same thing, but it feels like I do it very conservatively.It’s a badge of honor to be in your 40s and 50s in this industry. I am constantly engaging with people who are 15-20 years younger than me at work. That can be daunting. So I do the part: I get my hair colored every few weeks, I get Botox. I’m doing everything I can to look my age, but young for my age. You want to say, “I’m really proud to be 48!” But only because you want people to say, “Oh my God, you’re 48? I thought you were 40!”I love my job. But do I worry as every year passes? Yes. Sometimes when my younger colleagues say the year they graduated college, I am absolutely flummoxed. In my more insecure moment, I worry if I’ve aged out of my job. I hope the answer is no.

title: In the footsteps of the Victorians on the Isle of Man | Isle of Man | The Guardian
description: Steam trains, horse-drawn trams and glorious coastal paths are all part of the adventure on a new self-guided walking tour of the island
Author: Phoebe Smith
Headline: Steam trains, horse-drawn trams and glorious coastal paths are all part of the adventure on a new self-guided walking tour of the island
Content: On the coast path high above the west coast town of Peel.Photograph: Phoebe SmithView image in fullscreenOn the coast path high above the west coast town of Peel.Photograph: Phoebe SmithIsle of ManIn the footsteps of the Victorians on the Isle of ManSteam trains, horse-drawn trams and glorious coastal paths are all part of the adventure on a new self-guided walking tour of the islandPhoebe SmithTue 11 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 06.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the shores of Douglas Bay, I could barely see the sand. Crammed on to the beach, on every available inch, were tourists bustling for the best spot. Luckily, I wasn’t there at the same time. I was looking at a black and white photograph taken some 135 years earlier, displayed in the Manx Museum in Douglas, the Isle of Man’s capital. When I’d stepped off the ferry earlier that day, the crescent-shaped beach was still there – but the crowds weren’t.The self-governing British Crown dependency in the Irish Sea has always been a haven for outsiders. From the early hunter-gatherers who ventured here in 6500BC, to the Irish Celts (who brought over Christianity in the fifth century) and Vikings who established Tynwald (one of the oldest continuous parliaments in the world) to the Victorian tourists who transformed it into a popular holiday destination.Tourism boomed after the advent of steamboats in the 1830s, bringing hundreds of thousands to the island. Visitor numbers rose from 60,000 a year in 1863 to 350,000 by 1887. Last year, there were 329,613 visitors.View image in fullscreenThe seafront at Douglas in the late Victorian era.Photograph: Photo Art Collection/Alamydouble quotation markOn the horse-drawn tramway, tourists shared benches with local people carrying shopping bags while children squealed with delightI’d come here to try out Inntravel’s new self-guided walking holiday, a four-night, single-centre package with a booklet full of hikes to try each day and a Go ExploreHeritagePass, which offers unlimited public transport and entry to many attractions. It promises a car-free adventure using footpaths and heritage railways to explore more than just the coast.Arriving in Douglas byferry from Heysham, Lancashire, early on a Sunday morning, the capital was barely stirring. Along the promenade, black guillemots and herring gulls outnumbered people. Grand Victorian hotels, painted in bold blues, greens and yellows, lined the waterfront. TheTower of Refugesat on its tiny islet, illuminated by a sliver of sunlight cutting through the cloud.I climbed aboard the island’s 150-year-old horse-drawn tramway. Tourists shared benches with local people carrying shopping bags as children squealed with delight as the horse trotted along the seafront.Swapping literal horsepower for electricity, I boarded the narrow-gauge railway towardsGroudle Glen. Taking Inntravel’s advice, rather than heading there directly, I hopped off at a request stop nearGarwick Beach, a woodland-backed pebbled cove on theRaad ny Foillan(the Way of the Gull), a 100-mile coastal path that circles the island and is well-known to long-distance hikers.View image in fullscreenDouglas marina.Photograph: Joshua Burgess/Getty ImagesThe variation on this walk was that the trail led inland throughBallannette nature reserve, where wrens loudly trilled from the brush and greylag geese bobbed across the lakes. The path then diverted to the ruins ofSt Adamnan’s churchwith its Celtic crosses dated from between the seventh and 10th centuries. Finally, I reached the fairytale setting of Groudle Glen, where the wheel at the watermill churns and the sunlight spools through the tree canopy of beech, birch and larch.That evening I settled into theHalvard hotel,a 20-room boutique property in the heart of town, dining at its restaurant, which makes pub grub (burgers, pasta, stew) with local Manx ingredients, served with views of the sea.The next day I headed west on another Victorian legacy: the island’ssteam railway. Atthe Level, a request stop so short only passengers in the last carriage can disembark, Gore-Tex-clad hikers stepped off the train clutching walking poles. But with my insider guide in hand, I continued to Port Erin and rejoined the Raad ny Foillan. Purple spring squill and bright yellow gorse lined the path as it climbed and fell in a rollercoaster of colour, rabbits darting at my feet.View image in fullscreenA view of the Calf of Man.Photograph: AlamySoon I reached one of the island’s highlights: the Calf Sound, where the Calf of Man, a small island separated from the mainland by half a mile of sea is home to a colony of grey seals, accessed by boat trip.My route continued along the water but then diverted inland to Cregneash, one of the last strongholds of the Manx language – a type of Gaelic – and the oldest open-air folk museum in the British Isles (founded in 1938). Here, costumed guides explain traditional crofting life while rare four-horned Manx Loaghtan sheep graze nearby and prehistoric stones stand in a circle above the village – things I would have missed had it not been for my recommended detour.Rejoining the coast, I reached the Chasms, where the remains of an 1898 tourist cafe – which had to run with no water or electricity – cling dramatically to the cliffs. Though it closed in the 1960s, walkers and climbers still come to peer down into the sea-carved fissures below. I finished the day with the daily catch and chips in Port Erin before catching the bus back to Douglas, stomach and heart full.double quotation markPerhaps the island’s greatest success will not be resurrecting its Victorian heyday, but offering travellers the chance to explore without turning an ignition keyFor my last full day I placed my trust in the Inntravel guide again and headed to Peel, the island’s medieval capital, where the remains of Peel Castle dominate St Patrick’s Isle, connected to the mainland by an artificial causeway. Wandering amid ruins, I listened to tales of former residents – including monks, kings, the military and the Moddey Dhoo (the legendary black dog said to haunt the castle’s ramparts) on an audio guide, included with the Go Pass.Lunch was a paper tray of queenies – locally caught scallops simply pan-fried in butter – from the Fish Bar stall at the harbour before I climbed toCorrin’s Folly, built in 1806 by a wealthy landowner. Once more my guidebook took me away from the well-known coast and inland, toKnockaloe, site of one of the largest first world war internment camps in the British Isles – now just fields. More than 23,000 internees passed through its once barbed-wire perimeter, includingJoseph Pilates, who developed his eponymous exercise system while interned here. I followed directions to a bus stop to head home, wandering through pretty woodlands and along the banks of a stream.View image in fullscreenCregneash village is one of the last strongholds of the Manx Gaelic language.Photograph: David Chapman/AlamyBack in Douglas that evening, sampling locally brewed beer atWine Down, it was easy to imagine those black-and-white photographs filling with colour once more. But perhaps the Isle of Man’s greatest success will not be resurrecting its Victorian heyday, but rather offering the chance for travellers to explore without ever turning an ignition key. Given the climate crisis and rising carbon emissions, that makes this place feel less like a throwback and more of a glimpse into the future of sustainable travel.The trip was provided by Inntravel. title: Can I make my house less dusty? I spent four weeks experimenting to find out | Homes | The Guardian
description: Some household surfaces do attract more dust – but changing your home’s climate can make a difference
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Some household surfaces do attract more dust – but changing your home’s climate can make a difference
Content: ‘I’m not imagining things… some surfaces really are better at collecting dust.’Composite: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreen‘I’m not imagining things… some surfaces really are better at collecting dust.’Composite: Guardian DesignHomesCan I make my house less dusty? I spent four weeks experimenting to find outThe phrase ‘dust magnet’ isn’t completely metaphorical. Some household surfaces do attract more dust – but changing your home’s climate can make a differenceIlana BeanTue 11 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 19.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.For years, I’ve complained about an Ikea shelf in my home that seems to attract dust at an impossible speed. Eventually, my frustration gave way to curiosity: what’s actually happening, scientifically? Is there anything I can do about it, besides just continuously dusting?The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.I’m not imagining things, says Nisa Salim, a materials engineer and associate professor at Swinburne University of Technology. While an object’s placement in the home and airborne particle levels make a difference, some surfaces really are better at collecting dust.Clean like you mean it: the ultimate guide to spring cleaning your homeRead moreLarge particles settle by gravity, but finer ones are influenced by Van der Waals forces – weak molecular attractions that strengthen when there’s more contact between a particle and a surface, says Salim. Rough, porous materials have more contact points, giving dust more opportunities to stick.My shelf doesn’t feel rough, but Salim says “even if a surface appears smooth to the naked eye, at the microscopic level it may contain tiny peaks, valleys and defects that can trap particles”.The phrase “dust magnet” isn’t completely metaphorical, either. Some surfaces literally attract dust through electrostatic forces, which resemble magnetic attraction. When materials rub together, electrons can transfer between them, leaving surfaces charged; because many dust particles also carry charges, they’re often drawn to these surfaces.Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best readsAcrylic, PVC, polyester and polypropylene are poor electrical conductors, so they hold on to electrical charges longer. Metal, by contrast, conducts electricity well, so it passes charge along and neutralises quickly. Without that lingering static charge to attract fine particles, metal surfaces collect less electrostatic-charged dust.It’s also not surprising if your home seems unusually dusty at certain times of year. “Humidity or water molecules in the air help electrical charges dissipate from surfaces,” Salim says.During colder, drier months, or in air-conditioned spaces, there’s less moisture to neutralise electrostatic charges, so dust clings more stubbornly.Can I make my furniture less dusty?After consulting with Salim, I ran a month-long experiment testing small tweaks based on dust science to see what makes a difference in my own home. Instead of my dust-magnet shelf, I tested a coat rack made of similar materials because it was smaller and easier to monitor.Week one: control conditionsView image in fullscreenIlana Bean’s dusty coat rack, week one.Photograph: Ilana BeanFirst, I unplugged my air purifier and dehumidifier and measured how much dust naturally accumulated over one week.In each photo, including this one, I’ve swiped a finger through the dust to make the contrast more visible. Here’s what the starting point looked like.Week two: anti-static sprayView image in fullscreenThe coat rack on week two, sprayed with an anti-static product.Photograph: Ilana BeanAfter dusting and wiping the coat rack, I sprayed it with an anti-static product, which would theoretically reduce electrical charge and, in turn, dust.I left the right side untreated for comparison. It doesn’t show up well in photographs, but everyone who saw it in person – and concentrated for a moment – identified that the left side was slightly less dusty.Verdict:Since the results are nearly imperceptible, I can’t recommend anti-static spray as a dust solution.Week three: adjusting the humidityView image in fullscreenIlana Bean’s dusty coat rack, week three, after the dehumidifier had been running.Photograph: Ilana BeanI usually run a dehumidifier at all times, because my bathroom fan is weak, but had turned it off for the experiment. Since dry air increases static cling, I wanted to test whether my usual attempts to control humidity were actually contributing to my dust problem, so I plugged it back in for a week.Verdict:My dehumidifier habit may have been working against me, because the drier conditions definitely produced a dustier coat rack.Week four: running an air purifierView image in fullscreenIlana Bean’s dusty coat rack, week four, after the air purifier had been running.Photograph: Ilana BeanThis idea is more intuitive. Air purifiers, particularly ones fitted with Hepa filters, reduce the concentration of airborne particles. If you have less dust in the air, you get less dust on any given surface. I cleaned the coat rack, unplugged my dehumidifier and plugged in myair purifierinstead, placing it about a metre from the coat rack.Verdict:After one week the coat rack collected noticeably less dust than in any previous test. I was, admittedly, disappointed. I’d hoped the humble anti-static spray would turn my life around, but I’m crowning the air purifier the winner.What does a low-dust home actually look like?View image in fullscreenGentle House in Brunswick, Melbourne, designed by interior design firm The Stylesmiths.Photograph: Kate Enno PhotographyRichard Misso, an interior designer and creative director of the Stylesmiths, says he spends a lot of time thinking about dust.His clients want homes that are beautiful but low maintenance. So he points them away from dark floors, glass surfaces, open shelving, excessive decoration and intricate joinery.He says that although gloss surfaces collect slightly less dust, matte finishes are often lower maintenance, because they’re more visually forgiving when dust inevitably lands.Misso cites Melbourne’s Gentle House, which was designed by his company. The Brunswick home has a “calm, pared-back” palette from its timber, brick and stone materials, rather than decorations that require frequent cleaning, he says.Ultimately the easiest way to have a low-dust home is simple: plan fewer places for it to collect in the first place.Explore more on these topicsHomesAustralian lifestyleInteriorsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Houseplant hacks: can willow water act as a rooting hormone? | Houseplants | The Guardian
description: This is one of those rare homemade concoctions that works, though it might not outperform a good commercial product
Author: Gynelle Leon
Headline: This is one of those rare homemade concoctions that works, though it might not outperform a good commercial product
Content: You can make willow water from twigs.Photograph: Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenYou can make willow water from twigs.Photograph: Getty Images/iStockphotoHouseplant hacksHouseplantsHouseplant hacks: can willow water act as a rooting hormone?This is one of those rare homemade concoctions that works, though it might not outperform a good commercial productGynelle LeonTue 11 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 06.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe problemPropagation is where good intentions go to die. You take a cutting, pop it in water and wait. Sometimes you are rewarded with roots, sometimes not. So the internet offers an organic aid that sounds almost too folkloric to be true: brew your own rooting hormone from a willow tree.The hackWillow contains indolebutyric acid, auxin (a plant hormone that is the main active ingredient in commercial rooting powders), along with salicylic acid, better known as the basis of aspirin.The methodCut a few thin willow twigs, ideally fresh new growth taken in late winter or early spring when the hormone is most concentrated. Strip off any leaves, cut the stems into short pieces and lightly crush them. Then steep them in a jar of boiling or cold water for 24 to 72 hours, until the water takes on a faint colour. Strain out the twigs. Stand your fresh cuttings in the willow water to root.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHouseplant hacks: does putting gravel at the bottom of pots improve drainage?Read moreThe testI made a batch from twigs I found under a local willow tree and used it to root pothos and tradescantia cuttings, alongside a control group in plain water. The willow-water cuttings rooted faster and none of them rotted. Two of the plain water cuttings grew shorter roots more slowly; the rest went limp.The verdictThis is one of the rare homemade hacks that stands up. Indolebutyric acid promotes growth, while salicylic acid helps protect the cutting from bacteria and fungi that cause rot. It won’t outperform a good commercial hormone on a difficult plant, but for everyday houseplant propagation, willow water is ancient wisdom that genuinely works.Explore more on these topicsHouseplantsHouseplant hacksGardening adviceGardensfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: They cannot even flush their toilets: life in east London blocks where taps often run dry | Water | The Guardian
description: Devons Road estate residents describe months-long ordeal of not being able to wash, clean or cook for much of the day
Author: Nimra Shahid
Headline: Devons Road estate residents describe months-long ordeal of not being able to wash, clean or cook for much of the day
Content: Chagford House, Devons Road estate, which has been affected by water shortages, with supply turned off for hours each day.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianView image in fullscreenChagford House, Devons Road estate, which has been affected by water shortages, with supply turned off for hours each day.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianWaterThey cannot even flush their toilets: life in east London blocks where taps often run dryDevons Road estate residents describe months-long ordeal of not being able to wash, clean or cook for much of the dayHundreds in London flats left without regular running water since last yearNimra ShahidandDamien GayleTue 11 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChristmas Day in eastLondon. Beatrice Asante empties a bag of potatoes into her kitchen sink and turns on the tap. Nothing. She turns it off and on again. Still nothing. What now?Asante rushes out to the only shop that is open, the local Nisa convenience store. She buys several big plastic bottles of water. Enough, she thinks, to make dinner and to last until the taps start running again.Seven months later and as parts of the country brace for a fifth heatwave, Asante still cannot rely on tap water. She is one of hundreds of householders in housing association flats on the Devons Road estate in Tower Hamlets who have been left for up to a year without a reliable supply. Only now, after months of delay, is the landlord mobilising to have the problem repaired.It is difficult to understand just how much we rely on running water – until it is taken away. Residents of the nine blocks affected have been left unable to properly wash themselves, clean their homes or cook. For long stretches each day, they cannot even flush their toilets.View image in fullscreenBeatrice Asante: ‘You can’t put a price on it. Water is essential.’Photograph: Linda Nylind/The Guardian“You can’t put a price on it,” Asante says. “Water is essential. Even if you haven’t got food, [if] you can drink water or have a very nice bath, you are OK.”Rajia Begum and Jasmine Begum are two mothers living and raising their families in east London. Both have been without a reliable supply of water this year.Like others with whom the Guardian spoke, they often only get running water in the middle of the night. “Everything [we] do is after 1 o’clock at night,” Rajia says. “We can’t sleep. [Instead] we do cooking, washing toilet, everything.”In July, she went three days without any water at all. Her landlord, Poplar Harca, sent the family three five-litre bottles. But when one toilet flush requires five litres, 15 litres is insufficient to keep a household going. “We can’t clean,” she says. “It’s a messy house. Because without water how can it be possible?”View image in fullscreenWater bottles stored in the flat, ready for the next outage.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianTrying to raise children without a reliable supply of water presents particular problems. Rajia says her two daughters refuse to use the toilet at home because it is unclear when it can be flushed. As a result, they have become unwell.In this deprived part of east London, many residents of these estates are in poverty, or are affected by disability. For many, English is their second, or even third language. They are among the most marginalised people in the capital. But it seems remarkable that so many can have gone without water for so long without action being taken.View image in fullscreenAbdul Hai had a stroke in June. His wife believes he can no longer use his right side because of the stress from being without water for months.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianThe first time Poplar Harca came to deliver water to Razna Begum’s home after she made a number of attempts to get through to their phone line, the landlord came to check her taps turned on. “We are not lying, what would we do for our taps to turn on? We’ve had no water for the last eight months,” she says.The 64-year-old lives on the Devons estate with her youngest son, who has severe eczema, and her husband, Abdul Hai, who had a stroke in June and is now mostly bedbound.Razna believes her husband can no longer use his right side because of the stress from being without water for more than eight months. His visiting carers have advised that he should stay hydrated in the current heatwave. “Sometimes I think my husband could have a heatstroke because there’s no water,” she says.“We have emailed our Tower Hamlets mayor but no one has replied. They have stayed silent,” she adds. “This is a first-world country but there is no water.”View image in fullscreenA group of residents at Devons Road estate. Razna Begum (third from left) says: ‘We have emailed our Tower Hamlets mayor and councillor but no one has replied.’Photograph: Sadaf MoosviA Poplar Harca spokesperson said: “We recognise the disruption and frustration that intermittent low water pressure has caused residents, and we understand the impact this has had on day-to-day activities such as washing, cleaning and cooking. Residents continue to receive water, although pressure levels can fluctuate and, at times, may be insufficient for some households’ needs.“As soon as we became aware of the issue in December, we worked with Thames Water to investigate the cause, who confirmed that pressure to the affected buildings remains above the minimum level required under Ofwat’s guaranteed standards scheme.”The landlord said it did not need to pursue an emergency route to fit the pumps to fix the problem and therefore had to follow a statutory consultation process with leaseholders before major works could proceed.“Our focus has been on maintaining support for affected residents – including supplying bottled water on request as quickly as possible, providing alternative washing facilities and offering additional assistance to residents with support needs – while progressing the permanent solution as quickly as the statutory process and technical works allow.”View image in fullscreenA letter from the housing association Poplar Harca explaining the delays to the works to rectify the pressure problem.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianA spokesperson for Tower Hamlets council said: “We recognise the significant disruption and inconvenience that water supply issues have caused for affected residents and understand the concerns that have been raised.“Although the delivery and maintenance of water services within these buildings is a matter for the landlord, Poplar Harca, the council and the mayor’s office are working with them throughout to escalate residents’ concerns, seek updates on remedial works, and ensure appropriate support arrangements are in place, including provisions for vulnerable residents and access to bottled water where required.”Explore more on these topicsWaterLondonSocial housingHousingCommunitiesWater industryLocal governmentfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Matilda in pieces: what one mother’s suicide reveals about the carers broken by the system | Carers | The Guardian
description: Parent-carers of disabled children are exposed to chronic levels of extreme stress and often reach crisis point before help is available – then they face a ‘fight for basic support’, experts say. This is Matilda Davis’s story
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: Parent-carers of disabled children are exposed to chronic levels of extreme stress and often reach crisis point before help is available – then they face a ‘fight for basic support’, experts say. This is Matilda Davis’s story
Content: Evidence heard at Matilda’s inquest showed a person engulfed by stress in the final weeks of her life.Photograph: GuardianView image in fullscreenEvidence heard at Matilda’s inquest showed a person engulfed by stress in the final weeks of her life.Photograph: GuardianCarersMatilda in pieces: what one mother’s suicide reveals about the carers broken by the systemParent-carers of disabled children are exposed to chronic levels of extreme stress and often reach crisis point before help is available – then they face a ‘fight for basic support’, experts say. This is Matilda Davis’s storyJosh HallidayTue 11 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 05.54 EDTShareTwo days before she died, Matilda Davis issued a plea on Facebook. Sharing a study that found more than 40% of parent-carers had considered suicide, she called for “greater awareness, action and change” in Britain’s broken social care system. “This speaks the words I can’t,” she wrote.Matilda, known as Tilly to her family and friends, had spent years battling for support in a regime that close observers and those who rely on it often say is increasingly confusing, fragmented and difficult to navigate.Her seven-year-old son, Jude – not his real name – has significant disabilities. She was, her friends said, an “absolutely inspirational” mother, juggling care for Jude’s five-year-old sister Lilly – also a pseudonym – alongside his appointments at therapy, physio, hospital and two schools, as well as the significant financial and administrative burden.She cherished every moment with her children. “Tilly cared more than anyone I know,” said her sister Georgina Davis, 35. “It was what she lived for.”On 3 October last year, Matilda, 36, was found dead in the bathroom of their home in Stratford-upon-Avon in the West Midlands.She had killed herself a day after saying she felt “completely exhausted” by her responsibilities, and “paralysed with anxiety” about the prospect of her looming divorce from her estranged husband, who the Guardian has chosen not to name.View image in fullscreen‘Tilly cared more than anyone I know,’ Georgina Davis said of her sister Matilda. ‘It was what she lived for.’After Andy Burnham promised the biggest reforms to social care in a generation, experts said Matilda’s death showed how carers were being “pushed to breaking point” by a broken system.“Health and social care services in England are failing disabled children and their parents are being left to pick up the pieces,” said Dr Siobhan O’Dwyer, one of Britain’s leading experts on family carers.“In his speech, the prime minister acknowledged that without support unpaid carers can break. But what does it mean to break? For Matilda it meant death by suicide, it meant dying alone and in pain because services failed to fully appreciate the impact of the caring role and the troubled marriage, and it meant leaving behind the children she loved more than anything else in the world.“That is a break that can never be healed, but it was entirely preventable. If the government really wants to stop other carers breaking, it’s going to need more than a heartfelt speech. It’s going to need real action.”View image in fullscreenMatilda Davis had struggled with her mental health since her son became critically unwell shortly after his birth. She gave up work as an art teacher to care for him full time.Composite: Guardian‘I won’t be here much longer’Evidence heard at Matilda’s inquest earlier this year, including GP records and disclosures to professionals, showed a person engulfed by stress in the final weeks of her life.Last August, she told her GP she was worried about her “ability to cope emotionally with the daily demands as a parent-carer living with a home environment, which is becoming increasingly stressful, full of anxiety and worry … My absolute focus is to ensure [Jude and Lilly] are spared the turmoil of the unrest and upset in the house.”Matilda had struggled with her mental health since Jude became critically unwell shortly after his birth. But two days before she died, she was in the “slight depths of ruin”, she told a friend in a voice note.“I’m just in pieces and I’m trying to hold it together with the children, but it’s so physically taxing and emotional with what I’m dealing with [Jude] alone,” she said. “I’m just breaking really. I’m just completely broken. I haven’t really got any physical strength in me.”Matilda had given up work as an art teacher to care for Jude full time.Social workers had not carried out a family care assessment, where professionals assess what support they might need, for almost four years by the time she died. They were due to visit the following week to carry out an updated plan.View image in fullscreenMatilda Davis told her divorce lawyer her day-to-day life was packed with ‘appointments, rehabilitation, admin, emails, phone calls, transporting/commuting’.On 2 October, Matilda told her divorce solicitor the worry was “overwhelming”. “My capacity to earn is basically nothing and will be long term,” she said.Her day-to-day life was packed with “appointments, rehabilitation, admin, emails, phone calls, transporting/commuting”, she said, which would become more complex over the coming years with Jude’s schooling and health needs.With her marriage coming to an end, Matilda said she was “desperately fearful” about the future of the family home, as she had sacrificed years of earnings to care for Jude full time. “The estate agents will not accept me as a non-earning single occupant and I have absolutely no where else suitable to go,” she said the day before she died, the inquest heard. She said she felt “financially trapped” and that it was “both physically and emotionally relentless at times”.That morning, her husband called social services to say he was concerned about Matilda’s mental health.He said she had expressed suicidal thoughts that morning by saying: “I won’t be here much longer and then you will all have to look after yourselves.”Social workers are obliged to act on welfare concerns within 24 hours and visited Matilda at home at 2pm the following day, a Friday.A note of the meeting, shared at the inquest, detailed how Matilda was “visibly upset and tearful” when they arrived and “expressed significant anxiety” about the visit.The coroner, Deborah Sewell, noted that Matilda spoke of the “emotional and psychological strain arising from relationship conflict, financial pressures, and the ongoing divorce proceedings”. Matilda told the social workers she had hit her head on the door in front of the children that morning “as a manifestation of emotional frustration”.Before they left the meeting, social workers suggested her husband look after the children that weekend and that Matilda stayed with her parents. She was reluctant to leave, having already expressed concern about how Jude would manage without her.When the social workers left at 2.30pm, Matilda “appeared calm” and there was “no indication of any suicidal ideation”, the note of the meeting recorded. Minutes later, she was dead.At the inquest in March, social workers admitted they did not ask Matilda whether she had thoughts of suicide despite knowing she was in significant distress. Nor was she directed to crisis organisations.Neither social worker who visited her that day had undertaken suicide prevention training. When told it is best practice to ask someone directly whether they have plans to kill themselves if they have expressed suicidal thoughts, one said: “Well, I’ve not done the training.”Asked whether they were concerned that Matilda had said a day earlier she “won’t be here much longer”, which they were told by her husband was a suicidal thought, the social worker added: “Obviously it is concerning she said that but she wasn’t using the word ‘suicide’.”Sewell issued a rare prevention of future deaths report in April to direct Warwickshire council to make suicide prevention training mandatory for 600 members of staff.The council said: “We extend our deepest sympathies to the family and all those affected by this tragic loss. Following Matilda’s death and the subsequent coroner’s inquest, we have implemented enhanced suicide prevention training for all social workers to equip staff with skills to identify when parents and carers need additional support and to help them to access it.“In addition, all agencies involved with this case will participate in a review to look closely at all the circumstances leading up to Matilda’s death. The purpose of the review will be to make recommendations for improving services and support.”View image in fullscreenMatilda Davis with her son. In the garden of his primary school in Birmingham, two apple trees and a rose bush have been planted in her memory.‘Love does not mitigate the overwhelming pressure’Inresearch publishedin 2024 – and shared by Matilda two days before her death – the University of Birmingham found 42% of parent-carers had thought about suicide, many times higher than the general population.Those caring for significantly disabled children are exposed to chronic levels of extreme stress that are “compounded by other factors like poverty, domestic abuse, or social isolation”, said O’Dwyer, who led the research.She said social workers often had an “excess of professional optimism” about parents’ ability to cope with the pressures of caring for children with complex needs, particularly when they saw a devoted, loving mother – and it was often women who took on primary care responsibilities – and would think she would never act on thoughts of self-harm because she loved her children so much.“But it is possible to love your children andbe pushed to the point of suicide,” O’Dwyer said. “Love does not mitigate the overwhelming pressure of caring for a disabled child in a broken system.”Contact, a charity for families with disabled children, said parents often reach crisis point before help was available and had to “fight for basic support”. Anna Bird, its chief executive, said parent-carers were being “squeezed from every direction: by the cost of living crisis, reduced services; and a support system that is increasingly confusing, fragmented and difficult to navigate”.In the garden of Jude’s primary school in Birmingham, two apple trees and a rose bush have been planted in Matilda’s memory. Twenty miles away in Stratford, her friends at a family club have raised money for a bench engraved with her name and a number for the Samaritans suicide helpline.Her sister Georgina described Matilda as “the most incredibly devoted mother”, draining her savings and driving hundreds of miles a week to get Jude the support he needed.“She would tell me how she had to really fight to get what she wanted and needed for [Jude],” she said. “[Often talking about] how exhausting it is having to continually have to battle to get the provision he so needs.”Matilda’s friend Francesca Roberts, a nursery manager, said she was constantly in awe of her ability to go “far beyond what any parent should have to do simply to access proper care and support”.“She absolutely adored her children and dedicated every part of herself to them,” she said. Matilda was “one of the most caring, devoted, and selfless people I have ever known,” she added. “She was the village that everybody dreams of having around them.”In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.org
