title: Canadian airline cancels flight after child refuses to wear seatbelt  | Airline industry | The Guardian
description: Flight from Victoria to Toronto forced to return to terminal after repeated attempts to secure child in seat failed
Author: Olivia Bowden
Headline: Flight from Victoria to Toronto forced to return to terminal after repeated attempts to secure child in seat failed
Content: The airport was closed by the time the incident was resolved, forcing passengers to travel the following day.Photograph: Graham Hughes/The Canadian Press/APView image in fullscreenThe airport was closed by the time the incident was resolved, forcing passengers to travel the following day.Photograph: Graham Hughes/The Canadian Press/APAirline industryCanadian airline cancels flight after child refuses to wear seatbeltFlight from Victoria to Toronto forced to return to terminal after repeated attempts to secure child in seat failedOlivia Bowdenin TorontoTue 11 Aug 2026 10.03 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 17.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Canadian airline cancelled a flight from Victoria to Toronto after a child refused to wear a seatbelt.The child was standing in their chair as the 6 August Porter Airlines flight taxied towards the runway, the airline said. Repeated attempts by an accompanying parent and crew to secure the child in their seat failed, so the crew elected to return to the terminal and have the two passengers disembark as “the aircraft could not take off in this unsafe condition”, it added.Brad Cicero, a spokesperson for the airline, told the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC) that all passengers had to disembark, as the time needed to remove only the child and their parent and refile paperwork meant the plane could not take off before the airport closed at 12:30am.“We apologise for the effect this had on other passengers, who were able to depart on a flight the following day,” he told the broadcaster.Singapore Airlines tightens seatbelt rules after turbulence flight deathRead morePassenger Aryeh Kozuchtold the Canadian Pressthat the child was not being unruly, and that online comments admonishing the parents did not “empathetically capture the situation”.“They just kept hiding under their seat,” he said. “If they got forced into [being] strapped in, they just kind of slid out underneath.”“This was a child that was in a tube with 150 people … They’re obviously terrified, and their response was to try and hide under the seat in front of them,” he said. “That’s so different than a kid running around and screaming.”Hillary Hertzberg, another passenger, said the airline could have acted faster. “It took for ever,” Hertzberg told CBC. “The kid eventually got off the plane at 11.30 so we had been on the flight for almost an hour at that point.”Porter Airlines said passengers were rebooked on a different flight the following day.Explore more on these topicsAirline industryCanadaAmericasAir transportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Scores dead in Colombia after powerful earthquake strikes west of country | Colombia | The Guardian
description: Quake of 7.4 magnitude collapses and severely damages buildings in several major cities, including Cali and Pereira
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Quake of 7.4 magnitude collapses and severely damages buildings in several major cities, including Cali and Pereira
Content: Rescuers race to find survivors as Colombia rocked by 7.4-magnitude earthquake – videoColombiaScores dead in Colombia after powerful earthquake strikes west of countryQuake of 7.4 magnitude collapses and severely damages buildings in several major cities, including Cali and PereiraTom Phillips, andThomas Grahamin BogotáTue 11 Aug 2026 06.14 EDTFirst published on Mon 10 Aug 2026 10.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 100 people died after a powerful earthquake struck westernColombia, collapsing and severely damaging scores of buildings in major cities including Cali and Pereira.The US and Colombian geological surveys reported that a 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck at 7.34am local time on Monday, with its epicentre in the western department of Chocó. It was felt in neighbouring Venezuela, still reeling from a deadly double earthquake on 24 June.The quake killed at least 132 people and more than 570 were injured as of Monday afternoon, according to the Colombian Association of Capital Cities, a group coordinating cities across the country.View image in fullscreenRescue workers raise their fists to call for silence as they attempt to find people under the rubble of a collapsed building in Cali.Photograph: Sergio Acero/Reuters“The ⁠national government has all of its capabilities deployed to protect lives, assist affected communities and deliver aid wherever it is ​needed,” Colombia’s president, Abelardo de la Espriella, said in a national address at about 1pm local time upon declaring ‌a national state of emergency. “The first priority is rescuing the people trapped under the rubble.”Western Colombia appeared to have suffered the most serious damage. Authorities reported 27 deaths in the Valle del Cauca department, 40 deaths in Pereira, the capital of Risaralda department, and at least two in Manizales, the capital of Caldas.The mayor of Manizales, Jorge Eduardo Rojas Giraldo, said at least 12 buildings and 20 homes had been partially or completely or destroyed.Map locating the epicentre of the earthquakeIn a video post, he told citizens to be “completely ready” for aftershocks. “Do not go back into the buildings yet. I know this isn’t easy but stay outside for a little while at least because there could be an aftershock.”Social media videos showed people searching for victims in the wreckage of a four-storey hotel in Cali and a woman sprinting from a building as it collapsed in Manizales.One videoshowed part of San José church in Pereira collapsing as palm trees around it shook.Another videopublished by the newspaper El Tiempo captured the moment a building gave way in Manizales.View image in fullscreenLocal people and rescue workers search for people under a collapsed building in Cali’s La Alameda neighbourhood.Photograph: Samir Rojas/Getty ImagesThe mayor of Cali, Alejandro Eder, said at least 20 buildings collapsed in his city and people were trapped inside.“Right now, we are trying to map out what has happened, firstly to protect lives and secondly to be able to push ahead with any kind of rescue that might be necessary,” he said, urging citizens to stay calm.He told residents to check their buildings for structural damage. “If you do not feel safe, if you see very large cracks, please leave the building.”In an interview, the mayor of Pereira, Mauricio Salazar, said 65 buildings had collapsed, with victims thought to be trapped in at least 15 of them. Five of the city’s hospitals were reportedly inundated with the injured.Buildings damaged after strong earthquake hits ColombiaRaúl Andrés Buitrago, the head of customer service at a business in Pereira, said he was leaving for work when the seismic alert on his watch went off.“There are often little tremors here,” he said. “But I’d never felt an earthquake like this. It started softly, softly, softly, then it felt like it was getting stronger every second.”He spoke of “horrible” scenes as he fled outside on to the street in the city centre, which is home to many old buildings. “The roofs started to fall in. The buildings collapsed in on themselves. The panic was terrible. They were the four longest minutes of my life.”View image in fullscreenRescuers work in Cali in the early hours of Tuesday morning.Photograph: Sergio Acero/ReutersThe governor of Chocó, Nubia Carolina Córdoba, said people had been injured and buildings severely damaged in the department’s capital, Quibdó.De la Espriella, who took office on Friday, said he would lead the government response. “Colombia has a president whose heart aches for his people and who will do everything in his power to help them in the most difficult moments,” he said in a video post.View image in fullscreenA woman carries her cat after an evacuation in Bogotá.Photograph: Raúl Arboleda/AFP/Getty ImagesDe La Espriella visited Quibdo where he promised rent subsidies for those who had lost homes, and then travelled to Cali. Authorities ‌in Cali, Armenia and Manizales announced curfews, with Cali’s mayor saying threats of looting had forced him to deploy police and military personnel to the streets. De La Espriella promised 1,000 additional security personnel for the city.Aviation authorities said the airports were damaged in Pereira, Manizales, Quibdó, Cartago, Armenia and Buenaventura.View image in fullscreenThe cathedral of Manizales was damaged in the earthquake.Photograph: John Jairo Bonilla/APNeighbouring Venezuela wasstruck on 24 June by twin earthquakesthat devastated the country’s northern coast, killing more than 6,000 people.The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the Trump administration – which hasthrown its weight behind Colombia’s new rightwing president– would provide $15.5m in emergency aid.Explore more on these topicsColombiaEarthquakesAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Colombia quake leaves more than 110 dead – as it happened | Colombia | The Guardian
description: This blog is now closed
Author: Tom Ambrose
Headline: This blog is now closed
Content: 21h ago01.04 EDTClosing summaryWe’re about to wrap up this live coverage of Colombia’s devastating earthquake but you can read an updatedfull report here– and below is a recap of the day’s news. It’s now a little after midnight local time.Search and rescue efforts were under way early on Tuesday in dozens of cities and towns in western Colombiaafter a powerful earthquake struck the region.At least 110 people were killed after the 7.4-magnitude quake struck on Monday morninglocal time, toppling buildings, damaging hospitals and infrastructure and trapping people beneath the rubble in Colombia’s strongest earthquake this century.More than 2,700 people had been reported missingby Monday night.New president Abelardo de la Espriella – sworn in just days earlier – declared a state of emergencyand said in an address to the nation that his government had deployed all of its capabilities “to protect lives, assist affected ‌communities and deliver aid wherever it is needed”.“The first priority is rescuing the people trapped under the rubble,” de la Espriella said after about 1,600 buildings had been damaged, including at least 61 that completely collapsed.Colombian volunteers and rescuers were sifting through rubble into Monday evening searching for survivors.A person among those who joined a make-shift crew in Cali – western Colombia’s largest city – said: “We are trying to get everyone out alive.”View image in fullscreenVolunteers help remove debris at a collapsed building in Pereira, western Colombia.Photograph: Gabriel Aponte/Getty ImagesLocal officials confirmed deaths across several regions, including the coffee region of Risaralda.Among the worst-hit areas was the city of Pereira, with at least 40 deaths reported; the department of Chocó, with at least 12; and the neighbouring Valle del Cauca department with at least 27, including 15 in Cali, Colombia’s third most populous city.The quake hit the remote Chocó region about 7.30am local time and was felt as far as Bogotá, the national capital, about 400km (250 miles) away,as well as in neighbouring countries Ecuador, Venezuela and Panama. The epicentre was in San Jose Del Palmar, a community of about 4,800 people, and the initial quake was followed by two aftershocks of 2.8 and 4.8 magnitude.Authorities ‌in the cities of Cali, Armenia and Manizales announced curfews in the aftermath of the quake, with Cali’s mayor saying threats of looting had forced him to deploy police and military personnel to the streets.The US state department announced it would provide $15.5mfor emergency shelter, food and other aid. Governments across Latin America also offered help.The earthquake comes less than two months after back-to-back quakes devastated parts of Venezuela, killing more than 6,100 people.ShareUpdated at01.32 EDT

title: The RBA likely believes it won’t need to hike rates again – but the worst thing it could do is say that out loud | Reserve Bank of Australia | The Guardian
description: When it comes to the Reserve Bank, there’s a whiff of a parent making a threat they have no intention of carrying out
Author: Patrick Commins
Headline: When it comes to the Reserve Bank, there’s a whiff of a parent making a threat they have no intention of carrying out
Content: The Reserve Bank of Australia board held rates at 4.35% on Tuesday, before the RBA’s governor Michele Bullock said ‘inflation remains too high’.Photograph: Mark Baker/APView image in fullscreenThe Reserve Bank of Australia board held rates at 4.35% on Tuesday, before the RBA’s governor Michele Bullock said ‘inflation remains too high’.Photograph: Mark Baker/APReserve Bank of AustraliaAnalysisThe RBA likely believes it won’t need to hike rates again – but the worst thing it could do is say that out loudPatrick ComminsEconomics editorWhen it comes to the Reserve Bank, there’s a whiff of a parent making a threat they have no intention of carrying outGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastTue 11 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 17.28 EDTShareEvery parent makes threats in an effort to get their kids to behave – and every parent hopes they won’t have to follow through.Some (most?) parents even make threats they have zero intention of carrying out.There’s more than a whiff of this strategy coming through in the Reserve Bank’s communication.RBA interest rates: Reserve Bank holds cash rate at 4.35% but threatens more hikes if neededRead moreThe RBA board in a unanimous decisionheld rates at 4.35%on Tuesday, as was widely anticipated.Thelast time they hiked rateswas in May, so about three months ago.Lots of water has flowed under the bridge during that relatively brief time, but the central bank’s latest forecasts show inflation still getting back to around the RBA’s 2.5% target in about a year’s time.The impact of the Middle East andhigh fuel priceshas not proved as immediately inflationary as feared, although the lingering effects of the global oil shock could take 1-2 years to fully flow through the system.And after three back-to-back rate hikes earlier in the year, “the economy appears to be slowing as expected”, the RBA board said in its statement.Even thehousing downturnis leaning against the need for another rate hike (although what’s happening in the property market “is not the main game” and won’t stop them hiking again if they need to).Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailBut in her press conference, Michele Bullock did not sound like a central bank governor who believes things are breaking her way.“Inflation remains too high, and the board remains concerned about the upside risks,” Bullock told journalists after the rate announcement.“We’ve already raised three times, and we will go again if we need to.”Bullock even delivered a rare personal view on what she thought would happen.“And I think, personally, that it’s quite possible we might need to go, but we’ll wait and see what the data tells us,” she said.View image in fullscreenThe RBA’s governor Michele Bullock speaks during a press conference in Sydney.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersBullock and the RBA’s rate-setting board really, really want us to know they are prepared to hike again.Again, this is despite the fact that inflation has come in lower than expected since the board last met, and unemployment a little higher.Yet, if anything, Bullock’s warnings have become even more strident.Why? Because at this point in the cycle, and despite their protestations, it’s highly likely that the board hopes and believes it won’t need to hike again.But the worst thing bank officials can do is say that out loud.As Bullock said: “It’s important people believe that we will act if we need to.”That heightened expectation of another rate hike can do a lot of the RBA’s work for it.Look at financial markets: the implied chance of another cash rate increase by the end of this year jumped from 53% before the decision, to 67% by the time Bullock had wrapped up her press conference.This is the real power of central bank “jawboning”, as we used to call it.Bullock and her fellow board members will be hoping inflation behaves before we all stop believing they will follow through on their threats.Explore more on these topicsReserve Bank of AustraliaAustralian economyInterest ratesInflationanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Former judge Baka elected new Hungarian president in another break from Orbán era – as it happened | Europe | The Guardian
description: The new president is a former judge on the European Court of Human Rights
Author: Jakub Krupa
Headline: The new president is a former judge on the European Court of Human Rights
Content: 09.26 EDTFormer judge Baka elected new Hungarian president in another break from Orbán eraFormer ECtHR and Hungarian Supreme Court judge András Baka has been elected the new Hungarian president.146 votes were cast: 140 in favour, and six against.András Baka, the nominee of the governing Tisza Party for president and former Supreme Court president, attends the presidential election during an extraordinary plenary session of the Parliament in Budapest, Hungary.Photograph: Zoltán Balogh/EPA72-year-old Baka is another example of the new government’s clear break with the Orbán era:the lawyer was removed from the post of the president of the Supreme Court in 2011 by the then prime mnister, three years before his term was set to expire. He later won a case at the European Court of Human Rights against Hungary.In his acceptance speech, Baka said he believed Hungary “reached a period in its history when a serious reflection is needed about the functioning of the state,” after the last two decades of “a serious crisis” under the previous government and with deep societal divisions.He will replace Viktor Orbán loyalistTamás Sulyokwho stood down – or was effectively removed – from the post last month.ShareUpdated at10.13 EDT

title: Hotel prices in Europe jump before total solar eclipse | Travel & leisure | The Guardian
description: Rooms in Icelandic capital Reykjavík cost double usual rate and Spain also enjoying strong bookings
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Rooms in Icelandic capital Reykjavík cost double usual rate and Spain also enjoying strong bookings
Content: Tourists in Reykjavik have been shelling out £587 on average for a room, according to Lighthouse Intelligence.Photograph: Oliver Sved/AlamyView image in fullscreenTourists in Reykjavik have been shelling out £587 on average for a room, according to Lighthouse Intelligence.Photograph: Oliver Sved/AlamyTravel & leisureHotel prices in Europe jump before total solar eclipseRooms in Icelandic capital Reykjavík cost double usual rate and Spain also enjoying strong bookingsEurope’s total solar eclipse: the best place to see itKalyeena MakortoffTue 11 Aug 2026 06.50 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 17.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHotel prices have surged in key European cities as hundreds of thousands of tourists flock to see the first total eclipse visible from the continent this century.Iceland’s capital, Reykjavík, has seen one of the biggest jumps in hotel room prices, being one of the few accessible locations to see the full eclipse before evening on Wednesday.Tourists there have been shelling out $793 (£587) on average to secure a room on Wednesday, a 98% jump compared with the same day last year, according to data from the travel and hospitality data group Lighthouse Intelligence.Spain is also steeling itself for an influx of tourists, as one of the best places on the European continent toview the total solar eclipse. The finance ministry said on Monday that it expected 460,000 overseas tourists to visit specifically to see the eclipse.The rate for a room in A Coruña in the north ofSpainwas up 135% compared with last year to $451 on average, while prices in Mallorca, where the eclipse is expected to be visible on the horizon at sunset, were up by 24% at about $448. In Santiago de Compostela and Bilbao, hotel room prices have risen 34% and 67% respectively.Solar eclipse mapAccommodation in small towns and villages in the eclipse’s path, as well as makeshift observatories set up by local enthusiasts, have been booked for months. There have been reports of US travellers taking part in house exchanges with people living in Spain’s Castilla y León, which is one of the best regions to view the eclipse.However, authorities in Spain are worried about an increased risk of fires, with police expecting 1.5m more car journeys than usual on Wednesday. They have warned that extraordinarily dry temperatures mean the smallest spark could lead to devastating forest fires, while traffic could end up blocking access for emergency vehicles if fires break out in rural areas.Authorities will undertake out a massive police operation and safety campaign, with plans to deploy 35,000 officers to help minimise risks. Virginia Barcones, the secretary general for civil protection and emergencies at Spain’s interior ministry, said: “We’ve had an extremely tough summer in Spain, with yet another series of major forest fires. That’s why we must restrict any kind of activity that could generate a spark.”Parking on hard shoulders or close to dry vegetation has been banned in Spain, as have barbecues and fireworks. The València region has closed its natural parks and banned walking on rural footpaths.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs of Monday evening, three large wildfires were burning in the provinces of Huelva, Segovia and Huesca. Fires have already scorched about 200,000 hectares this year – six times more than by the same date in 2025, according to the environment ministry.For those unable to make the journey, the US space agency Nasa has installed four high-powered telescopes in the small village of Villalibado in north-west Spain in order to livestream the eclipse to more than 10 million people.A partial solar eclipsewill be visible across the UKon Wednesday, where it will reach its maximum coverage at 7.12pm in London.Explore more on these topicsTravel & leisureSolar eclipsesIcelandSpainEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Heathrow says need for expansion clear as it loses title of Europe’s busiest airport | Heathrow airport | The Guardian
description: Air transport hub in west London reports 7.86m passengers in July, compared with 8.15m for Istanbul’s new airport away from the city
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: Air transport hub in west London reports 7.86m passengers in July, compared with 8.15m for Istanbul’s new airport away from the city
Content: Heathrow airport’s July passenger total was 1.5% down compared with the same month last year.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAView image in fullscreenHeathrow airport’s July passenger total was 1.5% down compared with the same month last year.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAHeathrow airportHeathrow says need for expansion clear as it loses title of Europe’s busiest airportAir transport hub in west London reports 7.86m passengers in July, compared with 8.15m for Istanbul’s new airport away from the cityGwyn Tophamand agenciesTue 11 Aug 2026 04.02 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 17.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIstanbul airport has overtaken Heathrow as Europe’s busiest airport by passenger numbers, leading theLondonhub to say its “case for expansion has never been clearer”.Figures published on Tuesday showed 7.9 million passengers passed through Heathrow’s terminals in July, compared with Istanbul’s 8.15 million.Heathrow’s passenger numbers for July fell, while London Stansted and Manchester both had record traffic for the month.For more than two decades before the pandemic, Heathrow served more passengers than any other European airport, according to annual figures from the trade body Airports Council International.EasyJet agrees to £5.7bn takeover by US private equity firmRead moreThe UK’s biggest airport, located in west London, lost its pre-eminent position in 2020 amid coronavirus travel restrictions before regaining it in 2023.Heathrow’s July passenger total was 1.5% down compared with the same month last year, partly due to the war on Iran, while the Turkish hub recorded a 2.3% increase.Heathrow’s two runways operate at near full capacity, and it is seeking government permission to build a third. A £33bn expansion plan would enable it to accommodate 150 million passengers a year.The airport said: “The case for expansion has never been clearer, as Heathrow was overtaken in July by Istanbul airport as the busiest hub in Europe.“Our plans will ensure the country gets the infrastructure it needs to stay competitive and will deliver all-important economic growth.”The comparison, however, may not fully bolster Heathrow’s case. The current main Istanbul airport was only opened in late 2018 and built on a brand new site away from the city and residential neighbourhoods, gradually replacing the existing Ataturk airport as the main international hub. It has a vastly bigger footprint and is able to operate 24 hours a day.The Turkish boom also owes much to its location near the Gulf, which has become the crossroads of international air travel.Istanbul airport’s chief executive, Selahattin Bilgen, said the news was “a significant milestone for our airport”.“Thanks to our three independent runways, which can be operated simultaneously 24 hours a day, our advanced operational capabilities and high capacity, we have successfully overcome the capacity constraints faced by many major global hub airports,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“With the addition of our fourth runway, which is set to become operational by the end of this year, we aim to take this growth even further by increasing the capacity we provide to airlines and passengers while elevating the quality of our services to the next level.”The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, launched a consultation on the renamed Heathrow expansion national policy statement in June, setting out the conditions for the third runway to go ahead.The then chancellor, Rachel Reeves, said at the time that she was determined to get “spades in the ground” in the current parliament, and for it to be built by 2035.Andy Burnham, however, has previously expressed concerns over Heathrow expansion, saying the plans divert infrastructure investment “away from the north and traps it in London”.Heathrow’s chief executive, Thomas Woldbye, said: “Expanding Heathrow will help ensure the UK remains home to Europe’s leading hub and continues to benefit from the trade, investment and tourism that increased connectivity will bring.”London Stansted said it had recorded the busiest month ever in July, welcoming 3.1m passengers, a 6.3% increase year-on-year.Manchester also had a record July, serving 3.4m passengers.Explore more on these topicsHeathrow airportAir transportAirline industryTransportEuropeHeathrow third title: Gangs using Airbnb-type rentals as drug stash houses, top Belgian official says | Airbnb | The Guardian
description: Flexible short-term bookings used to store and pack drugs and stash weapons and cash, says Ine Van Wymersch
Author: Jennifer Rankin
Headline: Flexible short-term bookings used to store and pack drugs and stash weapons and cash, says Ine Van Wymersch
Content: Cocaine weighing approximately 200kg at the federal police East Flanders station in Dendermonde in June 2021.Photograph: Nicolas Maeterlinck/Belga/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCocaine weighing approximately 200kg at the federal police East Flanders station in Dendermonde in June 2021.Photograph: Nicolas Maeterlinck/Belga/AFP/Getty ImagesAirbnbGangs using Airbnb-type rentals as drug stash houses, top Belgian official saysFlexible short-term bookings used to store and pack drugs and stash weapons and cash, says Ine Van WymerschJennifer Rankinin BrusselsTue 11 Aug 2026 03.47 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 12.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAirbnb-type short-term rentals are being used as stash houses by criminal gangs for money, drugs, weapons and people, Belgium’s lead official in charge of countering drugs has said.The booming e-commerce sector is helping “enormously” to facilitate organised crime, Belgium’s national drug commissioner, Ine Van Wymersch, said.Authorities did not have a precise idea of the scale of the problem but criminals were taking advantage of the flexibility offered by short-term booking platforms, she told the Guardian.“You need someone to pick up a cargo from the harbour. You don’t know exactly when the boat will arrive. Well, you can hire anAirbnbapartment or studio for three days. It’s very flexible. If the boat is not coming to Antwerp but going to Marseille, there is free cancellation.”She said short-term rental companies had “a very good legal purpose” but needed to be more resilient to avoid abuse by criminals.View image in fullscreenIne van Wymersch said her priority is going after criminal money, which she describes as the ‘heart’ of the ‘multi-headed monster’.Photograph: Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP/Getty ImagesAt the beginning of August, police seized 3.3kg of cocaine and €4,845 (£4,140) in cash from an apartment rented on Airbnb in central Brussels, which was believed to have been used for storing and packing drugs, the news agency Belga reported. In 2024 when 11 people were sentenced for their role in a vast drug trafficking operation between Belgium and the UK, it was revealed that drugs worth €21m were seized from an Airbnb rental in Staden, West Flanders.A representative for Airbnb in Belgium declined to comment but directed the Guardian to recent remarks by Clément Eulry, Airbnb’s country manager for France and the Benelux.Hetold De Staandardthat such criminal bookings represented an extreme minority among the millions the company processes annually. He said every case was one too many and the company undertook various measures, including using artificial intelligence to identify suspicious bookings. He said reports of problematic renters were always notified to police and local authorities.Short-term rentals are only one facet of the modern economy making life easier for organised crime.Van Wymersch cited the ease of setting up anonymous email accounts, encrypted communications, cryptocurrency and the ubiquity of parcel delivery. “The fact that e-commerce is booming business is facilitating enormously organised crime.”She said delivery firms were also “very at risk” of being instrumentalised by organised crime, because “it is not a suspicious situation any more when you see that there is a white van stopping at your neighbour’s house and … a small box handed over”.View image in fullscreenAntwerp port, one of Europe’s main gateways for cocaine.Photograph: Olivier Hoslet/EPAVan Wymersch became Belgium’s first-ever national drug commissioner in 2023 after Antwerp was firmly established asone of Europe’s main gateways for cocaine.Her appointment followed a wave of drug-fuelled violence and threats. In 2022 the then Belgian justice minister had to live under police protection after an allegedplot to kidnap him was uncovered. Antwerp endured a spate ofgrenade attacks and the fatal shooting of an 11-year old girl, the victim of a conflict between rival drug gangs.Last year an anonymous investigative judge – who was forced to live in a safe house for four months – warned that Belgium riskedbecoming a narco statein an excoriating critique of the government’s response.The narco state warning originated with Van Wymersch. She agreed, she said, with her earlier opinion that “if we don’t do anything, we are at risk to become a narco state … where you don’t know any more who are the good guys and who are the bad guys”.Her priority is going after criminal money: “This multi-headed monster only has one heart and that’s the money.”Her strategy means targeting small businesses – hairdressers, nail bars or night shops – used for laundering money. Her message to local authorities was that they needed to inspect and investigate “the dodgy shop” in their neighbourhood: “It matters because all these small businesses are one big network.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShe said criminal gangs had changed their modus operandi, exploiting small business, rather than using the “big money-laundering constructions” of the past.Organised crime had morphed from top-down pyramid hierarchies bonded by trust into looser anonymous networks where criminals “don’t know to which network they are belonging any more”, she added.Illicit activities are outsourced to different gangs, who specialise in money laundering, procuring or using weapons. “It is really crime as a service and it’s very opportunistic,” she said.View image in fullscreenA 2019 seizure of heroin in Felixstowe in the UK. The seizure was made after British intelligence identified a container vessel suspected of carrying a large drugs shipment en route to Antwerp.Photograph: National Crime Agency/EPAAfter a rapid rise through Belgium’s judicial system, Van Wymersch is known for articulating an “iceberg strategy” to combat organised drug crime.The shootings and explosions are the visible part of the iceberg, she said, while below the waterline are harms not always linked to organised crime, from people killed by drivers under the influence, to victims of drug-fuelled domestic violence and sexual offences.While stressing the importance of the police, she said society needed to guarantee young people a stake to prevent them being drawn into drug gangs – essentially melting the iceberg. “We need to invest in warming up the temperature of the water,” she said citing education, anti-poverty strategies, housing and adequate pay for delivery workers.In Brussels, police recorded 101 shootings in 2025, reported by local media to be a record high, often resulting from turf wars between gangs. Van Wymersch sees a link between the increase in shootings and social problems, “because the people that are shooting are people without any perspective”.In Brussels 12.8% of people aged 15-29 are not in education, employment or training – above the national average – although numbers have been on a downward trend since the millennium.“It is naive to believe that a purely repressive approach will reduce the number of shootings,” Van Wymersch said. “We will see fewer shootings only when there are fewer vulnerable people. In fact, we need to strengthen the resilience of society as a whole.”The European Holiday Home Association, which represents Airbnb and other platforms, said the companies were best placed to respond.Van Wymersch said her team planned to be in touch with online booking platforms: “What we want to know now is what are the criteria for suspicious booking, what can we learn from that, how can we help you to be more resilient.”Explore more on these topicsAirbnbBelgiumEuropeDrugs tradeDrugsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Human rights groups sue Trump administration over ‘crippling’ ICC sanctions | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Lawsuit challenges executive order targeting international criminal court for investigating Israeli crimes in Palestine
Author: Alice Speri
Headline: Lawsuit challenges executive order targeting international criminal court for investigating Israeli crimes in Palestine
Content: People take part in a demonstration in defense of the international criminal court at Piazza Ugo La Malfa in Rome, Italy, on 16 July 2026.Photograph: Simona Granati/Corbis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople take part in a demonstration in defense of the international criminal court at Piazza Ugo La Malfa in Rome, Italy, on 16 July 2026.Photograph: Simona Granati/Corbis/Getty ImagesTrump administrationHuman rights groups sue Trump administration over ‘crippling’ ICC sanctionsLawsuit challenges executive order targeting international criminal court for investigating Israeli crimes in PalestineAlice SperiTue 11 Aug 2026 11.10 EDTFirst published on Tue 11 Aug 2026 10.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFour prominent US human rights organizations have accused theTrump administrationof using its “crippling” sanctions regime against the international criminal court (ICC) to undermine global efforts to prosecute war crimes and crimes against humanity.In alawsuitfiled in federal court on Tuesday, the groups – the American Friends Service Committee, the Center for Constitutional Rights, Human Rights Watch and the Open Society Institute – argued that the administration’s targeting of the ICC, as well as of groups and individuals affiliated with it or assisting its work, amounts to a “blatantly illegal attack on international justice”, the groups said.The suit challenges Trump’s February 2025executive order, which authorized sanctions on ICC officials, judges and others working to support its investigation of Israeli crimes in Palestine – one of 18 investigations into war crimes and crimes against humanity the Netherlands-based tribunal is overseeing.US groups sue Trump administration claiming ICC sanctions violate first amendmentRead moreThe US state department and justice department did not immediately respond to requests for comment.The US government has long opposed and sought to impede the work of the court – of which it is not a party – but those attacks escalated after the ICC prosecutor issuedarrest warrantsin November 2024 for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and former Israeli defense minister Yoav Gallant over crimes committed in Gaza. The US responded by sanctioning ICC prosecutors, judges, three leading Palestinian human rights groups andFrancesca Albanese, the UN special rapporteur on the situation of human rights in Palestinian territory.Earlier this summer, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, also escalated efforts against the ICC, announcing a campaign aimed at “dismantling” it by pressuring member states to leave the court.Those attacks, and Trump’s executive order, undermine access to justice for victims of major human rights violations and criminalize the work of those seeking to combat impunity by collaborating with the court – including the plaintiffs in the case – in violation of both constitutional protections for free speech and association and US obligations under international law, the lawsuit argues.“The Trump administration took the extraordinary step to not only deny Palestinians and victims of US torture equal access to justice, but to criminalize and punish them, their lawyers and advocates, and their partners,” said Katherine Gallagher, a senior attorney at the Center for Constitutional Rights who represents victims before the ICC. “All victims of international crimes – from Sudan and Ukraine toPalestineand Afghanistan – need and deserve to have an independent and strong ICC able to fulfill its mission of ending impunity, without fear or favor.”The individuals placed under US sanctions over their work for the ICC have been subjected to travel bans, have had their bank accounts closed or frozen, and access to digital services denied. Because of the dominance of US financial and technology institutions, the sanctions have trickled down and affected their ability to access services in other countries as well.But the sanctions also affected rights groups not directly targeted – including the four plaintiffs – by hindering their ability to represent victims before the court, make legal and policy submissions to it, or collaborate with the sanctioned Palestinian groups on litigation, advocacy campaigns, research and humanitarian aid efforts.“Because of the sanctions regime and the threat of severe criminal and civil penalties ... if I continued my work as a lawyer as before, I would have been or could be prosecuted or fined,” Gallagher said in a press conference held by the groups on Tuesday. “I have therefore ceased actively practicing before the ICC. [...] The government cannot dictate which clients lawyers can represent, which defendants are off limits from accountability, and what venue for justice and accountability are permissible.Shawan Jabarin, the director of the human rights group Al Haq, one of the Palestinian organizations targeted by the Trump administration over its work with the ICC, told the Guardian inan interviewlast year that the sanctions had left the group unable to access its bank accounts or process donations, leaving about 45 people without pay.But Jabarin also said the impact of the sanctions had extended beyond logistical matters and created a climate of fear by which longtime allies had cut communications with the group to avoid running afoul of the sanctions regime, with potential punishments of up to 20 years in prison and exorbitant fines.“Most of them – if not all – they stopped working with us or engaging with us formally and openly,” Jabarin said at the time of several US groups with which Al Haq had collaborated in the past. He had called on those partners at the time to “fight back with all means”.Tuesday’s lawsuit follows onefiled last monthby Democracy in the Arab World Now (Dawn), a Washington-based advocacy group focused on US foreign policy in the Middle East, and the New York-based Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide, as well as legal challenges brought by some of the sanctioned individuals themselves, includingAlbanese’s familyandthree sitting ICC judges.James Goldston, executive director of the Open Society Justice Initiative, a program of Open Society Foundations, which the Trump administration alsoexplicitly threatenedlast year, called the sanctions “an assault on the rule of law, independent judges and prosecutors, and civil society in the United States and around the world”.“Independent courts can function only when judges, prosecutors and rights advocates are free to do their work without fear of political retaliation. We believe that no one is above the law,” he said in the press conference on Tuesday. “The executive order shields the perpetrators of war crimes from scrutiny while punishing those who pursue accountability. Justice must be fair and impartial, not only directed at America’s adversaries.”Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationInternational criminal courtUS politicsLaw (US)PalestineIsraelMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Syrian court sentences Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia for war crimes | Syria | The Guardian
description: Verdict relates to atrocities committed during the country’s 14-year civil war in which about 500,000 people died
Author: William Christou
Headline: Verdict relates to atrocities committed during the country’s 14-year civil war in which about 500,000 people died
Content: Bashar al-Assad (pictured on the poster) and his brother Maher, who was also sentenced to death, fled to Moscow in December 2024.Photograph: Omar Sanadiki/ReutersView image in fullscreenBashar al-Assad (pictured on the poster) and his brother Maher, who was also sentenced to death, fled to Moscow in December 2024.Photograph: Omar Sanadiki/ReutersSyriaSyrian court sentences Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia for war crimesVerdict relates to atrocities committed during the country’s 14-year civil war in which about 500,000 people diedWilliam Christouin BeirutTue 11 Aug 2026 06.40 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 17.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Syrian court has sentenced the country’s former presidentBashar al-Assadand his brother Maher to death in absentia for crimes against humanity and war crimes during the 14-year civil war, in which about half a million people died.The two men fled to Moscow after being ousted by a lightning rebel offensive in December 2024 whichtoppled the dictatorial regime in just 11 days.The former president and his brother, who commanded the feared fourth division and was considered the regime’s top security official, oversaw a brutal crackdown in which government forces killed, arrested and tortured indiscriminately to crush protests that started in 2011.The court said Bashar al-Assad had been sentenced to death for crimes of “premeditated and intentional murder of more than one person and of children” as well as “torture, arbitrary arrest and crimes against humanity”.View image in fullscreenBashar al-Assad in 2023 at the signing of a  comprehensive programme of strategic and long-term cooperation between Iran and Syria in Damascus.Photograph: Matin Ghasemi/Borna News/ATPImages/Getty ImagesIt said it would pursue international legal avenues to try to prosecute the two men, but Russian officials have previously declined requests to extradite its former Syrian allies.The court also sentenced Atef Najib, Assad’s cousin and the former head of political security in Daraa, to death. Najib was responsible for the torture of a group of 15 young boys who had graffitied anti-Assad slogans on a wall in 2011 – an event that kicked off mass protests in the southern Syrian province, which then spread to the rest of the country.Najib’s trial was highly publicised, with pictures of him listening to proceedings while dressed in a prison uniform and held in a cage in court. The Syrian government has presented his trial as a landmark case in its pursuit of transitional justice, something experts say is key to healing divisions in the country.View image in fullscreenAtef Najib on trial in Damascus.Photograph: Mohammed Al Rifai/EPASyria has experienced explosions of violence in the post-Assad era. About 1,500 mostly Alawite civilians were killed in a wave of retaliatory killings in March 2025 after militants loyal to al-Assad attacked security forces. Al-Assad belonged to the Islamic Alawite sect – a minority group in Syria – and enjoyed strong support in the group’s coastal heartland during his rule.In July 2025, more than 1,700 people were killed in massacres in the Druze-majority province of Suweida when local fighting evolved into sectarian killings. Low-level violence has continued in northern Syria until the present day, particularly targeting Alawite civilians.View image in fullscreenSyrians celebrate the ruling outside the palace of justice in Damascus.Photograph: Bakr Alkasem/AFP/Getty ImagesSyrian authorities have taken steps towards transitional justice, establishing committees and arresting Assad-era officials, in an effort to end intercommunal violence.Al-Assad became president in 2000 at the age of 34, inheriting power from his father, Hafez. He had trained as an ophthalmologist in London and was not initially supposed to be president, but became the heir after his brother, Basil, died in a car accident.Though styled as a young reformer who was supposed to allow some liberalisation in Syrian politics and its economy, his legacy was largely defined by his brutal response to the country’s revolution. Under his rule, Syria’s fearsome security apparatus was given a free hand to arrest, torture and kill civilians on an industrial scale.Explore more on these topicsSyriaBashar al-AssadWar crimesMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: As conflict in the Middle East intensifies, India’s relationship with Israel deepens | World news | The Guardian
description: An Amnesty International report reveals that the country is now a key part of Israel’s weapons supply chain. Plus, Assam floods, student anger spreads and a song to put in rotation
Author: Niha Masih
Headline: An Amnesty International report reveals that the country is now a key part of Israel’s weapons supply chain. Plus, Assam floods, student anger spreads and a song to put in rotation
Content: Narendra Modi is greeted by Benjamin Netanyahu in Jerusalem last February.Photograph: Abir Sultan/EPAView image in fullscreenNarendra Modi is greeted by Benjamin Netanyahu in Jerusalem last February.Photograph: Abir Sultan/EPAThis Is IndiaWorld newsAs conflict in the Middle East intensifies, India’s relationship with Israel deepensAn Amnesty International report reveals that the country is now a key part of Israel’s weapons supply chain. Plus, Assam floods, student anger spreads and a song to put in rotationDon’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereNiha MasihTue 11 Aug 2026 02.55 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 04.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHello, and welcome back to This IsIndia.For this week’s newsletter, I’m looking at India’s evolvingrelationship with Israel, and how it has deepened as conflict swept across the Middle East. Why is it that India has formed an even closer bond with a country that has faced mounting international isolation and backlash over a military campaign in Gaza that has left the territory in ruins andkilled more than 70,000 Palestinians, – many of whom were children?Under Narendra Modi, India’s ties with Israel have taken on a different character, for a country that once championed the Palestinian cause and led the Non-Aligned Movement. To better understand it, I turned to Stanly Johny,Indian foreign policy expertand the international affairs editor at the Hindu. He told me it isn’t just a political or diplomatic shift, “it’s also at the strategic and defence level”.The evolution of India’s role was revealed in a recent Amnesty International investigation, which showed that India was now a key part of Israel’s weapons supply chain. This represents a fundamental change. For years, New Delhi had primarily been a major customer of Israeli weapons. But, through joint ventures and manufacturing partnerships, it is now a “significant contributor” to Israel’s weapons production, according toAmnesty, which offers the most extensive account so far of the scale of India’s involvement since the war in Gaza began.Indian companies, including state-owned enterprises, have delivered drone warheads, artillery shell casings, small arms parts and military vehicle components to Israeli military suppliers despite the substantial risk these could end up in weapons deployed in Gaza, it added.By examining publicly available shipment-level trade data, Amnesty said it traced hundreds of thousands of weapons components shipped from Indian factories to Israeli military suppliers between 7 October 2023 and 30 November 2025, including:390,516 small arms parts for military grade weapons564,970 parts of explosive ordnance298 components of military vehiclesMany western nations, including Britain, haverestricted or bannedarms supply to Israel over its conduct in the war, citing risks that the weapons could be used to commit or facilitate violations of international humanitarian law. (The United States accounts forthe overwhelming shareof major arms transfers to Israel.)An independent United Nations commission of inquiry concluded in September that Israel hadcommitted genocide in Gaza, and earlier this year another commission found that Israel is continuing to commit genocide bydeliberately targeting Palestinian children. Separately, the international criminal court hasissued an arrest warrantfor the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, accusing him of committing war crimes.Yet, the Amnesty report hasn’t resulted in any large-scale public debate or political backlash in India, despite some scattered media coverage. Johny believes this is a result of the support for Israel by Modi’s voter base. “There is a clear ideological confluence between Hindutva and Zionism,” he said. In rightwing circles in India and elsewhere, he argues, Israel is increasingly seen as a bulwark against the expansion of Islam.View image in fullscreenModi has long cultivated a personal rapport with Netanyahu.Photograph: Kobi GideonHindu nationalists have long admired Israel, viewing it as a model of a nationalist state that can assert itself in a volatile neighbourhood. Author PankajMishra chronicled this affinity ina 2017 essay, writing that his grandfather was among high-caste Hindus who saw Israel as an example of how to deal with Muslims “in the only language they understood: that of force and more force”.The war on Gaza doesn’t appear to have significantly shifted views. APew Research surveypublished in June found that more Indians view Israel favourably (32%) than unfavourably (28%). This is in contrast tothe decline of supportfor Israel in many western countries, including the United States, since the war.Modi, for his part, has cultivated a personal rapport with Netanyahu. In 2017, he becamethe first Indian prime minister to visit Israel, and Modi’s visit to Israel earlier this year came just 48 hours before Israel and the United States launched their attacks on Iran. The optics ofModi huggingNetanyahu on the tarmac, coupled with New Delhi’s noticeablymuted responseat the outbreak of war, were a clear sign of where India’s political establishment stands. It has not gone unnoticed. In July, after the US vice-president, JD Vance, rebuked Netanyahu by calling the US Israel’s “only powerful ally” left in the world,Netanyahu shot back: “We have some other friends, like a small country called India. It has 1.4bn people, and boy, do we have tremendous support there.”The government has previously declined to give a direct answer about weapons supplies to Israel. When asked in parliament in2024, external affairs minister S Jaishankar said that information is not in public domain and that exports of military products are guided by “national interest”. Amnesty identified three state-owned Indian companies – Munitions India Limited, India Optel Limited and Advanced Weapons and Equipment India Limited – supplying Israel with weapons, which it said, could expose India to the hazard of “complicity in ongoing genocide in Gaza”. Foreign ministry spokespersonRandhir Jaiswal responded thatIndia’s exports are governed by national laws and international obligations.The pushback has largely come from human rights activists, student bodies, trade unions, India’s left-leaning parties and theCongress party. The courts have offered no recourse, either. In 2024, a group of civil servants, activists and academicspetitioned the supreme court, demanding India suspend its military exports to Israel. The court dismissed the case, ruling that the matter fell within the discretion of the executive.“In India, you don’t see any anger towards the government for its relationship with Israel, despite the allegations the Israeli government is facing,” Johny said. This, he believes, is a sign that foreign policy debates in India are being stripped of moral concern.Weapons aren’t the only thing India has sent to Israel during this period. Thousands of Indian workers have also gone to Israel, in many instances toreplace Palestiniansbarred from entering the country after 7 October 2023. Last year, the governmenttold parliamentthat more than20,000 Indian workers, in construction work and caregiving, had moved to Israel after an agreement signed in November 2023.India, meanwhile, has shored up its own arms supplies from Israel. Between 2021 and 2025, New Delhi was Israel’s largest defence customer, accounting for 29% of total arms sales, according toStockholm International Peace Research Institute.But for Johny, India’s growing closeness to Israel is beginning to come at a cost. The war in Iran threatens India’s energy security and could have wider economic repercussions across the Gulf, home to a large Indian diaspora. “India has to continue to stay engaged with Israel, but it is important to restore balance to its approach to west Asia,” he said, adding that it needs to forcefully defend its own interests.What else we’re reading aboutView image in fullscreenTens of thousands have been displaced by floods in Assam.Photograph: Hafiz Ahmed/ReutersAssam floods |Floods in thenorth-eastern state of Assamhave killed 100 people and displaced tens of thousands of people. Three districts in particular – Sivasagar, Charaideo and Jorhat – have been hit hard. Deforestation and excavation, along with extreme rainfall induced by climate change, couldbe responsiblefor the unprecedented flooding, the Indian Express reported.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is IndiaNiha Masih takes a look at the stories, ideas and news makers of modern IndiaEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionStudent anger |After demonstrations over examination paper leaksrocked the central government, fresh protests have broken out in Jharkhand over alleged irregularities in state recruitment exams. Students marching to the State Assembly were met with tear gas, water cannons and baton charges. The state governmentagreed to scrap three exams, which will be held afresh.Skims debut |Kim Kardashian’s shapewear brand, Skims, is coming to India in partnership with Reliance Brands. It willopen storesin Delhi and Mumbai. Founded in 2019, Skims raised$225m in capital last year, valuing the company at $5bn.Vibe checkView image in fullscreenThe real people in Mumbai dealing with the impact of monsoons.Photograph: Yash ShethMumbai’s monsoon has been the backdrop of many Bollywood romances. But failing infrastructure means that life in the metro can become a logistical nightmare and a health hazard. The Mumbai-based photographer Yash Sheth (@yashsheth3) focuses his lens on this tumult with striking images that capture the rawness of the moment. And somewhere in between lies the magic of the rains. See more images from the monsoon serieson his Instagram page.Guest shelfA recommendation from someone with great tasteAnkur Tewari (@ankurtewari), singer and songwriterI’m tripping on the songFunk You, Pay Me, by Dhanji and Karan Kanchan, with a sample by RD Burman. The groove is super infectious and slaps, and Dhanji’s flow and the grain in his voice makes you want to move your body. These64 barscan make your day. (Ankur’s new album, Mr Faarigh, is out on 20 August.)Count itA number worth knowingView image in fullscreenChief minister of Uttar Pradesh state, Yogi Adityanath, whose administration outspends Modi on advertising.Photograph: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP£530mThe Yogi Adityanath-led state government in Uttar Pradesh has spent approximately £530m (Rs. 6800 crore)on advertisements and publicity since it came to power eight years ago, according toan analysis by Newslaundry. That’s more than the central government’s ad spend, which has been in power longer, the report said.Get in touchIt’s Independence Day on Saturday. We would love to hear from you: what does freedom mean to you? Tell us about moments, choices or things that make you feel free. Share your feedback by replying to this, or emailing us atthisisindia@theguardian.comand we may include your response in a future issue.Explore more on these topicsWorld newsThis Is IndiaIndiaSouth and central AsiaAmnesty InternationalNarendra ModiBenjamin NetanyahuIsraelnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Trump reportedly hid in catering container to board secret flight in Turkey amid Iran threat | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: Elaborate ruse was used to transport president to military flight from Air Force One in July
Author: Coral Murphy Marcos
Headline: Elaborate ruse was used to transport president to military flight from Air Force One in July
Content: 2:13Trump 'secretly switched planes via catering truck' amid Iran threat | Deconstructed – videoDonald TrumpTrump reportedly hid in catering container to board secret flight in Turkey amid Iran threatElaborate ruse was used to transport president to military flight from Air Force One in JulyCoral Murphy Marcosand agenciesTue 11 Aug 2026 02.46 EDTFirst published on Mon 10 Aug 2026 22.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump departed on a secret military flight from Turkey to Britain last month when the White House said he was flying aboard ⁠Air Force One, in an extraordinary ruse – prompted by an Iranian assassination threat – that involved hiding the president in an airport catering container, according to reporting from the Washington Post and the New York Times.The operation took place when Trump was in Ankara for a Nato summit with world leaders,according to the Post. The president reportedly boarded the old Air Force One jumbo jet in view of television cameras, and then was secretly shuttled minutes later to a smaller plane via an airport catering truck typically used to load meals and other supplies preflight, a US official told the Post.An official also confirmed the operation to theNew York Times. The Guardian has reached out to the White House and the US Department of Defense for comment.Trump boards and disembarks old Air Force One despite flying in separate plane for securityTrump’s actual location was concealed from journalists and some White House staff. A US official told the Post that a credible threat to Trump involvingIranset the “deception operation” in motion.The administration previously claimed that Trump left Turkey on 8 July on the former Air Force One. The president had alsoannounced on Truth Socialthat he would use the “former Air Force One” rather than the plane that flew him there, a new Boeing 747-8 gifted by Qatar.The trip to the Nato summit was the first international travel for the new plane, whose speedy upgrades triggered questions over its cost and security, ⁠and took place as hostilities escalated with Iran, which bordersTurkey.Before departing Ankara, Trump said on Truth Social that he would use an older, baby blue Air Force One plane “for old time’s sake” to RAF Mildenhall ⁠in Britain while the new plane stopped at the same base so US service members stationed there could tour the aircraft.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onplatform.x.com. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueA similar operation took place in 2000, when Bill Clinton used an unmarked executive jet to fly into Pakistan while sending his formal Air Force One as decoy.On this occasion, the journalists who thought they were traveling with Trump on the older Air Force One reported being advised to keep their window shades in the press cabin closed. The Post said some White House staff also believed the president was on board.When asked later by reporters why they had to keep their shades shut during the flight, Trump said it was because they were “probably on ​a dangerous flight”. He went onto say: “But if I go, you go. Right?”The C-32A carrying Trump flew to Britain, arriving at about 10.20pm local time with the older Air Force One and media arriving minutes later, the Post reported.The New York Times reported: “Mr Trump was brought by vehicle from the third plane that he had arrived on to the older Air Force One, boarded it through a different entrance and strode down the step from the upper left-side door as he would typically do, according to [a] US official.”Trump’s traveling press pool reported he climbed down the stairs of the older Air Force ⁠One at 10.56pm local time. He gave press a peace sign but didn’t walk over ​to talk to them. He then spent some ​time greeting service members before walking to the new, ​Qatar-donated plane.When asked for comment on the revelation of a secret flight on a third plane, the ​White House provided a statement ‌from Steve Cheung, the communications director, ​saying the Qatari-donated jet has been ​fitted with high-level security protocols that ensure the safety of the president and his staff.“As the president has said recently, there are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal to address those threats,” Cheung said. It was the same statement provided to the Post.Maanvi Singh and Reuters contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpUS-Israel war on IranIranMiddle East and north AfricaTurkeyTrump administrationNatonewsShareReuse this content

title: The return of the caspian tiger: how a species feared extinct has come back to Kazakhstan | Wildlife | The Guardian
description: The wild capture and release of a female big cat into a nature reserve is the first step towards reintroducing a population that hasn’t been seen for 70 years
Author: Patrick Greenfield
Headline: The wild capture and release of a female big cat into a nature reserve is the first step towards reintroducing a population that hasn’t been seen for 70 years
Content: A tiger is released into Kazakhstan's wilderness as part of a repopulation programmeThe age of extinctionWildlifeThe return of the caspian tiger: how a species feared extinct has come back to KazakhstanThe wild capture and release of a female big cat into a nature reserve is the first step towards reintroducing a population that hasn’t been seen for 70 yearsThe age of extinction is supported byAbout this contentPatrick GreenfieldTue 11 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 06.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn 31 July, “Umit” – which means hope in Kazakh – was released into a nature reserve on the edge of Lake Balkhash after more than a decade of careful planning to return the caspian tiger to the region. With this release,Kazakhstanbecame the first country to restore its tiger range after they had been thought extinct, with the last reliable sighting in the country recorded more than 70 years ago.Umit – a wild-caught female tiger transported from the Russian far east – will be joined by more big cats in the coming years, with plans to establish a self-sustaining population of about 50. A wild-caught male flown from Russia is still being monitored by authorities and will be released when he is judged fit to survive alone. Two wild tiger cubs are also being reared on the reserve in special enclosures, with as little human contact as possible, and are likely to be released into the marshlands next year, to feast on boar, deer and kulans, a type of wild donkey.“Today, we became witnesses of a truly historic event,” declared Yerlan Nysanbayev, Kazakhstan’s environment minister, after the release. “There is a lot of work ahead on monitoring tigers and forming a stable population, but today the first and very important step has been taken.”Amur tiger in Kazakhstan after being released into the wildernessThe caspian tiger was considered extinct in the 1970s after decades of fur hunting, habitat destruction and eradication campaigns. Its range once spanned from eastern Turkey to north-west China, including Armenia, Azerbaijan, Iran and swathes of central Asia, mostly in forest highlands and along the edges of lakes and rivers, particularly inTugai foreststhat were widely destroyed for agriculture.It was officially declared extinct in 2003, but a scientific breakthrough just six years later laid the foundation for the recent release. DNA analysis of the tiger’s genetic historyrevealed thatthe caspian tiger and the amur tiger found in eastern Siberia were almost identical, with populations probably intermingling until the early 1900s before they were isolated by hunting. What became known as the caspian tiger spread west from Siberia and were separated from the amur tiger by a single letter of genetic code.A map of Kazakhstan and surrounding countries“For all intents and purposes, this is the return of the caspian tiger, only this time they flew instead of walking,” said Dale Miquelle, an authority on Siberian tigers who headsWildlifeConservation Society’s Russia programme. “The idea of bringing back a subspecies of tigers that has disappeared is very exciting. This is as close as we’re going to get to that process.”Today, it would be practically impossible for the caspian tiger to re-establish its former range. A2017 feasibility study identifiedtwo places in the region with enough suitable habitat to re-establish populations, both in Kazakhstan. The most promising was thought to be Ile-Balkhash, where Umit was released, which the Kazakh government made a nature reserve in 2018.While this summer’s release is the first example of a cross-border tiger translocation, there have been several successful releases in the Russian far east as part of efforts to restore the amur tiger’s former range. One scheme involved rescuing orphaned cubs whose mothers had been shot by hunters in Siberia, and then releasing them into former ranges when they were strong enough. The project, which Miquelle worked on, was a huge success – especially because there was no human contact with the young big cats.“The success rate was pretty close to 100% after the release. These animals adapt amazingly quickly. One young female killed a Himalayan black bear within 24 hours of being released and others have learned to hunt on their own in the wild really quickly,” he says.But it is not all good news. Wild tigers have suffered a catastrophic century, withnumbers fallingfrom about 100,000 at the beginning of the 20th century to about 5,500 today. In many parts of Asia, they are still declining – and facing new threats from climate breakdown and disease. In recent years in Russia, African swine fever wiped out enormous numbers of wild boar, a tiger’s favourite prey,causing many totarget human settlements. Ensuring there is enough food for the returning caspian tigers is key to their survival, says Miquelle.“I am very hopeful this can work. In Russia, a number of translocations resulted in the recolonisation of tiger habitat. So there’s a blueprint that suggests that this can work as long as there is suitable habitat and sufficient prey,” he says.Find moreage of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reportersRebecca Ratcliffe,Phoebe WestonandPatrick Greenfieldin the Guardian app for more nature coverage.Explore more on these topicsWildlifeThe age of extinctionExtinct wildlifeAnimalsKazakhstanSouth and central AsiaRewildingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Burnham urged by 50 police leaders to prevent early release of PC Harper’s killers | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: Letter signed by every chief constable in England and Wales warns early release could weaken trust in justice system
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Letter signed by every chief constable in England and Wales warns early release could weaken trust in justice system
Content: Ministers are urgently seeking to free up spaces in overcrowded prisons across England and Wales.Photograph: Jeff Morgan/AlamyView image in fullscreenMinisters are urgently seeking to free up spaces in overcrowded prisons across England and Wales.Photograph: Jeff Morgan/AlamyPrisons and probationBurnham urged by 50 police leaders to prevent early release of PC Harper’s killersLetter signed by every chief constable in England and Wales warns freeing pair could weaken trust in justice systemPeter Walker,Rajeev SyalandCaroline DaviesTue 11 Aug 2026 18.47 EDTFirst published on Tue 11 Aug 2026 13.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham is facing an unprecedented mass call from police chiefs to block the early release of PC Andrew Harper’s killers, as unions warned his emergency plan to create more space in jails risked causing confusion or leading to prisoners being freed by mistake.A letter signed by 50 police leaders across the UK, including every chief constable in England and Wales, called on the prime minister to do everything in his power to stop the killers benefiting from a programme designed to free up prison space, saying there was “a profound strength of feeling across policing” that this should not happen.Burnham said earlier he recognised “the depth of public concern” about the proposed early release of Harper’s killers and announced a change to the early release scheme, intended to exclude prisoners convicted of the most serious offences by freeing up new prison places.In their letter, released late on Tuesday night, the leaders, who included the Met commissioner, Mark Rowley, Greater Manchester’s chief constable, Stephen Watson, and the National Crime Agency director general, Graeme Biggar, said: “When the state asks people to run towards danger on behalf of the public, they should be able to trust that the justice system will stand behind them when the worst happens.“Pc Andrew Harper’s case also raises a wider question.“When someone is sentenced for an exceptionally serious offence, how much confidence can victims, bereaved families and the public place in that sentence if subsequent changes to release arrangements result in an offender being released significantly earlier than originally anticipated?”The letter, which was signed by police chiefs from forces across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, added: “Officers and staff understand that the law must be applied as it stands. But they will question what message this sends about the value placed on their service and sacrifice when they put themselves in harm’s way to protect others.“Police officers and staff see first-hand the impact serious crime has on victims and their families. They support people through some of the most difficult moments of their lives and ask them to place their trust in the justice system.“That trust is vital and should not be weakened. We are also collectively concerned that an approach to early release which does not sufficiently distinguish the most serious offending risks undermining public safety, victim confidence and wider confidence in the criminal justice system.”Earlier, unions had warned that Burnham’s plan to stop the early release of PC Harper’s killers, Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, and other serious offenders could increase the risk of some more dangerous prisoners being released by mistake.It was also announced on Tuesday that probation staff had voted overwhelmingly to go on strike due to what they said were unrealistic workloads, in another blow to the proposals announced by the prime minister.How viable are plans to free up prison space in England and Wales?Read moreWhile the vote by members of Napo was not directly connected to the early release plans, the probation officers’ union has previously criticised the proposals as rushed.After an uproar about the proposed release of Harper’s killers, Burnham said on Tuesday morning that he had instructed the justice secretary, Alex Norris, to find more prison spaces so the pair and other serious offenders would not be freed.Writing on Facebook, Burnham said places could be provided by removing foreign offenders more quickly, finding a way to release lower-risk prisoners stuck in jail on indeterminate sentences, and “making greater use of the entire prison estate, including using the female estate for male offenders”.Downing Street had said on Monday that there was no feasible way of exempting just a handful of prisoners from the scheme to block the release of Cole and Bowers, who were sentenced to 13 years for Harper’s manslaughter. Under the scheme, they were due to be freed in January.View image in fullscreenJessie Cole (left) and Albert Bowers, two of three men sentenced over PC Andrew Harper’s death.Photograph: Thames Valley police/PATom Wheatley, the president of the Prison Governors’ Association, said further changes to the scheme could lead to prisoners being wrongly released. “Mistakes are more likely due to having to recalculate sentences against a very tight deadline,” he said.Wheatley said removing overseas prisoners was likely to be difficult as many would resist this and a number did not have proper documentation. He said victims would also want to be sure that anyone sent back to their home countries would properly serve their sentence there.Mark Fairhurst, the national chair of the Prison Officers’ Association, said placing men in women’s prisons would require investment and retraining. “Repurposing women’s prisons to accommodate male prisoners is not something that can simply be achieved by changing the sign above the door,” he said.“There would inevitably be additional staffing, training, security and operational requirements. The physical design and facilities of women’s prisons are not necessarily suitable for a male population, and those differences would need to be properly assessed before any decision was taken.”The Ministry of Justice said it was disappointed by the Napo strike vote and it would continue to engage with the union. Officials in Norris’s department are understood to be working at full speed on preparing detailed and workable plans to free up prison space by September.When the early release scheme was announced, there were exemptions for prisoners convicted of rape, serious child sexual abuse and grooming offences but not manslaughter, prompting pressure to block the release of Harper’s killers, including from police and his family.Officials initially said it would be unrealistic to just block the release of Cole and Bowers and that exempting all manslaughter cases risked not creating enough prison spaces to ease the crisis. But in his Facebook post and speaking to reporters on a later visit to Derbyshire, Burnham said he was aware of the strength of public feeling about the plans.View image in fullscreenPC Andrew Harper was killed in Berkshire in 2019.Photograph: Thames Valley police/PA“It’s my job to speak up for the public on this issue,” he said during the visit. “I take that duty very seriously indeed, and I’m confident that there’s more that can be done, and will be done to address public concern.”He said on Facebook: “I am increasingly confident that a more focused approach along these lines will allow us to reduce the number of people released early and, in the case of the most serious offenders like those convicted of the killing of PC Harper, prevent their early release altogether.”Harper, 28, was fatally injured when he got caught in a strap attached to the back of a car and was dragged down a country road as the killers fled the scene of a quad bike theft in Sulhamstead, Berkshire, in 2019.Cole and Bowers, two of three men sentenced over the police officer’s death, are due to be released halfway through their 13-year sentences, having been convicted of manslaughter in 2020. A petition demanding an intervention has nearly 900,000 signatures.The early release changes were part of the Sentencing Act passed earlier this year that cut the minimum amount of time many offenders would have to spend in prison.Explore more on these topicsPrisons and probationUK criminal justiceIndustrial actionTrade unionsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Richard Tice accused of ‘nasty tactics’ over legal threat to the Guardian | Richard Tice | The Guardian
description: Reform deputy leader condemned for seeking disclosure of documents that could reveal reporter’s sources
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Reform deputy leader condemned for seeking disclosure of documents that could reveal reporter’s sources
