Content: Richard Tice’s lawyers wrote to the Guardian over reporting about financial transactions that were referred to the National Crime Agency.Photograph: Thomas Krych/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenRichard Tice’s lawyers wrote to the Guardian over reporting about financial transactions that were referred to the National Crime Agency.Photograph: Thomas Krych/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockRichard TiceRichard Tice accused of ‘nasty tactics’ over legal threat to the GuardianReform deputy leader condemned for seeking disclosure of documents that could reveal reporter’s sourcesGuardian staffTue 11 Aug 2026 14.15 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleReform’s deputy leaderRichard Ticehas been accused of using “nasty tactics” in an attempt to intimidate journalists and deflect attention from his own financial affairs after issuing a legal threat to the Guardian.In a letter sent from his lawyers, a Guardian correspondent was singled out for her reporting on a series of Tice’s financial transactions that were referred to the National Crime Agency.Tice is now suing the NCA, claiming that the information could only have come from an officer within the agency.In a separate letter to the Guardian, Tice’s lawyers made clear they would be seeking disclosure of documents that could reveal the details of sources.John Whittingdale, a former Conservative culture secretary, condemned the move.“The essence of a free press is that journalists can use verified information from sources without being forced to reveal who they are. This betrays a failure to understand how important that principle is to journalism.”Margaret Hodge, the peer and former Labour MP and anti-corruption campaigner, said: “It is never acceptable for individuals to seemingly abuse our laws to silence investigative journalism and close down public criticism. That’s why we need to urgently reform our laws to stop rich people using their wealth to close down legitimate scrutiny.”Jemimah Steinfeld, the chief executive at the Index on Censorship, added: “This has the appearance of an attempt to force a journalist to break the golden rule: that sources must be protected.“This has been vital public interest reporting by the Guardian. The sources of such journalism are sacred. If the facts are incorrect, then they can be challenged, but the sources should not be chased down.“This appears to be a tactic designed to not only silence journalists but those who talk to them. It is a nasty tactic and we should all be concerned.”Theo Bamber, the chief executive at the News Media Association, said that “robust protection for journalists’ sources is absolutely fundamental to ensuring that reporters can scrutinise authority and hold the powerful to account on behalf of the people impacted by their actions and decisions.“The use of legal threats by an individual or organisation trying to force journalists to disclose their confidential sources is an attack on this important principle, and one that must be resisted at every turn.”Tice and Reform’s leader,Nigel Farage, have been under intense scrutiny in recent months because of a continuing investigation by the Guardian into their financial affairs.The Guardian revealed in a series of detailed reports that Reform UK received a secret £1m donation via a fundraising vehicle run by Tice and asecret £5m giftmade to Farage shortly before he announced he would stand in the 2024 general election.The Guardian also revealed that these and other transactions were reported by bankers to the National Crime Agency over fears they could involve laundered money.Throughout its reports the Guardian has referred to financial industry sources.Tice has suggested in a document filed at the high court that the Guardian’s award-winning City editor, Anna Isaac, could not have had sources at multiple banks.The tangled financial web at the heart of Reform UKRead moreIn legal correspondence sent directly to Isaac, Tice’s lawyers suggested he is seeking to unmask sources based on his own assessment of the reporter’s work.Farage has also issued proceedings against the NCA.A GNM spokesperson said: “Richard Tice’s legal threat against the Guardian appears to be a calculated attempt to deflect attention away from legitimate questions about his financial affairs and the funding ofReform UK.“Instead of providing answers to those questions, he seems intent on intimidating journalists and seeking to expose sources.“The Guardian will oppose these attacks on the freedom of the press and will not be deterred from public interest-driven investigations into politicians and the parties they represent.”Farage previously claimed – without providing any evidence – that the details of the £5m gift must have come from Russian spies hacking his phone.The Guardian described Farage’s claim as “absurd” and “an attempt to deflect attention from legitimate scrutiny of his financial affairs”. The spokesperson added: “Nigel Farage is once again hiding behind a baseless attack on the media rather than facing up to scrutiny from journalists and politicians.”Explore more on these topicsRichard TiceReform UKNigel FarageThe GuardianNewspapers & magazinesNational newspapersNewspapersnewsShareReuse this content

title: The Office actor Lucy Davis says she has incurable stage four breast cancer | Breast cancer | The Guardian
description: Star, 53, says disease has metastasised to her bones and it is too late for chemotherapy
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Star, 53, says disease has metastasised to her bones and it is too late for chemotherapy
Content: Lucy Davis in 2008. She played the receptionist Dawn in The Office.Photograph: Ian West/PAView image in fullscreenLucy Davis in 2008. She played the receptionist Dawn in The Office.Photograph: Ian West/PABreast cancerThe Office actor Lucy Davis says she has incurable stage four breast cancerStar, 53, says disease has metastasised to her bones and it is too late for chemotherapyNadeem BadshahTue 11 Aug 2026 13.55 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLucy Davis, the actor best known for playing Dawn Tinsley in The Office, has said she has incurable stage four breast cancer.The 53-year-old said she was diagnosed a year and a half ago and the disease had metastasised to her bones including her spine, right hip and ribs. She said it was too late for chemotherapy.Davis wrote on Instagram on Tuesday: “As of now, I’m trying to live out whatever might be left of my life in as fun a way as I possibly can.“I always like to find the teachable moments in anything negative that happens. And cancer has not disappointed in that regard; there’s a lot I have learned from it, and I’m grateful for that.“As some of you will know, the pain can really be something else. Standing and walking for too long a time can be hard, and I need to use a wheelchair sometimes (so if you see me toddling around in one, feel free to give me a push!).”Davis, the daughter of the comedian Jasper Carrott, said one of the most important things that had helped her was humour, asking her friends and family to poke fun at her “as much as possible” and to not treat her like a “sick person”.“There’s nothing that will make you feel more unwell than being treated as if you’re unwell,” she added.“I’m not scared of whatever comes next. I’m at peace with it. I’ll see my Gracie [her late dog] sooner than expected, and for me leaving my physical body just means going home. Any and all grieving is for my family; it’s far harder for them than for me.”Davis rose to fame playing the receptionist Dawn in the original version of The Office, which followed the lives of workers at the Slough paper merchant Wernham Hogg, with the show’s co-creator Ricky Gervais playing the manager David Brent.She played Hayley Jordan on BBC Radio 4’s The Archers for nearly 10 years and appeared in the 2004 comedy Shaun of the Dead opposite Simon Pegg and in the Netflix series Chilling Adventures of Sabrina.She said she would continue working for animal rights and would like to keep working as an actor, a job she said was one of the “biggest joys” of her life.She said: “For those of you on a similar journey to mine, I do wish you well. Cancer asks a lot from us, physically and mentally. And we all get to do it however we choose.”Explore more on these topicsBreast cancernewsShareReuse this content

title: Driver who broke sound barrier sets new speed record in hydrogen-powered car | Utah | The Guardian
description: British driver Andy Green reached 406.320 mph in car powered by two hydrogen internal combustion engines
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: British driver Andy Green reached 406.320 mph in car powered by two hydrogen internal combustion engines
Content: Andy Green after breaking the land speed record for diesel-powered vehicles in Bonneville Salt Flats, Utah, on 22 August 2006.Photograph: Richard Meredith-Hardy/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAndy Green after breaking the land speed record for diesel-powered vehicles in Bonneville Salt Flats, Utah, on 22 August 2006.Photograph: Richard Meredith-Hardy/ShutterstockUtahDriver who broke sound barrier sets new speed record in hydrogen-powered carBritish driver Andy Green reached 406.320 mph in car powered by two hydrogen internal combustion enginesAssociated PressTue 11 Aug 2026 13.48 EDTFirst published on Tue 11 Aug 2026 08.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe only person to break the sound barrier in a car earned another world record on Tuesday in a show of force for hydrogen power.British driver Andy Green reached 406.320mph (653.908km/h) in a car powered by two hydrogen internal combustion engines with a combined 1,600 horsepower, setting the record for that vehicle category, according to the Fédération Internationale de l’Automobile, the international governing body of motor sports.The 64-year-old retired Royal Air Force pilot rocketed across the crystalline crust at Utah’s famous Bonneville Salt Flats in a 32-ft (9.75-meter) car engineered by British construction equipment manufacturer JCB. The engines, adapted from those used in the company’s heavy machinery, mix pressurized hydrogen gas with air and ignite it to create bursts of power.To be clear, Tuesday’s feat didn’t come close to approaching the overall land-speed record, which Green set with jet power in 1997. That year, he climbed into the Thrust SSC, a black needle sandwiched between two cartoonishly large jet engines, and drove it to an outright record of 763.035 mph (1,227.985 kph), breaking the sound barrier and achieving a feat no one has come close to matching. His runs in Nevada’s Black Rock desert produced sonic booms that shook the nearby town of Gerlach.Footage from 1997 shows Andy Green’s fastest land speed world recordIn 2006, Green also set the land-speed record for a diesel-powered car – 350.092 mph (563.4 kph) – at the Bonneville Salt Flats. He returned there Tuesday with the goal of beating that mark using hydrogen power, which he has called the “fuel of the future”.In targeting his diesel speed, Green easily topped the previous hydrogen combustion world record of 185.5 mph (298.5 kph). He had a 10-mile (16-km) straightaway to build speed. A few dozen JCB staff members and reporters watched from a distance through cameras and binoculars.A remnant of a prehistoric lake bed, the Bonneville Salt Flats are about 100 miles (160 km) west of Salt Lake City and sit atop a shallow aquifer that cools the tires. The low-friction surface and dry desert air are conducive to speed and have beckoned drivers since the first race there in 1914.Green was no stranger to speed when he took his first racing job. He had been flying supersonic military jets when he spotted a 1994 British newspaper ad seeking a high-speed driver to break the sound barrierGreen did not approach supersonic speeds on Tuesday, but JCB engineers hope his feat with hydrogen power will shake up the clean-energy industry.The company’s chairman has argued that hydrogen can better handle the demands of heavy industries than electric power.Hydrogen is only as clean as its source, and the vast majority is currently produced from fossil fuels. JCB signed a deal to buy green hydrogen, which is created using renewable energy but makes up a tiny fraction of global hydrogen production.Explore more on these topicsUtahWorld recordsAutomotive industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Abusive’ man found guilty of harassing Stella Creasy MP on tube train | Crime | The Guardian
description: Clifford Wilby, 63, blocked the Walthamstow MP from leaving, filmed her and talked about her ‘failings as a member of parliament’
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Clifford Wilby, 63, blocked the Walthamstow MP from leaving, filmed her and talked about her ‘failings as a member of parliament’
Content: Clifford Wilby, who also filmed the MP on his mobile phone, was found guilty of using threatening, abusive, or insulting words or behaviour to cause harassment, alarm, or distress.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAView image in fullscreenClifford Wilby, who also filmed the MP on his mobile phone, was found guilty of using threatening, abusive, or insulting words or behaviour to cause harassment, alarm, or distress.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PACrime‘Abusive’ man found guilty of harassing Stella Creasy MP on tube trainClifford Wilby, 63, blocked the Walthamstow MP from leaving, filmed her and talked about her ‘failings as a member of parliament’Nadeem BadshahTue 11 Aug 2026 13.46 EDTFirst published on Tue 11 Aug 2026 13.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 63-year-old man has been found guilty of harassing the Labour MPStella Creasyafter he was “abusive and aggressive” to her on a tube train.Clifford Wilby, of eastLondon, saw the MP for Walthamstow in July 2025 on a Victoria Line train, Westminster magistrates court heard.He blocked her from leaving the tube carriage and started talking to her about knife crime and her “failings as a member of parliament” and then filmed her on his mobile phone, the court heard.Other passengers intervened and got in between them before Creasy left the carriage.Sarah Madden, prosecuting, said the pair first met during a Zoom meeting in 2024 in Creasy’s capacity as an MP. The meeting was terminated due to Wilby’s behaviour.Creasy, giving evidence from behind a screen, said during the online meeting he “made a series of very serious allegations”, became abusive and “referred to the fact he had been diagnosed as a psychopath”.She said he started to make a complaint about a constituent and she reminded him that she could not discuss somebody else’s case.He became “abusive, aggressive” and they terminated the conversation, said Creasy.View image in fullscreenStella Creasy, the Labour MP for Walthamstow.Photograph: Nicola TreeCreasy said that on 15 July last year she had boarded a Victoria line train and was intending to move further down the train at the next stop, and looked up to get off the train and made eye contact with the defendant.“He said ‘are you Stella Creasy?’, at that point my memory kicked in and I made the connection because I knew his face, he then confirmed he was Clifford Wilby,” said the MP.“He stood up and blocked my ability to leave the carriage, he began talking to me about his concerns about my constituent, he was shouting although the tube train is a loud environment.”She added: “Obviously I was concerned that I was in an enclosed space with him. He was very close.“I stated very clearly this wasn’t an appropriate conversation to be having.”Creasy said at this point she was backed up against the door of the carriage and was holding her hands out as a gesture “to say stop”.She got off the train at Finsbury Park by exiting through another door further up the carriage.Tess McCarthy, defending, put to the MP that she could have got off the train as the incident continued to which Creasy replied “no”.Wilby said he had been hoping to continue the conversation about the constituent on the tube but the MP “became quite agitated” and he was “quite shocked by her reaction”, so he pressed record on his phone “for my safety”.He added: “At no point did I stand in front of her. When I first spoke to her she was actually getting off the train and she turned around to speak to me, I stood up because it was noisy.”The defendant also denied telling Creasy in 2024 he had been diagnosed as a psychopath.The deputy chief magistrate Tan Ikram found Wilby guilty of using threatening, abusive, or insulting words or behaviour to cause harassment, alarm, or distress and adjourned sentencing until 8 September for reports.Explore more on these topicsCrimeStella CreasyLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: ICE to spend up to $20m on gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks | ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) | The Guardian
description: According to manufacturer, shock ‘is usually effective in bringing individuals into compliance in less than three seconds’
Author: Maanvi Singh
Headline: According to manufacturer, shock ‘is usually effective in bringing individuals into compliance in less than three seconds’
Content: ‘Introducing gloves that can so easily be used to deliver terrible pain in encounters is a recipe for harm to the public,’ said one critic.Photograph: Ryan Murphy/APView image in fullscreen‘Introducing gloves that can so easily be used to deliver terrible pain in encounters is a recipe for harm to the public,’ said one critic.Photograph: Ryan Murphy/APICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)ICE to spend up to $20m on gloves that can deliver painful electric shocksAccording to manufacturer,  shock ‘is usually effective in bringing individuals into compliance in less than three seconds’Maanvi Singhand agenciesTue 11 Aug 2026 19.35 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 19.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleICE plans to spend up to $20m (£15m) to purchase thousands of gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks for officers and agents by March, according to anotice published Mondayby the Department of Homeland Security.The devices, called Glove (Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter), are manufactured by Compliant Technologies LLC of Lexington, Kentucky.According to the manufacturer, “the discomfort associated with the stimulation is usually effective in bringing individuals into compliance in less than three seconds and leaves no burns, marks or scars”. The company has advertised the device as a “humane, low-optics, de-escalation solution for many situations facing our men and women in uniform”.The gloves have previously been used in settings such as jails in the US.View image in fullscreenGlove (Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter).Photograph: Compliant Technologies LLCCompliant Technologies says the devices function as a normal pair of patrol gloves until officers press a switch to activate their electrical mode. The gloves must be applied directly to someone’s skin to deliver a pain stimulus that typically helps an officer gain compliance within seconds, according to the company.“It’s immediate and sharp, and it will distract you. I call it like a bee sting,” said John Peters, president of the Institute for the Prevention of In-Custody Deaths, who is studying how the device has been used. “If the officer is getting any type of resistance from the person, this is certainly an effective tool.”Civil rights advocates expressed alarm at the plan, saying ICE officers already face criticism for their use of force with little oversight or accountability while enforcing Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.Jenn Rolnick Borchetta, deputy project director on policing at the American Civil Liberties Union, told the Associated Press that she questioned the use of the devices for civil immigration enforcement.“ICE spent the last year showing this country they are too quick to use force. Now they will be able to deploy electric shocks with the slight push of a button that maybe nobody else can see them do,” she said. “Introducing gloves that can so easily be used to deliver terrible pain in encounters is a recipe for harm to the public.”Peters said he believed ICE’s planned purchase would likely be the largest from the company to date. He said he could envision ICE officers using the gloves to help remove uncooperative subjects from cars and houses and in and out of detention facilities.The manufacturer warns the device should not be used as punishment, against people merely exhibiting “verbal defiance or belligerence” or on high-risk populations such as children, pregnant women or elderly or disabled people.Jeff Niklaus, the founder and CEO of Compliant Technologies, wrote in an email: “Unfortunately, we are unable to speak on this subject.”Explore more on these topicsICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Trump administrationUS immigrationUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nvidia links with Wall Street firms for $500bn AI financing deal | Nvidia | The Guardian
description: Apollo, BlackRock, Goldman Sachs and KKR among those working with chipmaker to fund infrastructure
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Apollo, BlackRock, Goldman Sachs and KKR among those working with chipmaker to fund infrastructure
Content: Nvidia counts Google, Amazon, Microsoft and Facebook owner Meta among its customers.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenNvidia counts Google, Amazon, Microsoft and Facebook owner Meta among its customers.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersNvidiaNvidia links with Wall Street firms for $500bn AI financing dealApollo, BlackRock, Goldman Sachs and KKR among those working with chipmaker to fund infrastructureKalyeena Makortoffand agencyTue 11 Aug 2026 04.34 EDTFirst published on Tue 11 Aug 2026 02.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNvidia ⁠has struck a deal with six large Wall Street firms to raise ⁠more than $500bn (£370bn) to fund the datacentres, chip factories and power stations needed to fuel the artificial intelligence boom.The Nvidia chief executive, Jensen Huang, said on X that it marked “a major milestone for Nvidia and the AI industry”, as he posted a photo of himself smiling and giving a thumbs up alongside finance bosses involved in the deal, including the head of Goldman Sachs, David Solomon.He confirmed that Nvidia, which has a market value of $5.3tn, had signed memorandums of understanding with Goldman, Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield and KKR to offer funding for what the industry calls “compute”, referring to hardware such as datacentres and chips that are used to run train and build AI.“Many great AI companies, enterprises and AI clouds have demand for compute but do not yet have access to financing at the scale or cost required to build quickly,” Huang said, adding that the funding “will make AI factories more accessible to the companies, industries and nations building the future”.The move highlights how rising demand ⁠for AI computing capacity is drawing institutional investors, as governments, companies and ​startups race to build out ‌datacentres. Big tech companies have signalled that spending on AI ‌was likely to surpass $730bn this year. However, there have been concerns over the link betweenhigh valuations of tech companies and the need for vast investments to support their ambitions.Last month, the Bank of England warned that AI developments could pose a risk to financial stability, particularly if the companies who take on debt end fail to deliver sustainable profits, or face big disruptions.“The pace of investment is unprecedented historically,” the Bank of England said in itsfinancial stability report in July,noting that AI companies were increasingly taking on debt “to support investment in infrastructure”.“If the scale of AI debt financing grows as expected over the coming years, an adverse shock to AI companies that results in losses or affects their ability to service debt could more materially affect global financing conditions,” it said, suggesting that it could lead to a credit crunch in which it would be harder and more expensive for businesses and households to secure loans.The Bank also warned banks and private credit firms to consider they may not be getting the full picture about the risks they were taking in relation to the AI industry. “Given the different funding sources from which AI companies are drawing, and different levels of transparency in those arrangements, it may be difficult for financial firms to be aware of the full extent of their direct and indirect exposures to the AI ecosystem and AI companies,” policymakers said. “This could increase the risk that exposures to developments in AI are greater than anticipated, or not fully reflected in firms’ risk management.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNvidia said the funding arrangements would “create dedicated pools of ⁠capital at significant scale at attractive rates” for its customers. The ​company did ​not disclose the financial terms, ​investment commitments by individual firms or a timetable for ​deploying the planned $500bn.“Every industrial revolution has been built on infrastructure: electricity, transportation, communications and computing, with every build-out enabled by external financing,” Huang said. “AI factories are the infrastructure of the intelligence era.”Explore more on these topicsNvidiaTechnology sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: HCA workers push for higher pay and more staffing amid billions in profits: ‘I’m struggling’ | US unions | The Guardian
description: Largest for-profit hospital system and operator in the US reported $6.8bn in profits, while employees find it difficult to make ends meet
Author: Michael Sainato
Headline: Largest for-profit hospital system and operator in the US reported $6.8bn in profits, while employees find it difficult to make ends meet
Content: HCA Sunrise hospital workers protesting in Las Vegas, Nevada, on 6 August 2026.Photograph: Jason Karsh, SEIU Local 1107View image in fullscreenHCA Sunrise hospital workers protesting in Las Vegas, Nevada, on 6 August 2026.Photograph: Jason Karsh, SEIU Local 1107US unionsHCA workers push for higher pay and more staffing amid billions in profits: ‘I’m struggling’Largest for-profit hospital system and operator in the US reported $6.8bn in profits, while employees find it difficult to make ends meetMichael SainatoTue 11 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 16.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUnion workers with HCA Healthcare, the largest for-profit hospital system and operator in the US, are holding picket protests across the country as they push for pay and staffing increases in a new contract.The hospital system has over300,000 employeesin the US and the UK, with 22,000 US workers represented by the Service Employees International Union (SEIU) who are in contract negotiations with HCA. Workers areaskingfor a pathway to a $25 an hour minimum wage, improved wage scales and raises that match the increased cost of living, along with benefits including paid vacation, sick time and bolstered work protections.Esther Reyes, a single mother of three children, has worked as an environmental services technician at the HCA-owned Las Palmas hospital in El Paso,Texas, for the past two years, and said she constantly struggles to make ends meet on her $16.80 an hour salary.“Sometimes I need to decide, maybe this month I pay the water bill, then another pay for gas, but most of the time I’m not able to pay for everything,” Reyes said.Ahead of contract negotiations, Reyes and her co-workers in El Paso are set to hold an informational picket outside the hospital this week, with picket protests planned at over a dozen HCA hospitals inCalifornia, Texas, Nevada, and Florida.Reyes explained prices have been going up but salarieshave remained stagnant, and it’s a constant battle figuring out how to cover basic necessities.“I’m struggling. I struggle a lot. If they gave us the raise we want, it would be a huge blessing,” Reyes added. “I work for my family. I work for my kids. If I don’t get enough for everything, how am I supposed to cover all they need?”HCAreported$6.8bn in profits in 2025, a 17.8% increase from 2024. In early 2026, the companyauthorizeda $10bn stock buyback program. Sam Hazen, the HCA CEO,receivedmore than $26.5m in total compensation in 2025, 420 times more than the median compensation for HCA employees at $62,955.“We also see HCA’s profit reports, and that they are having great returns, and their profit is increasing. Meanwhile, the people doing the work are not being compensated appropriately,” said Jody Domineck, a pediatric nurse with over 20 years at HCA Sunrise hospital and medical center in Las Vegas, the largest hospital in the state, and secretary-treasurer of SEIU Local 1107. “Our work is how they’re making billions. We are just asking for fair compensation.”Domineck noted that despite the increased profit, the hospitals continue to face staffing shortages that affect both workers and patients.“There’s been multiple studies that show that the more patients you have, the higher the risk is to all patients,” said Domineck, who joined her co-workers to hold a rally around their contract demands outside the hospital on 6 August.In 2025, Nevada’s Republican governor, Joe Lombardo,vetoeda bill that would have established safer nurse-to-patient ratios throughout the state. HCA members are now trying to get similar ratio guarantees into their next contract.“I personally have had to walk away from a parent when their child was having a procedure, and that parent was crying in the hallway alone,” Domineck said. “I had to walk away from them because I had to see my other patients, and that was one of the kind of moments that broke me, because I, with all of my being, wanted to be there and comfort that parent, but I had to walk away to continue to provide care for the other patients, and those are the decisions nurses have to make when they have more and more patients.”A spokesperson for HCA emphasized a small number of HCA Healthcare affiliated hospitals are engaged in individual negotiations with local SEIU chapters and shared a statement on the Sunrise hospital negotiations in Las Vegas,Nevada.“At Sunrise Health System, we value every member of our team and remain committed to reaching a fair agreement through good-faith negotiations,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “While we respect our employees’ right to peacefully demonstrate, portraying this as a patient safety issue is inaccurate. The outstanding issues are about compensation. We believe the best place to reach an agreement is at the bargaining table, and we look forward to continuing negotiations on August 11 and 12.”Explore more on these topicsUS unionsUS healthcareHealthcare industryNevadaTexasFloridaCalifornianewsShareReuse this content

title: Delivery drivers to be paid minimum $31.30 an hour across Australia in ‘world-leading’ decision  | Gig economy | The Guardian
description: Fair Work Commission issues a new minimum standards order for gig workers to come into effect 17 August
Author: Catie McLeod
Headline: Fair Work Commission issues a new minimum standards order for gig workers to come into effect 17 August
Content: Under the changes, delivery platforms will have to organise and pay for personal accident insurance that ‘provides a reasonable minimum level of cover’ for their workersPhotograph: Martin Berry/AlamyView image in fullscreenUnder the changes, delivery platforms will have to organise and pay for personal accident insurance that ‘provides a reasonable minimum level of cover’ for their workersPhotograph: Martin Berry/AlamyGig economyDelivery drivers to be paid minimum $31.30 an hour across Australia in ‘world-leading’ decisionFair Work Commission issues a new minimum standards order for gig workers to come into effect 17 AugustGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastCatie McLeodConsumer affairs reporterTue 11 Aug 2026 04.25 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 05.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDelivery drivers in Australia will be paid a minimum rate of $31.30 (US $22.05/£16.35) an hour and insured for injuries on the job under a landmark agreement approved by the industrial umpire that could set a precedent in other countries.The Fair Work Commission (FWC) on Tuesday issued a new minimum standards order for gig workers who perform on-demand delivery of food, drinks, or groceries, and the operators of the digital platforms who engage their services.Hospitality recruitment app Supp calls gig-workers contractors. Some users say it leads to casual work without entitlementsRead moreThe Transport Workers’ Union, representing the gig workers, had jointly applied with major platforms DoorDash and UberEats for the new protections in 2024, after years of talks.After taking public submissions on new standards for the industry, including from gig workers and other interested parties including Amazon and Auspost, FWC has greenlit the conditions, to come into effect from 17 August.The deal is likely to have involved concessions from either side of the negotiating table, including the union agreeing to call the workers “employee-like”.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailIn a joint statement on Tuesday, the TWU, UberEats and DoorDash said the new standards would provide an “industry-wide safety net for hundreds of thousands of [workers] while preserving the flexibility that sits at the heart of on-demand work.”The TWU national secretary Michael Kaine said the new standards were “world-leading”.Under the new standards, workers will be responsible for maintaining third-party insurances on the vehicles they use for deliveries, so if they get in an accident and damage another vehicle the delivery platform will not be liable for the cost.On the other hand, delivery platforms will have to organise and pay for personal accident insurance that “provides a reasonable minimum level of cover” for their workers, although experts have previously pointed out this is open to interpretation.While they were proposed by the TWU, UberEats and DoorDash, the conditions are expected to apply to any on-demand platforms that sell food, drinks or groceries, as well as the people they hire on an ad hoc basis to deliver products.The new conditions include “safety net” pay rates for workers, who will initially receive hourly rates ranging from $31.30 to $32 depending on the class of vehicle – for example, whether they are riding a push bike or driving a car.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe minimum rates – which are designed to ensure delivery workers are paid even if they are, for example, waiting for a restaurant – will increase by 50 cents from 1 January 2027.The new standards cover a range of issues and, among other provisions, are intended to provide clearer dispute resolution and workers the right to unpaid time off.The TWU, DoorDash and UberEats made the joint application to the FWC after the Albanese government introducedworkplace reforms in 2023, which included empowering the industrial umpire to set minimum standards for gig workers.The workplace relations minister, Amanda Rishworth, on Tuesday said the resulting standards were a “milestone”.“This [FWC] order is a big step in delivering Australia’s world-leading gig worker protections and means food delivery workers don’t have to trade off flexibility for fairer protections,” she said.Explore more on these topicsGig economyUberCouriers/delivery industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Hotel prices in Europe jump before total solar eclipse | Travel & leisure | The Guardian
description: Rooms in Icelandic capital Reykjavík cost double usual rate and Spain also enjoying strong bookings
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Rooms in Icelandic capital Reykjavík cost double usual rate and Spain also enjoying strong bookings
Content: Tourists in Reykjavik have been shelling out £587 on average for a room, according to Lighthouse Intelligence.Photograph: Oliver Sved/AlamyView image in fullscreenTourists in Reykjavik have been shelling out £587 on average for a room, according to Lighthouse Intelligence.Photograph: Oliver Sved/AlamyTravel & leisureHotel prices in Europe jump before total solar eclipseRooms in Icelandic capital Reykjavík cost double usual rate and Spain also enjoying strong bookingsEurope’s total solar eclipse: the best place to see itKalyeena MakortoffTue 11 Aug 2026 06.50 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 17.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHotel prices have surged in key European cities as hundreds of thousands of tourists flock to see the first total eclipse visible from the continent this century.Iceland’s capital, Reykjavík, has seen one of the biggest jumps in hotel room prices, being one of the few accessible locations to see the full eclipse before evening on Wednesday.Tourists there have been shelling out $793 (£587) on average to secure a room on Wednesday, a 98% jump compared with the same day last year, according to data from the travel and hospitality data group Lighthouse Intelligence.Spain is also steeling itself for an influx of tourists, as one of the best places on the European continent toview the total solar eclipse. The finance ministry said on Monday that it expected 460,000 overseas tourists to visit specifically to see the eclipse.The rate for a room in A Coruña in the north ofSpainwas up 135% compared with last year to $451 on average, while prices in Mallorca, where the eclipse is expected to be visible on the horizon at sunset, were up by 24% at about $448. In Santiago de Compostela and Bilbao, hotel room prices have risen 34% and 67% respectively.Solar eclipse mapAccommodation in small towns and villages in the eclipse’s path, as well as makeshift observatories set up by local enthusiasts, have been booked for months. There have been reports of US travellers taking part in house exchanges with people living in Spain’s Castilla y León, which is one of the best regions to view the eclipse.However, authorities in Spain are worried about an increased risk of fires, with police expecting 1.5m more car journeys than usual on Wednesday. They have warned that extraordinarily dry temperatures mean the smallest spark could lead to devastating forest fires, while traffic could end up blocking access for emergency vehicles if fires break out in rural areas.Authorities will undertake out a massive police operation and safety campaign, with plans to deploy 35,000 officers to help minimise risks. Virginia Barcones, the secretary general for civil protection and emergencies at Spain’s interior ministry, said: “We’ve had an extremely tough summer in Spain, with yet another series of major forest fires. That’s why we must restrict any kind of activity that could generate a spark.”Parking on hard shoulders or close to dry vegetation has been banned in Spain, as have barbecues and fireworks. The València region has closed its natural parks and banned walking on rural footpaths.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs of Monday evening, three large wildfires were burning in the provinces of Huelva, Segovia and Huesca. Fires have already scorched about 200,000 hectares this year – six times more than by the same date in 2025, according to the environment ministry.For those unable to make the journey, the US space agency Nasa has installed four high-powered telescopes in the small village of Villalibado in north-west Spain in order to livestream the eclipse to more than 10 million people.A partial solar eclipsewill be visible across the UKon Wednesday, where it will reach its maximum coverage at 7.12pm in London.Explore more on these topicsTravel & leisureSolar eclipsesIcelandSpainEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Infantino’s opponents developing new framework for running world football | Fifa | The Guardian
description: Uefa, Concacaf and AFC are working together on a new framework for running world football to replace what they regard as Fifa’s system of patronage
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Uefa, Concacaf and AFC are working together on a new framework for running world football to replace what they regard as Fifa’s system of patronage
Content: The Fifa president, Gianni Infantino (left), and his counterpart at Uefa, Aleksander Ceferin.Photograph: Christophe Ena/APView image in fullscreenThe Fifa president, Gianni Infantino (left), and his counterpart at Uefa, Aleksander Ceferin.Photograph: Christophe Ena/APFifaInfantino’s opponents developing new framework for running world footballUefa, Concacaf and AFC working together on systemFifa has ignored calls for an independent reviewExclusive byMatt HughesandNick Amesin SalzburgTue 11 Aug 2026 13.32 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 18.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGianni Infantino’s opponents are working together to produce a new framework for running world football to replace what they regard as a system of patronage that Fifa has adopted since he replaced Sepp Blatter as president 10 years ago.Repeated calls from Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation for an independent review of Fifa’s governance have been ignored by Infantino since his plan tosell off 21% of the World Cupwas made public a fortnight ago, and the rebels are now understood to have taken matters into their own hands.Donald Trump says it would be a ‘terrible mistake’ to replace Fifa’s Gianni InfantinoRead moreA source with knowledge of the discussions told the Guardian that the three confederations are working on producing a policy document to demonstrate how the world governing body could evolve in the future.Those involved have been empowered to ask existential questions such as what Fifa’s precise role should be, how it should be structured and what governance model should be adopted. Financial distribution among member associations is also a key consideration, particularly with an eye on how best to deploy funds from Fifa’s estimated $5bn (£3.7bn) reserves.If Infantino refuses to engage then the new framework is likely to be adopted by a challenger at the presidential election next year, or could even serve as a template for a breakaway organisation.Afterreleasing a joint statementon Monday, which called for “leadership that serves football, not seeks to command it”, Uefa, Concacaf and the AFC let it be known that they have begun preliminary discussions about organising new competitions if the standoff with Fifa’s leadership persists.View image in fullscreenUefa officials are meeting in Salzburg where the Super Cup takes place on Wednesday between Paris Saint-Germain and Aston Villa.Photograph: Gintare Karpaviciute/ReutersAt present the Under-20 Women’s World Cup next month could take place without European teams, asUefais maintaining that its members will boycott the tournament, unless Fifa moves quickly to set up an independent review of the World Cup sell‑off debacle and provide legally binding assurances that such a move will not be repeated.The Concacaf president, Victor Montagliani, is seen as the most likely presidential challenger to Infantino at this stage – although, as he told the Guardian in June, his current focus is on being reelected as president of the North and Central American confederation next year.It seemed significant, however, that the joint statement released on Monday contained strong echoes of a speech given by Montagliani at the Fifa congress this year in Vancouver, where he said: “Let me be frank, leadership is not about power.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAustralia falls into line with AFC stance but stops short of calling for Infantino’s headRead moreSenior figures from European football are gathering in person for the first time since the Fifa Forward Enterprise scandal broke, with a number of meetings expected in Salzburg – where the Uefa Super Cup final will be held on Wednesday – over the next two days.The Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin, will hold talks with Nasser al-Khelaifi, the chair of European Football Clubs, aimed at reinforcing the continent’s unity in demanding a change at the top of Fifa.Uefa continues to hold firm in its pledge to boycott Fifa competitions, having not received its desired assurances that there will be no recurrence of the issues that caused the current crisis.Explore more on these topicsFifaGianni InfantinoUefaFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: The last lap at Lloyd Center: how America is losing its mall ice rinks | Sport | The Guardian
description: The rink where Tonya Harding first skated was an affordable community institution for six decades. Its closure echoes the disappearance of mall ice across the US
Author: Talia Barrington
Headline: The rink where Tonya Harding first skated was an affordable community institution for six decades. Its closure echoes the disappearance of mall ice across the US
Content: Jerry and Tally Leonard skate at Portland’s Lloyd Center on 4 August. The married couple, both in their 70s, had skated together at the rink for nearly 60 years.Photograph: Michael Hanson for The Washington Post via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJerry and Tally Leonard skate at Portland’s Lloyd Center on 4 August. The married couple, both in their 70s, had skated together at the rink for nearly 60 years.Photograph: Michael Hanson for The Washington Post via Getty ImagesSportThe last lap at Lloyd Center: how America is losing its mall ice rinksThe Portland rink where Tonya Harding first skated was an affordable community institution for six decades. Its closure echoes the disappearance of mall ice across the USTalia BarringtonTue 11 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen theLloyd Center shopping mallfirst opened its doors in 1960, it boasted a unique feature: an ice rink. In the nearly seven decades since, that ice rink – first outdoor, then enclosed by a glass ceiling that sheltered mall-goers from the elements – became a cultural epicenter for Portlanders.Children accompanying parents on errands spotted peers gliding across the ice and begged for lessons. Shoppers, taking a break from the stores, watched idly from the three levels that looked out over the ice. At Christmas, a giant tree adorned the middle of the rink, making Lloyd Center an essential part of the holiday season.Deemed important enough for a stop on Bobby Kennedy’s campaign trail in 1968, famed as the site of Tonya Harding’s first steps on ice in 1973, the rink provided generations with a fun, easy and affordable space to skate. Even asmalls have declinedin America, attendance at the Lloyd Center rink endured, supporting aLearn To Skate USAprogram with one of the highest enrollment rates in the nation.But last Saturday that allcame to an end, when skaters laced up at Lloyd Center for the last time, and the mall, along with its rink, was finally shuttered.Lloyd Center’s demise is not isolated. For decades, ice rinks served as both spectacle and public amenity at shopping malls across the US, placing a sport often associated with private clubs directly in the path of ordinary families. But as aging malls have closed or been redeveloped, many of those rinks have disappeared, eliminating some of the most visible and accessible entry points to skating.“The environment is pretty special,” said Wendy May, 69, the day before the closure. “Because people on the upper levels are watching, a regular skater can feel like they’re performing. And there’s a lot of public skaters, so a lot of people are taking their first strokes and glides on this ice. There are birthday parties, and it’s a community center in a big way.”That feeling of community extended beyond the rink boards. Coaches and skating moms described how in recent years Lloyd Center had become a haven for teens and adults to socialize, with chess and bridge clubs, mall walkers, Zine meet-ups and residents seeking respite from smoky summers filling the space despite the emptying store fronts.double quotation markMall rinks made skating part of ordinary public life: a casual skater could step on to the ice without joining a team or academy“I watch high school and college students use that third floor for study groups,” said Lloyd Center coach and Pacific Ice Academy co-director Alec Schmitt. “I watch on the first floor on Saturdays, while I’m teaching classes, groups of trading card swaps and collector swaps.”The rink, which was never a standard competitive size, was further reduced during a 2016 renovation to a perfect oval shape, so young skaters who had dreams of competing, often ended up taking lessons at other, full-sized rinks. But still skaters returned to Lloyd Center, where they’d made friends, where the atmosphere was more relaxed, and where many said they felt most at home. Schmitt, who has coached for more than 10 years, said Lloyd Center was “unequivocally, the most inclusive rink I’ve ever been a part of”.Lydia Finch, now co-director of the Pacific Ice Academy at Lloyd Center, began skating in the mall at four years old, and even after she started training full-time at a bigger rink, still found herself back at Lloyd Center. “Every single week I would still go there Tuesdays and Thursdays and practice in the afternoons after school,” said Finch. When she graduated high school and started college, a position opened up there for teaching Learn To Skate classes, and she described the shift to coaching as a “full-circle moment”.With the closure of Lloyd Center,Portlandhas now been left without a rink within the city limits. Part of Lloyd Center’s appeal was its central location near the light rail and bus routes as well as several highways, offering a diverse range of skaters easy access to a sport that has been known for its exclusivity.That distinction is central to what is being lost nationwide. Purpose-built skating complexes may offer larger and better ice, but many are situated on the suburban fringe, difficult to reach without a car and heavily booked by hockey teams or competitive skating clubs. Mall rinks made skating part of ordinary life: a child could discover the sport while running errands with a parent, and a casual skater could step on to the ice without first joining a team or academy.That accessibility, along with the efforts of coaching staff to make pricing straightforward and affordable, was working. According to US Figure Skating’s vice-president of membership, Elise Preston, Lloyd Center had the largest Learn To Skate USA program in Oregon with nearly 800 participants last season. The next largest program in Oregon is less than half of the size, with about 300 skaters. Management at the Lloyd Center rink recorded an average of 700 class enrollments per multi-week session.View image in fullscreenSkaters enjoy the ice skating rink inside Lloyd Center last week ahead of Saturday’s closing day.Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty ImagesHowever, even for those who can commute, it isn’t as simple as shifting to another rink. The three nearest facilities already have full rosters of coaches, compete for ice time with hockey, and in some cases are even unable to add young skaters to their academy programs. Coaches like Finch and Schmitt have been left with the impossible options to move away from family to be near other rinks, or quit the job they love.“A lot of us are looking at having to potentially drive two hours north or south to Tacoma, Washington, or to Eugene – and that’s if we can get our students to make that commute,” Finch said. A few have been commuting three hours to Snoqualmie. “A lot of coaches are having to find other jobs. I already work as a medical assistant aside from coaching, so I’m not stressed for support, financially.”But she talks about the huge emotional toll of losing the relationships she had built with her skating students and their families. “A lot of my students, as well as myself, don’t want to have to part ways,” she added.Julie Weber, whose daughter began skating at Lloyd Center at three years old, said that her daughter will continue to skate when and where she can, but that she will take a year off from competing due to the time it takes and the financial hardship of traveling to other rinks. “I talk to parents every day, asking: ‘What is this gonna mean for your kid? Can you go to these other rinks? Can you even get there? Can you even afford it? Will they still compete?’” she said.Weber, along with May and several other parents and adult skaters reeling from the rink’s closure, serves on the board of the newly-formedBridgetown Ice Skating Collective(BISC), a non-profit hoping to establish a new ice rink to support the local demand. Part of the devastation, many explained, was that in the approximately five years since the demolition of the mall was announced, developers had suggested a new rink would be part of the plans.“We were trying to turn lemons into lemonade,” Weber said. “Lloyd is busting at the seams, and we all knew it’s too small an ice sheet to do the many things that coaches and people want to do here.” Maybe, they all thought, a full-sized ice rink was actually just what the community needed.That was until February, when it became clear that the owners, KKR Real Estate Finance Trust Inc and Urban Renaissance Group, did not have plans to build a new location for the rink.After a final appeal was rejected, BISC is now actively seeking endorsement and funds for a temporary rink, before a more permanent municipal solution can be set in motion. May said there is interest from local council members and some investors, but she’s unsure how long it will be before a new ice surface will be ready for skaters.On the final day of the mall’s 66-year tenure, from early in the morning to late into the evening, the community poured into the Center to pay their final respects. In numbers estimated at the thousands, locals skated, mall-walked and reminisced as they said goodbye to such a long-standing stalwart of Portland’s downtown area.“It’s a huge loss in so many ways,” Webber said. “But we’re still family. We’re going to run into each other at other rinks. We’ll find those sparks of joy. And I think it’ll work out. We’ll just stay strong. I’m optimistic.”Explore more on these topicsSportPortlandFigure skatingUS sportsWest CoastfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: New York Jets’ Qwan’tez Stiggers in hospital after collapsing during practice | New York Jets | The Guardian
description: The cornerback was taken to hospital by ambulance after he briefly lost consciousness during a joint practice with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The cornerback was taken to hospital by ambulance after he briefly lost consciousness during a joint practice with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers
Content: Qwan'tez Stiggers has become an important part of the Jets’ special teams unit.Photograph: Phelan M Ebenhack/APView image in fullscreenQwan'tez Stiggers has become an important part of the Jets’ special teams unit.Photograph: Phelan M Ebenhack/APNew York JetsNew York Jets’ Qwan’tez Stiggers in hospital after collapsing during practiceCornerback loses consciousness during joint practiceTeam indicate 24-year-old is recovering wellAssociated PressTue 11 Aug 2026 15.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNew York Jets cornerback Qwan’tez Stiggers was taken to a hospital by ambulance after he briefly lost consciousness during a joint practice with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Tuesday.Jets coach Aaron Glenn said the 24-year-old Stiggers was conscious and talking on the field before being put on a stretcher and taken for further examination. There was no immediate word on Stiggers’ condition, but Glenn indicated the cornerback was recovering well.“He was able to talk and I want to make sure I go and see him after this, just to make sure I’m good with everything,” Glenn said. “But for the most part, he was good.”The Jets and Buccaneers were in the middle of special teams drills when Glenn said Stiggers came to the sideline.“He actually fell out,” Glenn said. “The good thing is, he was conscious. Our guys did a hell of a job, just like most medical staffs around this league do in situations like that, and they took the necessary steps just to make sure that we do everything we can to be on board when it comes to those situations.”Several Jets teammates took a knee near the sideline and others formed a prayer circle after Stiggers collapsed. After several minutes, he was placed on a stretcher and carried into the ambulance as fans seated near the area clapped in support.“It was very sad, very emotional,” running back Breece Hall said. “You get on your knee and say a prayer for him and hope he’s OK.”Added defensive tackle Harrison Phillips: “What’s been shared to us is things are on the up and up.”Practice resumed after a stoppage of 10 minutes while Stiggers was being attended to.Stiggers is entering his third season with the Jets after being a fifth-round draft pick in 2024. He was one of that draft’s feelgood stories: he had no college football experience and was the first player drafted directly from the CFL since Miami took Jermaine Haley in 1999.In 29 games, including five starts, with New York, Stiggers has 35 tackles, two fumble recoveries and three passes defensed. He is also one of the Jets’ top special teams players.Explore more on these topicsNew York JetsNFLUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Does Sophie Cunningham benefit from white privilege? Of course she does | WNBA | The Guardian
description: One of the player’s WNBA rivals said the Fever guard is treated differently from her Black peers. There’s plenty of evidence to back that statement up
Author: Etan Thomas
Headline: One of the player’s WNBA rivals said the Fever guard is treated differently from her Black peers. There’s plenty of evidence to back that statement up
Content: Sophie Cunningham has hauled in lucrative endorsement deals this season.Photograph: Paul Beaty/APView image in fullscreenSophie Cunningham has hauled in lucrative endorsement deals this season.Photograph: Paul Beaty/APWNBADoes Sophie Cunningham benefit from white privilege? Of course she doesEtan ThomasOne of the player’s WNBA rivals said the Fever guard is treated differently from her Black peers. There’s plenty of evidence to back that statement upTue 11 Aug 2026 04.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 09.59 EDTShareWhite privilege. An accusation that triggers multitudes of white people in America as if you had insulted their mother. Mention racism, and people may debate you. Mention discrimination, and people may even listen. But say the words “white privilege”, and suddenly defenses go up, outrage erupts, and people start explaining why privilege couldn’t possibly have anything to do with what everyone just witnessed with their own eyes.Which brings us to DiJonai Carrington and Sophie Cunningham.Etan ThomasIn Saturday’s WNBA game between Chicago Sky and Indiana Fever, Carrington was ejected after being assessed a Flagrant 2 formaking contact with Cunningham’s head and neck areawhile attempting to defend her in transition. Carrington, who is Black, maintained she was making a play on the ball and didn’t intentionally hit Cunningham, who is white. Even Cunningham’s coach at the Fever, Stephanie White, said she did not believe Carrington intentionally went out to hurt Cunningham.Carrington acknowledged she should have been penalized for the foul. But after her ejection, shewent on social mediaand posted those two words many white people seem to fear so much: “WHITE PRIVILEGE”.Predictably, Carrington’s words became as controversial as the foul itself. But instead of dismissing Carrington’s accusation, we should ask why she posted the words that she did –she has saidthey had nothing to do with the officiating decision itself. What happens when Cunningham, a white woman, is the aggressor, and what happens when she is the “victim”?We’ve already seen the first scenario. In June 2025, Cunningham committed a Flagrant 2 foul against Connecticut Sun guard Jacy Sheldon. Cunningham wrapped Sheldon up as she drove toward the basket,sent her to the floor, and ignited an altercation. Cunningham was correctly ejected and fined by the WNBA.If we are going to discuss racial double standards, we shouldn’t manipulate facts. Cunningham was ejected in 2025, just as Carrington was ejected in 2026. The referees treated both players the same –as Carrington herself appeared to suggest. Instead, the white privilege is found in what happened next.As my co-host on The Collision podcast, Chuck Modi,pointed outafter Cunningham’s 2025 foul, a significant portion of the public didn’t transform her into a dangerous menace threatening the integrity of women’s basketball. Instead, she was lauded as an enforcer. She was the teammate willing to protect Caitlin Clark, a player whom many on the right see as a delicate white flower who needs protecting at all costs. Cunningham also became immensely marketable.Her TikTok following explodedfrom 300,000 to over one million, and she was flooded with lucrative marketing opportunities.double quotation markWhen Cunningham fouls an opponent, she’s an enforcer. When Carrington does the same, she’s a dangerRingpartnered with Cunninghamin an advertisement that explicitly played off her image as the Fever’s “protector”. The campaign converted the symbolism of her retaliatory foul into a branding opportunity: Cunningham protects her teammates; Ring protects her home.Think about that. A white player is ejected, and emerges with exponentially more followers, an “enforcer” identity, and lucrative endorsements.Now imagine if Carrington had been flooded with endorsement deals built around being an “enforcer” after her foul on Cunningham. Would America think that was cute? Would television personalities laugh and celebrate her toughness? Or would she be described with words like “dangerous”, “dirty” and “thug”?That question isn’t hypothetical, either. Look at what happened when Carrington fouled Cunningham.Carrington’s foul was immediately framed by commentators as something larger than basketball. Cunningham was portrayed not simply as the recipient of a Flagrant 2, but as another whiteWNBAplayer being victimized by an increasingly dangerous culture within the league. We’ve heard similar rhetoric surrounding Clark for years: opponents aren’t merely fouling her; they are targeting her, jealous of her, and trying to hurt her. The racial subtext matters because the villains in this narrative are disproportionately Black women, while the white players like Clark and Cunningham are portrayed as in need of protection.View image in fullscreenSophie Cunningham and DiJonai Carrington confront each other during Saturday’s game.Photograph: Icon Sportswire/Getty ImagesThen the Carrington-Cunningham incident went somewhere very strange: Florida’s attorney general, James Uthmeier, got involved.Uthmeier saidhe would be willing to charge players with assault and battery if they committed hard fouls in Florida.This is, of course, ridiculous, and Uthmeier – no doubt grandstanding for a certain demographic of conservative voters – knows it. Quite apart from the fact that Florida doesn’t have an WNBA team, we are talking about professional basketball. Hard fouls have existed since Dr James Naismith hung a peach basket on a wall. Players have been clotheslined, elbowed, shoved, and involved in fights. Flagrant fouls exist precisely because sports already have mechanisms to distinguish basketball contact from excessive contact. Yet suddenly, we are discussing criminal prosecution.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWould we be having that conversation if Cunningham had fouled Carrington? We don’t have to guess. When Cunningham committed her retaliatory Flagrant 2 against Jacy Sheldon, where was Uthmeier? Where were the threats of assault charges, the politicians warning the WNBA, or the television segments asking if Black women were safe from prowling white women?That’s what privilege looks like. When Cunningham fouls an opponent, she’s an enforcer. When Carrington does the same, she’s a danger.This isn’t the first time Cunningham has become a cultural phenomenon. In June, she pointed at Phoenix Mercury’s DeWanna Bonner during an on-court confrontation. The image exploded across social media, accumulating tens of millions of views as Cunningham’s pointbecame a meme. People described it as hilarious, petty, and iconic – and there’s no denying it was entertaining.But in considering white privilege,I posted an image on social mediaof Cunningham as a Black WNBA player and asked: How would it be viewed if the roles were reversed? If a Black player followed a white opponent around the court, staring her down and pointing in her face for 20 seconds. Would she still be called adorable? Or would she be described as threatening, aggressive, classless, and hostile?That’s why conversations about white privilege cannot stop at whether two players received the same foul classification on the scorecard.We could test this. Take every comparable WNBA flagrant foul over the last several seasons involving contact to the head or neck. Separate the incidents by the race of the offending player and the race of the recipient. Examine the headlines and social media posts. How frequently do the words “hard foul” come up versus “cheap shot”, “brutal”, “assault”, “targeted”, or “clobbered”?That would be a far more meaningful investigation of white privilege than screaming about playing “the race card.”Privilege isn’t always receiving something someone else didn’t. Sometimes privilege is being granted innocence of interpretation. It’s having your aggression interpreted as toughness, your confrontation as personality, your retaliation as loyalty, your defiance as humor, and your anger as passion. Meanwhile, someone else’s aggression becomes violence, confrontation becomes hostility, retaliation becomes assault, and anger becomes evidence that she is dangerous.White privilege doesn’t require Cunningham to ask for it or be racist. It doesn’t require every referee, journalist, or politician to consciously think: “She’s white, so I’m going to treat her differently”.Privilege operates through assumptions, sympathy, and framing – through whose aggression gets contextualized and whose gets criminalized.So when Carrington talks about white privilege, instead of becoming enraged, America should examine why those two words make people angrier than the double standard she’s asking them to examine. The question isn’t simply whether white privilege exists in the WNBA. The real question is: How much more evidence do people need before they’re willing to admit that it does?Explore more on these topicsWNBABasketballUS sportsIndiana FeverChicago SkycommentShareReuse this content

title: Arthur Fery ready to test himself at Masters level after Wimbledon run | Tennis | The Guardian
description: Arthur Fery, Britain’s surprise Wimbledon semi-finalist, will return to competition in the Cincinnati Open
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Arthur Fery, Britain’s surprise Wimbledon semi-finalist, will return to competition in the Cincinnati Open
Content: Arthur Fery took a holiday and training block after his memorable performance at Wimbledon.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenArthur Fery took a holiday and training block after his memorable performance at Wimbledon.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianTennisArthur Fery ready to test himself at Masters level after Wimbledon runBriton reached SW19 semi-finals as a wildcardWorld No 36 has first-round bye in CincinnatiTumaini Carayolin CincinnatiTue 11 Aug 2026 17.45 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArthur Fery believes he is at the start of a new chapter in his career as he returns to competition for the first time since his surprise run to the Wimbledon semi-finals as a wildcard.Fery will compete for the first time in a month at the Cincinnati Open this week, after opting to take a short holiday and training block following the most demanding fortnight of his career at Wimbledon.“It’s the first time that I’ve broken through like that and I’m going to be able to play only tour events, so I’m looking forward to that,” he said.Vondrousova’s antics put tennis doping tests in spotlight – a far cry from football’s view | Tumaini CarayolRead moreFery arrives in Cincinnati at his career-high ranking of No 36 and despite this being his first direct entrance into a Masters 1000 event he is seeded No 32 and will receive a first-round bye. He awaits either James Duckworth of Australia or a qualifier in round two, with a potential meeting with the fifth seed Alex de Minaur looming in round three.Although Fery’s new ranking is a great achievement in itself, its most important utility is the opportunities it opens up for his scheduling. It has massive implications for the 24-year-old’s career as he will now be able directly to enter the main draw of all regular events on the ATP tour.Until now, Fery had spent his professional career competing at the lower-level ATP Challenger events. He sat outside the top 150 at the beginning of the grass court season, still far from being ranked highly enough to directly enter most ATP events.Fery’s ranking of No 114 at Wimble­don appeared to position him for months of trying to bridge the gap between the two tours, a tricky undertaking that requires players to choose between competing in ATP Challenger events and the qualifying rounds of ATP tour events. Instead, he will completely bypass that stage.Perhaps the most pressing question surrounding Fery after such an unexpected run was how representative his performances at Wimbledon were of his actual level. Fery showed his mental toughness and skill throughout the tournament, dragging himself from the brink of defeat in consecutive five-set wins, against Zizou Bergs and Grigor Dimitrov, before dismant­ling the French Open finalist Flavio Cobolli to reach the semi-final, where he lost against Alexander Zverev.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHowever, this was also a unique situation – competing on grass, in front of a home crowd and against players unfamiliar with his game has its benefits. These tournaments will allow him to see exactly how his game matches up to the elite. Fery, for his part, believes completely that this is where he belongs. “I was always confident that I could play with top players. But yeah, now having the ranking to back it up is really great. And obviously you’re playing great players week in, week out, so it’s difficult.“It’s a difficult sport with fine margins, so you’ve got to have a lot of self-belief. I think it comes from just proving to myself that I have beaten top players and if I do the right things and train well, I feel good on court when I’m with those top guys.”Explore more on these topicsTennisArthur FeryWimbledon 2026newsShareReuse this content

title: Portland Thorns and USWNT star Olivia Moultrie out for season with ACL injury | NWSL | The Guardian
description: The Portland Thorns midfielder is likely to miss the Concacaf W Championship after suffering a season-ending knee injury in training
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Portland Thorns midfielder is likely to miss the Concacaf W Championship after suffering a season-ending knee injury in training
Content: Portland Thorns FC midfielder Olivia Moultrie in action during the first half of an NWSL match against the Washington Spirit in March.Photograph: Terrance Williams/APView image in fullscreenPortland Thorns FC midfielder Olivia Moultrie in action during the first half of an NWSL match against the Washington Spirit in March.Photograph: Terrance Williams/APNWSLPortland Thorns and USWNT star Olivia Moultrie out for season with ACL injury20-year-old injured right knee during Thorns trainingMidfielder had five goals and five assists this seasonMoultrie likely to miss Concacaf W ChampionshipAgenciesTue 11 Aug 2026 16.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePortland Thorns midfielder Olivia Moultrie has been placed on the season-ending injury list because of an ACL injury, the National Women’s Soccer League team announced Tuesday.Moultrie, who also plays for the US national team, injured her right knee during training last week, the team said.“Heartbroken doesn’t even begin to sum up all of the feelings right now,” Moultrieposted to Instagram. “To be taken away from something you love more than anything is a feeling I never wanted to experience. I know there is a reason this path has been chosen for me and I can’t promise everything but I can promise I’ll be back and I’ll be better.”Moultrie, 20, had five goals and five assists for the Thorns this season. She signed with Portland in 2021 after she successfully sued theNWSLover a rule prohibiting teams from signing players under 18.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram.
