title: Djed Spence nears Tottenham exit with Inter in talks over £25.6m move | Tottenham Hotspur | The Guardian
description: Tottenham are prepared to allow Djed Spence to join Inter, with the England defender expected to cost around €30m
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Tottenham are prepared to allow Djed Spence to join Inter, with the England defender expected to cost around €30m
Content: Djed Spence on the ball for England against Argentina in their World Cup semi-final.Photograph: Ian MacNicol/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDjed Spence on the ball for England against Argentina in their World Cup semi-final.Photograph: Ian MacNicol/Getty ImagesTottenham HotspurDjed Spence nears Tottenham exit with Inter in talks over £25.6m moveEngland defender keen on move to Italian championsUdogie and Porro set to be Spurs’ first-choice full-backsEd AaronsTue 11 Aug 2026 12.22 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 17.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTottenham are prepared to allow Djed Spence to join Inter, with the England defender expected to cost around €30m (£25.6m).Spence – who started four games at the World Cup, including the semi-final against Argentina – has fallen further down the pecking order at Spurs after the arrival of Andy Robertson from Liverpool. He signed a new four‑year contract in north London at the start of last season but is believed to be keen on joining the Italian champions, with Destiny Udogie and Pedro Porro expected to be Roberto De Zerbi’s preferred full‑backs this season.Men’s transfer window summer 2026: all deals from Europe’s top five leaguesRead moreTalks are ongoing over a fee for the 26-year-old as Inter search for a replacement for Denzel Dumfries, who joined Real Madrid this summer. But personal terms are not believed to be an issue and an agreement is likely to be reached that will see Inter pay only slightly more than the £20m fee Spurs paid to sign Spence from Middlesbrough in 2022.Inter also held talks with Tottenham over a potential move for Cristian Romero but the Argentina defender looks poised to join Atlético Madrid for a fee of €40m. They have yet to agree a fee but Romero is expected to move to La Liga despite interest from elsewhere, including the Premier League champions Arsenal.On Monday, Spurs – who have spent almost £240m this summer on new players, including Sandro Tonali for a club‑record £92.5m, confirmed that Micky van de Ven has signed a new five-year contract. “It’s clear the direction the club wants to go in and I want to be a part of it. I’m excited about what’s to come,” the Netherlands defender said.Crystal Palace, meanwhile, are in talks to re-sign Evann Guessand on a season-long loan from Aston Villa. The Côte d’Ivoire forward spent the second half of last season at Selhurst Park and was part of the side that won the Conference League in May, although Palace decided not to take up an option to sign him earlier in the summer. The south London club are also expected to complete deals for Anan Khalaili from Union Saint‑Gilloise for £21m and Zavier Gozo from Real Salt Lake for £11m.Explore more on these topicsTottenham HotspurInternazionaleEuropean club footballSerie ATransfer windownewsShareReuse this content

title: Apple TV eyes US broadcast rights to the Open as foray into sports broadcasting continues | The Open | The Guardian
description: Apple TV has joined the battle to win US rights to golf’s Open Championship in the streaming platform’s latest move into sport
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Apple TV has joined the battle to win US rights to golf’s Open Championship in the streaming platform’s latest move into sport
Content: New Zealand's Ryan Fox celebrates winning this year’s Open.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersView image in fullscreenNew Zealand's Ryan Fox celebrates winning this year’s Open.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersThe OpenApple TV eyes US broadcast rights to the Open as foray into sports broadcasting continuesNBC is current US broadcaster of tournamentStreaming services making inroads into live sportsExclusive byMatt HughesTue 11 Aug 2026 13.10 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 13.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleApple TV has joined the battle to win US rights to golf’s Open Championship in the streaming platform’s latest move into sport.The Guardian has learned that Apple has had preliminary discussions with the R&A about bidding for the Open, whose current US deal with NBC expires in 2028.The formal tender process will take place at the start of next year, with the R&A also expecting interest from Apple’s fellow streamers Netflix and Amazon in a major challenge to traditional broadcasters.NBC has had live rights to the Open since 2017 when it outbid existing holders ESPN to secure a 12-year deal, but now appears in danger of losing its foothold. NBC’s Open rights are shared with media company Versant, who operate theGolfChannel.Apple has followed other streaming companies in experimenting with sports rights in recent years, and appears intent on adding to its portfolio, particularly in the US.A 10-year deal worth $2.5bn for Major League Soccer rights has not been a success, with both parties agreeing to terminate the contract three years early amid disappointing viewing figures. But Apple has not shelved its sporting ambitions and last year secured a five-year deal worth $750m for exclusive Formula One rights in the US.A source with knowledge of Apple’s plans told the Guardian that the company remains committed to investing in sports rights, and will continue to search for the right properties.“We have an excellent partnership with NBC and Versant which has delivered significant benefits forThe Open, the AIG Women’s Open and our other championships and international matches,” a spokesman for the R&A said in response to the Guardian.“As we look ahead to the next US media cycle for the R&A’s rights, we expect to enter discussions with our incumbent partners NBC and Versant in due course. We will also continue to monitor the evolving broadcast landscape and the wider interest in our rights.”Explore more on these topicsThe OpenApple TVEuropean TourGolfTV streamingUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Premier League 2026-27 preview No 5: Brighton | Premier League previews 2026-27 | The Guardian
description: Fabian Hürzeler has lost key players including Welbeck and Van Hecke with Brighton needing squad depth to cope with the demands of European football
Author: John Brewin
Headline: Fabian Hürzeler has lost key players including Welbeck and Van Hecke with Brighton needing squad depth to cope with the demands of European football
Content: Georginio Rutter will be a key man for Brighton this season. Photograph: Ashley Western/ShutterstockFabian Hürzeler has lost key players including Welbeck and Van Hecke with Brighton needing squad depth to cope with the demands of European footballByJohn BrewinTue 11 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGuardian writers’ predicted position:9th (NB: this is not necessarily John Brewin’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)Last season’s position:8thProspectsLast season’s final day in May featured Brighton fans and players united in celebrating qualification for the Europa Conference Leaguedespite losing 3-0 to Manchester United. Considering West Ham and Crystal Palace have won the competition since its inception, lifting that trophy becomes a target to aim for.How realistic is that? Beyond the Thursday-Sunday schedule playing in the Conference League demands, it has been a summer of change within the ranks. James Milner did not celebrate as Europe was reached. By then he had decided he would retire. Danny Welbeck was last season’s outstanding forward for Brighton, one of the best in England, and hasfollowed the now traditional trade routeto Chelsea. Him turning 36 in November adds a note of curiosity to that transfer. Thus, the veteran class, each older than their head coach, Fabian Hürzeler, still just 33, is reduced to Pascal Gross, Lewis Dunk and the reserve goalkeeper Jason Steele. Solly March not being offered a new contract was another break from the past, a surprise to a long-serving and popular player whose injury problems counted against him.Jan Paul van Hecke, last season’s best defender, has beensold to Tottenham for £52m, with the teenager Luka Vuskovic coming in the opposite direction. If Brighton supporters are wondering about their club’s slew of new signings then their Premier League peers will be watching as closely, such is the industry’s respect for the club’s recruitment. The Jamestown Analytics company owned by Tony Bloom, Brighton’s financier, is a football Rosetta Stone, admired and coveted. It is not, though, completely infallible; there have been a number of busts.Fans hugely enjoyed being in the Europa League three seasons ago, reaching the last 16, but it had a deleterious effect at home, stretching resources and relations with the then manager, Roberto De Zerbi. Brighton finished a disappointing 11th. Better is hoped for this time around.Past five seasonsOff-field pictureSafe standing is being expanded in the South Stand of the Amex, as part of a £40m modernisation project. The work will take place during September’s extended international break and is a drive towards enhancing the atmosphere. The ownership is among the most mindful of the matchday experience in English football. For Albion fans seeking a middle ground between the posh seats and pre-match drinks in the concourse, there’s the opening of the 1901 Pub, a “hybrid traditional pub and premium matchday lounge designed for a more relaxed fan experience”. With a capacity of 660, membership starts at £173 a month.Owner-fan relationshipThere can be no doubt that Brighton’s continued success relies on the patronage and funds of Bloom. The club’s supporters are more than aware of this. Last season, Bloom’s involvement withHearts’ chase for the Scottish titledemonstrated he has wider horizons, though his key priority will always be the hometown, boyhood club. In January, “the Lizard”, as he is known in the gambling circles he made his fortune, increased his Brighton investment with a £107m loan, making for an overall loan amount of £400m. Without Bloom’s financing and his continued enthusiasm, Brighton would not be the established, model Premier League force they remain.The managerHürzeler has done much growing up in public. There have been points during his two seasons when doubts circled. In the boardroom, though, Bloom and his influential chief executive, Paul Barber, have kept faith in the still youthful Bavarian. As a new, three-year contract was announced in May, Bloom referred to a “clear playing identity”. Hürzeler can be fiery. His touchline behaviour does not always meet the approval of officials and opposing coaches but he enters the season as the fifth longest-serving manager in thePremier Leagueand will be showing off a severe hair remodelling unveiled in pre-season. Success in European football can burnish a growing reputation.Star signingView image in fullscreenNew arrival Luka Vuskovic’s playmaking abilities from the back are highly regarded.Photograph: Matt Impey/ShutterstockWill Tottenham rue never drawing on Vuskovic’s potential? Brighton hope so. He never played a match for Spurs but impressed on loan at Hamburg, where his reading of the game, positioning and maturity drew rave reviews. The signing of the experienced centre-back Pascal Struijk from Leeds means Vuskovic can be allowed time to develop but the Croatian’s playmaking abilities from the back may make him a long-term successor for the captain, Dunk. His fee, reported at £46m when Spurs paid £12m for him, suggests the demand for his talents. The hope and expectation is that the deal becomes regarded as a bargain.Stat attackThe two Manchester clubs were the only sides who scored more Premier League goals than Brighton in regular play last season. The Seagulls dropped down the standings a little once counterattacks were included but they had an identical rate for open play expected goals per game as Arsenal in 2025-26. There should be no shortage of chances for whoever picks up the goalscoring baton after Danny Welbeck’s departure.StatSet for a breakthroughPatience with new arrivals is part of the Brighton doctrines, players are given latitude and opportunity to bed in. A season’s grace is often granted, and Charalampos Kostoulas showed a few flashes of his talent during the 2025-26 campaign. With Welbeck departed, there is a vacancy to lead the line. The Greece international scored a brilliantoverhead kick against Bournemouthin January, and at 19, last summer’s signing from Olympiakos should receive more airtime than the two league starts he received last season. His Greek compatriot Stefanos Tzimas, back in training after an ACL rupture, can provide either competition or a partnership.World Cup impactWhen Jordan Henderson played master of ceremonies as England celebrated third place at the World Cup, he made sure Steele was given a medal for his acclaimed, appreciated work as training goalkeeper. It was an otherwise mixed summer for Albion players, with Maxim De Cuyper going furthest to the quarter-finals with Belgium. Diego Gómez was suspended forParaguay’s historic defeat of Germanythough featured in his country’s bruising exit at the hands of France. Yasin Ayari became the first Brighton player to score two World Cup goals in a game asSweden beat Tunisia 5-1. Michael Svoboda, the summer defensive signing from Venezia, did not play a single minute for Austria.Explore more on these topicsPremier League previews 2026-27Brighton & Hove AlbionPremier LeaguefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Emery positive about Aston Villa’s outlook despite summer exits as PSG await | Aston Villa | The Guardian
description: Ebullient manager takes his side to Salzburg to cross swords with the European champions in the Super Cup
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: Ebullient manager takes his side to Salzburg to cross swords with the European champions in the Super Cup
Content: Unai Emery speaks to the media at Stadion Salzburg.Photograph: Leonhard Simon/UEFA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenUnai Emery speaks to the media at Stadion Salzburg.Photograph: Leonhard Simon/UEFA/Getty ImagesAston VillaEmery positive about Aston Villa’s outlook despite summer exits as PSG awaitEbullient manager takes his side to Salzburg to cross swords with the European champions in the Super CupBen Fisherin SalzburgTue 11 Aug 2026 16.14 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 18.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne thing was almost instantly detectable as Unai Emery walked into a stuffy room inside the Red Bull Arena on the eve of Wednesday’s Super Cup againstParis Saint-Germain. After a summer of change, Aston Villa’s manager appeared uber-relaxed, confident his team will absorb a series of headline departures. He cracked a joke about his English improving and poked fun at John McGinn, impersonating his captain while next to him on the auditorium’s top table.Emery was in a jovial mood, then. But he was also switched on, alert to the frequency, the tone of the wave of questions at the beginning of his fourth full season in the job. “You ask about the changes of coaches and players, but McGinn is intelligent and his answer was fantastic,” Emery said with a smile. “When he arrived here [in 2018] they were in the Championship and every year since there have been changes and still the club has moved forward.Premier League 2026-27 preview No 2: Aston VillaRead more“If we compare ourselves to other clubs like Man City, Chelsea, Manchester United, Arsenal and Liverpool, we are competing with them. We don’t have their power … yet.”Emery spoke with an enthusiasm that will be music to the ears of Villa supporters fretting about the size of the task on his hands. Villa have sold Morgan Rogers, Youri Tielemans and Lucas Digne, the latter returning to PSG, for whom he could make his second debut against his former club. Villa would be tested again if Arsenal make a serious play for Ezri Konsa, who, together with Ollie Watkins and Emiliano Martínez, remains on holiday after World Cup duty. Three key coaching staff have also left, including the set-piece coach, Austin MacPhee. But Emery, the beating heart of the operation, as McGinn said, is still in the building.McGinn’s response was punchy when asked where expectations should be for the forthcoming campaign. “Similar to where it has been in the past few seasons,” he said. “I think we have consistently competed with the best in England, the best in Europe, no matter what the competition is. We will have our challenges. There is a lot of change, but when you look at other clubs around England there is a lot of change there as well: a lot of coaches changing, a lot of players changing.“But what we still have is our main core, same manager, same methods, same desire to achieve more. A lot of people thought we had reached our ceiling a couple of seasons ago, and we proved them wrong. We have still got the same hunger and desire to go and achieve more. Our job is just to integrate the new players and try and make them believe, in the same way the players in the last few seasons have believed. I’m really excited by the sort of ‘new Aston Villa’.”View image in fullscreenPlayers and staff of Aston Villa on the pitch at Stadion Salzburg.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesVilla, of course, did not want to lose Rogers. Chelsea paid £117m to sign the England midfielder, two and a half years after Emery asked Villa to pay £8m to take him from Middlesbrough. The same goes for Tielemans, who after a slow start established himself as one of Emery’s undroppables. Villa signed Tielemans on a free but sold the 29‑year‑old for £35m. Digne was an equally reliable performer, taking back the left-back spot from £38m buy Ian Maatsen.Emery knows the business but it was particularly interesting to hear him talk about the importance of the leverage Villa have gained off the back of the ride they have been on over the past few years. One of the most memorable nights was their pulsating quarter-final against PSG 16 months ago, a 3-2 second‑leg victory at Villa Park, when Gianluigi Donnarumma pulled off three superb saves to prevent Villa taking the game to extra time. Emery ended up on all fours after Willian Pacho blocked Maatsen’s goal-bound volley with 28 seconds to play.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The Premier League is the best league in the world and Aston Villa can now have better brands in the way we are,” Emery said. “I am so, so, so happy how the club is committed together with us. [I am so happy] with how we are getting better, keeping our consistency in the Premier League … the club is making a huge effort to try to be in the same direction as me. They are trying to extend Villa Park to achieve 50,000 supporters next season. We are increasing our budget through good results on the pitch, by sometimes selling some players and being consistent like we are, and as well expecting a high level, like we are more or less keeping.”Emery, who spent two years in charge of PSG, knows how these things work. PSG are no longer just a football team but a brand: see their megastore on London’s Oxford Street. PSG’s chief executive, Victoriano Melero, has talked of PSG competing with the likes of Real Madrid on the pitch but labels like the LA Lakers and Ferrari off it.Salzburg is the latest destination on Villa’s quest for success, with 6,000 Villa fans in tow. The stadium facade is plastered with images of McGinn and co celebrating their Europa League win in Istanbul in May. “I am feeling comfortable, happy, very demanding, even more than the last years,” Emery said. “We want more. We are not stopping here.”Explore more on these topicsAston VillaParis Saint-GermainUefa Super CupfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Arsenal’s Myles Lewis-Skelly offered to Manchester United as left-back solution | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: Myles Lewis-Skelly has been offered to Manchester United as a potential left-back option, with Arsenal wishing to recoup some of the £75m paid to Newcastle for Bruno Guimarães
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: Myles Lewis-Skelly has been offered to Manchester United as a potential left-back option, with Arsenal wishing to recoup some of the £75m paid to Newcastle for Bruno Guimarães
Content: Myles Lewis-Skelly made only five league starts for Arsenal last season.Photograph: Marc Atkins/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMyles Lewis-Skelly made only five league starts for Arsenal last season.Photograph: Marc Atkins/Getty ImagesManchester UnitedArsenal’s Myles Lewis-Skelly offered to Manchester United as left-back solutionChelsea also made aware of 19-year-old’s availabilityNewcastle’s Lewis Hall remains prime United targetJamie Jacksonin DublinTue 11 Aug 2026 08.09 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMyles Lewis-Skelly has been offered toManchester Unitedas a potential left-back option, with Arsenal wishing to recoup some of the £75m paid to Newcastle for Bruno Guimarães.Chelsea, it is understood, have also been made aware of the 19-year-old’s availability. Lewis-Skelly won the Premier League under Mikel Arteta last term, but whether the west London club will make a move for him is unclear.Men’s transfer window summer 2026: all deals from Europe’s top five leaguesRead moreLewis-Skelly, who made only five league starts and 36 appearances in all competitions in 2025-26, signed a five-year contract last summer. His prospective price is thought to be in the region of £45m.This is within the range of finance United have spent so far this summer, afterYouri Tielemans’s £35m movefrom Aston Villa and Andrey Santos’s arrival for £48m plus £2m of add-ons from Chelsea. United are now weighing up a move for the teenager.Newcastle’s Lewis Hall remains of prime interest for United but, after losing Guimarães, Sandro Tonali to Tottenham, and Anthony Gordon to Barcelona, the new Newcastle manager, Matthias Jaissle, is intent the 21-year-old England international does not also departRB Leipzig’s 28-year-old left-back David Raum is another in the position United may assess.Chelsea have already had a busy summer in the market, having spent over £300m on a raft of new signings. Maxence Lacroix and Marco Palestra have been brought in to bolster the centre and right of the defence respectively, while Morgan Rogers became the club’s record signing at a cost of £117m.But Xabi Alonso’s side have a hole on the left of their defence afterMarc Cucurella’s £52m move to Real Madrid. The 20-year-old Jorrel Hato, who featured for the Netherlands at the World Cup, was Cucurella’s deputy at left-back.Mason Mount missed training on Monday and Tuesday at United’s County Kildare summer training camp owing to a knock he received on a foot in Saturday’s 1-1 draw with Paris Saint-Germain in Gothenburg.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe the 27-year-old midfielder being stood down is a precautionary measure, it is understood, and he is also set to sit out Wednesday’s penultimate pre-season friendly against Leeds at Croke Park. The game at the 81,300 capacity venue is a sell-out.United’s final friendly before Michael Carrick’s team start the season on Saturday week at Hull is against Milan in Wroclaw on Saturday.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedTransfer windowArsenalnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I am quite optimistic’: Newcastle’s Jaissle on leading club after turbulent summer | Newcastle United | The Guardian
description: The former Al-Ahli head coach, chosen by the Saudi owners to replace Eddie Howe, admits ‘vacuum’ after sale of three key players
Author: Louise Taylor
Headline: The former Al-Ahli head coach, chosen by the Saudi owners to replace Eddie Howe, admits ‘vacuum’ after sale of three key players
Content: Newcastle is Matthias Jaissle’s first managerial job in Europe’s top five leagues.Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenNewcastle is Matthias Jaissle’s first managerial job in Europe’s top five leagues.Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/ReutersNewcastle United‘I am quite optimistic’: Newcastle’s Jaissle on leading club after turbulent summerThe former Al-Ahli head coach, chosen by the Saudi owners to replace Eddie Howe, admits ‘vacuum’ after sale of three key playersLouise Taylorat St James' ParkTue 11 Aug 2026 15.15 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMatthias Jaissle has been described as “fire” and a “rockstar”, but his formal “unveiling” as Newcastle’s manager revealed a rather more considered and conservative character than advertised.At the precise moment the clock struck 3pm on Tuesday the 38‑year‑old German walked into a packed media suite at St James’ Park. Before taking his seat on the stage Jaissle, wearing a smartly understated open-necked suit complete with a silk pocket square, took a deep breath and jumped down into audience, making a point of shaking everyone’s hand. It was a courteous and classy gesture.‘There is a clear vision’: Matthias Jaissle installed as Newcastle head coachRead moreOnce back on that podium, his evident excitement atexchanging Saudi Arabia’s Al-Ahli for the Premier Leaguewas tempered by the sort of realism inevitable at a club that,in Anthony Gordon,Sandro TonaliandBruno Guimarães, has just sold its three best players.“This is now a vacuum as you call it,”Eddie Howe’s successorsaid in his excellent English. “They were great characters, great players, ­experienced players. Obviously we are in that transition phase. My job is to make the best out of it all. I am quite optimistic. We are ambitious, that’s the most important thing and why I decided to come here. But it will not happen overnight. I’m pretty sure it will be a successful story. But we need time now.”Regular chats with the England head coach, Thomas Tuchel, promise to help minimise any culture shock. “It’s been a long connection,” he said. “Thomas was my youth coach when I was a youth player at Stuttgart. He was amazing, I really admire him.“He’s a really special coach and I’m looking forward to staying in touch with him, and getting insights on the league. That’s something I want to use for sure. But it’s also important to build your own opinions because every coach is their own human being and has their opinions and, ­sometimes players get stuck in a box. It’s ­important for me to be neutral about players.”Allied to a willingness to chall­enge assumptions, such refusal to take labels at face value hinted at the qualities that prompted David ­Hopkinson, Newcastle’s Canadian chief executive, to dub Jaissle “fire” and “a rock star”.View image in fullscreenNewcastle beat Valencia 2-1 in Jaissle’s first pre-season game in charge.Photograph: Clive Brunskill/Getty ImagesIf the one-time RB Salzburg manager’s brand of football – “front foot, intense, aggressive, vertical and, of course, also successful” – fits the latter tag, Newcastle fans have greeted him with an adaptation of a late 1970s Euro-disco hit.Where the Spanish female pop duo Baccara soared to No 1 with Yes, Sir I Can Boogie, travelling supporters attending the friendly win in Valencia last Saturday chorused: “Oh Jaissle I can boogie/You try me once, you’ll beg for more.”Jaissle said: “All my staff members already said they’re looking forward to sitting after a match in the bar and listening to the song. So let’s see about that! I heard it once and I was smiling. I’m really happy the fans already appreciate me a lot. The welcome from the fans was unbelievable when I was having a walk yesterday in the city. It was really giving me a nice feeling.”There were more “big smiles” when he recalled a phone call last month asking him if he would be interested in replacing Howe but, little more than 48 hours after arriving in Newcastle for the first time followinga training camp at La Mangain southern Spain, Jaissle is under no illusions as to the scale of the challenge ahead.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWith the needto comply with football’s spending ruleshaving seen the club pivot to buying young players with high resale potential – four of their five summer signings so far are aged 20 or younger – the immediate future remains opaque.Men’s transfer window summer 2026: all deals from Europe’s top five leaguesRead more“I’m long enough in the industry now that you cannot promise anything,” Jaissle said when asked what he aimed to achieve this season. “It makes no sense to promise you things now because I don’t know how things will look in one year. But it doesn’t make sense to see the negative. There will be more adjustments to the squad this summer. We still have time. I would say keep the optimism.”His cautiously upbeat mood will be bolstered further should Newcastle’s ongoing talks with Benfica about potentially signing their 23‑year‑old full-back Amar Dedic, who played for Jaissle at Salzburg and can operate on both the right and the left, conclude successfully.“I had a tour of St James’ Park two days ago,” Jaissle said. “When I entered the pitch here with my assistant coaches for the first time, we were looking at each other with smiles and goosebumps. It’s really special, an amazing stadium. I can’t wait to see it full.“When I received the call at the end of July and it was clearly most likely Eddie would quit there were no doubts or question marks. I had a big smile.”Explore more on these topicsNewcastle UnitedfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Liverpool, Jeff Bezos and mission creep off the field at Anfield | Soccer | The Guardian
description: In today’s Football Daily: An, ahem, prime example of modern football
Author: John Brewin
Headline: In today’s Football Daily: An, ahem, prime example of modern football
Content: Big Jeff Bezos there.Photograph: Abdul Saboor/ReutersView image in fullscreenBig Jeff Bezos there.Photograph: Abdul Saboor/ReutersFootball Daily newsletterSoccerLiverpool, Jeff Bezos and mission creep off the field at AnfieldSign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!John BrewinTue 11 Aug 2026 10.50 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 11.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTHIS MEANS MORE (MONEY)Far be it for Football Daily to make cheap gags [wait, what? – Football Daily Ed] relating to the involvement of Amazon founder and master of the universe Jeff Bezos in a consortiumbuying around 30% of Liverpool FC. Will new signings arrive via prompt delivery but end up next door at Everton? How will fans rate the packaging? Etc, etc. There’s also the involvement of Eduardo Saverin, the Facebook co-founder poking his head in. Though long ago unfriended by Mark Zuckerberg, Saverin still ranked No 56 on Forbes’s billionaires list. These are seriously rich men, and among the planet’s chino class, to quote Vladimir Putin, “soccer is popular”. The Geopolitics World Cup posh seats were full of those eyeing up deals on a frontier hardly new to investors from the USA USA USA, but where there may be much more gold to strike. See Gianni Infantino’s misreading of the art of the deal as an, ahem, prime example.Bezos is no football man, barely known as a sports fan. Links with buying the Seattle Seahawks, his local NFL franchise, were speculative. He is, though, the third richest man in the world, according to appendage-measuring listicles. Amazon’s market value is higher than Brazil’s annual GDP. For certain people, that triggers arousal at the thought of their team being able to buy the biggest and best players in the world. Just imagine if their club was to spend, say, £446m in a single summer. How good would that be?For others, there is a regrettable mission creep towards a civic institution – one that, despite global fame, cleaves to its local community – being tossed around by venture capitalists. Though that process has been in train sinceTom Hicks and George Gillettarrived on Merseyside, full of huckster charm, almost two decades ago. The socialism and collectivism Bill Shankly envisaged for the club he made famous disappeared in the sepia-tinged rearview mirror. Football was a business even back in Shanks’ day but now attracts the richest suits of all; if Bezos is chancing his arm in football, what price Elon Musk or Google tycoon Larry Page are seen wearing the scarf of their chosen club? Oh joy.Current overlords Fenway Sports Group, who picked up the pieces from impending disaster in 2010, are, yes, a consortium of American venture capitalists. Their existential aim is to make as much loot as possible from an asset purchased for a knockdown price of £300m. It’s gone well. This mooted deal includes Bezos, Saverin and Amit Bhatia, a frontman you may recognise from when QPR fans celebrated their owners being richer than Roman Abramovich. That did not go well. The latest deal would value the club at £4.4bn. High-fives all round, though the doubles and trebles may take time. Liverpool enter the season with an imbalanced squad, unsuited to a manager whose arrival was generally seen as a Good Thing. If football is all about money, even the biggest money cannot solve every problem.QUOTE OF THE DAY“After careful consideration, we don’t feel it is right to proceed at this time without the necessary preparation in place, but we will remain in conversation with the club and see what is possible in the future” – one wealthy benefactor not entering the game – yet – is Turki Alalshikh, whose bid to buy a controlling interest in Derby will no longer proceed, with the club now off the market.RECOMMENDED LOOKINGHere’s David Squires on …the masochistic life of a Football League fan.View image in fullscreenIllustration: David Squires/The GuardianFOOTBALL DAILY LETTERSdouble quotation markHaving also boycotted the GWC and also being very concerned about the season to come, I sympathise with Ken Muir (yesterday’s Football Daily letters). But at least Hearts know who their manager is. Due to the absurd, months-long FA ‘investigation’ into the manager who’s clearly admitted culpability for the undisputed facts of Spygate, my club, Southampton, is in a horrid limbo. Surely it could have been done and dusted in a couple of weeks and Saints could have planned accordingly. But perhaps the FA blazers were too busy writing their letter of support to Gianni Infantino to worry about destabilising my football club” – Bob Cushion.double quotation mark‘It’s 15 years of frustration here at this club,’ says Rangers boss Derek McInnes (yesterday’s Quote of the Day.) Steven Gerrard and the sole object in his managerial trophy cabinet would like a word, Derek” – David Maddock.double quotation markGiven the surfeit of the recent GWC machinations, the blatherings and canvassing for Gianni to do one (or not) and the less-than-sportsmanlike attitude from members of the Argentina team, can we please have a reprise of the Football Daily’s erstwhile, eventually abortive, attempt to ‘STOP FOOTBALL’? It has to be worth a thought, before VAR, PGMOL and Arsenal’s Dark Arts Department™ get to work on the 2026-27 Premier League shenanigans, surely?” – Budgie Wright.If you have any, please send letters tothe.boss@theguardian.com.Today’s letter o’ the day winner is … Bob Cushion, who gets some Football Weekly merch. Terms and conditions for our competitions can be viewedhere.This is an extract from our daily football email … Football Daily. To get the full version,just visit this page and follow the instructions.Explore more on these topicsFootballFootball Daily newsletterfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Chelsea face Real Sociedad in WCL third qualifying round with riches at stake | Women's Champions League | The Guardian
description: Chelsea will face Real Sociedad in the Women’s Champions League’s third qualifying round, needing a victory over two legs to earn a place in the main league phase of the competition
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Chelsea will face Real Sociedad in the Women’s Champions League’s third qualifying round, needing a victory over two legs to earn a place in the main league phase of the competition
Content: Chelsea’s players celebrate a goal during a pre-season game against Auckland FC Women's Invitational XI.Photograph: Phil Walter/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChelsea’s players celebrate a goal during a pre-season game against Auckland FC Women's Invitational XI.Photograph: Phil Walter/Getty ImagesWomen's Champions LeagueChelsea face Real Sociedad in WCL third qualifying round with riches at stakeWSL team will be favourites against Spanish sideFinancial implications of missing out are significantTom GarryTue 11 Aug 2026 07.19 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 17.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChelsea will face Real Sociedad in the Women’s Champions League third qualifying round, needing a win over two legs to secure a place in the main league phase of the competition.The 2021 runners-up and six-time European semi-finalists are taking part in the qualifying stage by virtue of their disappointing third-placed finish in the Women’s Super League last season – their lowest league ­finish since 2019 – and they will be the favourites against the Spanish side.Jordan Nobbs ready to complete wishlist with Newcastle WSL dreamRead moreChelsea could have faced Ajax, Inter, Eintracht Frankfurt or the ­Austrian side St Pölten. They were unable to meet the big-name sides such as Real Madrid, Wolfsburg, Juventus or Paris Saint-Germain at this stage because of seedings. Sonia Bompastor’s team will hope to join Arsenal and Manchester City in the main phase of the competition.The potential financial implications of missing out on ­qualification are significant. All 18 clubs that take part in the league phase will receive a guaranteed minimum of €505,000 (£431,500), plus a further €60,000 for every league‑phase fixture they win and €20,000 for every draw, as well as prize money ranging from €10,000 to €180,000 depending on where they finish in the table, rising by €10,000 per position.Additionally, the eventual champions will receive €1,050,000 in prize money across the course of the knockout phase – including €500,000 specifically for winning the final – as there are six-figure sums on offer for each knockout-phase fixture.Chelsea will be at home for the first leg, which is scheduled to be played on 26 August, with the second leg in Spain scheduled for 2 September, three days before Chelsea’s WSL season opener, which is at home against Aston Villa on 5 September.Quick GuideWCL qualifying drawShowChampions pathSparta Prague v ServettePSV Eindhoven v HB KøgeBrann v Austria ViennaOH Leuven v Czarni SosnowiecLeague pathEintracht Frankfurt v Paris Saint-GermainSt Polten v JuventusWolfsburg v InterChelsea v Real SociedadAjax v Real MadridWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Chelsea have been strong contenders for the European title in recent years, reaching the semi-finals in three of the past four campaigns, but they lost to their rivals Arsenal in a dramatic quarter-final last term.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionReal Sociedad, based in San Sebastián, finished third in Spain’s top division last season behind Real Madrid and Barcelona. The ­qualifying draw was split into two sections, with a “champions path” for winners of their domestic divisions drawn ­separately to the “league path” which contained domestic runners-up and third-placed sides such as Chelsea.Køge, who eliminated the Scottish champions Hearts earlier in the ­qualification process, were pitted against PSV, while in the most eye-catching tie of the round Ajax will take on Real Madrid.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Champions LeagueWomen's footballChelsea WomennewsShareReuse this content

title: Flat racing’s biggest draw Bow Echo in shock retirement after training injury | Horse racing | The Guardian
description: The trainer George Boughey has announced the retirement of his superstar colt Bow Echo because of injury
Author: Tony Paley
Headline: The trainer George Boughey has announced the retirement of his superstar colt Bow Echo because of injury
Content: Bow Echo, ridden by Billy Loughnane, after winning the 2,000 Guineas at Newmarket in May.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAView image in fullscreenBow Echo, ridden by Billy Loughnane, after winning the 2,000 Guineas at Newmarket in May.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAHorse racingFlat racing’s biggest draw Bow Echo in shock retirement after training injuryUnbeaten colt’s career cut short after six racesBoughey: ‘He has given us some extraordinary days’Tony PaleyTue 11 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe trainer George Boughey announced on Tuesday the shock retirement of his superstar colt Bow Echo because of injury.The three‑year-old had cemented his reputation as the outstanding miler in Europe at the Glorious Goodwood meeting two weeks ago, defying the odds bycoming from what looked an impossible position a furlong out to win the Sussex Stakes.Goodwood great escape makes Billy ‘the Kid’ and Bow Echo public favouritesRead moreUnbeaten in three juvenile starts last season, the Night Of Thunder colt confirmed himself the best of his generation over a mile with a breathtaking victory in the 2,000 Guineas at Newmarket before overcoming trouble in running twice since, in the St James’s Palace Stakes at Royal Ascot and then when making it six successes from six outings when beating his elders in the epic Goodwood contest.Bow Echo was considered to be on the cusp of joining the small band of horses with a genuine claim to be a “public horse”, a thoroughbred in the process of transcending the sport and building a devoted following outside the racing cognoscenti. The colt’s popularity was enhanced bythe exploits in the saddle of Billy Loughnane, the baby‑faced 20‑year‑old now odds on to be champion jockey after a meteoric rise.The Newmarket-based Boughey had been preparing Bow Echo for a trip to France for the Prix Jacques le Marois in Deauville at the weekend, the latest staging post on the path to a crack at the top American milers at the Breeders’ Cup in the autumn, but has now confirmed the horse’s track career has been cruelly cut short.In a statement posted on X, the Newmarket trainer said: “It is with great disappointment that we have to announce that Bow Echo has had a setback and will be retired from racing. It has been the honour of a lifetime to train a horse like Bow Echo. He has given us some extraordinary days and taken everyone involved on a journey we will never forget. To retire unbeaten, having won the 2000 Guineas, St James’s Palace Stakes and Sussex Stakes says everything about what an exceptional racehorse he has been.Quick GuideGreg Wood's Wednesday tipsShowBeverley2.15 Ard As A Rock 2.45 Real Edition 3.15 King Sharja 3.45 Homestrait (nap) 4.15 Princess Niyla 4.45 Under The RadarSalisbury2.30 Forbidden Fire 3.00 Supreme King 3.30 Scommessa Sicura 4.00 Remi Mae 4.30 Felicitas 5.00 LondonerFfos Las3.37 Eskimo Pie 4.07 The Coffee Pod 4.37 Isabella De Vega 5.10 Ivat Ghia 5.40 Royal Bodyguard 6.10 A Daughters LoveKempton5.30 Friendly Force 6.00 Manaar 6.30 Percy’s Lad 7.00 Chalk Mountain 7.30 Grey Soul 8.00 Final Night 8.30 Forever Penywern 9.00 Crooked Path (nb)Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.“Bow Echo’s remarkable story began with his owner-breeder, the late Sheikh Mohammed Obaid and it is a great sadness that he was not here to see what a lifetime of breeding was able to produce. Bow Echo’s unbelievable constitution and extraordinary ability have set him apart.”As a grandson to the sire Dubawi he now looks likely to join him at Dalham Hall Stud for Darley, the breeding arm of Godolphin. Liam O’Rourke, director of studs, stallions and breeding at Darley and Godolphintold the Racing Post: “While it is very disappointing that we will not get to see Bow Echo on a racecourse again, he has been an outstanding flagbearer for his champion sire Night Of Thunder and is no doubt one of the most exciting stallions to retire to stud in recent years.“Although his injury will prevent him from running again, he is otherwise in great health and we are immensely proud of all his achievements.”Explore more on these topicsHorse racingHorse racing tipsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Keely Hodgkinson puts on shades and breezes into European 800m semi-finals in style | European Athletics Championships | The Guardian
description: The British runner’s time of 1min 57.28sec was her fastest in a heat, achieved in a race where she wore sunglasses on the track for the first time
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: The British runner’s time of 1min 57.28sec was her fastest in a heat, achieved in a race where she wore sunglasses on the track for the first time
Content: Keely Hodgkinson is a race away from a potential showdown with Audrey Werro and Femke Broeders-Bol on Friday night.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAView image in fullscreenKeely Hodgkinson is a race away from a potential showdown with Audrey Werro and Femke Broeders-Bol on Friday night.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsKeely Hodgkinson puts on shades and breezes into European 800m semi-finals in styleBriton wore sunglasses for first time in a race in victoryHodgkinson’s time of 1min 57.28sec her fastest in a heatSean Ingleat Alexander Stadium, BirminghamTue 11 Aug 2026 09.52 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 17.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKeely Hodgkinson breezed through the opening round of the 800m at the European championships with her ­fastest time in a heat – before laughing about why she had worn sunglasses for the first time in a race.“It’s sunny out there,” she joked. “I’m just trying not to get wrinkles and stop the need for Botox too early.”TheOlympic 800m ­champion’s time of 1min 57.28sec, easing down, showed that she is in prime condition for her ­likely showdown with the new Swiss ­superstar Audrey Werro and the ­multiple Olympic and world ­medallist Femke Broeders‑Bol on Friday night.“I felt really good,” Hodgkinson said. “I think that’s the fastest I’ve ever run in a heat. But I could feel the girls pushing on my shoulder. And, to be honest, running at that kind of pace is a bit more in keeping with my training, so it actually felt kind of nice. I had to slow myself down a bit. But I’ve got a day off now before the semi-final and I feel good.”The 24-year-old Briton revealed she has arrived in ­Birmingham ­having run a personal best in a camp in ­Portugal that she and her coach, ­Trevor Painter, use to gauge her ­fitness before major championships. “Portugal went really well,” Hodgkinson said.“I’m really happy and just excited to showcase where I’m at and hopefully have the performance I know I’m capable of. It’s always all about medals. They create legacy. This will hopefully be my fifth back‑to‑back title.”Next up is the semi-final on Thursday. If she makes it through she will not, however, be wearing the shades in the final on Friday. “No, it’s going to be nearly 10pm and I want to see everything,” she said with a laugh.Werro showed she, too, is in exceptional form as she made her time of 1:57.83 look like a jog in the park. Broeders-Bol also looked good as she continued her transition from the 400m hurdles with a similarly straightforward 1:59.96.Werro, of course,beat Hodgkinson in Stockholmin June in what was the third fastest time in history and she is not concerned about facing Britain’s best on home turf. “It’s always like all other championships,” Werro said.“It’s true that there are a lot of people here for her, but I think there are also a lot of Swiss people, so it’s a bit of a balance. It’s really great to be here at the European championships and I am expecting great things.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It’s a bit different because at the other championships I was never the best, the favourite athlete, and now it’s a little bit more pressure. But I think I can take this pressure and transform it to a positive thing. It gives me a lot of confidence to know I can run fast.”European Athletics Championships face backlash over ‘crazy prices’ and empty seatsRead moreExplore more on these topicsEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsKeely HodgkinsonAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: European Athletics Championships face backlash over ‘crazy prices’ and empty seats | European Athletics Championships | The Guardian
description: Keely Hodgkinson’s coach, and the BBC commentator Steve Cram have led a chorus of concern about high ticket prices causing lower attendances at the European Athletics Championships in Birmingham
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Keely Hodgkinson’s coach, and the BBC commentator Steve Cram have led a chorus of concern about high ticket prices causing lower attendances at the European Athletics Championships in Birmingham
Content: A backdrop of empty seats to the action on day two at Birmingham’s Alexander Stadium.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAView image in fullscreenA backdrop of empty seats to the action on day two at Birmingham’s Alexander Stadium.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsEuropean Athletics Championships face backlash over ‘crazy prices’ and empty seatsBirmingham’s Alexander Stadium half-full on MondayAthletes and fans join chorus of concern over pricesSean IngleTue 11 Aug 2026 09.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 18.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKeely Hodgkinson’s coach, and the BBC commentator Steve Cram have led a chorus of concern about high ticket prices causing low ­attendances at the European ­Athletics Championships in Birmingham.Fans have also criticised the high food prices at the Alexander Stadium, with a barbecue pork roll costing £18.50, a bratwurst hot dog £15, and a bottle of water £3.95.Keely Hodgkinson puts on shades and breezes into European 800m semi-finals in styleRead moreOfficially there were more than 13,000 fans in the stadium on ­Monday night to seeAmy Hunt’s 100m gold medal. But to most observers the 23,000-capacity venue looked barely half-full. The timing is also more than a little awkward given that London’s bid team for the World Athletics ­Championships in 2029 is due to make its final presentation on ­Friday.For the start of the competition, ­category A tickets in the main stand cost £110, with cate­gory B ­tickets coming in at £90. However, those seats have been better filled than the cheaper seats for £60 (­category C) and £40 (category D).“Crazy prices,” Hunt’s agent, Nick Harwell, wrote after her brilliant victory on Monday ­evening. “Such a shame.”Cram, the BBC’s main athletics commentator and a former world 1500m champion, also acknowledged the low figures on Monday night. “A little disappointing in terms of spectators, I have to say that,” he said. “Particularly down the back straight there. There’s not very many people at all in those stands.”In Birmingham city centre there is also little sign that this ­prestigious event is taking place, and the empty seats in the £60 and £40 areas have led some to question whether Birmingham 2026 had done enough to attract casual supporters. Fans are being charged £22.50 to use the park‑and‑ride scheme – although there is a cheaper £17.50 park‑and‑walk option which is a 45‑minute stroll away.Jenny Meadows, who coaches Hodgkinson, acknowledged the issues in a post on X: “Hearing from fans re high ticket prices, parking issues and even people not knowing it was taking place,” she wrote.View image in fullscreenTicket prices, transport problems and timings have been pinpointed as some of the reasons for so many empty seats at the Alexander Stadium.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAA Birmingham 2026 spokesperson defended the ticket prices and said 50% of tickets were priced at £30 and lower with adult tickets starting at £10. “Birmingham 2026 is delighted with ticket sales for the Championships, which have far surpassed our targets,” the spokesperson said.“Friday, Saturday and Sunday evening sessions are ­approaching sellout, with several other ­sessions close to capacity. There are still opportunities to be part of the championships at incredibly good value, including the ‘Mondo’ £6.31 children’s ticket for Friday morning – named in honour of [the pole vaulter Mondo Duplantis’s] world record – while a family of four can attend for as little as £30.”However, the athletics commentator Sonja McLaughlan spoke for many when she posted on X about the prices, which will go up to a top price of £150 for the last three days of competition.“Actually a bit shocked at type of prices being charged,” she wrote. “It’s a shame for the athletes who deserve better. The sport has this precious window without football, free-to-air television exposure and it looks flat with such a sparse crowd.”In response to her post, some questioned why the empty seats were not being given away free to youngsters in athletics clubs and other sports clubs. Another fan said: “­Perhaps the worst prices I’ve seen at a ­sporting event. Not even ­Cheltenham ­competes with this.”Some have also raised questions about the late finishes – the last events finish after 9.50pm – and the ­suita­bility for families of having to walk a mile to the nearest train station or get a bus back to a park‑and‑ride scheme. It also did not help either that, on Monday night, junction 10-11 of the M6, near the ­Alexander ­Stadium, was closed.Explore more on these topicsEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Transfer roundup: Nottingham Forest seal £34m deal for Sporting’s Diomande | Transfer window | The Guardian
description: Nottingham Forest have signed Côte d’Ivoire defender Ousmane Diomande from Sporting, while Fulham have snapped up Shea Charles from Southampton
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Nottingham Forest have signed Côte d’Ivoire defender Ousmane Diomande from Sporting, while Fulham have snapped up Shea Charles from Southampton
Content: Ousmane Diomande in action for Sporting Lisbon against Benfica last season.Photograph: Pedro Nunes/ReutersView image in fullscreenOusmane Diomande in action for Sporting Lisbon against Benfica last season.Photograph: Pedro Nunes/ReutersTransfer windowTransfer roundup: Nottingham Forest seal £34m deal for Sporting’s DiomandeFulham sign Shea Charles from Saints for £30mChelsea’s Filip Jorgensen moves to Strasbourg on loanPA MediaTue 11 Aug 2026 07.47 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 08.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNottingham Forest have signed Côte d’Ivoire defender Ousmane Diomande from Sporting for an undisclosed fee, reported to be £34.2m.The 22-year-old centre-half, who featured in the Côte d’Ivoire’s World Cup squad, has agreed a four-year deal with Forest, who have an option for a further year.Men’s transfer window summer 2026: all deals from Europe’s top five leaguesRead moreForest’s chief football officer, George Syrianos, said: “He has fantastic experience for a defender of his age. Playing a crucial role in title winning teams and going into the latter stages of the Champions League puts him in a great position to integrate well here at Forest.”Diomande began his professional career in Denmark with FC Midtjylland and after joiningSportingin January 2023 he made 132 appearances for the Portuguese club in all competitions.He played a key role in Sporting’s run in the Champions League last season, starting both legs in their quarter-final defeat by Arsenal, and also played the full 90 minutes in Côte d’Ivoire’s World Cup group win against Curaçao.Fulhamhave signed midfielder Shea Charles from Southampton for a reported £30m fee, which would be a record deal for a Northern Ireland international. Charles, 22, has agreed a five-year contract, with a club option to extend by a further 12 months.“It’s a great club, with a really good vision – the manager [Alvaro Arbeloa] explained that to me. To be here is a massive privilege,” Charles said. “I hope to really kickstart my Premier League career. At such a good club as well, it’s perfect for me, and hopefully perfect for the fans as well.”Filip Jorgensen has joined Strasbourg on a season-long loan fromChelsea. The 24-year-old goalkeeper arrived at Stamford Bridge in 2024 from Villarreal and has made 36 appearances for the Blues.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJorgensen started all but one of Chelsea’s games in the Conference League last year and featured 12 times in all competitions. title: Buzzer-beaters and besties: the rivalries and friendships that make the WNBA | WNBA | The Guardian
description: From Comets-Liberty and Lynx-Sparks to Wilson-Gray and the StudBudz, the feuds and friendships that have shaped 30 years of the WNBA
Author: Jordan Robinson
Headline: From Comets-Liberty and Lynx-Sparks to Wilson-Gray and the StudBudz, the feuds and friendships that have shaped 30 years of the WNBA
Content: A’ja Wilson and Allisha Gray meet up after last week’s game at Gateway Center Arena at College Park in Atlanta.Photograph: Adam Hagy/NBAE/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA’ja Wilson and Allisha Gray meet up after last week’s game at Gateway Center Arena at College Park in Atlanta.Photograph: Adam Hagy/NBAE/Getty ImagesWNBA 30WNBABuzzer-beaters and besties: the rivalries and friendships that make the WNBAFrom Comets-Liberty and Lynx-Sparks to Wilson-Gray and the StudBudz, the feuds and friendships that have shaped 30 years of the WNBASign up to get WNBA 30 in your inbox every TuesdayJordan RobinsonTue 11 Aug 2026 15.57 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 15.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s Rivals Week in the W, and it’s already given us so manyspicy viral moments. But when I look at the matchups that headline the schedule, it made me think of all the different rivalries that have come and gone throughout the league’s 30 years – some rooted inhalf-court buzzer-beaters, others inbaseline jumper buzzer-beaters. Moral of the story: if there’s a buzzer-beater involved, it’ll likely turn into a team rivalry.And while therearetense rivalries, there are also fierce friendships in this league. The ones that make you giggle to yourself when they wind up guarding each other during a game, or they show off a special celebration as teammates. Today, I want to highlight both – because both are what makes the W worth watching.***The OG Rivalry: Comets v LibertyView image in fullscreenHouston’s Cynthia Cooper drives to the basket against New York’s Vicky Johnson at Madison Square Garden.Photograph: Nathaniel S Butler/NBAE/Getty ImagesThe Houston Comets were really everyone’s rivals for the first four seasons of the WNBA. They won four straight championships and swept the MVP awards, too. But there was one team that especially didn’t like their red-white-blue color scheme: the New York Liberty. Three out of the four championship trophies hoisted up by the Comets came at the Liberty’s expense. Ico-host a podcastwith Comets legend Sheryl Swoopes, and she tells me all that time that those two teamsdid not like each otherbecause “the Liberty were always the bridesmaids. They wanted to be the brides, but it just wasn’t their time,” Swoopes said.We also saw this rivalry re-emerge between Cynthia Cooper and Teresa Weatherspoon during the WNBA All-Star weekend, 26 years later. When Cooper poked fun at the Comets winning four straight titles on the Orange Carpet,T-Spoon responded: “This is why I’m so thankful that four championships don’t define me. Coop, I’m still salty about this, chill out!”The Libertyfinally got their first ’ship in 2024. The only thing that would’ve made it sweeter? If they’d beat the Comets to earn it.***Besties for the Resties: A’ja Wilson and Allisha GrayView image in fullscreenA’ja Wilson and Allisha Gray look on during this year’s All-Star Game in Chicago.Photograph: Tyler Kaufman/NBAE/Getty ImagesWhen A’ja Wilson and Allisha Gray are on the same court, you know it’s going to be comedy … afterwards. But while the game is going on, those two battle. Their friendship goes back to playing together and being roommates at South Carolina, when they won the national championship in 2017. Since then, we’ve had a courtside seat to their best friendship (and their careers) blossom before our eyes. They’ve been each other’s biggest supporters, and Gray even has her special PE of Wilson’s A’Two signature sneaker. Now that’s a serious friendship flex.***The Last Dynasty: Lynx v SparksView image in fullscreenThe Sparks’ Candace Parker handles the ball against Maya Moore of the Lynx during the 2016 WNBA finals.Photograph: David Sherman/NBAE/Getty ImagesThe Minnesota Lynx defined the decade by reaching dynasty status in the 2010s. With a killer lineup of Maya Moore, Lindsay Whalen, Seimone Augustus, Sylvia Fowles and Rebekkah Brunson, they were built to win. And that’s what they did. Out of the 10 finals that made up the decade, the Lynx appeared in seven and won four. But the rivalry with Candace Parker’s LA Sparks was must-watch TV. They matched up well with each other; at its peak, there were four MVPs and 12 gold medals across the two rosters.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the 2015 Western Conference semi-finals, the Lynx beat the Sparks 2-1 en route to their third championship. In 2016, they met in the finals, and a fallaway jumper by the Sparks’ Nneka Ogwumike with 3.7 seconds left decided their fate. The next year, the two would meet in the finals again, and it also went the five-game distance. This time it was Moore who hit a game-winning jumper with seconds left to give Minnesotatheir fourth championship in seven years. It was a heavyweight battle, and one of the best bouts in WNBA history.***You’re the Bud to my Stud: Courtney Williams and Natisha HiedemanView image in fullscreenCourtney Williams and Natisha Hiedeman walk the orange carpet during this year’s All-Star Weekend.Photograph: Geoff Stellfox/Getty ImagesHiiiii, twin 👋 There aren’t too many friendships where names morph into a world-renowned moniker synonymous with joy, laughter and 72-hour streams. The StudBudz duo of Williams and Hiedeman stems from the two being teammates in Connecticut starting in 2019. Since then, they’ve played together on the Minnesota Lynxwith matching pink hair,had Vogue photoshootsand countless livestreams, and have become key figures of theWNBA’s culture. Dubs in the chat!This is an extract from WNBA 30, where Jordan Robinson covers the biggest stories in the league on and off the court each week.Subscribe for free here.Explore more on these topicsWNBAWNBA 30BasketballUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Meta glasses banned from courts in England and Wales | Meta | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Court service says anyone trying to enter buildings with glasses will have them confiscated and returned when they leave
Author: Matthew Weaver
Headline: Exclusive: Court service says anyone trying to enter buildings with glasses will have them confiscated and returned when they leave
Content: Mark Zuckerberg wearing a pair of Meta glasses, which have been labelled ‘pervert glasses’ amid concerns about people taking videos without consent.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMark Zuckerberg wearing a pair of Meta glasses, which have been labelled ‘pervert glasses’ amid concerns about people taking videos without consent.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesMetaMeta glasses banned from courts in England and WalesExclusive:Court service says anyone trying to enter buildings with glasses will have them confiscated and returned when they leaveMatthew WeaverTue 11 Aug 2026 06.29 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 14.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCourts inEnglandand Wales have joined a number of restaurants, theatres and pubs in banning Meta glasses, amid a mounting backlash against what has been described as “spyware”.Last month courts inNew York announced a banon the controversial glasses, which can record video footage while being worn.Now His Majesty’s Courts & Tribunals Service (HMCTS), which is responsible for all criminal, civil and family courts in England andWales, has made clear that Meta glasses will be confiscated from anyone entering its judicial buildings.A spokesperson told the Guardian: “There are clear restrictions on taking images or videos within courts and tribunals which is why the use ofMetaglasses is prohibited.”Taking images or videos in court buildings is prohibited in the UK without official permission and can be prosecuted as contempt of court. While lawyers and members of the public are allowed to enter courts with smartphones, which can record both video and audio, theHMCTS made clear that no such exception would be made for smart glasses.A source said: “Users who bring Meta glasses into courts or tribunals will have them confiscated on entry and they will be returned when the owner leaves the building.”They said smartphones were allowed on the condition they would not be used for recording court procedures.Earlier this year, aclaimant was accused by a judge of wearing smart glassesin the high court and getting “coaching” through them while giving evidence.Laimonas Jakštys was told to remove the glasses during a case over the directorship of a property company. Raquel Agnello KC, sitting as a judge of the high court, said Jakštys had been “assisted or coached in his replies to questions put to him during cross examination”. Jakstys denied using the smart glasses to receive answers, and denied they were connected to his phone.HMCTS does not hold figures on the number of incidents of smart glasses being used or taken into courts.In February, members of the security team for Meta’s chief executive, Mark Zuckerberg, were seen wearing Meta glasses during a high-profile trial in California about social media addiction.The judge, Carolyn B Kuhl,threatened the security guards with contempt of courtif they had recorded any of the proceedings.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNew York’s court system said it was banning smart glasses to ensure “individuals cannot surreptitiously record court proceedings”. It added: “No individual possessing smart glasses will be permitted to enter a UCS [unified court system] facility unless they voucher the smart glasses for safekeeping by uniformed personnel while the individual remains in the facility.”Last year Meta sold 7m pairs of the glasses, which cost between £269 and £469.Fears about Meta glasses being used to film people, especially women, without their consent has led to them being labelled “pervert glasses”. A number of restaurants, theatres and pubs in the UK, including Wetherspoons, havebanned Meta glasses over privacy fears.A spokesperson for Meta said the company did not want to comment on the court ban. They said when the glasses were recording a pulsing light was visible to people in the vicinity, and that frequently updated tamper detection technology is deployed to stop users covering this light during recordings.This article was amended on 11 August 2026 to correct the name and abbreviated form of HM Courts and Tribunals Service (HMCTS)Explore more on these topicsMetaUK criminal justiceCameras in courtContempt of courtEnglandWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Spotify to distinguish AI artists from real people – and stop recommending them | Spotify | The Guardian
description: Music streaming platform creates ‘AI persona’ label that will appear on profiles and track listings in crackdown on fake performers
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Music streaming platform creates ‘AI persona’ label that will appear on profiles and track listings in crackdown on fake performers
Content: AI-generated artists will be labelled as an ‘AI persona’ on their profile, in search and in track listings.Illustration: Spotify UKView image in fullscreenAI-generated artists will be labelled as an ‘AI persona’ on their profile, in search and in track listings.Illustration: Spotify UKSpotifySpotify to distinguish AI artists from real people – and stop recommending themMusic streaming platform creates ‘AI persona’ label that will appear on profiles and track listings in crackdown on fake performersDan MilmoGlobal technology editorTue 11 Aug 2026 09.40 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 17.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSpotify is to label AI artists and exclude them from algorithm recommendations as part of a crackdown on fake performers.The world’s largest music streaming platform is creating a label for AI-generated artist identities called “AI personas” that will appear on the artist profile and on track listings on playlists.It means that from September AI-generated artists such as theVelvet Sundownwill carry the persona label and will be blocked from personalised recommendations by default. The aim is to differentiate these deepfake artists from real performers who might lose out on streams to artificial rivals.Spotify said: “True artist-fan connection can only be built on a foundation of trust and authenticity. In music, that means listeners need to be able to trust that the artist behind the music is who they say they are. That’s more essential than ever in the age of generative AI.”Last year Spotify revealed it had removed 75m spam tracks from its platform over a 12-month period as AI tools created a flood of fake music. Spotify’s legitimate catalogue stands at 100m tracks.Spotify will allow music creators to reveal if their identities are AI-created – and will then label them as an AI persona – but it will not rely on self-disclosure alone. The company said it would use human review and AI investigative tools to determine if artists were fake. Although the new rule technically applies to AI “identities”, Spotify says AI-generated profiles are invariably a front for AI-made tracks as well.The company said: “Listeners have been clear in telling us that they don’t like seeing an artist profile that seems human, only to find out that the persona is AI-generated.”Last year there was debate about the origins of the Velvet Sundown – a 70s-style US rock band – before the band’s social media channels confirmed the subterfuge. A statement described the group as an AI creation that was “somewhere in between” human and machine.The Velvet Sundown has 117,000 monthly listeners on Spotify but its page has no clear AI labelling, although the artist profile describes the four-piece as a “synthetic music project”.In January there was further discussion about Sienna Rose, a soul singer who entered Spotify’s viral top 50 but did not appear to be real, having never played a gig or released any videos despite releasing a prolific burst of material over a 10-week period. The Spotify profile for Rose, who has more than half a million monthly listeners, does not clarify whether she is AI or not.Explore more on these topicsSpotifyAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: Meta faces expensive child safety reckoning | Meta | The Guardian
description: Also: Google executives jump ship in race for AI dominance
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Also: Google executives jump ship in race for AI dominance
Content: Mark Zuckerberg arrives to the Los Angeles superior court on 18 February 2026 in Los Angeles, California.Photograph: Jill Connelly/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMark Zuckerberg arrives to the Los Angeles superior court on 18 February 2026 in Los Angeles, California.Photograph: Jill Connelly/Getty ImagesTechScape newsletterMetaMeta faces expensive child safety reckoningAlso: Google executives jump ship in race for AI dominanceDanielle AbrilTue 11 Aug 2026 08.04 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 13.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHello, TechScape readers! Danielle Abril, editor of the Guardian’sReworked serieson AI and the future of work, filling in for Blake Montgomery this week. Major legal battles againstMetaover child safety are playing out in courts across the US – and the tech giant is losing. Recent rulings raise big questions about social media companies’ responsibility to their youngest users. Meanwhile, more key executives have jumped ship fromGoogleas it battlesOpenAIandAnthropicin the race for AI dominance, and Meta’s smartglasses face a fearsome backlash. Let’s dig in!Meta latest legal loss piles on the pressure as child safety concerns growThe pressure on social media giants including Meta is mounting, as courts work through a growing pile of cases and deliver devastating, expensive rulings, one after another. Meta’s repeated losses underscore how serious thechild safety crisishas becomefor social media companies and may force them to change how they operate to avoid further costly legal exposure.The latest blow came last week, after a New Mexico court hit Meta with anorder to pay $567minto a teen mental health fund to remediate the harm its platforms have caused children. The penalty adds to the$375m finealready on the court’s books after a jury determined in March that Meta negligently permitted damage to children’s mental health and hid what it knew about child sexual exploitation on its platforms. In a Los Angeles court, also in March, Meta washeld liablefor $4.2m in damages for designing platforms that addict and hurt children. The California case paved the way for hundreds of plaintiffs who have filed similar cases, which could cost Meta billions and force major changes to its products.But New Mexico is just the latest of many headaches in store for social media companies including Meta. The company is facing 42 lawsuitsfiled by states across the US, plus thousands more, along with YouTube,TikTokand Snap, brought by state attorneys general, school districts and individual families.At the center of the battle is the growing concern that social media companies harm its youngest users withaddictivefeatures thatpropel issuessuch as depression, anxiety and suicidal thoughts. The plaintiffs’ goal is to hold companies accountable and enjoin them tochange their products– everything from stricter age verification to usage limits and safety banners promoting protection features.“This is a cautionary tale of hubris,” said Karen North, a professor at University of Southern California who studies social media. Tech companies “seemed to believe they had safe harbor, and this wasn’t their problem”.Government-ordered remedies are a partial fix at best. For example, the New Mexico court orderedMetato improve its age verification tools, which use artificial intelligence to analyze signals such as the ages of users’ friends and the content users post and consume. It also asked Meta to develop a prediction model that could determine if users were under the age of 13. These measures will probably flag more underage users for better protection.But broadly, AI has a track record ofmisprofiling people, which will probably leave some underage users undetected. Meanwhile, inadequate age verification checks have left Australia’sbanon social media for children under 16 largely ineffective, according torecent research. Only a small percentage of those surveyed were required to provide official ID, and a significant portion said they bypassed the restrictions by using a fake account or a VPN.Meanwhile, tech companies are already skirting some trials through private settlements. Last week, TikTok settled three lawsuits from young people over claims its app harmed their mental health. Last month, a lawsuit filed against Meta in Los Angeles wasdroppedafter the plaintiff settled with YouTube, TikTok and Snap. In June, companiesreached a settlementwith a Kentucky school district that sued over platforms’ addictive designs that caused harm.Children’s safety on social media is no longer a peripheral issue for tech giants. It’s a growing risk to companies’ bottom lines. And the outcome of a federal case against Meta, brought by attorneys general from 29 states set for trial later this month in Oakland, California, could set the tone (and price) for the thousands of cases ahead.But, as North says, child safety is probably the tip of the iceberg. “At what point do they decide you don’t have to be a child to be harmed?” It starts with “young people and then vulnerable people and then all people”.The backlash to Meta’s smartglasses‘I’ve definitely lost followers’: influencers face backlash over Meta ‘pervert glasses’ contentThis man was secretly snapped by someone with smartglasses. He’s not alone in calling that a violation of privacyTell us: do you believe you have been filmed by Meta’s smartglasses without your consent?Restaurants, pubs and theatres ban Meta’s ‘spy glasses’ over privacy fears‘I’m not spying’: how Meta’s smartglasses have divided opinionskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGoogle faces executive shake-up as it battles for AI supremacyView image in fullscreenDemis Hassabis, then CEO of DeepMind Technologies, listens during a debate at an AI summit at Imperial College London on 9 July 2025.Photograph: Ludovic Marin/ReutersGoogle’s AI division is facing an internal leadership shuffle amid a heated external talent war, as frontier labs race to build the most capable large language models and capture the biggest market share.News broke last week that Google’s DeepMind CEO, Demis Hassabis, isstepping downfrom day-to-day leadership of the famed AI unit. He will serve as the chair of DeepMind, chief scientist for Google parent Alphabet, and continue as the CEO of Isomorphic Labs, the drug discovery company that spun off from Google. Meanwhile, Google’s current chief scientist, Jeff Dean, a 27-year veteran, and three colleagues are leaving to launch Discovery Loop, a startup the tech giant is backing. The news caused the company’s stock to drop 4%, and it had yet to rebound as of this newsletter.The executive shake-up follows the exits of other key leaders, several of whom have jumped to competitors in the last year, andreports of poor morale and delayed releases– Gemini 3.5 Pro ismonths late and counting.
