With executives exiting and releases delayed, the pressure to keep pace is only mounting, especially as Google continues to trail OpenAI in the AI race.ChatGPT is still decidedly in the lead, with 1.11 billion monthly users as of May, according to data from the market intelligence firm Sensor Tower. While Gemini has steadily started to close that gap, with help from a strong Android user base and integrations across Google’s ecosystem, it lags behind with 662 million monthly users in the same month. Claude, meanwhile, has seen a spike ingrowththis year but trails both at 245 million monthly users, though Anthropic hascapturedmore business customers andhigher marginsthan OpenAI by focusing its bot on coding and technical tasks.Still, while Google’s exits may be among the most senior and seemingly consequential, they’re part of a broader turnover happening across AI labs as competition for a minusculepool of top talent intensifies. Which labs can hold on to those major players will shape who leads the AI race in the future.The wider TechScapeBernie Sanders calls on Silicon Valley to ‘pause AI development’ in interest of humanityRising number of UK children report seeing explicit deepfakes of themselvesThe White House’s plan to vet potentially dangerous AI is cloaked in secrecy‘This is very real redlining’: outrage in Little Rock as two datacenters loomSafety fears as scientists make first viruses designed by AISpaceX beats revenue expectations in first earnings report after IPO crashExplore more on these topicsMetaTechScape newsletterSocial mediaGoogleAI (artificial intelligence)OpenAIAnthropicComputingnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: AI’s potential climate benefits outweighed by role in boosting fossil fuels, study finds | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Modelling finds AI-driven productivity gains in coal, oil and gas enable more emissions than applications in renewables avoid
Author: Ajit Niranjan
Headline: Modelling finds AI-driven productivity gains in coal, oil and gas enable more emissions than applications in renewables avoid
Content: Estimates suggest AI will create close to £370bn in cumulative value for fossil fuel companies between 2026 and 2030.Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreenEstimates suggest AI will create close to £370bn in cumulative value for fossil fuel companies between 2026 and 2030.Photograph: AlamyAI (artificial intelligence)AI’s potential climate benefits outweighed by role in boosting fossil fuels, study findsModelling finds AI-driven productivity gains in coal, oil and gas enable more emissions than applications in renewables avoidAjit NiranjanTue 11 Aug 2026 05.15 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 11.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAI-driven productivity gains enable more planet-heating pollution from fossil fuels than they avoid from renewables, astudyhas found.Researchers modelled the technical potential for AI to boost clean power generation along with projections for how it can help produce coal, oil and gas. Across 64 scenarios, they found net yearly carbon pollution rose by 0.47-1.8 gigatonnes, or about 1-5% of the energy sector’s annual emissions.The study is the first to quantify the climate impact of AI across the full power sector. Previous research has explored its indirectclimate benefits– such as reducing renewable downtime and optimising electricity grids – while ignoring the extra pollution from increasing productivity in drilling oil wells and extracting gas.“What most studies have done so far … is compare the datacentre energy use with the emissions savings AI has,” said Lynn Kaack, an assistant professor of computer science and public policy at the Hertie School who provided feedback on a draft of the research. “They completely omit this picture of AI causing increases in emissions.”View image in fullscreenA solar array installed in a river in Bangladesh.Photograph: Bipul Ahmed/NurPhoto/ShutterstockThe researchers found net emissions only fell in scenarios where AI did not increase productivity in the fossil fuel sector. If clean and dirty energy facilities were to adopt AI at similar rates, they found, the productivity gains for renewables would have to outpace those for fossil fuels by at least four times for emissions to break even.Holly Alpine, a co-author of the study and a former Microsoft employee who left to co-found the Enabled Emissions campaign group, said the research team used a conservative assumption that AI adoption would happen at the same rate for fossil fuels and renewables.“Fossil fuel applications are already happening at scale today – real contracts, real deployment, with evidence from industry operators and financial analysts,” she said. “Renewables applications are still largely at the pilot or academic-study stage – more speculative, more dependent on deployment barriers like permitting and interconnection getting resolved.”The InternationalEnergyAgency estimates that AI could boost technically recoverable oil and gas reserves by 5% and cut the cost of deepwater offshore projects by 10%. Oil and gas executives have been enthusiastic about the extra fuel that AI has allowed them to find, and celebrated its emerging impact as “the next fracking boom”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘Just an unbelievable amount of pollution’: how big a threat is AI to the climate?Read moreSaudi Aramco said last year that it had embedded AI “in everything”, increasing productivity and the number of wells, while earlier this summer Equinor attributed 27 discoveries on the Norwegian continental shelf to new seismic technologies and AI. The findings include the Lofn and Langermann oil wells, which the company said was the largest discovery it operated in 2025. “AI was key, from automated data interpretation to efficient well planning,” it said in a video at its capital markets day in June.Rystad Energy, an independent research and energy intelligence company based in Oslo, estimated in May that digitalisation and AI would create close to $500bn (£370bn) in cumulative value for fossil fuel exploration and production companies between 2026 and 2030 – the result of more efficient operations, increased production, and shorter development timelines. “The returns are already visible in the industry,” its analysts wrote, citing hundreds of millions of dollars in reported AI-related savings from Equinor and Abu Dhabi’s Adnoc.Climate scientists and energy experts have been troubled by the rapid construction of increasingly large and energy-hungry AI datacentres, which are typically powered by burning fossil gas. The researchers did not factor datacentre energy demand into their calculations but found AI enables productivity gains in the fossil fuel sector that result in emissions at least three times current estimates for datacentres.They cautioned that the results were a “directional and structural finding, not a precise forecast”, though the broad relationship held true across every scenario and sensitivity test they ran.Ketan Joshi, an independent climate analyst who was not involved in the study, said the AI sector was “fundamentally hungry for fossil fuels” and that the impacts went well beyond data centres driving fossil fuel use.“Even within some parts of the climate movement, there is still a denial that an unchecked tech industry will inherently boost fossil fuels,” he said. “Simply asking companies to throw a few scraps of cash at renewable projects is not enough to ensure the industry operates safely.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Climate crisisFossil fuelsRenewable energyGreenhouse gas emissionsEnergynewsShareReuse this content

title: How to buy a bike: expert tips for finding the right budget, frame and fit | Cycling | The Guardian
description: Whether you’re commuting, training or riding for fun, we asked specialists to break down what to know before you buy – from specs and safety to price
Author: Paddy Maddison
Headline: Whether you’re commuting, training or riding for fun, we asked specialists to break down what to know before you buy – from specs and safety to price
Content: Paddy Maddison enjoys the ‘meditative’ process of climbing coastal roads on his trusty steed.Photograph: Paddy Maddison/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPaddy Maddison enjoys the ‘meditative’ process of climbing coastal roads on his trusty steed.Photograph: Paddy Maddison/The GuardianThe FilterCyclingHow to buy a bike: expert tips for finding the right budget, frame and fitWhether you’re commuting, training or riding for fun, we asked specialists to break down what to know before you buy – from specs and safety to priceThe best bike locks for every budgetPaddy MaddisonTue 11 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.For me, cycling is therapy. It’s calming, meditative and uncomplicated. But there’s a catch. To experience the simple joy of riding a bike, you first have to navigate the maddeningly complex process of buying one.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Make no mistake: this is not a straightforward case of marching into Halfords, saying, “One bike, please!” and leaving with a shiny new steed. But, while complicated, it needn’t be stressful.Before you buy, ask yourself three questions: how will I use it? How much am I willing to spend? And what features do I want? Based on your answers, this guide will arm you with what you need to make a confident, informed purchase – no engineering degree required.To help, I’ve enlisted two experts: David Arthur, founder of cycling-tech YouTube channelJust Ride Bikes, and Stephen Roche, owner of bike-fitting and custom-build studiothe Bike Tailor.How to buy a bikeWhat type of bike do you need?View image in fullscreenChain reaction: start your bike search by getting to know the different types available.Photograph: Paddy Maddison/The GuardianThe best bike for you depends largely on where and how you intend to use it. To make matters more confusing, the bike industry is constantly coming up with new types of bicycles. Thankfully, they can all be grouped loosely into one of five main categories.HybridBest for:running around townHybrids fuse elements from road and mountain bikes, prioritising comfort for everyday use. They’re popular in urban environments when journeys are short, and speed isn’t a primary concern. They’re usually among the most affordable options, too. “These bikes are perfect for commuting and casual leisure cycling due to the flat handlebar and upright riding position,” says Arthur. “That said, they can feel slow compared with road bikes.”View image in fullscreenScott Metrix 30 EQ bike£949 at Scott SportsView image in fullscreenTrek Verve lowstep equipped 2027£800 at Team Cycles£800 at Evans CyclesRoad bikeBest for:riding farther, faster on paved surfacesWith drop handlebars that allow the rider to get low down and tuck in, road bikes are made to go fast. They’re designed for aerodynamic efficiency and low weight, featuring slick tyres that roll smoothly over tarmac. “The downside is that the low-slung riding position can be uncomfortable at first,” says Arthur. “The relatively narrow tyres combined with a stiff frame can be jarring on rough roads.”View image in fullscreenVan Rysel Shimano 105 Di2 Endurance£2,999.99 at DecathlonGravel bikeBest for:hopping between tarmac, towpaths, bridleways and light trailsThe fastest-growing category in cycling, this relatively new breed of bike is essentially an off-road version of a road bike. It still has the drop bars and fundamental shape, but with wider tyres to grip on rough ground, lower gears for traction on unpaved ascents, and a longer wheelbase for increased stability. “Gravel bikes are designed to handle a variety of terrain,” says Arthur. “They’re the perfect all-rounders – as at home on country lanes as they are blasting through a forest or tackling the daily commute. The trade-off is they’re slower than road bikes on the road and less capable than mountain bikes on the rough stuff.”View image in fullscreenCanyon Grizl CF 6£1,899 at CanyonView image in fullscreenLiv Devote 2£1,199 at TredzMountain bikeBest for:full-blown off-road ridingIf you intend to do most of your riding away from roads and paths, a mountain bike could be a good option. They have thick, knobbly tyres for grip on loose surfaces, flat handlebars for increased control, and often feature suspension to smooth out bumps when riding on rough ground. “These comfort-focused features – including easy gearing and a relaxed riding position – make mountain bikes great for beginners,” says Arthur. “Unfortunately, big tyres and suspension systems add weight and mechanical complexity.”View image in fullscreenTrek Marlin 4 Gen 3£525 at Tredz£525 at Cycles UKView image in fullscreenBoardman MHT 8.6 women’s mountain bike£650 at Halfords£650 at TredzCargo bikeBest for:reducing car useA cargo bike offers a genuine alternative to travelling by car. These bikes often have a large platform or bucket at the front or rear that can be filled with anything from shopping to children, allowing you to transport large loads with relative ease. “Many cargo bikes have pedal-assist motors too,” says Arthur. “But they’re expensive and bulky to store, so you’ll need the money and the space first.”View image in fullscreenTrek Fetch+ 4 750Wh electric cargo bike£4,500 at Trek BikesFolding bikeBest for:city living and short commutesFor those without much storage space, housing something the size of a pony isn’t realistic. This is where folding bikes come in. With smaller wheels and compact frames, these metal bikes can be packed away quickly when not in use, conserving floor space.Born in London during the 1970s,Bromptonhas a well-deserved reputation as one of the most reliable names in the category. Its genericisation has made it a household name, but it is by no means the only option. Dahon, for example, also makes excellent folding bikes, often at a slightly lower price. That being said, if your budget can stretch to a Brompton, it’s perhaps worth forking out for the superior build quality.View image in fullscreenDahon Mariner D8£799 at DahonWhat else do you need?View image in fullscreenGet kitted out: consider essential and desirable accessories you’ll need once you have your bike.Photograph: Justin Paget/Getty ImagesHelmetHelmetsaren’t mandatory for cyclists in the UK, but most people still choose to wear one. It can be the difference between life and death if you have a nasty crash. Pick one that’s comfortable and adjustable for a snug fit. It should feel secure without any significant movement when you shake your head.LightsIf you’re cycling on the road at night,bike lightsaremandatory. Depending on where you’re riding, you’ll want them to see and/or be seen. By law, you should have a red light mounted on the rear and a white light mounted on the front.The best bike lightshave rechargeable batteries, multiple blinking and static modes, and can be removed or adjusted easily. The Knog Blinder came top in my test of bike lights; this mini set from the same range features a front and rear light.View image in fullscreenKnog Blinder mini square light£38.99 at Fawkes Cycles£52.99 at Ribble CyclesFor more, read thesafety essentials cyclists won’t leave home withoutskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLockA lock is a good idea if you’re using your bike to commute or run errands. The best ones are heavy and cumbersome but provide peace of mind if you’re leaving your bike unattended for extended periods. For 10 minutes here and there, something smaller and more discreet will usually do the trick. Wearable chain locks, such as the classic Hiplok, are a good middle ground, as they’re portable but still offer robust protection.View image in fullscreenHiplokLite wearable bike lock£42.75 at Fawkes Cycles£59.99 at HalfordsFor more, read our guide to thebest bike locks for every budgetBasic toolsMechanical issues can and do occur. The basic ones can be fixed at home or even in the middle of a ride, provided you have the right tools. A simple multitool is a cyclist’s Swiss army knife. It has several different Allen key heads for making adjustments to the bike, and some of the higher-end ones even include things like chain-link removers. You should also arm yourself with two pumps: a floor-standing track pump for home to inflate tyres quickly and easily, and a mini pump that can be shoved into a pocket, pannier or backpack for adding air on the go.View image in fullscreenLezyne V Pro 7 multitool£16.49 at Fawkes Cycles£16.99 at Merlin CyclesView image in fullscreenTopeak JoeBlow Max II floor pump£28.54 at Halfords£28.54 at AmazonView image in fullscreenTopeak Peakini II mini pump£14.99 at HalfordsLubeA bike’s chain, cassette and chainrings (known collectively as the drivetrain) will wear over time, but you can extend their life by keeping them lubricated. Choose a purpose-designed lubricant for dry or wet conditions based on where you ride, and apply it to the side of the chain that contacts the teeth of the cassette and chainrings. Do this approximately every 100 miles, or more frequently in wet weather.View image in fullscreenFinish Line dry chain lubricant, 60ml£4.99 at Tredz£9.99 at AmazonView image in fullscreenMuc-Off wet weather lube, 120ml£7.99 at Decathlon£5.99 at AmazonClothingHigh-visibility clothing is always a good idea if you’re riding on roads, but you may even want to consider things like padded shorts and close-fitting jerseys if you’re planning to ride longer distances for hours at a time. Padded “bib shorts” or “bib tights” have a soft foamy pad stitched into the seat to keep you comfortable on the saddle for longer.View image in fullscreenProviz men’s waterproof reflective cycling jacket£79.99 at Proviz£88 at Mountain WarehouseView image in fullscreenProviz women’s reflective active jacket£44.99 at Proviz£49.50 at Mountain WarehouseHow much should you spend?You can spend as much or as little as you like, but the experience improves noticeably as you move up through the prices … up to a point. The good news is that there are solid options to suit almost every budget. Pricing is a broad spectrum, ranging from a few quid for a Facebook Marketplace clunker to £12,000+ for a Tour de France-worthy “superbike”. Your best bet is to aim somewhere in the middle. Here’s what you can expect for your money.SecondhandThere are incredible deals to be had for those bold enough to navigate the used bike market. However, some rudimentary knowledge is essential to avoid a bad experience, so get to know yourSramfrom yourShimano(if that’s a foreign language to you, you know where to start Googling).Found something that looks like a good fit? Don’t just blindly go in offering the asking price. Instead, hunt online for the same bike and see what the going rate was when it was new. You can use that information, coupled with the age and current condition, to determine whether the price is fair or not. Make sure you’re comparing models from the same year. If the year isn’t stated on the listing, search Google Images for the exact same colourway, as manufacturers tend to change these annually. If you can find one the same, chances are it was made at the same time.A word on carbon: any used bicycle comes with the possibility of hard-to-spot structural damage, but the risk is greater with carbon. This material is strong and lightweight, which has made it the go-to for high-end bikes, but it can fail catastrophically if cracked even slightly. The trouble is, such cracks are often barely visible, so you’ll need to conduct a thorough inspection, looking for deep scratches, flaking paint or any other suspicious signs. If in doubt, you could always pay a professional mechanic to check it for you.In terms of where to buy, local bike-specific Facebook sales-and-wants groups often yield the best results: do a bit of digging to find the best ones in your area. Alternatively, eBay can be a safe bet, or, better still, spend a day visiting local bike shops to browse in person.Under £400At the bottom end of the price scale, you’re looking at basic entry-level bikes built with affordability in mind. Options in this bracket will be mostly low-grade aluminium or steel with budget components, such as mechanical brakes as opposed to more powerful hydraulic brakes. As a result, they’ll probably be heavy and clunky to operate. Plus, cheap parts tend to wear out faster. That’s fine for short, occasional miles or getting a feel for cycling, but if you want to spend hours in the saddle, you may find yourself shopping for an upgrade sooner rather than later.£500-£1,000Expect lighter aluminium frames and entry-level shifting-and-braking components (known collectively as groupsets) from reputable, industry-standard brands such as the aforementioned Shimano and Sram. Closer to £1,000, this may include hydraulic disc brakes, which provide superior stopping power, wet-weather performance and control when compared with their mechanical counterparts. This is a good place to aim for most people looking for a solid bike for commuting and leisure who aren’t concerned about having the “fastest this” or the “lightest that”.£1,000-£2,000Carbon fibre begins to creep in here – if not the full frame, then possibly fork and/or seatpost. Bikes in this bracket will generally be lighter and provide a noticeably smoother ride thanks to better-quality components, such as wheels, tyres and groupsets. Speaking of which, respectable mid-range shifting can be found easily for this sort of money, such as Shimano’s bestselling 105 system – affectionately referred to by some as “the groupset of the people” – which is renowned for offering excellent bang for the buck.£2,000+This is where things get serious. These are mid- to high-end bikes, probably featuring full carbon-fibre frames, premium groupsets, carbon wheels and possibly even electronic gears. On mountain bikes in this bracket, you should expect full suspension, and for cargo bikes, you’ll probably see mostly motor-assisted options.What should you look for?Frame materialAluminium, steel, carbon and titanium: these are the four most common frame materials, and each comes with its own benefits and drawbacks.“Carbon fibre is the most desirable material in cycling due to its low weight, stiffness and strength, but it comes with a premium price,” says Arthur. “But aluminium should not be ignored. It’s more common at lower prices, and it offers the best value for beginners.”Steel and titanium are good options, too. Both are easy to repair, but where steel is affordable and heavy, titanium is expensive and light.GearsIt’s easy to fall down a rabbit hole when trying to understand gears, but don’t get too caught up in it. Unless you’re a professional road racer, ignore the fancy stuff and focus on fuss-free functionality.“Don’t be swayed by flashy top-of-the-range electronic groupsets,” says Arthur. “A lot of cheaper groupsets still offer exceptional performance, and their simplicity leads to lower maintenance and cheaper replacement parts when things do eventually wear out.”TyresBroadly speaking, wide, knobbly tyres inflated to low pressures provide cushioning and grip on uneven ground, while narrow, slick tyres inflated to higher pressures are faster and more efficient on paved surfaces. Consider where you’ll be riding and which you value most: comfort or speed. Choose your rubber accordingly.BrakesBrakes are a divisive topic in the cycling world. Rim brakes, which work by gripping a braking surface on the outer edges of the rim, used to be the default. In recent years, they’ve been usurped by disc brakes, which use a rotor attached to the wheel’s hub. Many purists swear by rim brakes, praising their low weight and simplicity. But when it comes to pure stopping power, disc brakes win.Disc brakes come in two forms: mechanical and hydraulic. Mechanical disc brakes are cheaper and operate with a cable mechanism. Hydraulic disc brakes are more expensive and use hoses filled with brake fluid – much like the brakes in a car.“If your budget allows for an upgrade to hydraulic disc brakes, it’s worth spending the extra money,” says Arthur. “They offer far superior braking performance in all weathers and can genuinely boost confidence when riding fast.”SizeMost brands provide a chart to give you a loose idea of what size to go for based on certain measurements, but it’s always best to sit on different options before making a decision. The Bike Tailor’s Stephen Roche agrees, adding that you should know your measurements – height and inseam at a minimum – before you start shopping.“You can also look at the bike measurement known as reach,” he adds. “This is the horizontal distance from the bottom bracket to the top of the head tube. If you find that your arms are outstretched and you’re bending from the neck, you probably need a smaller frame size.”Another option, Roche suggests, is to pay for a professional bike fit. “It takes any guesswork out of the equation.”For more, read:The best bike lights to see and be seenThe best bike panniers and handlebar bagsHow to make your bike last longerPaddy Maddison is a consumer journalist, outerwear enthusiast and exercise addict. If he’s not hiking in the hills, he’s grinding up them on his bike, hurtling down them on his snowboard, or lacing up his running shoes and hitting the pavements. As a result, he gets plenty of time to put all the latest and greatest gear through the wringer for the FilterExplore more on these topicsCyclingThe FilterFitnessHobbiesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Virtue and a Sledgehammer – take a literal hammer to your past | Games | The Guardian
description: What do you do when you return to your home town, with your dead mother in your car boot, to find the inhabitants have been turned into robots?
Author: Malindy Hetfeld
Headline: What do you do when you return to your home town, with your dead mother in your car boot, to find the inhabitants have been turned into robots?
Content: Taking ‘20 pounds of physical media’ to her town … Virtue and a Sledgehammer.Photograph: Devolver DigitalView image in fullscreenTaking ‘20 pounds of physical media’ to her town … Virtue and a Sledgehammer.Photograph: Devolver DigitalSummer games previewsGamesVirtue and a Sledgehammer – take a literal hammer to your pastWhat do you do when you return to your home town, with your dead mother in your car boot, to find the inhabitants have been turned into robots?Malindy HetfeldTue 11 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the boot of her car, Pratelle carries the corpse of her mother and a giant sledgehammer. Her mission is simple: take the hammer to her home town. As you enter shops and homes through the door and leave them through the opposite wall, it becomes clear that the robots who either attack you or flee are all digital versions of your old neighbours.Pratelle, with her close-cropped hair and dungarees, read to me as a queer woman, but interestingly, testers of the game often mistook her as a man. The team at developer Deconstructeam and longtime collaborator Selkie Harbour didn’t anticipate this confusion but found it fits the character perfectly, especially in this setting based on a small Spanish town like those in which the developers grew up.“These towns are culturally living a couple of decades behind, especially regarding subjects such as queerness,” says game director, writer and Deconstructeam CEO Jordi de Paco. “Maybe these communities aren’t ready to acknowledge that they have other identities within them – and Pratelle is exactly that. She is someone who doesn’t fit the community, but her very existence makes the community ask questions about identity, even if it’s through confusion and anger.”View image in fullscreenDigital versions of your old neighbours … Virtue and a Sledgehammer.Photograph: Devolver DigitalMany of the robot villagers react to Pratelle with vitriol, but some flee or beg for their lives, which feels harrowing despite their identical bodies. The villagers remember what it was like to have a body, a plot point the full game will explore in detail.The most important part, however, is Pratelle’s story, which you uncover by hitting glass statues around town that contain fragments of memory. It seems as if Pratelle’s own sister turned everyone into robots, which is one of the reasons she rebels with what she calls “20 pounds of physical media”. But Virtue isn’t meant to be read as a critique of our increasingly digitised lives. Instead De Paco created a family story of a “sometimes embarrassing teenager” to contrast with the otherwise futuristic themes of the game.“Back in 2024 we designed a prototype with a pretty stereotypical story about transhumanism,” he says. “We had some friends play it and got the feedback that the themes were stale, so we decided to use the setting as more of a metaphor and came up with the feeling of not belonging. Suddenly the aesthetics and themes felt really powerful in contrast with the destruction of buildings and facing robots.”A game about straightforward destruction seems to fit oddly with Deconstructeam’s prior body of work, such as the thought-provoking narrative experiences The Red Strings Club and Many Nights a Whisper. “We’re constantly joking about this being our first actual game because you’re not making a proper game unless you destroy something,” laughs De Paco, who even tried to take a sledgehammer to a real ruin for research.“In Virtue, you’re being made to destroy the place you grew up in. Despite the combat, the game is a narrative experience. It’s not meant to be challenging; it’s more of an aesthetic choice. We think of Virtue like a walking simulator: you go through a space and solve the narrative, and the game isn’t designed around combat. We want everyone who plays this game to reach the end.”Virtue and a Sledgehammer is in development forPC. Release is planned for later in 2026Explore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsPCfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on AI money in US politics: not the way to hold an urgent democratic debate | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Amid public concern over the impact of new technology, Silicon Valley’s use of its wealth to influence specific election races is an unwelcome development
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Amid public concern over the impact of new technology, Silicon Valley’s use of its wealth to influence specific election races is an unwelcome development
Content: Demonstrators wave signs during a nationwide protest in July against AI data centre expansion in Imperial, California.Photograph: Sandy Huffaker/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDemonstrators wave signs during a nationwide protest in July against AI data centre expansion in Imperial, California.Photograph: Sandy Huffaker/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionUS politicsThe Guardian view on AI money in US politics: not the way to hold an urgent democratic debateEditorialAmid public concern over the impact of new technology, Silicon Valley’s use of its wealth to influence specific election races is an unwelcome developmentTue 11 Aug 2026 14.04 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 21.06 EDTShareAs the huge societal ramifications of artificial intelligence have become clear, some of the tech industry’s most senior figures have taken to writingthinkpieceson what comes next. The latest to do so is Mark Zuckerberg, who this weekpublished6,500 words making the case for a laissez-faire approach to AI development. Worrying too much about regulation, Meta’s CEO unsurprisingly opines, could lead to the United States falling behind in the race to own the future.Mr Zuckerberg’s plea for maximum autonomy is, of course, self-serving. Much of hisessay– which airily envisions “invention superpowers” for every entrepreneur and “an abundance of jobs in the future” – reads like unadulterated tech-utopianism. But the lobbying at least has the merit of being out there in the open. As midterm elections loom in the US, darker arts are also being used to counter popular concern about what AI will mean for a host of topics, from the labour market to child safety, the environment and cybersecurity.Replicating a strategy deployed by cryptocurrency backers in the 2024 election cycle, Silicon Valley ispouringhundreds of millions of dollars into Super Pacs – groups unaffiliated to political parties or campaigns – to ensure that voices sympathetic to its deregulatory AI agenda get elected. OpenAI’s co-founder and president, Greg Brockman, and Palantir’s co-founder, Jo Lonsdale, have given large sums to Leading the Future, an organisation dedicated to “identifying, maintaining, and growing pro-AI candidates”.Vastamounts are being spent to try to tilt the balance in individual contests, sometimes through disingenuous means.View image in fullscreenGreg Brockman, president of OpenAI.Photograph: Manuel Orbegozo/ReutersEarlier this summer, Leading the Future spent $6m on ads attacking Alex Bores, a New York state assemblyman and pioneer of AI regulation at state level. Rather than focus on his AI campaigning, the ads attacked Mr Bores’s progressive credentials, alleging that he had carried out tech work in the past for US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which he denies. Running for Congress in a Democratic stronghold, he lost a tight primary race after battling what was in essence a smear campaign.Countervailing forces are emerging.Guardrails Alliance, a union-backed Super Pac, is attempting to combat Leading the Future’s influence, while a bipartisan groundswell of opposition to datacentres is generating serious electoral clout. But as tech companies and their billionaire owners seek to shape and above all limit the scope of AI regulation, their influence is distorting debate in a political culture where thepowerof money already holds far too much sway.In his essay, Mr Zuckerberg urges that AI’s democratising potential be protected from those who believe “a small set of experts … should decide what is best for humanity”. He appears to miss the irony that an unelected tech oligarchy, to which he belongs, is already performing that function by default. Its pressure has been instrumental in persuading Donald Trump tocancelthe signing of an executive order which would have given the government the right to review new AI models. Its wealth is now being used to attack and undermine dissenting voices in the public square.If a democratic debate about the benefits and dangers of AI is to take place, such presumption must be fiercely resisted in the US and elsewhere. The semi-covert manipulation of political discussion is no way to map out an inclusive future in challenging times.Explore more on these topicsUS politicsOpinionUS political financingMark ZuckerbergAI (artificial intelligence)Super PacseditorialsShareReuse this content

title: Trump put a wrecking-ball through the East Wing – and through democratic norms | Francine Prose | The Guardian
description: Our children should be able to visit our nation’s capital without having to think about Donald Trump and about how much he did to deface it
Author: Francine Prose
Headline: Our children should be able to visit our nation’s capital without having to think about Donald Trump and about how much he did to deface it
Content: ‘I can’t have been the only person who was shocked and saddened by photos of the jagged, gaping hole in the White House’s east facade.’Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘I can’t have been the only person who was shocked and saddened by photos of the jagged, gaping hole in the White House’s east facade.’Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty ImagesOpinionDonald TrumpTrump put a wrecking-ball through the East Wing – and through democratic normsFrancine ProseOur children should be able to visit our nation’s capital without having to think about Donald Trump and about how much he did to deface itTue 11 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 12.12 EDTShareHistory has shown us how much dictators and aspiring dictators love building monuments to themselves. They enjoy reminding the world that they can do anything, no matter who is responsible for the physical labor or who will be paying the financial and human cost.They prefer outsized structures, heroic arches, towers and columns designed to prove that their signature and their esthetic will be with us forever, even after they’re dead, though dictators often seem to believe they are too powerful to die.There’s a chilling photograph of Hitler in the bunker beneath Berlin, not long before his suicide, contemplating an architectural model of the Austrian city of Linz which he had intended (and perhaps still intended) to rebuild to his specifications.In Tirana, Albania, is a bizarre glass pyramid that the tyrant Enver Hoxha constructed as a museum about his life, and in which he is now buried. In Rome’s EUR, Mussolini and his city planners designed a neighborhood scaled for the race of Fascist giants to which they imagined they belonged.So it comes as no surprise thatDonald Trumphas invested so much energy, sacrificed so much popular goodwill, and already spent a fortune on the East Wing ballroom, a project that will occupy an astonishing 90,000 square feet.I can’t have been the only person who was shocked and saddened by photos of the jagged, gaping hole in the White House’s east facade, ripped apart by a wrecking crew, and by pictures of the historic rose garden remade to resemble an outdoor food court at a mall.Also unsurprisingly, estimates of the building’s costs have varied widely, though it’s clear that the price tag will be in the hundreds of millions of dollars. ($400m is the most recent figure to have been mentioned.) Though the president has promised that the American tax payer will not be stuck with all or part of the bill, some of the money has already been diverted from publicly funded agencies such as the Secret Service.And there’s been precious little reporting about who is getting contracts for all this expensive work and about the nature of the contractors’ relationships (financial and personal) with the president.We were supposed to have been relieved and mollified to learn that the ballroom – a pleasure palace for the president and his most loyal and generous supporters – would occupy a mere 22,000 of those square feet. The remaining 68,000 would provide, as the president wrote in a post, “one big, expensive, and very complex unit, which is vital for National Security and Military Operations!” Beneath the ballroom, a six-story underground bunker, designed to protect our leaders in the event of an attack, will make Hitler’s roomy 3,000 square feet look, by comparison, like a studio apartment. Most recently, Trump discussed using the new building’s roof as a launching pad for killer drones and other lethal weapons.This clever use of the air space seems to have occurred to the president even after the US court of appeals for the District of Columbia circuit ruled, in a 2-1 decision, that he could not continue renovating the East Wing without congressional approval.According to Judges Patricia Millet and Bradley Garcia, “each president is a temporary tenant, not the owner, of the White House and its Executive Residence”. Brought by the National Trust for Historic Preservation, the reasoning behind the suit seems obvious: a temporary tenant cannot change a rental cottage into a skyscraper without the landlord’s permission.The legal requirement to ask permission from Congress has already been ignored by a president who has levied tariffs, attacked Venezuela, gutted government institutions and started a war with Iran – all without bothering to consult the elected senators and representatives.Now Trump has vowed to take the case before the US supreme court which, as we have seen, is inclined to support him, though there have been a few happy surprises when the majority of chief justices decided to uphold the constitution.Much of what Trump does seems pointless, illogical, a response to some passing whim. But let’s not forget that he has the instincts of an autocrat, that he is the heir to a playbook, a series of actions designed to attain and consolidate increasing power and control.This story has always been about more than a building, more than about the intentional desecration of a national symbol, of a handsome structure with a history and a meaning. We’ve seen how Trump feels about history when he accused the Smithsonian Institution of being anti-American for telling the truth about our past.Though the case was initially brought by Alison Hoagland, an architectural historian and a board member of the National Trust, who claimed that the ballroom was an “aesthetic, cultural and historical” affront, it was never as simple as asking a town board to rule that a neighbor can’t build a view-blocking three-story vertical addition on to his house. We know, as the judges must have known, that the whole thing is about control, about the reckless grab for absolute power and about the necessity to resist it.It might seem like a distraction – a relatively trivial concern – to worry about a building when our government agents are shooting and kidnapping innocent people on our streets. But it’s part of the same story, a narrative about the subversion – at once reckless and calculated – of our ethical and democratic norms.Like our response to the ruined reflecting pool and the proposed Trump triumphal arch, our reaction to the proposed ballroom is partly about our wanting our grandchildren and great-grandchildren to be able to visit our nation’s capital without having to think about Donald Trump and about how much he did to deface it.Francine Prose is a former president of PEN American Center and a member of the American Academy of Arts and Letters and the American Academy of Arts and SciencesExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: An HBCU has banned durags and bonnets. That reinforces anti-Blackness | AD Carson | The Guardian
description: Tuskegee University’s dress code is a marker of a harmful politics of respectability. In my academic career, it’s become all too familiar
Author: AD Carson
Headline: Tuskegee University’s dress code is a marker of a harmful politics of respectability. In my academic career, it’s become all too familiar
Content: ‘Debates about “proper attire” have polarized the country throughout its history.’Photograph: Mike Stewart/APView image in fullscreen‘Debates about “proper attire” have polarized the country throughout its history.’Photograph: Mike Stewart/APOpinionUS educationAn HBCU has banned durags and bonnets. That reinforces anti-BlacknessAD CarsonTuskegee University’s dress code is a marker of a harmful politics of respectability. In my academic career, it’s become all too familiarTue 11 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 08.01 EDTShareIn anticipation of the coming school year, the president of Tuskegee University, Dr Mark A Brown, sent welcome letters to students and their parents last month. Part of the message focused on theuniversity’s policy for student attire. A newly enforced dress code prohibits students from wearing “revealing clothing in class, to the cafeteria or in official settings like Convocation. They are also not able to wear bedroom shoes, bonnets, or durags to class or the cafeteria.” Dr Brown goes on to let the students know: “Faculty will be empowered to respond to students who are inappropriately dressed based on these guidelines.”The policy has produced polarized responses. Supporters believe that since the university is a private school, and Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs) have often been places where Black people learn discipline and earn entrance into the professional world, this dress code is simply reinforcing a tradition that calls for students to exhibit professionalism during their training. It harkens back to WEB DuBois’s idea of a “Talented Tenth”, which would consist of upwardly mobile Black leaders such as teachers and other professionals whose example of hard work and social standing would uplift the entire race.Dissenters like me largely concede that as a private HBCU, Tuskegee has the institutional authority to require dress codes, as any similarly situated institution does. But we believe the policy is ultimately rooted inpolitics of respectability, a set of assumptions I’ve grappled with throughout my own academic career. One of the damaging implications of such a dress code is the reinforcement of anti-Black standards that have been externally and internally imposed on Black people in the United States for decades and have never equaled success or safety.Howard University disenrolled over 500 students. Black college hopefuls seem to be losing ground on all sides | Saida GrundyRead moreIn fact, debates about “proper attire” have polarized the country throughout its history. This has been especially true when the conversations have been tied to violence. Black men returning to the US from war werelynched in their US military uniformsbecause white folks thought them “uppity” for trying to claim the honor and valor supposedly synonymous with military service.More recently, debates about clothing became a primary focus after Trayvon Martin was killed by George Zimmerman in 2012. The fact that the 17-year-old was wearing a hoodie apparently justified his killing: for some people, the outfit was enough to provoke the fear and apprehension Zimmerman claimed to feel.When Zimmerman was on trial, I was a high school teacher in Illinois. In that job, I usually wore a tie and a jacket to work. I fondly remember teaching many young students how to tie a half windsor or a bowtie. In 2013, I left that job to go back to school for a PhD. The week I arrived on Clemson University’s campus in South Carolina, George Zimmerman was found not guilty.At the university, things seemed different from when I was in Illinois. The classes were less diverse, and almost everyone assumed the formal way I chose to dress had more to do with religion than professionalism. For a person who isn’t very religious at all, it was strange to suddenly be asked if I was on my way to or from church on a weekday morning when I was teaching. Eventually, I decided that, if I was going to be misread, I would rather be comfortable.My work and research are about how arguments appeal to people. I believe that people are almost always engaging with the world in rhetorical ways. From how we choose to speak to our eye contact to the ways we dress, we are making and responding to appeals. To emphasize how these rhetorics work, I wrote my doctoral dissertation as a rap album titledOwning My Masters: The Rhetorics of Rhymes & Revolutions. I decided the project had to be a rap album, in part, to highlight how Blackness is read as a set of appeals that are offered through music, speech, form and more.Rap music was the most effective way to demonstrate the kinds of appeals I was interested in exploring. The project highlights how sometimes our commitments to “tradition” and our unquestioning adherence to notions of what is “proper” or “improper” might limit our ability to identify and resist some of the mundane versions of this violence. If I were a professor at Tuskegee, it would be brazenly hypocritical of me to enforce such a dress code given the work I do and how I do it. Because of this, I empathize with the students who havesounded off in responseto the public discourse.More generally, though, my professional investment in eschewing what’s considered “traditional” has created similar pushback that I can’t help but experience as personal in some ways. To take seriously the position of the supporters of policies like Tuskegee’s dress code, to me, seems to be a concession to self-harm. I experienced this as a graduate student at Clemson as the assumptions about religious fervor shifted to assumptions that I was a trespasser or interloper when I stopped wearing a tie to teach and started wearing T-shirts. These misreadings followed my work, even as I experienced what might be considered professional successes. In 2017, asnews of the rap album dissertation, my successful defense of it, and myappointment as a professor of hip-hopspreadacross the world, the same politics of respectability that couch so many of the defenses of the Tuskegee dress code were aimed at me and my work.People seemed unconvinced that making rap music to earn a PhD was a good thing. Like the current online discourse about young college students at Tuskegee and elsewhere wearing bonnets, durags and house shoes in public, criticism of my work said that rapping my research might make other Black people look bad. Others worried about whether a university should employ a professor of hip-hop. These concerns were mixed in with apprehensions about rigor, evaluation and the abandonment of traditional academic forms, but they all seemed to me to boil down to the perceptions of white folks.The ways these polarized debates have played out through history are part of the inspiration for my book,Being Dope. Rather than give in to those politics of respectability, I have continued to do the opposite. When it was time to be evaluated forpromotion and tenure, I submitted the portfolio of rap albums I’d been recording since I was appointed in 2017. The book is composed through forms that are often misread and less appreciated in academia. My inclusion of rap lyrics, personal essays and poetry in an academic monograph might be read as balking at the kinds of respectable preferences that would prohibit wearing a durag or flip-flops to an academic conference.The federal government isn’t America’s only authoritarian institution | Jan-Werner MüllerRead moreI think Being Dope offers a valuable perspective about the debates over the Tuskegee dress code. It wasn’t insolence that led me to ignore the people insinuating that my choices were disrespectful to the Black people who sacrificed so much to make it possible for me to study and become a professor. It was actually a commitment to the same cause – principles that we have expressed in defense of Trayvon Martin, Jordan Davis and so many other young people whose clothes and musical choices were used to excuse the violence done to them. Studying what is offered as “tradition” can challenge us to be better critical thinkers. Sometimes challenging those “traditions” can highlight the underlying violence and anti-Blackness that drives an institution like Tuskegee to make the clothing preferences of some people into a policy by which all students must abide.It’s also a reminder to those Tuskegee students and any reader willing to learn that trying to earn the understanding of people committed to misunderstanding you is a losing game. In a society committed to anti-Blackness, anything that might even vaguely be considered an expression of Blackness is subject to policing.Even after sticking to my convictions and earning tenure as a rapper, since I released the book, I have been chastised for daring to describe Black people by using the word “dope”. For some, it seems like an insult rather than an apt metaphor for how Black people have forever fought against the politics of respectability and recognized it for the kind of trap it is.This current focus on what young Black folks wear in public is a similar trap that has pulled our attention and ire away from more pressing issues like the actual safety and security of those students. I would hope we openly and unapologetically resist people and institutions that cling to questions of clothing, grammar, area codes, academic credentials and whatever else they have at their disposal to minimize the humanity of others and do them harm.AD Carson is associate professor of hip hop & the global south and a Shannon Center fellow for advanced studies at the University of Virginia, and the author of Being Dope: Hip Hop & Theory through Mixtape MemoirExplore more on these topicsUS educationOpinionRaceBlack US cultureUS universitiesRapcommentShareReuse this content

title: Drought, water rationing and dry rivers: our water crisis is here | Peter Gleick | The Guardian
description: It doesn’t have to be this way. We know what needs to be done
Author: Peter Gleick
Headline: It doesn’t have to be this way. We know what needs to be done
Content: ‘No new technology needs to be invented to provide safe water and sanitation to the billions of people who still lack it.’Photograph: Marco Bertorello/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘No new technology needs to be invented to provide safe water and sanitation to the billions of people who still lack it.’Photograph: Marco Bertorello/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionClimate crisisDrought, water rationing and dry rivers: our water crisis is herePeter GleickIt doesn’t have to be this way. We know what needs to be doneTue 11 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 11.56 EDTShareDisturbing news about our water resources is now constant and unrelenting. In just the past few weeks, media have reported that Puerto Rico issuffering a deep water crisisas severe drought has cut water supplies to thousands. TheRhine and Po riversin Europe areat record low levels. The seven states sharing theColorado Riverin the US arefighting over unprecedented shortages, while its major reservoirs have shrunk to their lowest levels since they were built.Hungary’s only nuclear power plant is on the verge of shutting down because there isn’t enough water in the Danube River to cool it. Toxic chemicals have been found inall English water bodies.Desalination plants in the Middle Easthave been bombedin the ongoing war with Iran and municipal water systems in the United Statesare being hacked.The worstEl Niñoin recorded history isunfolding in the Pacific, affecting weather and water around the world. Violence over wateris worsening, with more water-related conflicts than at any time in recorded history. And communities are mobilizing toblock water-hungry datacenters, concerned that their water resources will be drained away.As AI guzzles water and energy, we are already facing a choice: datacentres or homes? | John HarrisRead moreAt any given moment, there are always places around the world suffering from droughts or floods or experiencing water scarcity – a normal consequence of the natural variability of our climate and weather.But what we’re experiencing now is not normal; it is the direct consequence of accelerating human-caused climate changes, on top of decades of neglect and underinvestment in our water institutions and infrastructure.For years, climate scientists have warned that continued emissions of greenhouse gases from burning fossil fuels and other human activities would alter the planet’s climate, raise temperatures, disrupt weather patterns and worsen extreme events, raise sea levels, and accelerate the spread of disease vectors. Those warnings were ignored, dismissed, downplayed. And now we are reaping what we’ve sown.Yet our politicians continue to prevaricate, refusing to take actions to protect water resources; or worse, rolling back earlier efforts. The Trump administration’s EPA has halted efforts to regulate new water pollutants and weakened regulations put in place by previous administrations – both Democratic and Republican.The administration has also continued to push forbillions of dollars of cutsto other federal agencies that coordinate research on water resources and climate, including the National Science Foundation, the US Geological Survey, and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.If governments continue to fail to address water and climate crises, the coming decades will inevitably see worsening water-related violence and conflict and deteriorating public and ecological health.It doesn’t have to be this way. People care deeply about water. Inpollafterpoll, concern for water resources – both quantity and quality – consistently ranks at the top, above all other environmental challenges.Europe’s rivers are running dry, and the knock-on effects are disastrous | Yiannis BabouliasRead moreAnd we know what needs to be done. No new technology needs to be invented to provide safe water and sanitation to the billions of people who still lack it. The cost of providing water to all and cleaning up the consequences of unregulated and uncontrolled water pollutionis far less thanthe costs of failing to do so.Violence over shared water resources can be lessened by international agreements and diplomacy over shared watersheds – which is the focus of a majorFinnish water diplomacy initiative.Smart investments in water efficiency technologies and regulations and in advanced wastewater treatment systems canimprove the resilienceof existing water infrastructure to extreme events.Far more food can be grown with far less water with efficient irrigation systems, reducing pressures on overtapped aquifers and rivers.And the rapid expansion of renewable energy systems and the rapid phase-out of fossil fuels will both slow the rate of climate change and reduce the amount of water required to produce the energy we all require – a win-win.We also need more public education about both water threats and solutions by our schools and media, more bipartisan actions by our politicians, and more investment by governments, corporations and communities in the technologies and policies that we know work but are failing to pursue with the urgency the growing crises demand. Constant news about worsening water problems must not become the new normal.Peter Gleick is author of The Three Ages ofWater(2023) and When the Well is Dry: How Water Fuels Violence and Shapes Peace (2026)Explore more on these topicsClimate crisisOpinionWaterAccess to waterDatacenters – USMiddle East and north AfricaTrump administrationcommentShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s vaccine order is about feelings, not facts | Robert B Shpiner | The Guardian
description: There’s no evidence that vaccines cause autism, or that we should separate MMR shots. This order is dangerous
Author: Robert B Shpiner
Headline: There’s no evidence that vaccines cause autism, or that we should separate MMR shots. This order is dangerous
Content: ‘Studies were designed to answer whether vaccines are the cause of autism, and they have answered it. They are not.’Photograph: Anna Moneymaker/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Studies were designed to answer whether vaccines are the cause of autism, and they have answered it. They are not.’Photograph: Anna Moneymaker/Getty ImagesOpinionTrump administrationTrump’s vaccine order is about feelings, not factsRobert B ShpinerThere’s no evidence that vaccines cause autism, or that we should separate MMR shots. This order is dangerousTue 11 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 14.17 EDTShare“This is based on what I feel.” That was the president last September,explainingwhy he wanted the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine broken into three separate shots. On Monday, he signed anexecutive orderinstructing exactly that.Four decades in intensive care have taught me what a feeling costs once it becomes national policy. Children will be hospitalized who did not need to be. Some of them will die. No one can name those the vaccine has saved, because prevented harm is invisible by definition, and that invisibility is what makes preventive medicine easy to dismantle and hard to defend.The order rests on a single complaint, stated in the White House’s ownfact sheet: American children are recommended more vaccine doses than children anywhere in the developed world, 84 doses across 57 injections by 2024 against 23 doses in seven injections in 1980.Section 2of Monday’s executive order directs that the MMR be given as three single-disease shots, and that “to the maximum extent feasible, all childhood immunizations should be administered at separate medical visits”. Not only the MMR: every childhood immunization.No evidence supports the spacing. The most thoroughreviewof the American schedule ever conducted, by the Institute of Medicine in 2013, found no safety signal and no case for spreading doses out; a delayed-schedule trial, if held, could not ethically be run, because delay only lengthens the time a child is unprotected.Data is not enough: from Covid to measles, America must relearn risk communication | Lynne PeeplesRead moreThe president and Robert F Kennedy Jr, his health secretary, returned repeatedly to autism as the order was signed. A study in 2019followed657,461 Danish children and found no association between MMR and autism. Last month, researchersexamined2.56 million American children and found none between the timing of a first MMR dose and a later diagnosis. Those studies were designed to answer whether vaccines are the cause, and they have answered it. They are not.Under Trump’s order, the number of diseases every child is recommended to be protected against falls from 18 to 11. Seven are gone: hepatitis A, hepatitis B, rotavirus, influenza, Covid-19, meningococcal disease and RSV. Some are now recommended only for children already at high risk. The rest are moved to what the order calls “shared clinical decision-making”.Hepatitis B is the clearest example of the danger here. An infant infected at delivery has roughly a90% chanceof chronic infection, and the dose given in the first hours of life prevents about three-quarters of that transmission. Meningococcal diseasekills 10% to 15%of those it infects even when antibiotics start promptly, and up to one in five survivors is left with deafness or an amputated limb. RSV was theleading causeof hospitalization among American infants until universal immunization began in 2023; in the first season with those products widely available, hospitalization among infants under eight monthsfell by about 43%.This is a country that ended domestic polio, helped the world eradicate smallpox, and whose National Institutes of Health helped engineer the stabilized spike protein behind the first Covid vaccines. Its childhood immunization schedule has now been rewritten by a man with no medical training, who touted his own instinct. We have seen that instinct applied to medicine: in April 2020, shown data on disinfecting surfaces, heaskedat a televised briefing whether the same might be done inside the body, “by injection inside or almost a cleaning”.A president is entitled to be a layperson. Most are. The question is what a layperson’s instinct is doing where evidence belongs, and Monday’s answer is that it now sits there formally, with the federal government behind it.At the moment, the splitting instruction also cannot be carried out, and the order quietly concedes it, conditioning it on single-disease products becoming domestically available. None exist. Merck stopped making them in 2008 andtoldfederal advisers in 2009 that it would not resume, at the urging of pediatricians who warned it would mean more needles and longer vulnerability. Restoring them would take years.Suppose they existed. Federal survey datadescribeswho is unable to complete a multidose series: uninsured, low-income, renting, recently moved, more than one child at home. In a county with no pediatrician, one well-child visit already costs half a day of wages. Ask for three. Families with paid leave and a reliable car will manage it.Why America is failing its health report card | Robert B ShpinerRead moreThere is no margin left to spend. Kindergarten MMR coverage is92.5%, under the 95% needed to interrupt transmission, with exemptions at a record of 3.6%. There has been more measles this year than in any of the past 35 years, and in November the Pan American Health Organizationdecideswhether the country still qualifies as having eliminated it.What reaches an adult intensive care unit is the far end of these decisions. I spent the pandemic watching unvaccinated patients die of an illness they had been offered protection against. This year, our neurocritical care conference reviewed a child left with profound and permanent brain damage by the seizures of measles encephalitis. There is a vaccine that has prevented it since before I entered medical school.The provision that will outlast the argument was written for lawyers. School entry rules are state law, and no president can rewrite them. Section 4 instead directs the attorney general to pursue legal action against state laws that conflict with obligations to provide religious and medical exemptions. That is the Department of Justice aimed at the last enforceable layer of protection American children have.The order does not have to persuade a single parent. It only has to remove a recommendation, add visits, and point a government lawyer at a state legislature. A feeling cannot be tested, and it cannot be proven wrong. The children it reaches cannot be counted.Robert B Shpiner is an internist and clinical professor of medicine at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA. He has practiced and taught intensive care medicine for more than 40 yearsExplore more on these topicsTrump administrationOpinionUS healthcareDonald TrumpVaccines and immunisationHealthcommentShareReuse this content

title: Experts are warning: our AI arms race is putting humanity at risk | Stuart Russell | The Guardian
description: A recent letter signed by 1,367 researchers and engineers at frontier AI labs – mainly OpenAI, Anthropic and Google Deepmind – points to a dangerous moment
Author: Stuart Russell
Headline: A recent letter signed by 1,367 researchers and engineers at frontier AI labs – mainly OpenAI, Anthropic and Google Deepmind – points to a dangerous moment
Content: ‘The first is the need to coordinate to escape an arms race towards the edge of cliff.’Photograph: Ruhani Kaur/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The first is the need to coordinate to escape an arms race towards the edge of cliff.’Photograph: Ruhani Kaur/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)Experts are warning: our AI arms race is putting humanity at riskStuart RussellA recent letter signed by 1,367 researchers and engineers at frontier AI labs – mainly OpenAI, Anthropic and Google Deepmind – points to a dangerous momentTue 11 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 11.52 EDTShareIt is fashionable in certain circles to dismiss the catastrophic risks of AI. One often hears that “the real experts” who work on the technology every day are really not concerned at all; that only “doomers” and “luddites” espouse a “fringe” view from a “position of ignorance”; that all talk of potential catastrophe is just “science fiction”.Fortunately, anopen letterhas been published that lets us hear from the real experts who work on the technology every day, in their own words. And are they worried? Very.The letter states: “There is a real risk that capability development rapidly accelerates beyond our ability to understand or control the resulting systems.” It asks the US government to support “an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development”.AI systems going “beyond our ability to understand or control” would mean that we no longer have a say in whether we exist. AI systems escaping their confines and breaking into other companies’ computers – something that has become analmost daily occurrence– are an early warning.Democracy is at stake when foolish humans bet on machines being intelligent | Rafael BehrRead moreTo “pace the frontier”, as the letter asks, is to ensure that more advanced systems are developed and released only when it is demonstrably safe to do so. This requires a licensing process with strong verification of safety; registration of AI systems and the ability to monitor and terminate them when necessary; and enforceable international agreements. All of this takes time and is impossible to put in place once a real emergency happens.The concerns expressed in the letter about the rapid acceleration of AI capabilities have been bubbling up for some months under the heading of “recursive self-improvement” or RSI – that is, AI systems contributing to their own improvement, which then enables even greater contributions to their own improvement, and so on.This was the subject of the “Recursive” conference in mid-May in San Francisco as well as Anthropic’s RSI warning, “When AI builds itself”, in early June. Broader concerns about the safety and societal impacts of AI have also motivated the formation of theCoalition of Concerned AI Staff, which links together employees of all the major AI companies.The letter is signed by (at the time of writing) 1,367 researchers and engineers at frontier AI labs – mainly OpenAI,Anthropicand Google Deepmind. The list includes CEOs, co-founders, chief scientists and hundreds of well-known AI researchers, including many of my former students. These are the people who are driving the AI revolution while trying to fashion brakes and steering wheels at the same time. If these are not the experts, then there are none.What makes the letter so powerful is not just the first-person authority of the signers but the inclusion of personal statements from almost a hundred of them. The statements paint a much more detailed picture of what the experts really think. At least three major themes emerge.The first is the need to coordinate to escape an arms race towards the edge of cliff. Earlier this year at Davos, Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, and Demis Hassabis, the CEO ofGoogleDeepmind, both suggested they wanted to halt AI developmentif others would agree.“The world is locked in a deadly race towards an intelligence explosion … To survive, we must coordinate to slow down the race,” said one signer.Another wrote: “Once this becomes common knowledge – once all of us in China and the US and at the various labs see that all the rest of us also think we need to slow this down – that’s when coordination becomes possible.”The second common theme in the remarks is, as one signer put it, “the complete absence of credible plans for controlling ‘superintelligent’ AI systems”. “These are the facts: The AI industry has the explicit goal of building things smarter than humans … None of us yet know how to make sure these things stay under human control … This is, objectively, an insane and suicidal thing to do,” wrote another.Not surprisingly, these concerns lead to the third theme: real fear. “I currently feel quite afraid of all paths I see that don’t include a near-future negotiated slowdown.” “There is … a very dark future ahead of us if we don’t get this right.” And: “I want a world where my kids can have a full life not a world where they are wiped out.”These are not greedy employees trying to hype their stock valuations. They say the same things in private conversations, closed-door meetings and off-the-record chat groups.In the face of such real and well-founded fears, surely these trillion-dollar companies are devoting massive resources to ensure they don’t end our, and their own, existence? Wrong.How do we prevent AI agents from going rogue? It starts with a new kind of measurement | Bruce Schneier and Barath RaghavanRead moreOne researcher, quoted in a recentNew Yorker articleon the OpenAI systems that broke into Hugging Face, said: “If people actually knew what the safety culture looks like, even in the most safety-minded labs, then I think people would be genuinely much more freaked out.”According to one senior safety researcher at Anthropic, their best bet for avoiding an irreversible loss of control works like this: as soon as the superintelligent machine comes into existence, but before it’s had a chance to take over the world, we ask it how we can stop it from taking over the world, and we do what it says.This plan doesn’t fill me with confidence, and the Anthropic researcher gives it at best a 50% chance of working. It’s the same plan that IJ Good mentions in his famous1965 paperon the intelligence explosion: “The first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control.” I rather think that Good meant this remark sarcastically.The most powerful of all the personal signing statements is also the shortest: “Think of all we love.”Stuart Russell is a distinguished professor ofcomputer scienceat University of California, Berkeley, the president of the International Association for Safe and Ethical Artificial Intelligence and a Guardian US columnistExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionOpenAIAnthropicGoogleDeepMindcommentShareReuse this content

title: Does Sophie Cunningham benefit from white privilege? Of course she does | WNBA | The Guardian
description: One of the player’s WNBA rivals said the Fever guard is treated differently from her Black peers. There’s plenty of evidence to back that statement up
Author: Etan Thomas
Headline: One of the player’s WNBA rivals said the Fever guard is treated differently from her Black peers. There’s plenty of evidence to back that statement up
Content: Sophie Cunningham has hauled in lucrative endorsement deals this season.Photograph: Paul Beaty/APView image in fullscreenSophie Cunningham has hauled in lucrative endorsement deals this season.Photograph: Paul Beaty/APWNBADoes Sophie Cunningham benefit from white privilege? Of course she doesEtan ThomasOne of the player’s WNBA rivals said the Fever guard is treated differently from her Black peers. There’s plenty of evidence to back that statement upTue 11 Aug 2026 04.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 09.59 EDTShareWhite privilege. An accusation that triggers multitudes of white people in America as if you had insulted their mother. Mention racism, and people may debate you. Mention discrimination, and people may even listen. But say the words “white privilege”, and suddenly defenses go up, outrage erupts, and people start explaining why privilege couldn’t possibly have anything to do with what everyone just witnessed with their own eyes.Which brings us to DiJonai Carrington and Sophie Cunningham.Etan ThomasIn Saturday’s WNBA game between Chicago Sky and Indiana Fever, Carrington was ejected after being assessed a Flagrant 2 formaking contact with Cunningham’s head and neck areawhile attempting to defend her in transition. Carrington, who is Black, maintained she was making a play on the ball and didn’t intentionally hit Cunningham, who is white. Even Cunningham’s coach at the Fever, Stephanie White, said she did not believe Carrington intentionally went out to hurt Cunningham.Carrington acknowledged she should have been penalized for the foul. But after her ejection, shewent on social mediaand posted those two words many white people seem to fear so much: “WHITE PRIVILEGE”.Predictably, Carrington’s words became as controversial as the foul itself. But instead of dismissing Carrington’s accusation, we should ask why she posted the words that she did –she has saidthey had nothing to do with the officiating decision itself. What happens when Cunningham, a white woman, is the aggressor, and what happens when she is the “victim”?We’ve already seen the first scenario. In June 2025, Cunningham committed a Flagrant 2 foul against Connecticut Sun guard Jacy Sheldon. Cunningham wrapped Sheldon up as she drove toward the basket,sent her to the floor, and ignited an altercation. Cunningham was correctly ejected and fined by the WNBA.If we are going to discuss racial double standards, we shouldn’t manipulate facts. Cunningham was ejected in 2025, just as Carrington was ejected in 2026. The referees treated both players the same –as Carrington herself appeared to suggest. Instead, the white privilege is found in what happened next.As my co-host on The Collision podcast, Chuck Modi,pointed outafter Cunningham’s 2025 foul, a significant portion of the public didn’t transform her into a dangerous menace threatening the integrity of women’s basketball. Instead, she was lauded as an enforcer. She was the teammate willing to protect Caitlin Clark, a player whom many on the right see as a delicate white flower who needs protecting at all costs. Cunningham also became immensely marketable.Her TikTok following explodedfrom 300,000 to over one million, and she was flooded with lucrative marketing opportunities.double quotation markWhen Cunningham fouls an opponent, she’s an enforcer. When Carrington does the same, she’s a dangerRingpartnered with Cunninghamin an advertisement that explicitly played off her image as the Fever’s “protector”. The campaign converted the symbolism of her retaliatory foul into a branding opportunity: Cunningham protects her teammates; Ring protects her home.Think about that. A white player is ejected, and emerges with exponentially more followers, an “enforcer” identity, and lucrative endorsements.Now imagine if Carrington had been flooded with endorsement deals built around being an “enforcer” after her foul on Cunningham. Would America think that was cute? Would television personalities laugh and celebrate her toughness? Or would she be described with words like “dangerous”, “dirty” and “thug”?That question isn’t hypothetical, either. Look at what happened when Carrington fouled Cunningham.Carrington’s foul was immediately framed by commentators as something larger than basketball. Cunningham was portrayed not simply as the recipient of a Flagrant 2, but as another whiteWNBAplayer being victimized by an increasingly dangerous culture within the league. We’ve heard similar rhetoric surrounding Clark for years: opponents aren’t merely fouling her; they are targeting her, jealous of her, and trying to hurt her. The racial subtext matters because the villains in this narrative are disproportionately Black women, while the white players like Clark and Cunningham are portrayed as in need of protection.View image in fullscreenSophie Cunningham and DiJonai Carrington confront each other during Saturday’s game.Photograph: Icon Sportswire/Getty ImagesThen the Carrington-Cunningham incident went somewhere very strange: Florida’s attorney general, James Uthmeier, got involved.Uthmeier saidhe would be willing to charge players with assault and battery if they committed hard fouls in Florida.This is, of course, ridiculous, and Uthmeier – no doubt grandstanding for a certain demographic of conservative voters – knows it. Quite apart from the fact that Florida doesn’t have an WNBA team, we are talking about professional basketball. Hard fouls have existed since Dr James Naismith hung a peach basket on a wall. Players have been clotheslined, elbowed, shoved, and involved in fights. Flagrant fouls exist precisely because sports already have mechanisms to distinguish basketball contact from excessive contact.
