Yet suddenly, we are discussing criminal prosecution.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWould we be having that conversation if Cunningham had fouled Carrington? We don’t have to guess. When Cunningham committed her retaliatory Flagrant 2 against Jacy Sheldon, where was Uthmeier? Where were the threats of assault charges, the politicians warning the WNBA, or the television segments asking if Black women were safe from prowling white women?That’s what privilege looks like. When Cunningham fouls an opponent, she’s an enforcer. When Carrington does the same, she’s a danger.This isn’t the first time Cunningham has become a cultural phenomenon. In June, she pointed at Phoenix Mercury’s DeWanna Bonner during an on-court confrontation. The image exploded across social media, accumulating tens of millions of views as Cunningham’s pointbecame a meme. People described it as hilarious, petty, and iconic – and there’s no denying it was entertaining.But in considering white privilege,I posted an image on social mediaof Cunningham as a Black WNBA player and asked: How would it be viewed if the roles were reversed? If a Black player followed a white opponent around the court, staring her down and pointing in her face for 20 seconds. Would she still be called adorable? Or would she be described as threatening, aggressive, classless, and hostile?That’s why conversations about white privilege cannot stop at whether two players received the same foul classification on the scorecard.We could test this. Take every comparable WNBA flagrant foul over the last several seasons involving contact to the head or neck. Separate the incidents by the race of the offending player and the race of the recipient. Examine the headlines and social media posts. How frequently do the words “hard foul” come up versus “cheap shot”, “brutal”, “assault”, “targeted”, or “clobbered”?That would be a far more meaningful investigation of white privilege than screaming about playing “the race card.”Privilege isn’t always receiving something someone else didn’t. Sometimes privilege is being granted innocence of interpretation. It’s having your aggression interpreted as toughness, your confrontation as personality, your retaliation as loyalty, your defiance as humor, and your anger as passion. Meanwhile, someone else’s aggression becomes violence, confrontation becomes hostility, retaliation becomes assault, and anger becomes evidence that she is dangerous.White privilege doesn’t require Cunningham to ask for it or be racist. It doesn’t require every referee, journalist, or politician to consciously think: “She’s white, so I’m going to treat her differently”.Privilege operates through assumptions, sympathy, and framing – through whose aggression gets contextualized and whose gets criminalized.So when Carrington talks about white privilege, instead of becoming enraged, America should examine why those two words make people angrier than the double standard she’s asking them to examine. The question isn’t simply whether white privilege exists in the WNBA. The real question is: How much more evidence do people need before they’re willing to admit that it does?Explore more on these topicsWNBABasketballUS sportsIndiana FeverChicago SkycommentShareReuse this content

title: Melon-gate was a non-issue in Japan. How did it get elevated to a crisis in Australia? | Malcolm Farr | The Guardian
description: Anthony Albanese’s comments about melons given to him by Japanese prime minister Sanae Takaichi continue to make headlines weeks after they were made
Author: Malcolm Farr
Headline: Anthony Albanese’s comments about melons given to him by Japanese prime minister Sanae Takaichi continue to make headlines weeks after they were made
Content: Anthony Albanese and Sanae Takaichi. The Japanese government has insisted it is more concerned about the condition of its economy than a crudity pinned to the Australian PM.Photograph: Saeed Khan/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAnthony Albanese and Sanae Takaichi. The Japanese government has insisted it is more concerned about the condition of its economy than a crudity pinned to the Australian PM.Photograph: Saeed Khan/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionAnthony AlbaneseMelon-gate was a non-issue in Japan. How did it get elevated to a crisis in Australia?Malcolm FarrAnthony Albanese’s comments about melons given to him by Japanese prime minister Sanae Takaichi continue to make headlines weeks after they were madeFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastTue 11 Aug 2026 19.35 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 20.14 EDTShareThe government continues to face an all-out effort, led by parts of the media, to depictAnthony Albaneseas the Benny Hill of international diplomacy endangering Australia’s regional standing.There is ongoing anger – or so we’re told – over a crude double entendre from the Australian prime minister made over a month ago that indirectly involved his Japanese counterpartSanae Takaichiand her gift of two melons during her recent Australian visit.The incident initially produced the kind of sniggering usually found in a schoolyard, andgrave demands for public apologies.Australia’s prime minister refuses to apologise to Japanese counterpart over melon gaffeRead moreNow the opposition has now referred the leak of a diplomatic note sent by Japan to Australia to the federal police, prompting housing minister Clare O’Neil to declare the Liberals have“lost the plot”.There has been encouragement for Tokyo to deliver outrage and condemnation, with the issue resurfacing after former Japanese ambassador to Australia Shingo Yamagami criticised the exchange in The Australian on Monday.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailHowever, the Japanese government has insisted it is more concerned about the condition of its national economy than a crudity pinned to the Australian prime minister.“It was a non-issue in Japan, not even reported by any of the mainstream press,” Shiro Armstrong, professor of economics and director of the Australia-Japan Research Centre at the Australian National University, told the ABC last week.The controversy may be stored away in the minds of Japanese business and political figures for possible future use, but for now it seems to have a limited use.Yet some persistent media coverage of the prime minister’s comments – which were made last month on a podcast that encourages guests to shed any staidness – has elevated the matter to a crisis.“The fact is … here you and I are on our national broadcaster talking about the remarks of the Australian prime minister which implies being vulgar and crude to a female leader …. This is a national embarrassment,” Liberal Ted O’Brien sternly told ABC radio on Tuesday morning.There is a sneaky suspicion O’Brien liked that prominence, even though it was a relatively short element of the broader interview.The finance minister, Katy Gallagher, told ABC on Tuesday morning the melon comments “were not intended to be interpreted the way that our political opponents and some media outlets are reporting”.“I think they’ve been interpreted in a way that he never intended and absolutely rejects,” said the senator.But One Nation’s Barnaby Joyce argued – without supporting detail – that it would damage trade relations with Japan, but focused on Albanese.“He’s trying to be clever. It wasn’t clever for the fourth biggest economy in the world, an absolutely vital strategic partner in our defence,” he said.The tone of the offending podcast played a part in the controversy, possibly exceeding anything Albanese said. The host, comedian Nikki Osborne, led the way as she pressed Albanese with insinuations the melons were smuggled in under Takaichi’s clothing.“I don’t know, ‘I got a couple of melons,’” Albanese replied with a grin while gesturing to his chest.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat gesture condemned Albanese, and Osborne swiftly removed any doubt about his depiction.“She brought two? She just came in looking like Pamela Anderson,” she said.The prime minister replied: “She brought two, and they’re beautiful.”Anthony Albanese apologises ‘unequivocally’ for podcast comment about Kylie MinogueRead moreIt was the second time Osborne had pointed the prime minister into troubling territory, and he had obliged. On the first occasion he implied he would “shag” Kylie Minogue.Joyce perhaps was right when he said Albanese was “trying to be clever”.It is one thing for a prime minister wanting to reach younger voters through non-mainstream media, such as podcasts.However, there is a layer of dignity that comes with the office, and that should not be shed.Albanese refused to apologise for the comments in question time on Tuesday, saying Australia and Japan have “never been closer”.Hopefully he will absorb the lesson of the melons and apply a discipline to future, similar occasions.Meanwhile, there is a country to run.Malcolm Farr worked in the Canberra press gallery from 1991 to 2019, reporting mainly for the Daily Telegraph andnews.com.au. He has later contributed to Guardian Australia, Crikey and the ABCExplore more on these topicsAnthony AlbaneseOpinionAustralian politicsAustralian foreign policyJapanSanae TakaichicommentShareReuse this content

title: To all the betting shops littering our high streets: people power is coming and the odds are against you | Dawn Butler | The Guardian
description: Too many shops are blighting too many communities. With the rule change I fought for now on the horizon, ordinary people can fight back, says Labour MP Dawn Butler
Author: Dawn Butler
Headline: Too many shops are blighting too many communities. With the rule change I fought for now on the horizon, ordinary people can fight back, says Labour MP Dawn Butler
Content: Higher-stakes gambling machines can generate an average of £35,000 in gross yield per machine each year.Photograph: Islandstock/AlamyView image in fullscreenHigher-stakes gambling machines can generate an average of £35,000 in gross yield per machine each year.Photograph: Islandstock/AlamyOpinionGamblingTo all the betting shops littering our high streets: people power is coming and the odds are against youDawn ButlerToo many shops are blighting too many communities. With the rule change I fought for now on the horizon, ordinary people can fight backTue 11 Aug 2026 13.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 13.45 EDTShareHow much gambling do you want in your high street? Are you happy with all the betting shops, the problems they cause, the effect on your environment?It’s worth asking because for years, local councils have been expected to say yes to new gambling venues, even when communities made clear they did not want them. Now, undernew rules announced on Monday, that’s about to change. And about time.Speaking to local residents I hear a clear message time and again: people are fed up with seeing so much gambling where they live, while having little say over whether new venues open.I knew grappling with this issue would be an uphill battle. The gambling industry is lucrative and deeply embedded in our communities. When I looked into why councils were struggling to stop new betting shops, casinos and adult gaming centres opening, I discovered the problem.At the heart of it was the outdated “aim to permit” principle in theGamblingAct 2005. It meant councils were effectively working against a presumption that gambling premises should be permitted, leaving them limited ability to say no. This one principle is the root of the crisis on our high streets: it has stripped local people of any real power to shape their own communities, and let the industry expand largely unchecked.So in 2021 I started my campaign to put power back where it belongs: in the hands of councils and local communities. Today, after years of campaigning, I’m delighted to say that we’ve won.The government has announced it is scrapping aim to permit, giving councils and communities greater power over what happens on their high streets. This is a huge victory forLondon, and for communities nationwide. But it took years of pressure and persistence to get here.I took a minister to Harlesden high street to see the reality for themselves. I launched a petition so Londoners could make their voices heard. I organised a cross-party letter backed by more than 280 MPs, councillors, mayors and gambling reform advocates, including the then mayor of Greater Manchester, Andy Burnham. I took the campaign into parliament too, raising it at prime minister’s questions and leading a debate.During my summer tour last year, I took the campaign into communities across London, listening to what people wanted to see on their high streets, and meeting families affected by gambling harms, such as the campaigner Jackie Olden, who watched her mother’s lifespiral out of controlthanks to a slot-machine addiction.It was a shock to discover how much gambling machines generate: B3 (higher-stakes) gambling machines – essentially slot/fruit machine-style games, found in places such as betting shops, adult gaming centres and casinos – generate an average of £35,000 in gross gambling yield per machine each year – more than the roughly £26,400 a year earned by someone aged 21 or over working 40 hours a week on the national living wage. The scale of the problem is clear in Brent, where gambling premisesoutnumber supermarkets in 17 of Brent’s 22 wards. We have 81 licensed gambling venues across the borough. For my constituents, this is about improving the places they live and raise their families. People want to be proud of their high streets again.The consequences of gambling-related harm can be devastating.A 2023 reportestimated there could be between 117 and 496 gambling-related suicides in England each year. I’ve worked with campaigners and advocates with lived experience of gambling harm, and highlighted organisations such asGambling with LivesandGambling Harm UK, whose expertise helped make the case for reform.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI’m grateful to residents who signed my petition, representatives who backed my campaign, councils including Brent council that pushed for this change, and every reform advocate who helped build momentum. I’m also grateful to Andy Burnham, who followed through on his support by committing to make this bold change.Our high streets should work for local people – not for companies profiting from harm. No longer should residents feel powerless when they see changes on their doorstep. That is why scrapping aim to permit matters: it will make a real, tangible difference to people’s lives.With the support of Londoners and campaigners across the country, we fought, organised and delivered. So, this is your chance: take back your high streets. Get involved, hold your council to account – use these new powers to demand and shape the neighbourhoods you deserve.Dawn Butler is the Labour MP for Brent EastDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsGamblingOpinionPlanning policyCommunitiesLocal governmentLondonEnglandScotlandcommentShareReuse this content

title: Malcolm in the middle: what can Labor learn from Turnbull’s doomed attempt to govern from the centre? | Peter Lewis | The Guardian
description: Ten years after my first Essential column for the Guardian, another centrist government is confronting a global bin fire in the face of a resurgence of populism
Author: Peter Lewis
Headline: Ten years after my first Essential column for the Guardian, another centrist government is confronting a global bin fire in the face of a resurgence of populism
Content: Malcolm Turnbull, centre, Tony Abbott, left, and Janeatte Howard at a dinner in honour of the 20th anniversary of the Howard government in 2016.Photograph: Mike Bowers/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMalcolm Turnbull, centre, Tony Abbott, left, and Janeatte Howard at a dinner in honour of the 20th anniversary of the Howard government in 2016.Photograph: Mike Bowers/The GuardianOpinionEssential pollMalcolm in the middle: what can Labor learn from Turnbull’s doomed attempt to govern from the centre?Peter LewisTen years after my first Essential column for the Guardian, another centrist government is confronting a global bin fire in the face of a resurgence of populismTue 11 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 19.05 EDTShareIwrote my first column for Guardian Australia in August 2016, when the winds of chaos were sweeping the globe, the forces of division were finding their voice and a centrist leader named Malcolm was scrambling to hang on.A decade provides enough space to give events real definition in the rear-view mirror while more recent events still feel like passing traffic or roadkill. So, let’s strap ourselves into theEssentialDeLorean and go back to the future.Malcolm has just narrowly survived the double-dissolution election he foolishly called, having been forced to dig into his own substantial personal wealth to sandbag what would end up a one-seat majority.My debut columnis about Pauline Hanson, who has returned to the parliament for the first time in nearly 20 years. I link the backlash against the levels of immigration to a growing sense of economic insecurity, something I argue should beharnessed rather than rejected as extreme.Guardian Essential poll: Angus Taylor’s approval rating crashes and One Nation support plateausRead more“We’ve seen the rise of the outsider overseas, from Brexit to Le Pen to Trump and Sanders.One Nationis poised to become Australia’s expression of that international pushback on globalisation,” I write.In October, Malcolm and Bill Shorten, whose energetic leadership and ruthlessly truthy election campaign have put Labor back in the game,reach across the partisan dividein the name of social cohesion, issuing a joint rejection of discriminatory immigration policy.When Malcolm had wrested control from the political wrecking ball that was his long-term nemesis, Tony Abbott,I (like many progressives) wished him well, a centrist leader from the other side who would confront the future with a modicum of shared purpose.But bySeptember our pollshows the weakness of his position, especially for a man who had used Newspoll to justify his own challenge on a sitting PM who remains deeply embedded in the right’s echo chamber waiting to pounce back.In exile from his first leadership, Malcolm had made action on climate his cause celebre, donning the leather jacket to become a regular truth-teller on Q+A. In power he had begun the process of redesigning a working energy market after Abbott had destroyed the carbon trading scheme (CPRS) but was constantly stymied by thecoal club and the fossils in his own party.In 2016, the fossil fuel industry and its political and media mouthpieces have pivoted from denial to the reliability of renewables.When freak storms wiped out the South Australian grid, this was blamed on the fragility of the new technology rather than the urgent need to address climate chaos. Ten years on, batteries may be mainstream butthe hostility to renewable technology continues to be weaponisedeven as evidence of an impending climate catastrophe becomes more incontrovertible.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailMalcolm is battling a divided party fixated on culture wars; he manages to usher through atortuous but ultimately successful postal balloton marriage equality but can’t stifle the intermittent,unhinged breakouts, such as a confected fightover the Racial Discrimination Act.These identity schisms sow the seeds of the Liberal party’s ongoing identity crisis. Whenthe majority of Australians who see themselves as middle classcan’t name a party for them, the teal writing is already on the wall – and Abbott will be the first to fall.All this noise is diverting Malcolm from delivering on his big economic play, a national innovation drive to deliver “jobs and growth”, a pitch to the future that has failed to translate into votes when it is delivered totech start-upsrather than workers.As November approaches, the prospect of aTrump presidency is becoming more realand we are at pains to differentiate ourselves from the madness over there. Wehold our breathsand turn blue when the “red wall” breaks and the reality TV show conquers the White House.By year’s end we are in a state of existential limbo, Trump is elected but the full catastrophe is yet to begin.In 2016, all that will follow is yet to be: thatMalcolm will join the revolving door of PMs; that his treasurer will slip through the middleand morph into ScoMoand conjure anelection win from nowhere; that Albo will reinvent himself as Anthony andstumble into powerafter the pandemic and then secure anhistoric second-term majority.Pauline will spend the decade on the fringes, the occasional cosplay stunt, the shift in targets from Asians to Muslims, until the times arrive for her and support surges as afresh wave of anti-immigration populism, which stands as a proxy for economic inclusion.Ten years on it feels we have come full cycle: a centrist government is confronting a global bin fire in the face of a fresh resurgence of the nativist populism. Even Abbott is back trying to break his own party.Before the last electionI described Albo as the John Howardof his generation but, in character, perhaps he is closer to Malcolm, a leader trying to find a centre ground in a world that privileges the extremes.The (spin) doctor is in: the Albanese government is in good health, but that could all vanish in an instant | Peter LewisRead moreLooking back onmy 10-year opusit strikes me that I never once wrote anything remotely kind about Malcolm. Despite his integral role in the establishment of Guardian Australia, there was never any suggestion we should play nice. He was always such a big target:his self-assuredness, his lack of anything resemblingpopular cultural literacyand, most profoundly,his inability to rise to the level of his own rhetoric.So here goes. On the nation’s broad direction towards energy transition, innovation-driven prosperity, social cohesion, civility in public life and, of course, the need for a counterweight to Murdoch in the Australian media and a healthy scepticism of the US alliance, Malcolm was mostly right. But in assuming that being right is enough, Malcolm was ultimately wrong.It is to our collective detriment that he couldn’t execute but, a wasted decade on, a new government seeking to occupy the centre can learn things from his failure; not least the corrosive power of those who resist change by turning people against each other.Albo has things going for him that Malcolm never did – a unified base galvanised around a plan to govern; a thumping majority and a public that may be looking at the nihilism ofHanson but have not yet signed up to her actual agenda, whatever it is.The challenge for anyone trying to navigate the middle of the road is to keep their hands on the wheel and their foot poised between accelerator and the brake. The highway ahead is so uncertain, we need our driver to keep their eyes on the horizon.Peter Lewis is the executive director of Essential, a progressive strategic communications and research company that undertook qualitative research for Labor in the last federal election. He is the host ofBurning Platforms, a weekly podcast focusing on the politics of technology. His columns are accreditedProudly HumanExplore more on these topicsEssential pollOpinionAustralian politicsMalcolm TurnbullAnthony AlbaneseLiberal partyCoalitionOne NationcommentShareReuse this content

title: MPs shouldn’t face abuse. Neither should their staff – but here’s what we deal with every day | Estelle Warhurst | The Guardian
description: Some constituents are traumatised, others violent. It’s time the House of Commons protected the people who work at the grassroots of our democracy, says Estelle Warhurst, office manager for a Labour MP
Author: Estelle Warhurst
Headline: Some constituents are traumatised, others violent. It’s time the House of Commons protected the people who work at the grassroots of our democracy, says Estelle Warhurst, office manager for a Labour MP
Content: ‘In an MP’s email inbox are images that no one should see.’Photograph: osterman/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreen‘In an MP’s email inbox are images that no one should see.’Photograph: osterman/Getty Images/iStockphotoOpinionHouse of CommonsMPs shouldn’t face abuse. Neither should their staff – but here’s what we deal with every dayEstelle WarhurstSome constituents are traumatised, others violent. It’s time the House of Commons protected the people who work at the grassroots of our democracyTue 11 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 06.32 EDTShareBefore most people have finished their morning coffee, an MP’s staffer might have already dealt with a suicidal caller, a victim of domestic abuse or a threat of violence. We’ve been yelled at, cried at and sometimes even physically attacked, all in the course of managing a heavy caseload of constituents’ most intractable problems. So, when I read the results ofthe latest survey by the wellness working group (WWG)I was not surprised to learn that half of us are experiencing clinical levels of psychological distress.Psychological distress is a range of emotional or cognitive suffering, such as anxiety or depression, that impairs a person’s ability to cope with ordinary daily life and functioning. It makes you wonder why urgent action is not in place to support these staff members, who are holding together the day-to-day functioning of democracy as well as supporting constituents throughout the UK.As the office manager for the Labour MP for Preston, and an executive committee member for the WWG, I encounter this distress every day. In an MP’s email inbox are images that no one should see. These include murdered children, flayed animals, nude images and graphic pictures of war zones, all sent by constituents to try to strengthen their points or illustrate the reality of the situations they face. While photos are often triggering, so is some written communication from constituents who urgently need their MP’s help. Vivid descriptions of child abuse, domestic violence, physical ill health or the thoughts of people who are severely mentally ill or suicidal take a huge toll. The reality is that usually it is not the MP who opens these communications but a member of staff in their constituency or parliamentary office – often an office manager, sometimes a junior colleague who has just left university and hasn’t received any training at all. These teams also receive the racist or sexist language and the rape and death threats that are levelled at some members of parliament.Sometimes these communications are sent directly to the staff themselves, or staff are abused personally on social media. In my role at the WWG I speak weekly to colleagues who have beenphysically attacked, doxed (sharing someone’s person data online) and stalked. One told me how she lived in a small village, where a constituent found her address and knocked on her door to shout abuse at her. We all remember our colleagueAndrew Pennington, who was killed in 2000 while protecting the MP he worked for from a constituent with a sword. This kind of abuse seems to be increasing, yet support and protection for staffhas not kept pace. It’s little wonder that we are overwhelmed and at breaking point. A third of staff are considering leaving their jobs.Staff members are now at their lowest psychological point since the WWG began the survey in 2000, including the year of the pandemic – and I think that’s because the nature of the work is changing. The pressure for MPs and their staff to be always on is increasing with the expectation by some constituents that we should respond immediately to their emails and posts on social media. What many people do not understand is that an MP is supported by a very small number of staff and that each year our casework is increasing, both in volume and complexity. This has resulted in some offices having hundreds of emails backlogged. Staff are fighting to reassure people for whom we are struggling to find solutions. Obviously to each constituent, theirs is the most important case, but offices have to triage. Is there an immediate threat of death, destitution or disaster? These cases must be brought to the fore, pushing others further back in the never-ending list of work to be done.The survey too points to how many staff are working until late at night, logging on early in the morning and not taking lunch breaks, or their annual leave, to try to get on top of the workload. I know of staff who go into their offices at weekends to check the answerphone to see if their vulnerable constituent is still alive, and those who buy weekly shopping and deliver it to constituents who don’t receive any other support. Inappropriate? Most of us do this work because we care, we want to help people and we find it hard to see others in extreme distress.Contrary to popular opinion, the vast majority of members of parliament are honest, decent people who come into public service because they also care and want to make the country a better place. They care about their constituents and hire people who want to help them. However, like any large group of people, there are always a few who don’t have the right intentions. Some of those few expect their staff to work all hours and a small percentage expect their staff to work in unsanitary conditions, without running water or even toilet roll.In response to the annual survey the WWG provides a series of recommendations, and this year they are more urgent than ever. TheHouse of Commonsshould mandate specific training for staff, taking the decision for this out of the hands of the individual MPs who employ us. This would equip them with the skills to help constituents, and to protect themselves mentally and physically. Similarly, the House should make its recommended safety measures mandatory in all MPs’ offices – these include providing alarms and security counters, and ensuring that all surgeries are by pre-booked appointment only. The House of Commons has a duty of care to the staff who work in MPs offices – it should ensure that basic security measures are provided as a standard minimum requirement away from the parliamentary estate.If we expect MPs’ staff to absorb trauma, safeguard vulnerable people and keep constituency services functioning, then we also have a duty to equip and protect them. If we do not do this, the public ultimately feels the consequences, and we further erode faith in democracy.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEstelle Warhurst is the office manager for a Labour MP and an executive committee member for the parliamentary wellness working groupDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
