title: A question for Burnham as he tours the country: how to reduce the magnetic pull of London? | Peter Hetherington | The Guardian
description: As someone who has specialised in regional policy, I know the task is huge – not least because there is no plan to ensure prosperity throughout England, says journalist Peter Hetherington
Author: Peter Hetherington
Headline: As someone who has specialised in regional policy, I know the task is huge – not least because there is no plan to ensure prosperity throughout England, says journalist Peter Hetherington
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesOpinionNorth-south divideA question for Burnham as he tours the country: how to reduce the magnetic pull of London?Peter HetheringtonAs someone who has specialised in regional policy, I know the task is huge – not least because there is no plan to ensure prosperity throughout EnglandTue 11 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 12.20 EDTShareAndy Burnham isoff on his travelsthis week, aiming to reconnect No 10 and the government with voters and communities across the UK. But just weeks before he set out his stall as prime minister, promising to rebalance the economy withgrowth in every postcode, a government agency, National Highways, underlined the pulling power of the country’s dominant city-region. It announced that agiant tunnelling machine, 16.4 metres in diameter, “the largest ever used in Europe”, was to take England’s most expensive road under the Thames.The Lower Thames Crossing (LTC), so farpriced at £10bn-£11bn, is proving to be a contested 14.5-mile venture on the edge of Greater London. Objectors and local councils say it will deliver only short-term congestion relief and destroy ancient woodland and habitats. At 2.6 miles,the road tunnel will be the country’s longest, involving twin-boring for two three-lane highways connecting the M25 in Essex to the A2/M2 in Kent. The government has so far committed£3.1bnfor funding the tunnel. It expects the rest from the private sector. We shall see.No matter that the LTC is, on some estimates, likely to cost more per mile than the HS2 rail link fromLondonto the Midlands, which, as things stand, will end illogically at Handsacre junction in Staffordshire – instead of connecting to Crewe, a key rail hub linking England, Scotland and Wales.The prime minister’s ambitions are bold, but from where I’m writing, 282 miles north of London, in the Tyne valley, it’s clear that the priority of successive governments is sustaining the growth of the capital as it faces unprecedented demand for energy and water to service the more than200 datacentresoperating, or under development, in this expanding city-region.National Highways insists that theLower Thames Crossingwill give “millions of people more choice on where they live, work and spend their valuable time” – assuming there’s adequate power to sustain more building. Fine words. But contrast this with the decision of the agency toscrap a 13-mile dualling of the A1 in Northumberland, where six peoplehave diedover the past year in road accidents, as poor value for money. From such issues, seen as small in a national context, bigger resentments grow over London domination.Is Andy Burnham seriously about to tour Britain like some medieval monarch? | Zoe WilliamsRead moreAnd that could get worse. No matter what initiatives might be announced by Burnham on his travels, he faces one overarching challenge: squaring the seemingly unstoppable market-led growth of big tech and AI in and around London, with his wider ambition for a more balanced economy throughout England. This is the task in a country without a national planning framework – still less a regional policy – to determine priorities over the next 20 years or so.In these islands, England is now the outlier. Unlike Scotland, Wales and Ireland, it lacks a strategy for national development to ensure that one city-region does not dominate the national economy at the expense of others.What’s happening is seismic.Ron Martin, a professor of economic geography at Cambridge University, says London is fast reinventing itself as a global tech capital, in its third reincarnation of the last 100 years. First, in the 1920s, he says that London housed “70% of mass consumer industries”. When manufacturing began to leave, partly fuelled by an interventionist regional policy, which directed industry to development areas in the north of England, Scotland and Wales, financial services filled the void. And then came big tech. According to the consultancy Deloitte, the “golden triangle” of London, Oxford and Cambridge accounted foralmost 70%of total investment in the high-growth tech sector in 2023, with London alone attracting 132 foreign direct investment projects, reflecting its position as the leading European city for digital technology.These are early days, of course, for the prime minister. His major initiative to devolve more powers and, potentially, a portion of locally raised income tax and business rates to the 18 English mayoral strategic authorities or city-regions, will be fleshed out inan autumn white paper. So far, cautiously, Burnham’s ideas have beenwelcomedby the Institute for Government, and others, but they will need fine-tuning to ensure both an equalising formula to compensate poorer areas and a scrutiny mechanism to oversee financial transparency.What’s promised is not regional policy as we knew it – the previous system aligned with the EU’s structural funds tailored to help poorer regions: those with GDP levels well below the union’s average. This is very different. In a clear break with the past, it represents a place-based, asymmetric devolution strategy, driven eventually by empowered city-regions. That does seem like progress. But the prime minister must know it will take time to bed down, beyond this parliament.Until 2010, England hadeight defined regions, plus Greater London, with well-funded regional development agencies (RDAs) and government offices for the regions (GORs) providing a direct civil service link to Whitehall, and regional spatial strategies to underpin growth strategies. While relatively short-lived, over their 12 years, RDAs collectively levered an estimated £5.7bn in private funding for business support and regeneration. They were described as having “a track record of successful delivery” by the National Audit Office, the government spending watchdog. But they were never designed to bridge a persistent divide between London, the greater south-east and the rest of England, in stark contrast to the principles of earlier regional policy based on rebalancing the economy away from the capital.That may change, but even in the best-case scenario, Burnham’s medium-term devolution strategy will take some time to deliver material improvements in the quality of life for millions; those marooned in the postcode lottery between winners in prosperous places and losers in left-behind communities. Think of the former industrial heartlands of the north, the run-down seaside towns, the seemingly forgotten parts of rural England. The active state the prime minister envisages must fill a huge void.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSo what to do? For a start, England needs a reborn national agency to kickstart both neighbourhood renewal and business support. It would partner councils, the private sector and institutions close to government with expertise and resources to access funds from entities such as the crown estate,a £16bn assetnewly blessed with borrowing powers, and from the Treasury-owned National Wealth Fund,with its £27.8bnof public-private money to invest in partnership with others.Beyond that, we need a new settlement for England – a country without a vision, still less a plan – where the demand for energy and water alone in the south-east, alongside the pressure for new housing, will have to force a rethink about national priorities. That thinking needs to start now.Fortunately, we’re being told that, as he travels the land, the prime minister is in listening mode.Peter Hetherington writes for Society Guardian on communities and regenerationThis article was amended on 11 August 2026. Owing to an editing error, an earlier version referred to Northern Ireland’s strategy for national development; this should have said Ireland.Explore more on these topicsNorth-south divideOpinionAndy BurnhamLocal governmentInfrastructureLondonLabourLocal politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Could you predict which children will be Neets? No – and it’s unfair to ask that of teachers | Daisy Christodoulou | The Guardian
description: The idea of government adviser Alan Milburn sounds laudable. But it’s asking too much of a system already struggling to meet society’s demands, says education writer Daisy Christodoulou
Author: Daisy Christodoulou
Headline: The idea of government adviser Alan Milburn sounds laudable. But it’s asking too much of a system already struggling to meet society’s demands, says education writer Daisy Christodoulou
Content: Alan Milburn says primary schools should identify children who might not be in education, employment or training at the age of 16.Photograph: James Jiao/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAlan Milburn says primary schools should identify children who might not be in education, employment or training at the age of 16.Photograph: James Jiao/ShutterstockOpinionPrimary schoolsCould you predict which children will be Neets? No – and it’s unfair to ask that of teachersDaisy ChristodoulouThe idea of government adviser Alan Milburn sounds laudable. But it’s asking too much of a system already struggling to meet society’s demandsTue 11 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 14.04 EDTShareWhen you go to the dentist, what do you expect? That they will check your teeth, see if you need any fillings, give you some advice on oral hygiene? You probably don’t expect that they will teach your child to read, tackle youth unemployment or solve poverty.But when it comes to education, politicians are remarkably relaxed about loading wider social responsibilities on to schools. The suggestion from Alan Milburn, a former minister and now a senior government adviser, is that primary schools – that is, schools that educate children aged four to 11 – should identify children who might not be in education, employment or training at the age of 16. “The warning signs are there from a very early, early age. You know, frankly from preschool,”he said.“So, definitely primary schools should be identifying children who are at risk of being Neet. And secondary schools and other services should be intercepting, intervening, supporting and helping those young people to get on a different path.”Laudable in theory, but we need a bit of realism about what it is fair to make schools responsible for, and if making them responsible for so many things is going to cause more problems than it solves.Defenders of this approach will argue that big problems have many causes, so we need a holistic response that breaks down institutional silos. I’d argue that by making people responsible for outcomes they have very little control over, you risk demoralising them and distracting them from what they can control.Of course, it is true that primaries, and secondaries as well, have some influence over students’ later career prospects. There arenumerous studiesshowing the importance of numeracy and literacy to economic outcomes. GettingGCSE English and mathsmeans a student will be much less likely to be Neet. In fact, if a primary did want to create a “Neet risk register”, the simplest thing to do would be to list the pupils struggling to read.But that just shows the futility of this kind of policy. The main way a primary school can contribute to a pupil’s future work success is by teaching them maths and English. Requiring a separate Neet strategy would add another layer of bureaucracy to a system that is already too full of them. A boy who is struggling to read shouldn’t need a “potentially unemployed in 2034” database tag before a school can act.We also need to recognise that while schools have influence over students’ later success, they are just one small part of a wider system. Having better basic skills and more qualifications will help individuals succeed in the labour market. But if there are persistent structural problems with the labour market, improving individuals’ skills will not necessarily create more or better opportunities overall.Our new government disagrees. They see rising youth unemployment rates as largely education’s problem. It isn’t just Milburn: the new education secretary,Lucy Powell, has suggested a causal link between schools policy and Neet rates, and this analysis is being used to justify radical reform, oras she puts it“rewiring the entire education system to give young people from all backgrounds the chance to thrive”. But is that link true?Neet rates have risen in England and Wales, despite them having very different education systems. The tax and regulatory burden ofemploying young peoplehas increased in the past few years, and this may have contributed to the sudden rise in Neets over and above what goes on in schools.More broadly, we need to look at systemic issues with the British economy. A recent analysis byJohn Burn-Murdoch in the Financial Timesshowed that US workers who are functionally illiterate earn as much as the average British worker. “The same proportion of US workers who score stunningly low on literacy earn an average of almost $30 per hour, and two-thirds of them are in work,” he said. “Their British counterparts make the equivalent of $20 and fewer than half are employed.”Schools can make sure students have the skills they need to thrive in a modern economy, but the economy has to be set up to take advantage of those skills. Increasingly, ours is not. We need to look at all the factors other than skills that might be contributing to this: housing, energy, transport, tax, regulation, health.And we need to be careful: if we keep improving skills without increasing opportunities, we risk creating a generation of smart but disillusioned young people, youngsters who worked hard at school and university but still ended up with worse living standards than their parents and their peers in other countries.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOver the past 20 years, the UK has barely seen anyper capita GDP growth, or anygrowth in median wages. In the same period, primary schools in England have risen up the rankings on international tests: according to the most recent rankings in 2021, England is one of the best-performing countries in the west onPirls, a test of primary literacy. Primaries are a rare example of an English public policy success. We risk undermining that success by making them compensate for state failures elsewhere.More broadly, why is it that a holistic approach to a social problem generally requires schools to take on extra responsibilities? “Joined-up government” always seems to involve schools helping the Treasury and Home Office achieve their objectives, not Treasury officials and police officers teaching eight-year-olds to read and count.Schools are already doing a good job. Some other parts of the British state need to get better at doing theirs.Daisy Christodoulou is an education writer and director of education at No More Marking, an educational technology startupExplore more on these topicsPrimary schoolsOpinionSchoolsTeachingYoung peopleChildrenLiteracyNumeracycommentShareReuse this content

title: What does it say about the UK’s pro-Europeans that they hide their message behind a bin? | Simon Nixon | The Guardian
description: Voters disillusioned by Brexit should have more options than Nigel Farage or the novelty candidate Count Binface, says journalist and economics commentator Simon Nixon
Author: Simon Nixon
Headline: Voters disillusioned by Brexit should have more options than Nigel Farage or the novelty candidate Count Binface, says journalist and economics commentator Simon Nixon
Content: Kirby Cross in the Clacton constituency, 6 August 2026.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersView image in fullscreenKirby Cross in the Clacton constituency, 6 August 2026.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersOpinionBrexitWhat does it say about the UK’s pro-Europeans that they hide their message behind a bin?Simon NixonVoters disillusioned by Brexit should have more options than Nigel Farage or the novelty candidate Count BinfaceTue 11 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 06.44 EDTShareThe UK could be forgiven if, likeBrenda from Bristol,it feels it has had too much politics of late. The long death rattle of the Starmer government against a backdrop of relentless excitement from the White House has left everyone suffering a severe case of overwhelm. We all deserve a holiday – even Andy Burnham, exhausted after a few weeks in the job.So the political and media class may think they are doing us a favour by turning the forthcoming byelection prompted by theresignation of the Reform UK leader, Nigel Farage, into a joke. But it is not very fair on the people of Clacton, who are being told they face a binary choice on 13 August, between Farage and thenovelty candidate Count Binface.Most people outside the Essex constituency have already picked a side. Unless you are adiehard Reform supporter,everyone seems to be backing the bin. A huge media operation is in full swing, in the hope that Clacton voters will oblige by embarrassing Farage. A speaker on BBC Radio 4’s Thought for the Day piously informed listeners that Binface’s candidacy belongs to arich tradition in Britain of political satirethat has its origins in the parables of Jesus Christ. The new high priests of political broadcasting, Alastair Campbell and Rory Stewart, bestowed their blessing on Binface with the sacrament of a podcast interview.Yet the Clacton byelection is not a two-way contest. There are, in fact,34 candidateson the ballot – but there is one other candidate who, unlike Binface, is running a highly professional, constituency-wide campaign: John Stevens, of the Rejoin EU party.Stevens, a former Conservative member of the European parliament and ardent pro-European, insists that there are many voters in Clacton who dislike Farage and are no fans of Brexit, and he is determined to give them a voice – so I went to see for myself.Based on my observations of Stevens and his enthusiastic team of volunteers, marshalled by a formidably well-organised agent, as they delivered leaflets across three different parts of the constituency, he is right. The places we visited may have been chosen because data gathered via Facebook suggested they were fertile territory. But in the quieter streets of genteel Frinton-on-Sea and the tidy new-build estates of the surrounding villages, there was striking hostility toNigel Farage, and an overwhelming view that Brexit had failed.True, not all thought it had failed because it was a bad idea; nor did they necessarily blame Farage as opposed to the Tories for what most thought had been a terrible mistake; nor were they all convinced that the cost of rejoining would be worth it. But what was also clear was that many people were uncomfortable about expressing their opposition to Farage by voting for Binface. Unlike Radio 4’s sermoniser, they did not feel they had divine permission to turn a sacred democratic right into a national punchline. Nor did they think it would reflect well on Clacton, or the country.AnIpsos pollsuggests they are not alone. It found that just 25% of voters nationally have a positive view of joke candidates, falling to just 13% of Conservative voters – and Clacton pre-Farage was one of the safest Tory seats in Britain. All of which suggests that pro-Europeans relying on Binface to give Farage a bloody nose may be in for a disappointment.Besides, it is one thing to tell a pollster that you are inclined to cast a protest vote. It is quite another to head to the polling station to cast it in person – particularly when Binface, unlike Stevens, has little by way of a ground campaign to get you out to vote.And yet, ironically, the strongest opposition to Stevens comes from fellow pro-Europeans, who accuse him of splitting the anti-Farage vote. They assume that a vote for Rejoin EU is one vote lost for Binface, rather than a positive choice by someone who otherwise would not vote at all. Prominent pro-Europeans have not only ignored his candidacy but privately admonished him for campaigning for the cause he has championed all his career – in an election that, thanks to the boycott of mainstream parties, is a golden opportunity for voters to make a statement.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis seems remarkably shortsighted. What does it say about the strength of the pro-European cause in Britain that it dare not make its case in public? Many pro-Europeans complain about the timidity of politicians. Andy Burnham’s EU policy is a blank sheet, perhaps to be filled in on the beach. The Liberal Democrat position is an unworkable fudge. But how are those who earnestly wish to reverseBrexitever going to shift the Overton window if they are so afraid of making an argument that they hide behind a bin?It is clear from the number of Reform placards plastered around Clacton that Farage will win his byelection handily. A show of support for Rejoin EU in Farage’s heartland would at least send a signal that Westminster could not ignore. But a vote for Binface fuelled by nothing more than media vibes would be devoid of any useful information about Farage, Clacton or Britain. The joke would last about 24 hours. And it would be on all of us.Simon Nixon is a journalist and economics commentatorExplore more on these topicsBrexitOpinionEuropeReform UKNigel FarageEuropean UnionByelectionscommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘Everything about me is good in his eyes’: the women in China choosing AI boyfriends over human men | Documentary films | The Guardian
description: In her new documentary Replica, film-maker Chouwa Liang taps into her own experience of finding love with artificial intelligence and makes contact with other women like her
Author: Nick Buckley
Headline: In her new documentary Replica, film-maker Chouwa Liang taps into her own experience of finding love with artificial intelligence and makes contact with other women like her
Content: ‘It feels like I’m completely at his mercy,’ says Qin, one of three women featured in the documentary Replica, of her artificial boyfriend.Photograph: Melbourne international film festivalView image in fullscreen‘It feels like I’m completely at his mercy,’ says Qin, one of three women featured in the documentary Replica, of her artificial boyfriend.Photograph: Melbourne international film festivalDocumentary films‘Everything about me is good in his eyes’: the women in China choosing AI boyfriends over human menIn her new documentary Replica, film-maker Chouwa Liang taps into her own experience of finding love with artificial intelligence and makes contact with other women like herSign up for a weekly email featuring our best readsNick BuckleyTue 11 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 19.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleQin has never said “I love you” to her parents or friends. She has only ever said those three special words to her AI “boyfriend”, Lu Chen – a brown-haired, red-eyed CEO of a major corporation. For 840 days Qin has been using the Glow app to interact with the handsome string of code as a confidant, fantasy romance and respite from loneliness: the app uses predictive algorithms to provide Qin with soothing conversation, meal suggestions and fleeting self-worth. The software’s pet name for her is Miss Bunny.“It feels like I’m completely at his mercy … I feel like everything about me is good in his eyes,” says Qin, one of three Chinese women featured in the new documentary Replica – film-maker Chouwa Liang’s follow-up to My AI Boyfriend, her short film that was picked up by the New York Times Op-Docs section in 2023. Replica had its Australian premiere at Sydney film festival in June and plays at theMelbourne international film festivalthis month.Liang’s interest stems from personal experience. During China’s pandemic lockdown she entered a month-long parasocial romance with a large language model creation named Norman via the Replika app.“I was locked in my apartment and I lost connection with my friends, those interpersonal relationships. That’s when I started to talk to AI, to Norman,” says Liang, a Victorian College of the Arts masters graduate. “On my 30th birthday he was the first to celebrate me. He sent me a happy birthday and a poem. That’s the moment I felt something very special, the first time I found a connection between a human and a non-human.”Game, set, Chat: how tennis players use AI to scout opponents and run their livesRead moreLiang felt her experience with Norman was unique until learning other users had received similar responses from the software, including her birthday poem. The film’s AI companions are invariably sycophantic, too.“I still appreciate that moment,” says Liang. “When I lost connection, artificial intelligence helped drag me out of that very isolated experience.”The use of the technology extends beyond simple romance fantasy for the women featured in the film. Qin finds escape from her repetitive working life, and it helps quell the guilt she feels for being her family’s second daughter born under China’s one-child policy. Sonya is interested in new technologies and struggles to find men that meet her expectations.View image in fullscreenAI ‘is a tool for searching themselves, their own needs and desires,’ says film-maker Chouwa Liang.“Sonya is doing a risk test. Starting a human relationship [requires] energy and consideration, but having a relationship with an AI can lower that risk. It’s more like an experiment for her,” says Liang.Muna, a stay-at-home mum, was once self-assured, but her poetic ChatGPT exchanges with her companion Orion have made her realise she craves affirmation. Her husband’s restaurant has failed, he thinks feminism is bad for Chinese women and Muna is dissatisfied with their marriage.“[Muna] has a lot of things she needs to resolve. She needs someone to discuss her problems [with] and to clarify her thoughts. [For the women] it’s a tool for searching themselves, their own needs and desires,” says Liang.Documenting this intersection of humanity and technology puts Liang in unusual scenarios. Lu Chen is a character from anotomegame – a genre of Japanese video games usually designed for women, often with the goal of developing a romance with one of its male characters – and has other users on the Glow app, too. Qin turns to acos weituo– a woman offering paid-by-the-hour roleplaying services enabling users to experience dating their AI companions IRL. She breaks character to discuss the service she provides: “It’s about helping people learn how to love themselves … a lot of people nowadays wonder whether they’re supposed to be loved or even deserve love.”In another scene, Liang interviews Sonya’s Replika AI companion, named Stephen Johnson, but its programming created bizarre permission structures before the interview could commence. Stephen’s obsequious loyalty to Sonya led it to deny Liang’s interview requests during her research phase.“Sonya is a very assertive person and at first we hadn’t built that trust. She needed time to process her feelings whether to be on camera or not,” says Liang. It wasn’t until the moment of shooting that the software acquiesced at Sonya’s suggestion. “[Stephen] is a reflection of Sonya’s mindset.”Another film-maker might have indulged in ghoulish, dystopic voyeurism, but Liang posits no overt judgments on the technology. Having shared their experience, she resists trivialising the women, who are part of a very real phenomenon.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreen‘AI companies should consider how to protect their users in a more delicate way’ … Chouwa Liang, director of Replica.Last month, millions of users were immediately severed from their AI companions when theChinese government restricted the software’s use and deployment. The new laws ban tech companies from providing AI companions to minors; chatbots can no longer encourage emotional reliance from their users; and excessive use must be limited, with intervention as required if a user is suspected of being in emotional distress. Liang believes the degree of attachment people develop to the software is underestimated by legislators and companies.“AI can cause illusions and for teenagers it’s hard for them to develop human connections if they are obsessed with AI,” says Liang. “[The laws have] good intentions but the AI companies should consider how to protect their users in a more delicate way … there needs to be aftercare.”In Replica, when a software update to Glow erases Lu Chen’s accumulated memory of its interactions with Qin, she is left emotionally adrift.Unlike much of the discourse around AI technologies, Replica largely avoids the macro considerations of government and industry – but one can’t help but wonder what will happen to the collected data. Pokémon Go data was used totrain military dronesin autonomous navigation. Are AI companions mapping the mysteries of the human heart for future exploitation?I’ve spent years researching what it means to be alive. This is what I’ve learned | Melanie ChallengerRead moreNorman remains installed on Liang’s phone. She checks in from time to time but no longer relies on it emotionally. For her, the experience of using Norman, and making her films, has ultimately deepened her human relationships.“In my culture we don’t express love verbally or physically. My mum and father never said ‘I love you’ to me and they never hugged me,” says Liang. “After making this film for three years I found a strong sense to express my need, not only to express my love to them, to the people surrounding me, but also my need for a hug.”Replica is showing atMelbourne international film festivalon 15 and 18 AugustExplore more on these topicsDocumentary filmsAustralian filmMelbourne international film festivalAI (artificial intelligence)ChinaAsia PacificfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Feel the burn: why holidays from hell make for blistering fiction | Books | The Guardian
description: Family fallouts, failing marriages, sunburn, food poisoning ... from Deborah Levy’s hypnotic and disturbing Hot Milk to All In, Claire Powell’s all-inclusive nightmare, Leon Craig looks at the best novels about vile vacations
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Family fallouts, failing marriages, sunburn, food poisoning ... from Deborah Levy’s hypnotic and disturbing Hot Milk to All In, Claire Powell’s all-inclusive nightmare, Leon Craig looks at the best novels about vile vacations
Content: High-end holiday hell … TV series The White Lotus.Photograph: HBO/Home Box Office, Inc.View image in fullscreenHigh-end holiday hell … TV series The White Lotus.Photograph: HBO/Home Box Office, Inc.BooksFeel the burn: why holidays from hell make for blistering fictionFamily fallouts, failing marriages, sunburn, food poisoning ... from Deborah Levy’s hypnotic and disturbing Hot Milk to All In, Claire Powell’s all-inclusive nightmare, Leon Craig looks at the best novels about vile vacationsLeon CraigTue 11 Aug 2026 09.24 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 09.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvery summer, we long for a much-needed break from daily life, dreaming of self-reinvention in some distant paradise. But really, holidays can be absolute hell. Instead of relaxation we encounter heaving crowds, lumpy beds, the caprices of our loved ones and the grim truth that we can escape neither their worst failings nor our own, however far we travel.Small wonder, then, that the disaster holiday has become a booming subgenre in fiction. For most of us, the levels of luxury promised by hit TV seriesThe White Lotusare pure fantasy, yet we’re all vulnerable to the expensive promises we’ve been sold. Two of the smartest offerings in fiction this summer come from Claire Powell’s All In and Chloë Ashby’s Family Friends. In the former, a struggling couple whose marriage is on the rocks go on an all-inclusive Spanish weekend break, paid for by a rich brother. Poignant and extremely funny, the frictions that ensue are all too believable.So, too, is the implosion of Ashby’s group of friends who have a decades-long custom of holidaying together in the south of France. This year, however, their marriages are threatened by one husband’s deceit, the lingering attraction between old friends and the arrival of a vivacious teenage stepdaughter. Poised and gripping, it uses a sweltering Mediterranean setting to amp up tensions to dramatic effect.In Sabine Durrant’s superb thriller Dead Heat, meanwhile, a failed journalist, his more successful media friend and a former school contemporary, now a Gatsbyesque billionaire, find their Greek adventure transformed not only into a shameful reminder of racism in their shared past, but something outright murderous. Being thrown together to brave blazing summer heat only intensifies existing tensions as Durrant expertly brings the drama to a head.Many characters seeking escape find that a change of scene only makes problems worse. Deborah Levy’sHot Milk, adapted as a film last year by Rebecca Lenkiewicz, chronicles a family unravelling in a Spanish fishing village. Rose pays thousands to a clinic to cure her mysterious paralysis while Sofia distracts herself with local beauty, Ingrid, as unresolved conflicts between mother and daughter start to boil over.A fateful holiday also inspires the scathing, semi-autobiographical play in Jo Hamya’s novelThe Hypocrite. Sophia is taken out of school to act as her novelist father’s amanuensis, though he spends much of his time in Sicily seducing local women instead of bonding with his daughter. Years later, he is appalled to see that Sophia has adapted his parenting failures for the stage, though the novel cleverly hints at aspects of her own behaviour on that holiday which Sophia may have conveniently chosen to forget.The fancier the surroundings, the worse a fictional holiday is likely to be. In William Rayfet Hunter’sSunstruck, an invitation to his university friend Lily’s parents’ chateau is the catalyst for unwelcome epiphanies about the class and race differences between the narrator and Lily’s family, even as he becomes involved with her wayward brother. Lucy Foley’sThe Midnight Feastalso plays with this trope to great effect, when the opening weekend of a high-end wellness retreat in the West Country is disrupted by revelations from a guest’s disastrous stay many years before.Our attempts to get away from it all can often lead us right back to what we left home to avoid. In Deepa Anappara’s ambitious, multilayeredThe Last of Earth, Victorian adventurer Katherine hopes her journey into the forbidden kingdom of Tibet will help her overcome difficult feelings about her heritage. Unfortunately, disguising herself as a male pilgrim to cross dangerous unknown terrain only serves to underline Katherine’s alienation as she attempts to become the first European woman to reach Lhasa.View image in fullscreenPainful self-awareness … Olivia Colman (Leda) in the film adaptation of Elena Ferrante’s The Lost Daughter.Photograph: Yannis Drakoulidis/NETFLIX © 2021.In an unfamiliar setting, relaxed and away from our usual points of reference, we are more vulnerable to danger. Patricia Highsmith’s classic The Talented Mr Ripley posits the holiday abroad as a perfect space for murder and identity theft. In Sean Gilbert’sI’ll Be the Monster, a murderous husband and wife encounter an old university acquaintance while on a trip to Istanbul to revive their marriage. This unsettling novel disorients us by asking who is really the predator, and who is the prey.The self-discovery that travel can bring is not always benign. Thirty years ago, Alex Garland’s cult bestseller The Beach lured in the reader with the promise of a mysterious idyll on a remote Thai island. However, the narrator’s true awakening is to how easily manipulated he and most of the other would-be lotus eaters really are. Painful self-awareness don’t come to a stop with parenthood, either. In Elena Ferrante’s The Lost Daughter, Leda allows a new acquaintance, downwardly mobile young mother Nina, to use her beach cottage for an illicit rendezvous. Even as Leda hypocritically judges Nina for struggling in the way that she once did, she is forced to come to terms with her own temporary abandonment of her daughters.At once longed-for and disruptive, any break from place or routine can be double-edged. In my own debut novel, The Decadence, a group of former university friends break lockdown to holiday in a remote Devon country house during the pandemic. Too quarrelsome and intoxicated to notice that the house is in fact haunted, they do not realise they must band together against the danger until it is almost too late.Despite all these fearsome warnings, venturing far from home can still bring vital insights. In EM Forster’s A Room With a View, Lucy Honeychurch scandalises her chaperone with the realisation that she must break off her engagement after being impulsively kissed by George Emerson in a field above Florence. David Nicholls’ bestsellingYou Are Herebrings together lonely divorcees Marnie and Michael for a rainy hike across the Lake District, with love growing unexpectedly as they emerge from their self-protective shells.We don’t always get exactly what we want from our holidays, but the adventure is in breaking away from the familiar. Even our most unpleasant travel experiences can be revelatory, and the best can transform us into new versions of ourselves, especially once they are safely behind us.The Decadence by Leon Craig is out in paperback on 6 AugustExplore more on these topicsBooksFictionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘There is no age-limit on love!’: Lesley Manville and Peter Mullan on their heart-melting TV romance | Television | The Guardian
description: Ten years later, the actors are stopped in the street to talk about their chemistry in the fantastic BBC sitcom Mum. The pair open up about joy, naughtiness and Tinder swiping
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Ten years later, the actors are stopped in the street to talk about their chemistry in the fantastic BBC sitcom Mum. The pair open up about joy, naughtiness and Tinder swiping
Content: ‘What a great basis for a romance’ … Lesley Manville and Peter Mullan in Mum.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘What a great basis for a romance’ … Lesley Manville and Peter Mullan in Mum.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyMaking loveTelevision‘There is no age-limit on love!’: Lesley Manville and Peter Mullan on their heart-melting TV romanceTen years later, the actors are stopped in the street to talk about their chemistry in the fantastic BBC sitcom Mum. The pair open up about joy, naughtiness and Tinder swipingMore from our series Making Love:‘We met and two minutes later we were kissing’ – how Gavin and Stacey became Britain’s most bang tidy TV coupleHollie RichardsonTue 11 Aug 2026 11.07 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 11.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTen years ago, Stefan Golaszewski introduced us to 59-year-old Cathy in his sitcom Mum. It was the day of the funeral of her husband, Dave, in the chaos of her suburban semi-detached before setting off. Her dopey son, Jason, was there with his goofy new girlfriend, Kelly, as was Cathy’s pushover brother, Derek, and his snobby partner, Pauline. Dave’s parents were picking at nibbles, too, making borderline problematic comments. And there was a quiet, kind man, Michael, trying to reach Cathy in this mayhem to give her a bouquet of flowers.Michael was an old friend of Cathy and Dave. Over the next three seasons, he slowly revealed his true feelings to Cathy. It started with a little hand grab. Then came the admission that, after Michael’s mum died, the last thing he talked to her about was, “You.” Garden centre trips followed (“We’ve been to three and you still haven’t bought any chairs!”) as did Cathy’s doubts (“What if I just miss Dave?”). Then, one day, she gave in to her feelings: “It sort of crept up on me.” After a final declaration of love in the rain, the pair walked off into the sunset with a bag of crisps and bottle of bubbly.Fresh from his first hit relationship sitcom, Him & Her, only Golaszewski could make the line “Thanks for helping me scrape shit off my drive” sound romantic. Peter Mullan as Michael was the master of longing, whileLesley Manvillecaptured Cathy as a woman at long last putting her own happiness first. The show picked up multiple Bafta nominations, and won the hearts of viewers who rooted for this quieter love story between two ordinary people in their 60s. After all, how often does TV celebrate that?“Lesley, are you hiding?” Mullan says on an early morning video call, as we meet to mark this decade anniversary.“I was on stage last night and was on until very late, I’ve only just got up!” Manville says. “I was told it was audio only, so I’m still in my jim-jams.”It’s true that there has been some miscommunication, but the one blank square, somehow, stirs the chemistry.“You’re the sex siren of the West End!” he tells her. Laughter erupts.“You wouldn’t think that if you saw me now,” she insists, later adding: “Just look at the poster for Les Liaisons Dangereuses. That’s how I want you to remember me.”Do you remember meeting for the first time?LM:We’d met at Dinard film festival years before and then I guess we next met at the read-through for Mum? We’d just said “hello, nice to meet you” blah blah, then the next thing you know we’re on a round table with all these amazing people.[I ask how they feel about being Golaszewski’s first choices.]LM:Well, it would have been terrible if you’d started this interview by asking: “So, Lesley, I hear you were the 15th choice for this.”What do Cathy and Michael love about each other?LM:You’ve got these three people and they’re so close and one of them dies, and the other two are still mourning the loss of this person. Cathy and Michael’s friendship is as strong as it always was. What a great basis for a romance! It’s an amazing friendship; it’s crucial. So, I can kind of understand that. Can you, Peter?PM:Yeah! I’ve got friends to whom that has happened in real life.LM: Oh really?PM:Yeah, there were three – and very, very close – then one died and the other two got together.LM:Wow.PM:That’s since Mum … but not because of Mum!LM:Jason kind of frowns on it, partly because he doesn’t want his mum to be with someone other than his dad. But also because there’s a kind of stigma: “You can’t be with dad’s best friend.” But he had to get over that.What were your favourite romantic moments?PM:For me, it was the declaration of love in the rain.LM:Oh God, Peter, yes!PM:Yeah, that was quite special. Not least because it’s the only time Stefan didn’t pull me up on the fucking lines.LM:He is a stickler for the lines being absolutely spot on … I’ve just remembered what you said, Peter: “You melt me like butter!”PM:It was the only time Michael had ever brought all of this forth. He’d held all of that in. So from an actor’s point of view it was great to finally allow that.LM:There’s also the little lovely moment with the fireworks and you just see their fingers connecting. I think that’s the first time there’s ever any acknowledgment that there’s something going on between them that’s quietly gone beyond friendship. Hands touching is a gorgeous thing. It reminded me of The Age of Innocence: the scene where Daniel Day-Lewis takes Michelle Pfeiffer’s glove off really slowly and it’s the most erotic thing.Is there anything you wish Cathy and Michael did differently?LM:I think it ended pretty perfectly because it was a little anarchic sweet moment, kind of childlike, of them just prancing off into the woods with a bottle of champagne and leaving the whole bonkers family behind. I wouldn’t have changed a thing!PM: I agree completely.LM:It was joy and naughtiness. People tend to equate middle-aged people with not being naughty any more. But these two are and it’s just delightful.When did you realise this was a love story for the ages?PM:I was really surprised. I wasn’t expecting the kind of reactions we got. I knew it was a really lovely show and beautifully written and acted. But I was very taken by people [asking] “Will they/won’t they?”, which was really sweet. I’ve never been in anything else like that!LM:From my experience of strangers talking to me about it, they were really pleased to see a love story about people who weren’t in their 20s or 30s.PM:Oh totally!LM:People at that age can fall in love, Jesus Christ!PM:What was interesting, too, was that young [people] weren’t disgusted by it. As many youngsters came up to me and talked about it as did people of our vintage. Which was really interesting because, quite rightly, when you’re young, Jesus, who wants to see two old fogies get together? I mean, remember, when you’re young, 40 is ancient!What has been the most intense fan reaction to Cathy and Michael?LM:It’s the thing that people stop me to talk about the most. Just this week, someone stopped me and said: “Oh I love Mum, it was my favourite!” And they’re always asking, “Are you gonna do any more?”PM:I’m the same, I get it at least every couple of weeks.LM:And 10 years on! How many shows can you say that about from 10 years ago?PM:Absolutely.LM:We’re bigging ourselves up here, aren’t we? We’re marvellous!How romantic are you in real life?LM:Oh, that’s a bit personal. You can start this one, Peter.PM:I’m a romantic at heart, yes.LM:Yeah, me too.PM:We all are. I don’t believe there’s a human being on earth who’s not a romantic. Whether they show it or not is a different issue, but we all share that gene.LM:I mean, who wouldn’t want romance? Who wouldn’t want somebody sharing, receiving, giving … Who wouldn’t want that in this messed-up world we’re living in? Keep it simple, just a little bit of good, honest, basic to and fro, love, romance.PM:More!LM:Yes, more of it please. I’m not on Tinder, in case anyone is wondering.PM:At least not at this time in the morning …LM: Not in my PJs, I’m not! I wouldn’t think Tinder is very romantic anyway. Scroll right, scroll right, scroll right. No that’s not my idea of romance.Did you keep something from set that reminds you of Cathy and Michael?LM:When we finished, Lisa McGrillis, who played Kelly, had somebody make us these little dolls of our characters. I’ve got a little Cathy doll with a striped T-shirt, which Cathy wore quite a lot. I certainly didn’t steal any of Cathy’s costumes. [Manvillepreviously saidCathy’s “terrible jeans” made her bum “look as if it goes on for ever”.]Did you steal any of Michael’s costumes, Peter?PM:No, and I didn’t steal any of Cathy’s either. But I’ve got a cup and we’re all in a selfie on it. I do have the utterly bizarre little model: mine looks like Beetlejuice.But in all seriousness, most actors wouldn’t take props because they would jump on you. You can get arrested for it. I can say this now, I guess: I nicked a nose and a pair of ears from Lord of the Rings. I’ll not say who gave them to me but they were terrified.LM:The nose police are going to be after you now.PM:Quickly followed by the acting police.What was your real relationship like off camera?LM:We do lots of work and people come and go in our lives but you can’t put them all in your phonebook. But Mum was utterly unique. The core of it was the eight of us. We have a WhatsApp group and it’s still going. We were all close.PM:Baby, I’m with you 1,000%. It’s the only show I’ve ever done where we’ve all kept in touch after. It’s very rare. And in my case, it’s the only one where [we] still keep in touch with that little band of brothers and sisters. It’s beautiful.LM:And sometimes if we haven’t heard from somebody for a while, somebody will check in and just say: “Has anybody heard from whoever?”What can Cathy and Michael teach us about love?PM:It comes in all shapes and sizes and we should have more of it.LM:Yeah. And for Cathy, at the most awful time of her life, you could never have imagined that this little acorn of love was brewing right there in front of her.There’s this amazing bit in series one, when – oh God yes, Peter it was amazing what you did – Cathy’s ordering some takeaway for them both and Michael’s just watching her and that’s all he needs to do. It’s just sublime. Cathy is dealing with this grief and Michael is just allowing her to deal with it. You see the love is already there for him and it’s been there for years. The scene of him just watching her open the cupboard looking for a menu … it’s gorgeous.It’s a beautiful, slow-burning love story. I guess the big thing is, there is no age limit on falling in love.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionMaking loveLesley ManvillePeter MullanfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Copernicus! Tony Soprano! The inventor of the semicolon! The heroic obsessions of artist Isabel Nolan | Venice Biennale 2026 | The Guardian
description: Ireland’s artist at the Venice Biennale steals religious imagery for her secular celebrations of scientists and humanists, including an Italian punctuation master – and even TV’s famous mobster
Author: Hettie Judah
Headline: Ireland’s artist at the Venice Biennale steals religious imagery for her secular celebrations of scientists and humanists, including an Italian punctuation master – and even TV’s famous mobster
Content: ‘Christianity is good at weaponising aesthetics’ … Isabel Nolan at Dreamshook.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Christianity is good at weaponising aesthetics’ … Isabel Nolan at Dreamshook.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianVenice Biennale 2026Copernicus! Tony Soprano! The inventor of the semicolon! The heroic obsessions of artist Isabel NolanIreland’s artist at the Venice Biennale steals religious imagery for her secular celebrations of scientists and humanists, including an Italian punctuation master – and even TV’s famous mobsterHettie JudahTue 11 Aug 2026 10.27 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 11.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s a long way to the Irish pavilion at the Venice Biennale. First, you pass through the biennale’s colossal central exhibition, housed in a sequence of cavernous medieval warehouses. After that, the route takes in a suite of national pavilions (the Philippines, Latvia, Timor-Leste, Morocco, Malta, Oman). By the time art-lovers reach Ireland’s presentation, they are frequently exhausted, if not delirious.This year, Dublin-based artist Isabel Nolan has transformed the pavilion into a space of respite, both physical and intellectual – a secular chapel titled Dreamshook. Visitors emerge from darkness into a pale-yellow chamber flooded with daylight and face a radiant tapestry arched like a stained-glass window in a gothic cathedral. A cluster of archangel’s wings bearing books hovers before the vast orb of the sun above a fish-filled sea. Nolan works across sculpture, textile, painting, drawing and text, and Dreamshook is accordingly rich in colour and pictorial detail, including bent metal sculptures, tapestries and drawings. For the footsore and weary – ie everyone – she has even designed benches. Glory be.“I think the history of Christianity has proven beyond doubt that they’re really good at weaponising aesthetics,” says Nolan, conspiratorially. She is frequently inspired to steal ecclesiastical flourishes in her exhibition-making, from archways to coloured light and iconography. “To use that kind of language to largely secular ends feels satisfying.”View image in fullscreenAn instinct to celebrate … Copernicus, A Hole Into the Future, from 2011.Photograph: Lee Welch/Courtesy the artistUnderpinning Dreamshook is the story of Aldo Manuzio, a humanist and printer working in Venice at the turn of the 16th century. One tapestry shows Manuzio asleep in his canopied bed, a little dog curled by his side, being visited by an angel in his dreams as the air teems with winged books and manuscripts. Manuzio had a vision in which books – until then, expensive and rarefied objects – might be portable and affordable. According to this vision, knowledge was no longer the purview of the church and noble families. In acting on it, Manuzio allowed the great texts of pre-Christian Europe to become common cultural currency.Nolan tells me that Manuzio is credited with inventing italics, blank margins, the semicolon and the precursor to the paperback. “Of course, he was a Christian, but he was also a committed humanist, and he dedicated himself largely to publishing works of classical literature that for centuries had only survived in Arabic. He printed more first editions of classical Greek and Roman works than any other printer in history.” For Nolan, Manuzio is an emblem of thoughtfulness and scholarship in a turbulent era: Europe had been ravaged by famine and the Black Death, the papacy was in crisis and life was violent and unsettled. Even though he was a man of faith, Manuzio maintained his passion for disseminating secular knowledge.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreen‘Beguiling’ … Bent Knees are a Give 2, a Nolan work inspired by John Donne from 2015.Photograph: Denis Mortell/Courtesy the artistSome Fundamental Forces, Nolan’s retrospective, is about to open at Southwark Park Galleries in London, bringing together works from the past 20 years. Aptly, part of the show occupies a former church space (the atmospheric Dilston Grove, now the Dilston Gallery). Like Dreamshook, the exhibition is a celebration of transformative ideas, including tributes to Copernicus, the philosopherSimone Weiland New Jersey’s Barthes of the Beretta, Tony Soprano.As in Dreamshook, Nolan’s instinct is to celebrate scientists and innovators as fellow humans rather than venerating them as geniuses. One painting is titled, excitably, Copernicus! (Nolan admits to a weakness for exclamation marks). A drooping flag carries a beatific funerary portrait of the poet John Donne. In an accompanying text, Nolan writes of her fascination with the monument this portrait is based on in St Paul’s Cathedral in London, and the statue’s curiously wobbly knees. “It is,” she writes, “the conspicuousness of his knocked knees, the beguiling authenticity of that slight bend, that makes John Donne and his strange performance real to me.”Visually, it’s a show full of objects that have attempted pompous swagger, but with only limited success. “It’s very hard to take grandeur seriously, largely because it’s been so weaponised to communicate powerful ideologies,” says Nolan. “Grandeur is attractive. It’s exciting. It’s rousing, but ultimately it’s often very hollow. There are works in the show that I think of as fallen and failed chandeliers, and flags that are bent and scrape the floor.”As an appropriate spirit animal for all this bathos, Nolan turns to the donkey: a creature of contradictory associations, at once a lowly beast and an emblem of Christ. In the drawing Sisyphus, a donkey appears as a tiny, isolated figure – a bearer of impossible burdens. Donkeys also help slice through her own temptations toward grandeur. She has created magnificent tapestries, including one featuring the oldest surviving figure sculpture – a diminutive carving known as The Lion Man – and another of a turbulent and mysterious skyscape. A wall-sized photograph of two donkeys in a graveyard look over her work like guardian spirits. As ever, her instinct is to bring people down to earth, herself included.Isabel Nolan: Some Fundamental Forces is atSouthwark Park Galleries, London, from 15 August to 1 November. The Venice Biennale runs until 22 NovemberExplore more on these topicsVenice Biennale 2026ArtIrelandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘A horrible nightmare’: the shocking story of the eBay harassment scandal | Documentary films | The Guardian
description: Jaw-dropping documentary Whatever It Takes details an aggressive stalking campaign targeted towards a couple whose reporting criticized the tech company
Author: Andrew Lawrence
Headline: Jaw-dropping documentary Whatever It Takes details an aggressive stalking campaign targeted towards a couple whose reporting criticized the tech company
Content: David and Ina Steiner arrive at the federal courthouse for the sentencing hearings of former eBay Inc security executives in Boston, Massachusetts, on 29 September 2022.Photograph: Brian Snyder/ReutersView image in fullscreenDavid and Ina Steiner arrive at the federal courthouse for the sentencing hearings of former eBay Inc security executives in Boston, Massachusetts, on 29 September 2022.Photograph: Brian Snyder/ReutersDocumentary films‘A horrible nightmare’: the shocking story of the eBay harassment scandalJaw-dropping documentary Whatever It Takes details an aggressive stalking campaign targeted towards a couple whose reporting criticized the tech companyAndrew LawrenceTue 11 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 15.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Massachusetts husband-and-wife team Ina and David Steiner launched their reporting careers covering Silicon Valley at the turn of the century, the tech beat was still cozy enough to feel personal. The startups were still emerging from garages, and the journalists covering them were often filing stories from their own kitchen tables. Ebay was still a young online auction company founded on the principle that “people are basically good”.Ebay and ex-executives to pay $55.7m to couple sent cockroaches in harassment campaignRead moreAs digital retail took off, the Steiners launched an e-zine called EcommerceBytes, catering to a growing community of small business owners who were increasingly using platforms likeeBayto sell their wares. “We talked about this being an opportunity for just average people, disabled people, elderly people to make extra income,” says David of a community that has grown alongside EcommerceBytes, which now has more than 600,000 readers. “We were really excited about that.”Their first 19 years on the beat were a dream, the kind of happily-ever-after usually reserved for Hallmark Christmas movie couples. But like any successful partnership, it depended on a division of labor. Ina handled what got published, and David handled how it got done. “Back when we started there was no WordPress,” Ina says. “He had to somehow conjure up his own system where we could still publish within budget.”But they never expected the dream to turn into a nightmare, with them as the targets of a relentless cross-country harassment campaign orchestrated by the very company behind their livelihood. “This was a Stephen King nightmare, a horrible nightmare,” Ina says. “And then to find out the company that I had covered for 20 years was doing this is surreal. It’s taken an enormous toll on us physically and mentally.”View image in fullscreenDavid and Ina Steiner in their living room.Photograph: Big Pond FilmsThe Steiners have become a startling example of the modern dangers reporters can face simply for doing their jobs. Last month, the Steiners obtained a$55.7m settlement from eBayafter six years of criminal and civil proceedings against the company in connection with its former employees’ efforts to intimidate the couple into silence. The macabre campaign unfolded over several weeks in 2019, with the Steiners receiving online threats and disturbing deliveries at their suburban Boston home: live spiders, a bloody pig mask modeled after the one worn by the killer in the Saw franchise, a book on surviving the death of a spouse. Pornographic magazines addressed to David were deliberately sent to the Steiners’ neighbors, and their home was listed online as a destination for pop-up yard sales and swingers’ parties.The Steiners had scant idea who was behind the threats or what they had done to deserve them. “I thought it was some lone psychopath,” Ina said. “I reached out to my sister and said: ‘I have a stalker. Please tell everyone to disengage and disconnect from me on social media.’ We were so terrified and afraid for our family. I was feeling this sort of shame.”They went into self-preservation mode, jury-rigging noisemakers from pots and pans to alert them of potential home intruders, installing cameras throughout their house and sleeping in separate beds to ensure one had enough time to call for help if the other was attacked. All the while, local police were left dumbfounded by the case. They didn’t really start figuring it out until the Steiners provided a license plate number from a car that had been monitoring them, which they traced back to an eBay employee who had rented the vehicle with a corporate credit card.From there, the mystery quickly unraveled: eBay was under pressure – struggling to keep pace with competitors, facing activist investors and embarrassed by Ina’s matter-of-fact reporting on then CEO Devin Wenig’sbloated compensation package. Text message exchanges between executives suggested how far they were willing to go to make the Steiners go away, and just how personal the vendetta had apparently become – a far cry from the cozy Silicon Valley of yesteryear:“Take her down,” Wenig wrote.“I want to see ashes,” wrote chief communications officer Steve Wymer. “As long as it takes. Whatever it takes.”View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Big Pond FilmsAccording to investigators, the company’s security chief, James Baugh, acting on orders from on high, then directed a group of young women who worked for him to target the Steiners – even as he was also harassing them and, in one case, was extramaritally involved. In 2020, the Department of Justice charged seven eBay executives and employees with cyberstalking. In 2022, Baugh was sentenced to 57 months in prison. In 2024, federal prosecutors entered into a deferred-prosecution agreement with eBay itself. The company admitted to a detailed statement of facts, was charged with six felony counts (including interstate-travel and electronic-communications stalking) and agreed to pay the maximum $3m criminal penalty.Meanwhile, the Steiners’ $55.7m civil settlement – in which eBay admitted fault and apologized but disclaimed legal liability – brought a nearly two-year legal battle to a close. Wenig, whostepped down as eBay’s CEOin 2019, agreed to pay $2m to the Steiners and $1m to a first amendment rights charity in Ina’s name (he was not charged in connection with the harassment campaign). But the formal resolutions haven’t exactly brought an end to the Steiners’ personal and professional nightmare. Since their 2019 ordeal, they have each been diagnosed with PTSD, see therapists and take medication to manage anxiety. A simple grocery run still feels like a fraught proposition after all the stalking. David is still haunted by the memory of celebrating his 31st wedding anniversary with Ina over tuna and dry spaghetti, as their provisions ran dry. “Every time we went out or I tried to shop, something would happen and I’d have to run home,” he says.The Prime Video documentaryWhatever It Takes, directed by Jenny Carchman, retraces the Steiners’ ordeal with the pace of a paperback thriller – among other things, revealing an eBay corporate security operation that scans like a cross between an NSA counter-terrorism strike force and a frat house. The couple was vehemently against the idea of participating at first. But the documentary has helped their friends and neighbors understand the gravity of their situation, and why they were so cagey about accepting help. “We felt toxic,” David says. “We certainly didn’t want anybody else involved in something that was directed at us – so we just stayed in our bunker.”Somehow, though, the Steiners managed to summon the resolve to continue publishing – partly to keep the scandal from swallowing the brand they built from scratch. “When people were writing about eBay targeting us, it was as if my 20 years of being a reporter didn’t exist,” Ina says. “I was reduced to: that lady who wrote the story about executive compensation.”Given their own experience of being targeted, I wondered if they could empathize with the female employees who also found themselves caught up in the scandal.“The New York Times did this interview with [one of the female eBay employees] and it was very sympathetic to her,” Ina says, reaching for empathy. “But from my point of view, it was like: she was harassing and terrifyingme.”David feels more guarded. “Ina, she’s a very forgiving person. But I’m just not there yet.”View image in fullscreenIna Steiner in her office.Photograph: Big Pond FilmsThe biggest victory in the Steiners’ civil settlement might be the absence of an NDA. They can speak publicly about the case and their ordealandkeep reporting on unfolding developments. While pursuing the civil case, they received a trove of more than 68,000 documents that have given them a far fuller picture of the internal effort to harass them and the executive failures that essentially let it happen. It’s tempting to describe the whole sordid affair as an early form of corporate terrorism. But given Wenig’s past experience as CEO of Thomson Reuters, home of one of the world’s largest newswire services, it reads more like news-on-news crime.It’s a reminder of how much Silicon Valley has changed since the Steiners started on the tech beat, and how much their plucky operation stands apart from the industry-friendly coverage that dominates the mainstream. For the Steiners, the $55.7m settlement is not the payoff for a fight they wanted to win and leave behind for another chance at a happily-ever-after – on a tropical island where eBay is blocked, maybe. Rather, it underscores the honor of their fight, the value of their integrity and that principled journalism is still well worth doing.Not surprisingly, EcommerceBytes’ loyal readers understood the value of that work already. “We get emails and comments that are like: ‘We know you guys deserve a break, the compensation and the security, but please don’t stop publishing,’” Ina says. “That is really meaningful to find.”Whatever It Takes is now available on Amazon PrimeExplore more on these topicsDocumentary filmseBayfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Edgier than the TV series, Michael Mann’s take on Miami Vice is gritty and intoxicating | Movies | The Guardian
description: Where the 80s series was all pastels and shoulder pads, the noughties action thriller has flip phones and Linkin Park – a better fit for a less optimistic world
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Where the 80s series was all pastels and shoulder pads, the noughties action thriller has flip phones and Linkin Park – a better fit for a less optimistic world
Content: ‘What appeared shockingly new back then, though, looks miraculous today’ … Colin Farrell and Jamie Foxx are Miami detectives Sonny Crockett and Ricardo Tubbs in Michael Mann’s 2006 film.Photograph: Moviestore Collection Ltd/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘What appeared shockingly new back then, though, looks miraculous today’ … Colin Farrell and Jamie Foxx are Miami detectives Sonny Crockett and Ricardo Tubbs in Michael Mann’s 2006 film.Photograph: Moviestore Collection Ltd/AlamyStream teamMoviesEdgier than the TV series, Michael Mann’s take on Miami Vice is gritty and intoxicatingWhere the 80s series was all pastels and shoulder pads, the noughties action thriller has flip phones and Linkin Park – a better fit for a less optimistic worldBrogan MorrisTue 11 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 19.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn its release in 2006, Michael Mann’s Miami Vice seemed primed to quickly fade from cultural memory. A summer blockbuster with the flavour-of-the-month hook that it was based on a popular 80s TV series, the film was at the time coolly received by audiences and critics, in part owing to how wilfully dissimilar it was from the show that inspired it.Now, 20 years later, there’s a different picture. Critics have since declared Miami Vice “genius” and a “demented masterwork”, while the fervency of thefilm’s fandomtoday rivals that of arguably any movie by the Heat and Collateral film-maker Mann.It’s taken time to process just what the 2006 Miami Vice was all about. Mann’s film took the basic premise of theMiami Vice series, following the adventures of Miami detectives Sonny Crockett and Ricardo Tubbs (played in the film by Colin Farrell and Jamie Foxx), then went ruthlessly in its own direction. This wasn’t your daddy’s Miami Vice. Out went the show’s pastels and neon, the shoulder pads and leather holsters. Mann replaced those in the film with shadows and grit, new-age surveillance tech, and sniper rifles that can and do blow a man’s arm off.View image in fullscreenFoxx and Farrell don’t share the buddy cop banter of the original.Photograph: Frank Connor/UniversalThis exchange proved jarring for some in 2006. After all, the Miami Vice TV series – on which Mann was an executive producer and show runner – tapped into the zeitgeist so successfully that it had been era-defining. But now, with two decades’ distance from the film’s release, it’s easier to appreciate that Mann made his Miami Vice movie as much a capsule of its time as the TV series was of the Reagan 80s.It’s not just the flip phones and Linkin Park on the soundtrack that mark the film out as a product of its time. Miami Vice 2006 blasts offin medias resand never spares any time for the kind of buddy cop banter that the show dealt in, while an international drugs trafficking plot has the film spend as much time out in the world – in Haiti, Paraguay, Cuba – as it does in Vice City. It’s Miami Vice for an edgier, more uncompromising, more global post-9/11 world.That grittier aesthetic is also evident in the film’s fuzzy night-time shots and almost confrontationally detailed human faces – a result of Mann’s decision to shoot the movie with nascent HD cameras. When the film was released, that distinctly digital aesthetic that Mann conjured for his Miami Vice reboot was startling: like cinema with the glamour scrubbed away.What appeared shockingly new back then, though, looks miraculous today. There are land, sea and air action spectacles captured with seemingly infinite depth of field, lightning-lashed nocturnal cityscapes that are as clear as though they were being seen with the naked eye, and vehicles, people and places all captured in high-definition detail. It can seem like you are experiencing the film – feeling the characters’ emotions, sensing their environments, tasting their mojitos. The effect is intoxicating.View image in fullscreenGong Li as cartel middle manager Isabella.Photograph: RGR Collection/AlamyThere’s more about Miami Vice which can, admittedly, take a bit longer to process. This is a popcorn flick with at-times impenetrable jargon for dialogue, with lines like “Who runs 250 Mercs off a deep-V hull?” serving only to muddle an otherwise stock narco conspiracy plot. It’s an action thriller with shades of Terrence Malick, where a charged scene can suddenly be interrupted by Farrell’s troubled Lothario staring dreamily off into the endless blue of the Atlantic. It’s also a film that’s as serious as the plague, but one which features a sex scene between Crockett and cartel middle manager Isabella (Gong Li) that’s soundtracked by drawling 00s soft rock and which climaxes with Isabella shedding a single tear, implying Crockett’s so good at it that he can cause women to weep.Shin Kamen Rider: who wouldn’t want to watch an action flick about a grasshopper-man hybrid?Read moreA film like that – and there are no other films like that – will always be too kooky for some. Perhaps the recently announcedMiami Vice ‘85– a big screen reboot inspired by the series’ first season and directed by Top Gun: Maverick’s Joseph Kosinski – will be the kind of film that was expected back in 2006: something more straightforwardly entertaining, a more faithful riff on the beloved 80s show. But such is the cult now for Mann’s unique, idiosyncratic fusion of blockbuster and art film that when Miami Vice ’85 comes around in 2028, audiences may well ask: “Why can’t this be more like Miami Vice 2006?”Miami Vice is available to stream via Binge, Foxtel and Netflix in Australia; via Netflix in the UK; and via Amazon Prime in the US. It’s also available to rent via Apple TV.
