title: Yeehaw! Bring on the tap-dancing cowgirls! How the Edinburgh Military Tattoo suddenly got cool | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: With its marching bands, billowing flags and precision drills, the Tattoo has never exactly been cutting edge. But now an experimental theatre-maker has been let loose on it …
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: With its marching bands, billowing flags and precision drills, the Tattoo has never exactly been cutting edge. But now an experimental theatre-maker has been let loose on it …
Content: Hoedown at the castle … tap-dancers in action on opening night.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenHoedown at the castle … tap-dancers in action on opening night.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026Yeehaw! Bring on the tap-dancing cowgirls! How the Edinburgh Military Tattoo suddenly got coolWith its marching bands, billowing flags and precision drills, the Tattoo has never exactly been cutting edge. But now an experimental theatre-maker has been let loose on it …Mark FisherTue 11 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDusk has settled onEdinburghCastle and now a laser beam is scribbling a route across its ramparts and high into the sky. The voice of actor Richard Rankin is talking solemnly about lonely soldiers answering a call, while a ferocious light rises in the gatehouse. Out of it emerge scores of drummers and pipers, their sound both melodic and awe-inspiring. They crisscross the esplanade to the stirring lament of The Skye Boat Song.This is the Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo, an event often overlooked amid the festival cacophony – and yet its popularity eclipses any other event in the city. Last year, it played to 230,000 and raised £1.5m for charity. Like an outsize variety show, it is a formidable spectacle: fireworks, projections, flags dragged over the audience and a soundtrack that ranges from Carmen to Star Wars.double quotation markIt’s a living, breathing thing that speaks to the momentI speak to Susan from Aberdeen who is here with her daughter for the third year in a row. They love the highland dancing. “The atmosphere is amazing,” she says, delighted to be back. From New Zealand, Francesca tells me she is staying with family in Glasgow and is here for the night. “It’s a bucket-list item,” she says. “I was going to go when it toured to Auckland in February but I was told I had to see the original one first.”View image in fullscreenElectric dreams … the New Zealand army band at the castle.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianStaff Sgt Ross Yorkstone, drum major with the New Zealand army band, is equally pleased to be here. Performing for the sixth year, he can think of no equivalent. “The closest would be the Basel Tattoo but it’s nowhere near as big as this,” he says. “We always come here with our top A-game.”On a hot summer afternoon, I sit down with Alan Lane, the creative director, in West Princes Street Gardens to talk about the event’s phenomenal appeal. Our meeting place is deliberate: next to us is a statue of a kilted soldier with a rifle across his knees. He is the figure voiced by Rankin in A Call to Gather, the name of this year’s Tattoo show, and is looking poignantly towards the Scottish National War Memorial high above us in the castle grounds. Known as The Call 1914, the memorial is a tribute to the American expats who came to fight in the first world war. It is Lane’s inspiration. “It’s a celebration of those who will lend a hand,” he says. “If you’re my friend, I’m going to come when you call.”But which Alan Lane am I talking to? There seem to be two. One is the kind of man you would expect to be commanding a military display: a reservist who trained at Sandhurst as an officer in the Royal Engineers and who, as a wide-eyed 18-year-old, set his heart on directing the Tattoo. He is 1.9 metres tall (6ft 3in) and holds himself with a soldier’s bearing.View image in fullscreen‘I was obnoxiously leftwing’ … Alan Lane, who evacuated Sheffield Crucible as part of a show.Photograph: Duncan McGlynnThe other Alan Lane is more surprising. A lifelong member of the Labour party, he is the founding artistic director of Slung Low, the Leeds-based theatre company with a speciality in large-scale community events. He was behind Flood, a four-part epic with a cast of 58 for Hull, UK City of Culture, andCamelot: The Shining City, a dystopian fantasy in which the audience was evacuated from the Sheffield Crucible as part of the show.This Lane set up a community college on a doubledecker bus, took charge of a working men’s club and, for a year during the pandemic, coordinated afree food delivery service in Holbeck and Beestonin Leeds. He is a vegetarian who today has shown up in pink shorts. “Having run a food bank and working men’s club, there aren’t many theatre directors who are more obnoxiously leftwing than I was,” he laughs, keeping an eye on Bolt, his spaniel, who has come along for the walk.You can understand why Lane is not keen on singular thinking. If others see a contradiction in his background, he does not. “The beach commanders on D-day were part of the Labour cabinet five years later,” he says. “I don’t get how it isn’t leftwing to believe we need a military and that there is some honour in that.”double quotation markThis year, we’ve got the Americans and the Qataris in a show – that’s not by accidentStill, the organisation took some adjusting to. After his appointment in April 2024, he was kitted out with tweed, tartan and ties. He is not joking when he says that the Tattoo has a crisis meeting when attendance for the 8,800-capacity show drops below 96% – a figure that any arts company could only dream of. “But actually what I’ve found is, fundamentally, we’re not that different,” he says. And anyway, for Lane differences are there to be bridged. “Where that gets us to in this year’s Tattoo is a sharing of culture in order to understand each other,” he says. “This year, we’ve got the Americans and the Qataris in a show – that’s not by accident.”View image in fullscreenWords of wisdom … backdrop to the performance space.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianThe juxtaposition is plain to see. The Qatar Police Academy Band and Drill Team, with its sky-blue tunics, strident song and Islamic projections, comes on straight after a section called Bright Brave World in which US culture is represented by the Jackson 5, country music and tap-dancing cowgirls. Slogans of the nation’s founding principles are splashed across the castle walls: “All men are created equal”, “A new nation conceived in liberty”, “The pursuit of happiness”.Launched in 1950, the Tattoo established elements that remain to this day. There will always be marching bands and traditional songs, and they could not do without the lone piper, the solitary player on the ramparts who casts a spine-tingling hush across the audience.But every year, two-thirds of the event is created anew by the organisation’s own dancers and musicians – 133 of them, one of the largest amateur companies in the country. “In the same way you wouldn’t go: ‘Oh no, I’ve seen Scottish Ballet,’ you’d say: ‘What are they doing this year?’” says Lane. “They’re turning those skills and talents to a different story.”View image in fullscreenThe Qatar Police Academy Band and Drill Team at Edinburgh Castle.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianIf he is trying to capture the moment, this is nothing new. In 1962, the audience crowded on to the esplanade to dance to Chubby Checker’s Let’s Twist Again, a hit only a few months earlier. In 2022, theUS army Field Band brought hip-hop to the castle, with rappers Lamar Riddick and Nicholas Feemster taking to the mics for a cover of Clean Bandit’s Rather Be.“It’s a living, breathing thing that speaks to the moment,” says Lane. “The show has to have a specific creative intent at every moment. It’s not enough to say: ‘The New Zealand army band are coming – they’ll do their thing.’ There has to be something worth saying.”What, then, is worth saying in 2026? “People paying attention to each other’s cultures,” says Lane without hesitation. “This job involves me sitting with lots of military leaders telling me their plans for the next three or four years. All of them involve war. Notpreparingfor war – actual war. Looking five years out, every one of them says: ‘At that point, we are at war.’ This is a good time to be doing this show, where can we find common ground because they keep telling me war is coming.”View image in fullscreenLight fantastic … performers at the castle last week.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianBut what of those who see the Tattoo as acelebration of military might? Sensitivities feel especially acute this year, when the Tattoo, like the Edinburgh international festival, is marking the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence at the same time as the US is firing missiles at Iran. Is this really the best moment to bring on the US army Field Band performing the “best of Americana”?Magic tricks, Palestinian circus, and a ‘kinky Hamlet’: the must-see shows at 2026’s Edinburgh fringeRead more“The Tattoo doesn’t celebrate the military,” says Lane, unruffled by the suggestion. “I sit in meetings with people who wish it would do that, but it’s not our job. The Tattoo is unapologetically Scottish in its celebration of heritage. We genuinely love it. We’re zealots. But it doesn’t speak to militarism in those ways at all.”He continues: “The thing I’m sure of is: in times of difficulty, talk more, not less. The challenges for an American band to come here are real, and it would be very easy for them to decide they didn’t want to waste any political capital by coming. And it would be very easy for us not to invite them. I think we would be lesser for it because we would forget the great philosophical and poetic ideas of America. It’s brilliant to be reminded of them and to think: ‘Ah, this too shall pass.’”A Call to Gather, the Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo, is at Edinburgh Castle until 29 August. title: Mourinho review – if he didn’t want to open up, maybe he shouldn’t have starred in a docuseries… | Television | The Guardian
description: Football manager José Mourinho stars in a three-parter from the creators of Bros: After the Screaming Stops. Don’t expect it to be quite so entertaining…
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: Football manager José Mourinho stars in a three-parter from the creators of Bros: After the Screaming Stops. Don’t expect it to be quite so entertaining…
Content: José Mourinho, pictured in action in Mourinho.Photograph: NetflixView image in fullscreenJosé Mourinho, pictured in action in Mourinho.Photograph: NetflixTV reviewTelevisionReviewMourinho review – if he didn’t want to open up, maybe he shouldn’t have starred in a docuseries…Football manager José Mourinho stars in a three-parter from the creators of Bros: After the Screaming Stops. Don’t expect it to be quite so entertaining…Phil HarrisonTue 11 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmong his previous credits, the director of this mini-series Joe Pearlman can count the revelatory and hilarious 2018 film,Bros: After the Screaming Stops. That documentary worked brilliantly because its subjects seemed so sweetly but devastatingly lacking in discretion or self-awareness that everything they said landed like a line from a Christopher Guest parody. They couldn’t help themselves.In terms of a character study, storied football managerJosé Mourinhois a very different kettle of cold fish. Like the Goss twins, he takes himself very seriously indeed, but that’s pretty much where the similarities end. He’s something of a closed book. “You are pushing me to speak about myself,” he says, towards the end of the final part of this series. “And I don’t want to.” Which is fair enough but it does beg the question: why then, would you agree to be the subject of an in-depth three part documentary series?The answer, you suspect, has a lot to do with setting various records straight. Mourinho clearly feels he has been misunderstood and misrepresented. When he arrived in England, he self-applied the nickname The Special One. But, straight away, he bridles at the origins of this. “The Special One,” he claims, “is some special shit some guys in England thought up for me.” Mischievously, Pearlman then cuts directly to a clip of Mourinhodescribing himself thusat his first press conference as Chelsea manager. Although, to be pedantic (which Mourinho has every intention of being), he does say “Aspecial one”. This is a distinction he insists upon: it seems typical of a man who wants to establish his own narrative; have his cake and eat it.Many would argue that the next couple of hours of his story proves he has earned the right to do exactly that. For years, Mourinho was a fearsomely effective manager. In 2004, he won the Champions League from nowhere with FC Porto. His first spell at Chelsea was a tale of almost uninterrupted glory (although there might usefully have been a little more interrogation of both the sporting and moral implications of its bankrolling by Russian oligarch Roman Abramovich). While he was manager of Real Madrid, he single-handedly reversed the polarities of Spanish club football and won a frequentlyheated personal battle with then-Barcelona manager Pep Guardiola.The documentary doesn’t shy away from his frequently appalling behaviour along the way but nor does it ever quite get to the bottom of it. He seemingly relished battles with officials that were so acrimonious that his accusations against referee Anders Frisk led to Uefahaving to officially rule to clear him of any responsibilityfor Frisk’s subsequent resignation due to his family receiving threats from members of the public. His dealings with the media became the stuff of legend – he was paranoid, haughty and scornful. And he built teams in that image: sour, often spiteful, as difficult to like as they undeniably were to beat.Cultivating a siege mentality is an age-old tactic among managers of sports teams, but it’s fascinating to see how this works from the inside. Eventually, it becomes clear that being as insufferable as Mourinho on his worst days constitutes its own kind of courage. Because imagine if he failed? There was always a long way to fall. For a time, players responded. At various points, you’ll begin to tire of ex pros telling you how many walls they’d have run through for the gaffer – John Terry typically one-ups the rest of them by stating he’d have left the pitch “in a coffin” for Mourinho. The routine hyperbole of the beautiful game is embraced. Player after player claims that he created a family. But if these were families, they were frequently barely functional ones, without much staying power.For a while, this high wire act is gripping. But the patterns embodied by Mourinho’s managerial career soon become a little limiting for documentary purposes. He’s a manager of boom and bust; of diminishing returns. Why has he been unable to build anything more lasting? There’s plenty in Mourinho’s past that hints at vulnerability – his almost non-existent playing career clearly troubled him (“I still think I don’t belong to the tribe”), and he seems to carry an inferiority complex in relation to his father who was also a football coach – although a markedly less successful one. “I was so proud to be Mourinho’s son,” he says at one point. “He’s the opposite of me in that everybody loves him.”It’s almost certainly not Pearlman’s fault but these moments of confession; of vulnerability; of dropped guard don’t come quite often enough – or go quite deep enough – to make this film gripping to anyone beyond football aficionados. Mourinho freely admits that he doesn’t have much else in his life. We briefly meet his family for the first time about 15 minutes before the end of the concluding episode. “I know that they enjoy life much more without me,” he confesses.Like most prodigiously successful people, José Mourinho is clearly quite odd, and possibly, even now, as he prepares to take over once again at Real Madrid, slightly unfulfilled. You suspect he doesn’t want the world to see too much of this. Success is relative, in life, in football and in documentary making. Sometimes, it’s about the journey, not the arrival. One assumes that making a film about Bros was less exacting than this. It was probably a lot more fun too.Mourinho is on NetflixExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewJosé MourinhoDocumentaryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Ten Ways to Die Happy review – gameshow invites you to don a robe and treasure time | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Audience members are invited to examine what they will do with their lives in this earnest shared thought experiment
Author: Kate Wyver
Headline: Audience members are invited to examine what they will do with their lives in this earnest shared thought experiment
Content: Even if you are one of the chosen ones, the show’s pace remains fairly sedentary … Ten Ways to Die Happy.Photograph: Sisifo ProductionView image in fullscreenEven if you are one of the chosen ones, the show’s pace remains fairly sedentary … Ten Ways to Die Happy.Photograph: Sisifo ProductionEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewTen Ways to Die Happy review – gameshow invites you to don a robe and treasure timeUnderbelly, Bristo Square, EdinburghAudience members are invited to examine what they will do with their lives in this earnest shared thought experimentKate WyverTue 11 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 15.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you could hold the years of your life in your hands like coins, would you choose to spend them differently? This is the thoughtful, earnest tone of Ten Ways to Die Happy, an existential but somewhat formulaic Italian production (performed here in English) created by Emanuele Aldrovandi and Jacopo Giacomoni. In this gentle gameshow, we are asked not just to consider how we would use the finite time we have, but to put this thought experiment into practice.Eight people are plucked at random from the audience. My number is called, so I don a white robe, choose a new name for my new life, and take a seat on stage. Perla Ambrosini is our ethereal host, standing in fabric armour in a shallow pool of water. Each of us has a tray of flowers that we throw into the pool, every plastic bud representing the “energy” available to invest in work, art and family. Once our supply is up, we’re dead.Ambrosini efficiently guides us across the years, Dungeon Master-like, through fumbling sex, consuming grief and boring jobs. Over the course of our lives, we control little counters to mark our levels of happiness. “The aim of the game,” Ambrosini tells us, “is to die happy.”Spin Cycle review – romcom hits full speed as couple air their dirty laundryRead moreThere’s no doubt the show induces more of an elevated heart-rate if you’re on the top table – though there are opportunities for broader audience participation. But even if you are one of the chosen ones, the show’s pace remains fairly sedentary.Some of the interaction is cringe, and while there’s never a sense that you’ll say something wrong, neither is there ever a truly difficult dilemma, nor a decision that feels more poignant than if you were casually playing the board game Catan. While the performance is conducted with an intense sense of ceremony, the drama of the actual game would be improved by greater stakes. But in its blunt reflections and visual confrontations, Ten Ways to Die Happy is a welcome reminder that we should all make the most of the time we have.AtUnderbelly, Bristo Square, Edinburgh, until 31 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalFestivalsTheatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Spin Cycle review – romcom hits full speed as couple air their dirty laundry | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: There is crackling chemistry between Zofia Zerphy and Rhiannon Bell while their washing gets done but this play remains a puzzle
Author: Kate Wyver
Headline: There is crackling chemistry between Zofia Zerphy and Rhiannon Bell while their washing gets done but this play remains a puzzle
Content: ‘How will you use your 50 minutes?’ … Zofia Zerphy, left, and Rhiannon Bell.Photograph: Sofia Salazar StuderView image in fullscreen‘How will you use your 50 minutes?’ … Zofia Zerphy, left, and Rhiannon Bell.Photograph: Sofia Salazar StuderEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewSpin Cycle review – romcom hits full speed as couple air their dirty laundryUnderbelly Bristo Square, EdinburghThere is crackling chemistry between Zofia Zerphy and Rhiannon Bell while their washing gets done but this play remains a puzzleKate WyverTue 11 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 14.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNames go missing like lost socks in this laundry-based, amnesia-laced romcom. With crackling chemistry but a holey structure, Zofia Zerphy’s Offie award-winning story of a queer meet-cute asks what you hold on to once a relationship is over, and whether it’s ever better to forget the mistakes you both made.In the liminal space of a launderette, with their encounter framed by a washing machine’s 50-minute timer, Kitt (Zerphy) and Noel (Rhiannon Bell) talk over each other at full speed. “How will you use your 50 minutes?” Kitt asks. Their connection is easy and instant as they use them to bicker and flirt, discussing art, exes and the correct laundry tabs to use. Kitt is the rich, confident American, more privileged than Noel, the messy, Northern Irish, non-binary stranger. Except they don’t feel like strangers. With Bethan Rose’s direction making the most of the small stage, the pair lean close over the whirring machines, unpacking the ways they’ve been shaped by past relationships, and admitting they’ve both dated someone very like the other. In fact, they could swear they’ve met before.Roleplay review – Fleabag producer scores again with one woman’s life as a ‘slutfluencer’Read moreAs memories are tumbled up, this breezy romcom devolves into an airing of dirty laundry. Occasionally slipping into shouting matches, the story sings when they admit their feelings slowly, almost side-on, like Noel inspecting Kitt as if she’s one of their sculptures, tracing a tingling line from wrist to shoulder on her skin.The memory-loss set-up creates a thrilling puzzle, but it’s never pieced together. No explanation is given for the selective memories that build the story, so we have no idea why one remembers something when the other doesn’t, or what prompts that memory to fade. Without this structural scaffolding, the mystery loses its momentum. The attraction between Kitt and Noel is evident. We just need to understand the rules of their memory-muddled world to feel our 50 minutes is well spent.AtUnderbelly, Bristo Square, Edinburgh, until 31 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalFestivalsTheatreComedy (Stage)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Harriet Dyer: Easily Distra … review – how to sell a single shoe on eBay and other stories | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: A comic on the verge of the big time offers one ‘very silly hour’ around the highways and byways of her madcap life
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: A comic on the verge of the big time offers one ‘very silly hour’ around the highways and byways of her madcap life
Content: Semaphores punchlines with windmilling physicality … Harriet Dyer.Photograph: Matt StrongeView image in fullscreenSemaphores punchlines with windmilling physicality … Harriet Dyer.Photograph: Matt StrongeEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewHarriet Dyer: Easily Distra … review – how to sell a single shoe on eBay and other storiesMonkey Barrel, EdinburghA comic on the verge of the big time offers a ‘very silly hour’ around the highways and byways of her lifeBrian LoganTue 11 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 10.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAformer winner of the Sean Lock awardfor comic originality, Harriet Dyer richly delivers on that promise of oddity in her latest show, Easily Distra … As its title suggests, you can shelve any expectation of coherence or narrative consistency here: it’s 55 minutes of switch-backing reminiscence, as Dyer meanders across the landscape of her peripatetic life. From Cornwall to Birmingham to Bristol, our scatty host moves and moves on, and yet eccentric incident follows her everywhere. The real-world Harriet may justifiably be nonplussed by this (in quite the backhanded compliment, an old school friend tells her she’s not changed at all since she was four years old) – but no doubt it’s a gift to her comedy.Not that her comedy needs gifts: an increasingly familiar TV face, she’s teetering on the verge of the big time. But here in a cave in Edinburgh, it’s hard to imagine a more marginal figure, a tattooed West Country screwball rummaging her props bag for DIY comedy accoutrements, semaphoring punchlines with a windmilling physicality and oral SFX. Previous fringe shows, including 2022’s acclaimedTrigger Warning, have addressed more significant subject matter, but this one is “a very silly hour indeed”, in her own estimation, as our host fantasises about growing feathers, accidentally sells a single shoe on eBay and memorialises the occasion when a seagull filched her beekeeping brother’s bratwurst.Cathy review – snappy comedy with a perfect role for Elaine C SmithRead moreThere’s material that contains within it the germ of several fringe shows, like the routine about her closeted gay dad, or another about her teenage enthusiasm for alcohol. While mental health is not the emphasis here of a performer whoopenly engages with that subject elsewhere, there are plenty of jokes whose battiness only barely conceals something more troubling – like the one about breaking her own arm to escape a dead-end job. Yikes. But quirky is persistently the top-note in Easily Distra …, and Dyer keeps things upbeat with consistently strong gags (see the one about the roundabout, or the “al dente” variety of traffic accident) and arresting anecdotes. It adds up to nothing more, nor less, than a divertingly dotty autobiographical standup hour.AtMonkey Barrel, Edinburgh,until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Edinburgh festivalFestivalsComedy (Culture)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Spotify to distinguish AI artists from real people – and stop recommending them | Spotify | The Guardian
description: Music streaming platform creates ‘AI persona’ label that will appear on profiles and track listings in crackdown on fake performers
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Music streaming platform creates ‘AI persona’ label that will appear on profiles and track listings in crackdown on fake performers
Content: AI-generated artists will be labelled as an ‘AI persona’ on their profile, in search and in track listings.Illustration: Spotify UKView image in fullscreenAI-generated artists will be labelled as an ‘AI persona’ on their profile, in search and in track listings.Illustration: Spotify UKSpotifySpotify to distinguish AI artists from real people – and stop recommending themMusic streaming platform creates ‘AI persona’ label that will appear on profiles and track listings in crackdown on fake performersDan MilmoGlobal technology editorTue 11 Aug 2026 09.40 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 17.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSpotify is to label AI artists and exclude them from algorithm recommendations as part of a crackdown on fake performers.The world’s largest music streaming platform is creating a label for AI-generated artist identities called “AI personas” that will appear on the artist profile and on track listings on playlists.It means that from September AI-generated artists such as theVelvet Sundownwill carry the persona label and will be blocked from personalised recommendations by default. The aim is to differentiate these deepfake artists from real performers who might lose out on streams to artificial rivals.Spotify said: “True artist-fan connection can only be built on a foundation of trust and authenticity. In music, that means listeners need to be able to trust that the artist behind the music is who they say they are. That’s more essential than ever in the age of generative AI.”Last year Spotify revealed it had removed 75m spam tracks from its platform over a 12-month period as AI tools created a flood of fake music. Spotify’s legitimate catalogue stands at 100m tracks.Spotify will allow music creators to reveal if their identities are AI-created – and will then label them as an AI persona – but it will not rely on self-disclosure alone. The company said it would use human review and AI investigative tools to determine if artists were fake. Although the new rule technically applies to AI “identities”, Spotify says AI-generated profiles are invariably a front for AI-made tracks as well.The company said: “Listeners have been clear in telling us that they don’t like seeing an artist profile that seems human, only to find out that the persona is AI-generated.”Last year there was debate about the origins of the Velvet Sundown – a 70s-style US rock band – before the band’s social media channels confirmed the subterfuge. A statement described the group as an AI creation that was “somewhere in between” human and machine.The Velvet Sundown has 117,000 monthly listeners on Spotify but its page has no clear AI labelling, although the artist profile describes the four-piece as a “synthetic music project”.In January there was further discussion about Sienna Rose, a soul singer who entered Spotify’s viral top 50 but did not appear to be real, having never played a gig or released any videos despite releasing a prolific burst of material over a 10-week period. The Spotify profile for Rose, who has more than half a million monthly listeners, does not clarify whether she is AI or not.Explore more on these topicsSpotifyAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: Juilliard Orch/Royal Academy Symphony Orch / Salonen/Frang review – student players let rip, eventually | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: Esa-Pekka Salonen led an orchestra of players from London’s Royal Academy of Music and New York’s Juilliard School through 20th-century classics with Vilde Frang the electrifying soloist in Berg’s Violin Concerto
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: Esa-Pekka Salonen led an orchestra of players from London’s Royal Academy of Music and New York’s Juilliard School through 20th-century classics with Vilde Frang the electrifying soloist in Berg’s Violin Concerto
Content: Taking no prisoners … Salonen conducts the Royal Academy and Juilliard students.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouView image in fullscreenTaking no prisoners … Salonen conducts the Royal Academy and Juilliard students.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouProms 2026ReviewJuilliard Orch/Royal Academy Symphony Orch / Salonen/Frang review – student players let rip, eventuallyRoyal Albert Hall, LondonEsa-Pekka Salonen led an orchestra of players from London’s Royal Academy of Music and New York’s Juilliard School through 20th-century classics with Vilde Frang the electrifying soloist in Berg’s Violin ConcertoErica JealTue 11 Aug 2026 09.13 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 10.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHot on the heels of the National Youth Orchestra’s Prom, here was another outstanding student ensemble: an orchestra recruited half-and-half from London’sRoyal Academy of Musicand New York’sJuilliard School, brought together byan exchange schemefunded by the RAM alumnus Elton John.Esa-Pekka Salonentook no prisoners as he whipped the players through three great 20th-century works.They tore smartly into the start of Stravinsky’s Symphony in Three Movements, an exacting work requiring pinpoint-precise playing, which it mostly received. It felt as though Salonen was working hard to maintain that precision, though, and the performance didn’t quite achieve the buoyancy that would have let the music dance. Here and elsewhere in the programme, some of the music’s bright colours felt a little muted. Perhaps, for all Salonen’s guidance, this is one area in which there is no substitute for years of experience – in the ability to play to a venue and, for the wind and brass principals in particular, to fill a hall of this size not only with the instrument’s sound but with its character.View image in fullscreenSeamless … Vilde Frang.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouThe slow waltz in the first movement of Berg’s Violin Concerto had its own momentum thanks partly to the rapport between the orchestra andVilde Frang, who made the solo violin’s orations sing seamlessly, occasionally harshening her tone to soulful effect. The second movement’s clarinet chorale was played with touching softness and simplicity. Frang then led the strings, section by section, into the climactic elegy, slowly turning 360 degrees to face each player as she did so: one soloist morphing, movingly, into a whole body.There was more electrifyingly soft playing at the start of Bartók’s Concerto for Orchestra, the string tremolos little more than a disturbance in the air. This work was where the orchestra turned the dial up and came into its own: the strings full-bodied, the wind characterful, especially in the little duets of the second movement, the brass and percussion dynamic. The encore was the Galop from Stravinsky’s Suite No 2, and it was as if this tongue-in-cheek piece finally gave the players permission to let rip – to find the larger-than-life character lacking earlier on.Available on BBC Soundsuntil 12 October. The Promscontinue until 12 September.Explore more on these topicsProms 2026Classical musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: I Give You My Silence by Mario Vargas Llosa review – Nobel laureate’s final novel is a love letter to Peru | Books | The Guardian
description: This fascinating, eccentric book becomes a quirky primer on Peruvian music and culture
Author: Marcel Theroux
Headline: This fascinating, eccentric book becomes a quirky primer on Peruvian music and culture
Content: Striking a chord … Mario Vargas Llosa.Photograph: Leonardo CendamoView image in fullscreenStriking a chord … Mario Vargas Llosa.Photograph: Leonardo CendamoBook of the dayBooksReviewI Give You My Silence by Mario Vargas Llosa review – Nobel laureate’s final novel is a love letter to PeruThis fascinating, eccentric book becomes a quirky primer on Peruvian music and cultureMarcel TherouxTue 11 Aug 2026 06.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen I Give You My Silence was published in Spanish in 2023 its author, the Peruvian Nobel laureateMario Vargas Llosa, rightly predicted that it would be his final novel. He died last year at the age of 89. I Give You My Silence may have been completed with the spectre of death approaching, but there is nothing morbid about this book, which is an eccentric love letter to Vargas Llosa’s native country and, in particular, its music.The novel’s quixotic hero is a music journalist called Toño Azpilcueta. Toño always hoped to be a professor of Peruvian music, but as the novel opens, he’s earning a meagre living teaching at a girls’ school and writing articles for specialist magazines. Luckily, he’s subsidised by his longsuffering wife, Matilde. Toño is a recognisable type: the impecunious cultural obsessive. If he were British, he would be fanatical about free jazz, or some obscure Delta bluesman. But this is Peru and Toño’s particular infatuation is thevals,a Peruvian musical style that fuses the European waltz with African and indigenous Latin American traditions.One evening, Toño gets an invitation to see an unknown guitarist called Lalo Molfino, who blows him away with his incredible virtuosity. Before Toño has time to digest the musician’s brilliance, he learns of his sudden death. With the help of a small gift of money from a friend, Toño embarks on a project to write a biography of Molfino. “This book would be an homage to his talent, but also much more: he would at last put to paper those ideas about the Peruvianvalshe had entertained so often.”Toño’s Big Idea is that thevalsis going to save Peru, and possibly humanity. Its blended heritage, he explains, points a way past the trauma that colonialism, racism, dictatorship and terrorism have inflicted on his country. Toño’s quest to write the book involves sleuthing, research, interviews, a journey along Peru’s Pacific coast to Molfino’s birthplace, and battles with his own demons – in particular, a phobia about rats.Coming to this book with, I think, the median British knowledge of Peru (Machu Picchu, the Shining Path, ceviche, Paddington Bear), it took me a moment to orient myself. I knew nothing about the country’s music and I didn’t realise that Cecilia Barraza, an important recurring character, is a real-life Peruvian singer. (It’s a bit like having Patti Smith turn up in a novel.) Nor did I clock to begin with that the novel is really two books in one. The odd-numbered chapters are a third-person account of Toño’s attempt to research and write the biography. Most of the even-numbered chapters are excerpts from the final work, I Give You My Silence. These end up forming a quirky primer on Peruvian music and culture. It includes essays on the history of thevals; the lives of the musicians who created it; thecajon, a distinctive Peruvian percussion instrument; Spanish as a regional lingua franca; andhuachafería, a concept that Toño sees as a key part of Peru’s identity. Huachaferíaholds huge significance for both Toño and Vargas Llosa. The novel’s translator, Adrian Nathan West, tells us in a helpful afterword that “dictionaries typically define it aspretension”.Toño is much more effusive: “Huachaferíacan be brilliant, but it is rarely intelligent: it is intuitive, verbose, solemn, melodic, imaginative and above all maudlin.”double quotation markGentle, impractical dreamers, Vargas Llosa seems to be saying, bring their own kind of changes into the worldThis is, in fact, a perfect description of the book that Toño himself is writing, which includes the grandiose and impossible claim that “this book you hold in your hands, reader, will be the starting point of a true revolution that will pull our Peru up from poverty and sorrow, restoring its glory and its creativity, making it a place where all are truly equal and putting an end to the sad divisions of its people”.Toño’s mission is clearly bonkers, but he approaches it with a heroic single-mindedness that wins the reader over. And the form the novel takes allows Vargas Llosa to have his cake and eat it too: giving Toño space to explore his ideas in detail, while simultaneously having fun pointing out how overheated they are.For instance, one of Toño’s chapters tells the story of a love affair between Toni Lagarde and Lala Solórzano, a white man from a middle-class neighbourhood and a poor black woman from a rough one. Thanks to a shared interest in music, they meet, fall in love and get married. For Toño the polemicist, it’s proof of the redemptive power of thevals. But Toni and Lala reappear through the novel as he works on his book, gently pushing back at Toño’s efforts to make them emblematic of anything. “You’re the only ones who are free. And music opened your eyes. It made you two aware,” Toño tells them. “You’ve got a theory there, but there are lots of theories,” is Toni’s tactful answer. In another chapter, a psychiatrist who’s helping Toño deal with his rat phobia gives his book a much more savage assessment, calling it “a pointless, incoherent mass of undeveloped ideas”.Vargas Llosa’s own implied verdict on Toño’s idiosyncratic attempt to save the world by writing a book about Peruvian music is more nuanced and tender. Vargas Llosa, of course, shared his central character’s idealism. At the time the novel takes place, in the early 1990s, Vargas Llosa was also on a failed mission to save Peru, running unsuccessfully to become his country’s president. And just as Toño sees something poignant and important in the maligned quality ofhuachafería,Vargas Llosa finds heroism in his unworldly protagonist.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGentle, impractical dreamers like Toño, he seems to be saying, bring their own kind of changes into the world. One small proof of this is that by the novel’s end, I had followed Toño up the Pacific coast of Peru on Google Maps to the tiny settlement of Puerto Etén, tried to find a recipe for Lala’s quince marmalade online, made avalsplaylist on Spotify and searched the prices of return flights to Lima. If I ever make it there, I’ll be sure to pack this fascinating and engaging book.I Give You My Silence by Maria Vargas Llosa, translated by Adrian Nathan West, is published by Faber (£20). title: You Won’t Get Free of It by Rachel Aviv review – a subtle study of the mother-daughter bond | Books | The Guardian
description: The most complex of female relationships is thrown into sharp relief in this moving series of essays
Author: Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Headline: The most complex of female relationships is thrown into sharp relief in this moving series of essays
Content: Rachel Aviv.Photograph: Rose Lichter-MarckView image in fullscreenRachel Aviv.Photograph: Rose Lichter-MarckBooksReviewYou Won’t Get Free of It by Rachel Aviv review – a subtle study of the mother-daughter bondThe most complex of female relationships is thrown into sharp relief in this moving series of essaysRhiannon Lucy CosslettTue 11 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRachel Aviv has a profound interest in the vagaries of human psychology: Strangers to Ourselves, her last book, profiled five people whose psychiatric states resisted straightforward explanation, testing the limits of the mental health system. A Pulitzer finalist, Aviv has become known for rigorous, penetrating journalism that is as empathic as it is insightful. Now comes You Won’t Get Free of It, six stories of mothers and daughters, all originally published in the New Yorker.Madness runs through this book, too, in the stories of Linda Bishop, a woman who, upon discharge from hospital after a psychotic break, holed up in an abandoned farmhouse and tried to subsist on apples alone, and of Mary, a woman whose delusions and paranoia were only seemingly cured as a side-effect of chemotherapy. It’s also there in the childhood memories of the psychologist Elizabeth Loftus – a professional court witness for those who have been accused of abuse, one of whom was Harvey Weinstein. Loftus’s mother was found drowned, perhaps as a result of suicide. In Aviv’s masterly profile, she teases out a conclusion that leaves you pondering the extent to which this memory expert can rely on her own recollections, and what that says about her particular line of work.Of the mother representing madness, Marguerite Duras said: “Our mothers always remain the strangest, craziest people we’ve ever met.” Yet there is psychological instability here on the part of daughters, too: Hannah Upp, whose story opens the collection, suffered from fugue states that would lead to her eventual disappearance. Aviv compassionately chronicles her mother’s desperate quest to find her.double quotation markAviv’s investigation into Munro’s failure to protect her daughter Andrea from abuse is the standout piece hereIn the preface, Aviv writes about her interest in the “hide and seek” dynamic of mother-daughter pairings, and indeed, each of these stories could be said to represent an acting out of that game. What is interesting is that Aviv, too, is a player. “It was as if I had failed to see the drama on the mother’s side, too – her particular longings and humiliations and needs,” she writes, of her own journalism.Aviv admits to a previous “deficit of curiosity” about mothers. It is admirable how clear-eyed she is about these failures of imagination, which became apparent only after she herself became a mother. In Bishop’s case Aviv neglected to mention, or consider, the possible impact of a baby given up for adoption when Bishop was a young woman. “I had not even asked a follow-up question,” Aviv admits, and you can feel her embarrassment. She has gone back and remedied the “imbalance” for the purposes of this collection, but the discussion itself prompts a fascinating question: to what extent does a woman’s motherhood – or lack thereof – contribute to her perspective as a writer?It is not a question with an easy answer, not least in the case of novelist Alice Munro. Aviv’s investigation into Munro’s utter failure to protect her daughter, Andrea, from the abuse of her partner, Gerry, is the standout piece here. While it is claimedMunro knew of the abuse, was able to make reference to it in her art (Aviv’s tracing of it through Munro’s writing is meticulous), she chose not to act. That choice – the cowardice of it – and its lifelong repercussions for her daughters may never have come fully to light were it not for the persistence of several journalists, Aviv included. Munro emerges a pathetic figure; I have been unable to read her since.However our mothers behave, the fact is we will never truly know them. Aviv writes, not entirely comfortably, of how she is essentially living out her own mother’s dream career. The editorial comments she leaves on Aviv’s work – such as a note about caring for a suicidal friend on an article about mental illness – constitute for her daughter a “chronic delusion of reference”. It’s a neat theory – but as a writer whose mother sometimes gives similarly self-reflective feedback, I found myself wondering if what we have here is simply a mother’s insistence that she was, and remains, a person, if her daughter would only care to look.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories.
