title: Never Had a Chance review – a slice of gritty British Asian life with a side of drug dealing and addiction | Movies | The Guardian
description: Two likely lads in their 20s deal with problematic lives that dramatically intersect in this persuasive London drama
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: Two likely lads in their 20s deal with problematic lives that dramatically intersect in this persuasive London drama
Content: ‘True to its milieu’ … Never Had a ChancePhotograph: PRView image in fullscreen‘True to its milieu’ … Never Had a ChancePhotograph: PRMoviesReviewNever Had a Chance review – a slice of gritty British Asian life with a side of drug dealing and addictionTwo likely lads in their 20s deal with problematic lives that dramatically intersect in this persuasive London dramaLeslie FelperinTue 11 Aug 2026 08.55 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 08.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis gritty crime drama unfolds entirely within the Punjabi community in London’s Hounslow district, a plausible demographic situation in which white people are so peripheral to the story that they are little more than extras. In fact watching this well-crafted, if somewhat melodramatic, debut for director Jazz Bhalla makes one wonder why there aren’t more films made in the UK with entirely British Asian casts. Here, it doesn’t makes the film better or worse, but it certainly feels realistic and true to its milieu.The story revolves around two best friends in their 20s, Ravi (Amar Chaggar) and Jay (Jayant Singh), likely lads who spend a lot of time hanging out, getting high or drunk and ending nearly every sentence with the word “bro”. On the face of it, Jay seems like the one with a more stable situation at home, living with his middle-class parents; while Ravi, who has a criminal record due to a drug bust, lives in a bedsit and is estranged from his mother ever since his father died and she remarried, much to the chagrin of his bossy older sister (Parvinder Shergill). But Ravi manages to get a job working for a building supply merchant, which compels him to start waking up at dawn and considering the downside of always being hung over. Plus, he might be in with a chance with pretty fast-food vendor Sukhi (Tina Sharma), an ambitious young woman keen to get away from her alcoholic father and drug-dealing brother.It gradually becomes clear that, for all his charm and chat, Jay isn’t all that put together either. For starters, he has a growing gambling addiction, which isn’t helped when he gets a wodge of cocaine to sell for another drug dealer and starts getting high on a supply that isn’t really his at all. It’s not hard to see how all these dramatic freight trains might converge into one big conflagration of bad choices and worse luck, and that overdetermination is something of a flaw here.But Bhalla, who has previously worked mostly as a gaffer on other films, draws solid performances out of his cast, and the package as a whole is persuasive throughout, never more so than when it is evoking the faintly toxic yet jovial world of men in strip-lit social clubs, shooting pool and trash-talking one another just to pass the time – even though, to paraphrase Samuel Beckett, it would have passed anyway.Never Had a Chance is in UK cinemas from 14 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmCrime filmsDrama filmsLondonreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Momo and the Time Thieves review – kids’ fantasy jaunt sticks the boot into capitalism | Movies | The Guardian
description: This new adaptation of Michael Ende’s 1973 fantasy novel contains some neat parables for our digitally nihilistic age, but even a mystical tortoise can’t save it it from monotony
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: This new adaptation of Michael Ende’s 1973 fantasy novel contains some neat parables for our digitally nihilistic age, but even a mystical tortoise can’t save it it from monotony
Content: One urchin to save them all … Momo and the Time Thieves.Photograph: Constantin FilmView image in fullscreenOne urchin to save them all … Momo and the Time Thieves.Photograph: Constantin FilmMoviesReviewMomo and the Time Thieves review – kids’ fantasy jaunt sticks the boot into capitalismThis new adaptation of Michael Ende’s 1973 novel contains some neat parables for our digitally nihilistic age, but even a mystical tortoise can’t save it it from monotonyLeslie FelperinTue 11 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 06.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMomo – the 1973 fantasy novel by German author Michael Ende, who also wrote The Neverending Story – has been adapted in live and animated forms before, in 1986 and 2001. This latest version, too, is ostensibly a live-action film – but it’s been made with so many visual effects it might as well have been a cartoon. Still, the residual human element represented by the cast feels necessary, given the story is about the dangers of letting capitalism suck away our ability to enjoy the moment.Over the years, readers have posited all kinds of metaphorical interpretations of the plot, which involves a world where grey beings arrive and con everyone into literally “banking” their time, so as to have it all to themselves. Only the urchin Momo, here played by teen actor Alexa Goodall (whose gorgeous supernova of ginger curls is practically another character in the film), can save the world.For this iteration of the Momo-verse, the greys suck not on the time-burning cigars of the book, but on vape-like gadgets that they huff voraciously, like Frank Booth in a fairytale remake of Blue Velvet. Their targets – the normal people of the vaguely Italianate, kitschy dream town where this all takes place – bank their time with smartwatch-style bracelets that come with apps, presumably in a dig at our device-obsessed, time-sucking culture. How lucky that this has found its way to release just as the international discourse about stopping children from having access to social media has come to a boil.That said, kids may be less thrilled by the idea of watching this than scrolling through TikTok; it’s a lot longer than your average cat meme and not quite as much fun. Director Christian Ditter’s script is thin on jokes, and the solution to all the story’s problems feels all too easily arrived at, via a deus ex machina setup with mystical flowers and a very fake-looking tortoise puppet with messages that magically appear on her shell.Martin Freemanseems to be somnambulating through it as the Oz-like hero, not having nearly as much fun as Claes Bang as the grey’s leader – cinema’s current favourite baddie for hire.Momo and the Time Thieves is in UK cinemas from 14 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmScience fiction and fantasy filmsFamily filmsFilm adaptationsMartin FreemanreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Nimrods review – Green Day’s early years inspire teenage kicks in amiable punk road movie  | Movies | The Guardian
description: San Francisco’s pop-punk pioneers Green Day loom large in this fun, puppyish film about a scrappy band desperate to meet their idols
Author: Laurence Phelan
Headline: San Francisco’s pop-punk pioneers Green Day loom large in this fun, puppyish film about a scrappy band desperate to meet their idols
Content: A lot of bounce … Nimrods.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyView image in fullscreenA lot of bounce … Nimrods.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyMoviesReviewNimrods review – Green Day’s early years inspire teenage kicks in amiable punk road movieSan Francisco’s pop-punk pioneers Green Day loom large in this fun, puppyish film about a scrappy band desperate to meet their idolsLaurence PhelanTue 11 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 04.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleInspired by their own youthful rowdy escapades – “our early days of driving around in a van, tired, hungry, out of gas, out of money, struggling, creating trouble” – here is an amiable road-movie comedy about, soundtracked by and briefly featuring Californian pop-punk stalwartsGreen Day. Like them, it is more pop than punk: a fundamentally sweet and puppyish teen comedy about dreaming big and following your heart, featuring three fundamentally decent, likable youths – for all that they indulge in some Superbad-style smutty banter, try to buy booze, steal the odd car, take magic mushrooms, skate, have green hair, get into mud fights and decline to tell their parents where they are going when they hit the road and head west from Kansas City to LA.Mason Thames, Kylr Coffman and Ryan Foust star as 17-year-olds Tommy, Fred and Chad – two jokers and a nerd – who make music together as Analog Dogs in Tommy’s garage. When they are pranked into thinking their ageing idols have heard their demo cassette and want Analog Dogs to open for Green Day at the Hollywood Palladium on New Year’s Eve, the boys have mere days in which to beg, steal or borrow a way of getting there. Along the way, they encounter assorted oddballs and supportive adults, enter a battle of the bands contest, meet a cute girl who is also in a band, and learn a bit about the true meaning and importance of friendship.The soundtrack – about 98% of which is by Green Day – is a bit one-note, but it’s got a lot of bounce. Likewise, the script is unsophisticated but enjoyably performed. The adult cast is spotted with comedy pros such as Fred Armisen and Bobby Lee, and there is a perfectly pitched turn as Tommy’s mom by Jenna Fischer from the US Office (and who is writer-director Lee Kirk’s wife). But it’s the teens who have to carry the weight of this film, and they are fun to hang out with for a couple of hours.Nimrods is in cinemas from 11 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmComedy filmsGreen DayPop and rockComedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Game of Thrones, Shakespearean? What fools these mortals be!  | Theatre | The Guardian
description: The Mad King may bring more dynastic disputes and dotty despots to the RSC – but a ‘mayhap’ or a riddling aphorism does not a Shakespeare play make
Author: Michael Billington
Headline: The Mad King may bring more dynastic disputes and dotty despots to the RSC – but a ‘mayhap’ or a riddling aphorism does not a Shakespeare play make
Content: Endless jousters … Game of Thrones: The Mad King.Photograph: Johan PerssonView image in fullscreenEndless jousters … Game of Thrones: The Mad King.Photograph: Johan PerssonTheatreGame of Thrones, Shakespearean? What fools these mortals be!Michael BillingtonThe Mad King may bring more dynastic disputes and dotty despots to the RSC – but a ‘mayhap’ or a riddling aphorism does not a Shakespeare play makeTue 11 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTShareAs a latecomer toGame of Thrones, I am struck by how many people tell me it is “very Shakespearean”. It is as if they need to justify its heady escapism and heavy reliance on bonking and brutality. But its debt to the Bard – apart from the rivalry between the houses of Lannister and Stark – rests mainly on the casting. Watching the first 11 episodes, I noticed four Lears past and to come (Julian Glover, David Bradley, Oliver Ford-Davies and Roger Allam), a Macbeth (Sean Bean), a Hamlet and Henry V (Iain Glen) and a Cassius (Michelle Fairley) among many others.Because it is presented by the Royal Shakespeare Company and staged by Dominic Cooke, who memorably directedThe Hollow Crownon television, we shall doubtless hear the same arguments aboutGame of Thrones: The Mad Kingat Stratford. But, although there are frequent nods to Shakespeare, they totally lack the resonance of the original. Our first sight of Michael Shaeffer’s King Aerys with a white beard, a leafy crown and no shoes almost screams “Lear on the heath”. But where Lear gradually declines into insanity (“O fool I shall go mad”) and comes out the other side, Shaeffer’s Aerys is a dotty despot from start to finish. The use of tournaments to settle dynastic disputes also reminds us of the opening of Richard II – but where that event is aborted and ultimately causes the king’s downfall, here the image of embattled jousters is endlessly repeated.View image in fullscreen‘How many crows may nest in a grocer’s jerkin?’ … Harmony Rose-Bremner as Lyanna Stark and Michael Abubakar as Eddard Stark in Game of Thrones: The Mad King.Photograph: Johan PerssonBut there are two other reasons why the use of tropes from the Stratford playwright doesn’t make a play Shakespearean. The most obvious is the language. Where Shakespeare allows even minor characters unforgettable verse (the first murderer’s “the west yet glimmers with some streaks of day” in Macbeth) or plangent prose (the second carrier’s “peas and beans are as dank here as a dog” in Henry IV Part I), Duncan Macmillan’s dialogue rarely glistens. There is a heavy dependence on riddling aphorisms (“Every step we take from our destiny leads us towards it”) and repeated archaisms (such as “mayhap” for “perhaps”) that put me in mind of Max Beerbohm’s magnificent parody of a historical drama, Savonarola Brown, where Lucrezia asks: “How many crows may nest in a grocer’s jerkin?”The other aspect of Shakespeare’s genius, signally missing here, is the ability to enliven dynastic conflict with social detail and to traverse the nation. Even in an early Marlovian play such as Henry VI Part Two, there is a wonderful scene where the seemingly sightless Simpcox is exposed as a faker. By the time we get to a masterpiece like the two parts of Henry IV, Shakespeare takes us from the council chamber and the battlefield into the Eastcheap taprooms and the Cotswold countryside. But in the nearly four hours of Stratford’s Games of Thrones, we get little sense of the impact of the struggle for power on the commonwealth. This is a story of feuding families and warring tribes with scant acknowledgment of its impact on the people who are simply battle-fodder.‘Can’t stop smiling!’ The wait is over for epic Game of Thrones prequel The Mad KingRead moreBut there is a larger point. While marginalising Shakespeare, the RSC seems fixated on fiction. After this play, inspired by the novels of George RR Martin, the company offers adaptations ofGeorge EliotandAlexandre Dumas. Yet there is a great historical novelist with genuine echoes of Shakespeare hiding in plain sight: Walter Scott. I know he is unfashionable but I have read most of theWaverley novelsand been astonished by their narrative vigour and richness of character. Jonathan Bate in The Genius of Shakespeare, while quoting the endorsement of the novelist’s greatness by a Marxist critic, makes the case for Scott’s indebtedness to the man from Stratford far better than I could and I would urge the RSC’s directors to read it.Of course, they could do something even more radical than ransack the library shelves for work that is supposedly “Shakespearean”. They could stage more of the plays that Shakespeare actually wrote – but that might be a step too far.Game of Thrones: The Mad King is at theRoyal Shakespeare theatre, Stratford-upon-Avon, until 5 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreRoyal Shakespeare CompanyGame of ThronesGeorge RR MartinWilliam ShakespeareDuncan MacmillanDominic CookecommentShareReuse this content

title: QFWFQ review – If On a Winter’s Night a Traveller is taken in a bold new direction | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Gregory Nussen spins Italo Calvino’s surrealist authorial intrusions into a fascinating, playful and political show
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Gregory Nussen spins Italo Calvino’s surrealist authorial intrusions into a fascinating, playful and political show
Content: Reinventor … QFWFQ by Gregory Nussen.Photograph: Sonya KaterinaView image in fullscreenReinventor … QFWFQ by Gregory Nussen.Photograph: Sonya KaterinaEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewQFWFQ review – If On a Winter’s Night a Traveller is taken in a bold new directionSummerhall, EdinburghGregory Nussen spins Italo Calvino’s surrealist authorial intrusions into a fascinating, playful and political showMark FisherTue 11 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 03.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow to adapt an unadaptable novel famed for its postmodern surrealism and authorial intrusions? For Los Angeles performer Gregory Nussen, there can be only one solution: a play built out of postmodern surrealism and authorial intrusions.That is what becomes of Italo Calvino’sIf on a Winter’s Night a Travelleras filtered, refracted and reinvented by Nussen and directed by Hannah Pilkes. What in 1979 was a head-spinning novel about the reader trying to make sense of the novel’s unrelated manuscripts becomes, with the actor’s charm, wit and storytelling chops, a playful one-person show that has a fierce political heart beneath its metatheatrical games.QFWFQ, the name adopted by Calvino as a narrator, is about the power of storytelling and the power of those who tell the stories. Nussen is drawn to the narrative freedom of improvisation – an overheard keyboard workout in a Helsinki church, Keith Jarrett free-associating on a rehearsal piano onThe Köln Concert– and to uncertain authorship, their interrupted tales repeatedly attributed to obscure European writers and never quite reaching resolution.But the polemical force of the show lies in Nussen’s own story and their American Jewish upbringing. They describe a teenage summer-camp trip to Israel via Auschwitz as a form of coercion, not just to do the invaluable job of remembering the Holocaust, but to promote a sense of perpetual threat and victimhood.The self-referential tricks fall into abeyance as Nussen rails against dominant narratives that have no place for them as a queer artist nor for the700,000 Palestinians displacedin the foundation of Israel. If those other stories cannot be told with empathy and openness, they imply, then it is time to call the unreliable narrators to account.AtSummerhall, Edinburgh, until 31 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalTheatreFestivalsItalo CalvinoreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Virtue and a Sledgehammer – take a literal hammer to your past | Games | The Guardian
description: What do you do when you return to your home town, with your dead mother in your car boot, to find the inhabitants have been turned into robots?
Author: Malindy Hetfeld
Headline: What do you do when you return to your home town, with your dead mother in your car boot, to find the inhabitants have been turned into robots?
Content: Taking ‘20 pounds of physical media’ to her town … Virtue and a Sledgehammer.Photograph: Devolver DigitalView image in fullscreenTaking ‘20 pounds of physical media’ to her town … Virtue and a Sledgehammer.Photograph: Devolver DigitalSummer games previewsGamesVirtue and a Sledgehammer – take a literal hammer to your pastWhat do you do when you return to your home town, with your dead mother in your car boot, to find the inhabitants have been turned into robots?Malindy HetfeldTue 11 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the boot of her car, Pratelle carries the corpse of her mother and a giant sledgehammer. Her mission is simple: take the hammer to her home town. As you enter shops and homes through the door and leave them through the opposite wall, it becomes clear that the robots who either attack you or flee are all digital versions of your old neighbours.Pratelle, with her close-cropped hair and dungarees, read to me as a queer woman, but interestingly, testers of the game often mistook her as a man. The team at developer Deconstructeam and longtime collaborator Selkie Harbour didn’t anticipate this confusion but found it fits the character perfectly, especially in this setting based on a small Spanish town like those in which the developers grew up.“These towns are culturally living a couple of decades behind, especially regarding subjects such as queerness,” says game director, writer and Deconstructeam CEO Jordi de Paco. “Maybe these communities aren’t ready to acknowledge that they have other identities within them – and Pratelle is exactly that. She is someone who doesn’t fit the community, but her very existence makes the community ask questions about identity, even if it’s through confusion and anger.”View image in fullscreenDigital versions of your old neighbours … Virtue and a Sledgehammer.Photograph: Devolver DigitalMany of the robot villagers react to Pratelle with vitriol, but some flee or beg for their lives, which feels harrowing despite their identical bodies. The villagers remember what it was like to have a body, a plot point the full game will explore in detail.The most important part, however, is Pratelle’s story, which you uncover by hitting glass statues around town that contain fragments of memory. It seems as if Pratelle’s own sister turned everyone into robots, which is one of the reasons she rebels with what she calls “20 pounds of physical media”. But Virtue isn’t meant to be read as a critique of our increasingly digitised lives. Instead De Paco created a family story of a “sometimes embarrassing teenager” to contrast with the otherwise futuristic themes of the game.“Back in 2024 we designed a prototype with a pretty stereotypical story about transhumanism,” he says. “We had some friends play it and got the feedback that the themes were stale, so we decided to use the setting as more of a metaphor and came up with the feeling of not belonging. Suddenly the aesthetics and themes felt really powerful in contrast with the destruction of buildings and facing robots.”A game about straightforward destruction seems to fit oddly with Deconstructeam’s prior body of work, such as the thought-provoking narrative experiences The Red Strings Club and Many Nights a Whisper. “We’re constantly joking about this being our first actual game because you’re not making a proper game unless you destroy something,” laughs De Paco, who even tried to take a sledgehammer to a real ruin for research.“In Virtue, you’re being made to destroy the place you grew up in. Despite the combat, the game is a narrative experience. It’s not meant to be challenging; it’s more of an aesthetic choice. We think of Virtue like a walking simulator: you go through a space and solve the narrative, and the game isn’t designed around combat. We want everyone who plays this game to reach the end.”Virtue and a Sledgehammer is in development forPC. Release is planned for later in 2026Explore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsPCfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Fancy a Nobbly Bobbly? Or a Jelly Terror? The eye-popping guide to the greatest ice lolly wrappers ever | Design | The Guardian
description: From Fonzie to Elvis to the Daleks, from a Mini Milk to a Seaside Saucy to a Freak Out, incredibly rare vintage ice lolly wrappers have now been memorialised in a 96-page, nostalgia-inducing delight
Author: Daniel Dylan Wray
Headline: From Fonzie to Elvis to the Daleks, from a Mini Milk to a Seaside Saucy to a Freak Out, incredibly rare vintage ice lolly wrappers have now been memorialised in a 96-page, nostalgia-inducing delight
Content: Three greats … Happy Days, Rock Around the Choc and Zoom.Photograph: Trunk RecordsView image in fullscreenThree greats … Happy Days, Rock Around the Choc and Zoom.Photograph: Trunk RecordsDesignFancy a Nobbly Bobbly? Or a Jelly Terror? The eye-popping guide to the greatest ice lolly wrappers everFrom Fonzie to Elvis to the Daleks, from a Mini Milk to a Seaside Saucy to a Freak Out, incredibly rare vintage ice lolly wrappers have now been memorialised in a 96-page, nostalgia-inducing delightDaniel Dylan WrayTue 11 Aug 2026 04.52 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 08.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSeven years ago, Jonny Trunk entered the house of a hoarder in Stockport that was bursting at the seams with a goldmine of British ephemera from the last half century. “You couldn’t get into the house,” recalls Trunk, who is an avid pop culture collector, as well as a writer, DJ, broadcaster and record-label owner. “It was full of all this stuff he had collected indiscriminately.”Growing up in an orphanage in Surrey, John Townsend began collecting milk bottle tops and by the 1950s had amassed a huge collection of cigarette and tobacco cards. He then simply continued at full speed. “He never stopped collecting ephemera,” says Trunk. “If it was a printed piece of paper with something on it, he’d have it.” Townsend died in 2016, leaving every inch of his five-bedroom house, as well as the caravan and summerhouse, bursting with fizzy drinks cans, sweet wrappers, crisp packets, cereal boxes, flyers, cigarette cards and countless other items.View image in fullscreenLyons Maid Red Devil, Star Wars, Freak Out.Photograph: Trunk RecordsTrunk was given access to the collection – some of which featured in his 2020 book, Wrappers Delight – and he has now focused on one particular area from this vast haul for a new book: Fancy an Ice Cream? A Collection of Vintage Ice Lolly Wrappers. He bolstered this with his own personal collection. When Trunk posted some on Instagram in May, the rush of responses suggested there was a book in this. When he then announced one, film director Edgar Wright declared: “This is my dream book!”Over 96 pages, it’s an eye-popping collection of nostalgia-inducing icy delights from roughly 1970-80. There are familiar names such as Feast, Fab, Mini Milk, Nobbly Bobbly, Cider Lollies and Lemonade Sparkle, alongside long-forgotten designs that were specific to the era, featuring everything from Kevin Keegan football lollies to Star Wars, Dr Who’s Daleks and Fonzie from Happy Days. “Read about my fight against evil on the back of this pack,” reads one cartoon strip for Captain Rainbow’s lemonade and strawberry or banana lolly, complete with a chocolate dip base. One rock’n’roll themed ice lolly bears a wonky image of Elvis and features an Elton John trivia game on the wrapper.View image in fullscreenFizz Bang, Lord Toffingham, Cider Barrel and more.Photograph: Trunk RecordsThey clearly resonate with people. Trunk, who is 60, also sells prints, of everything from Lord Toffingham toffee ice creams to Lolly Gobble Choc Bomb, and gets requests from as far away as Las Vegas. “Some people now look at them from a design point of view,” he says, “because you’re seeing weird colours that don’t normally come together. And you see graphic styles that are now a bit lost. But it’s probably 75% nostalgia.”Trunk reckons it taps into a very particular period of childhood for a certain generation. “The peak period for these is around 1972-75,” he says. “That’s when a lot of those classics originated. And it was a grim time, wasn’t it? But summer in England was always a brilliant time and these wrappers are symbolic of that joy. They reflect that throwaway happiness of getting an ice-cream. Because when I was growing up, it was a real treat. We were lucky if we got one. I used to have to beg for 5p to get a Fizz Bang.”Trunk says it’s something of a miracle that a book like this could even exist, since 1970s ice lolly wrappers are far from durable. “They’re wax paper,” he explains. “And the other thing you’re dealing with, which makes them even more fragile, is they’re wet. So you’ve got wet paper. It’s also something you tear off, so they usually get destroyed.” All of which makes this collection a real one-off. “This stuff is so unbelievably, stupidly rare,” he says. “You’ve got no idea how rare an ice lolly wrapper from 1974 is. It’s ridiculous. Also, a lot of these only came out for a single season.”View image in fullscreenJelly Terror, Goal and Score ice lolly wrappers.Photograph: Trunk RecordsWithin a niche community, wrappers can exchange hands for £30 to £150 each. However, there is one that has eluded him and he’s now in a perpetual hunt for it: Walls’ Midnight Mint – a brown choc ice wrapper with an owl on it. “I’ve never seen one of those in however many years of collecting this stuff,” he says. “That would be the Holy Grail.”View image in fullscreenA Superman ice lolly wrapper.Photograph: Trunk RecordsGiven the scarcity of these wrappers and the lack of information about them, tracing down their designers is a problem. “It’s impossible,” says Trunk. “Unless someone comes out of the woodwork after this book and goes, ‘Oh, my mum did the drawing for the Fab lolly.’ None of it is ever credited. These places don’t keep archives. They were in-house designers and it was throwaway. Who was interested? This stuff was never seen as worth documenting properly. It’s such a shame.”● Fancy an Ice Cream? A Collection of Vintage Ice Lolly Wrappers is out now and available viaTrunk Records.Explore more on these topicsDesignCollectingFood & drink industryFoodfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: José Pizarro’s recipe for peach and moscatel granita | Food | The Guardian
description: Something light, cooling and refreshing to finish a big summer meal
Author: José Pizarro
Headline: Something light, cooling and refreshing to finish a big summer meal
Content: José Pizarro’s peach and moscatel granita.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The Guardian. Food styling: Aya Nishimura. Prop styling: Polly Webb-Wilson. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence.View image in fullscreenJosé Pizarro’s peach and moscatel granita.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The Guardian. Food styling: Aya Nishimura. Prop styling: Polly Webb-Wilson. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence.FoodJosé Pizarro’s recipe for peach and moscatel granitaSomething light, cooling and refreshing to finish a big summer mealJosé PizarroTue 11 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor me, the best desserts are often the simplest. In Spain, we often finish a meal with something light, something that refreshes rather than fills you up. This is exactly that. It has a lovely texture that sits somewhere between a drink and something you eat, and is perfect at the end of a long meal. It feels relaxed but still special, the kind of thing you enjoy on a warm day, when all you want is something fresh and uplifting.Peach and moscatel granitaWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appPrep5 minCook40 min, plus chillingFreeze3 hr+Serves6500ml moscatel wine125g caster sugar5-6lemon thyme sprigsPared zest of1 unwaxed lemon, plus the juice of ½ lemon6 ripe peaches or nectarinesPut the wine and sugar in a pan with the lemon thyme and lemon zest, then heat gently until the sugar dissolves. Add 500ml water and bring to a simmer.Lower the peaches into the liquid and poach for four to five minutes, until tender. Lift out the peaches with a slotted spoon, transfer to a plate or tray and leave to cool. Once cool enough to handle, remove the skins from the peaches and add these to the pan of poaching liquid. Put the peeled peaches in the fridge to chill.Bring the poaching liquid to a boil, then simmer for 15-20 minutes, until it reduces slightly and turns a lovely pink colour. Strain into a jug, pressing the juice from the skins, then stir in the lemon juice: you should have about 700ml syrup. Leave this to cool, then chill in the fridge until cold.Pour the chilled syrup into a shallow tray and put in the freezer for 30 minutes. Stir with a fork then repeat, stirring every half an hour or so. You will need to do this five or six times, until you have a lovely granita.Serve scoops of the granita with a whole poached peach, or cut the fruit in half and remove the stones.Explore more on these topicsFoodFruitSummer food and drinkIce-cream and sorbetSpanish food and drinkDessertrecipesShareReuse this content

title: How to jazz up a fruit salad | Chefs | The Guardian
description: Our panel says fresh is best, petals are pretty and booze can be beneficial – plus other upgrades for this retro summer classic
Author: Anna Berrill
Headline: Our panel says fresh is best, petals are pretty and booze can be beneficial – plus other upgrades for this retro summer classic
Content: Season the salad with salt to help draw out the flavour: Ravinder Bhogal'slabneh with watermelon berries, rose and pistachio dukkah.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Thea Hudson.View image in fullscreenSeason the salad with salt to help draw out the flavour: Ravinder Bhogal'slabneh with watermelon berries, rose and pistachio dukkah.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Thea Hudson.Kitchen aideChefsHow to jazz up a fruit saladOur panel says fresh is best, petals are pretty and booze can be beneficial – plus other upgrades for this retro summer classicAnna BerrillTue 11 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.How can I makefruit salads more interesting?Claire, via emailThere’s a fine line between a boring and brilliant fruit salad, and it comes down to treating it like you would any other salad. “It’s about layering, it’s about texture, it’s about contrast, it’s about colour,” says Gurdeep Loyal, author ofFlavour Heroes. That’s not to say it’s the time to be a maximalist, mind. “If you go for six fruits, then you get into the tinned fruit cocktail territory, so be discerning and use a magic triad instead,” he adds, “although don’t feel the need to use a playground mix of colours.” Sometimes it’s nice to have, say, three red things, so keep it in the family with a mix of strawberries, raspberries and a hybrid berry, like tayberries. That said, Loyal is of the strong opinion that “any fruit salad in the world” will greatly benefit from the addition of passion fruit.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Using nice, ripe fruit is a given, but it’s worth considering how you cut it, too : “A persimmon sliced on a mandoline, for example, is a really lovely thing.” Then, season with salt. “It’s the one thing people don’t do enough,” Loyal adds, although a pinch of brown sugar wouldn’t go amiss, either. And it’s hard to deny the transformative power of spices: “Cinnamon works incredibly well with berries; cardamom with tropical fruit; or try more savoury spices like cumin with mango or pineapple.” It would be a mistake to just stick to the spice rack, though: “Grating ginger on strawberries or mango (with a pinch of cinnamon and some lime, of course) will bring heat, as will freshly grated turmeric.”Then, there’s chilli, either a dusting of dried powder or flecks of the fresh stuff. “One of my favourite ways with watermelon is a sprinkle of aleppo pepper and grated frozen feta,” saysSabrina Ghayour, author ofPersiana One, although cantaloupe with pul biber, feta and torn basil is pretty good, too. But for extra oomph, Loyal is partial tohot chilli honey: “Put honey in a pan with finely diced chilli and a pinch of salt, let it infuse for five minutes, then use that to drizzle over mango and strawberries.”Herbs (torn, never cut) are another must: “Basil and tarragon have an amazing ability to amplify flavour,” says Loyal, and are just as good with berries as tropical fruit and melon. Otherwise, Ghayour combines coriander with peaches, pineapple or mango (plus, chilli, onion and lime juice) for salsa, to serve alongside grilled meat or seafood.Just like any salad, you’ll then want a dressing. “This could be citrus and a bit of honey or maple, a drizzle of olive oil, or just the juice that collects at the bottom of the bowl once you’ve salted it,” says Loyal. Although, as is so often the case, a tablespoon of alcohol always helps: “Try vodka with lime juice, a little maple syrup, and a pinch of cinnamon.”Last, don’t be shy when it comes to texture: Loyal deploys a topping of toasted peanuts or pine nuts, dukkah, or sesame seed brittle for crunch. And make it beautiful. “You don’tneedto add petals,” says Loyal – “but also why not?”Got a culinary dilemma?
